## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā
## Homage to that Blessed One
## Introduction to the Text

"Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi"—this exposition (niddesa) which shows these Three Refuges is the beginning of the Khuddakapāṭha text.

Now, in order to explain, analyze, and clarify the meaning of this (Khuddakapāṭha Pāḷi) through the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā, this is said:

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, the most excellent among those worthy of homage,
I shall perform the commentary on the meaning of some texts of the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Because the Khuddaka Nikāya is profound,
although such an exposition is very difficult for one like me who does not fully know the Dispensation (Sāsana).

However, since the decisions of the former great teachers remain uninterrupted until today,
and the nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher likewise remains as it was.

I desire to perform this commentary on the meaning, relying on both the Dispensation and the ancient decisions,
out of great devotion to the True Dhamma, and not out of a desire for self-exaltation,

nor for the purpose of disparaging others; listen to that (commentary which I shall explain) with a concentrated mind.
2:
## Defining the Khuddaka Nikāya

In this new commentary to be explained, since I have promised, "I shall perform the commentary on the meaning of some texts belonging to the Khuddaka Nikāya," I shall first define the texts of the Khuddaka Nikāya and afterwards perform the commentary on the meaning. The so-called Khuddakapāṭha is a portion of the Khuddaka Nikāya. The so-called Khuddaka Nikāya is a portion of the five Nikāyas. The five Nikāyas are—
Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya.
These five Nikāyas are profound in terms of both the Dhamma and the meaning.

Among those five Nikāyas, the thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta are called the Dīgha Nikāya. The one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta are called the Majjhima Nikāya. The seven thousand, seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta are called the Saṃyutta Nikāya. The nine thousand, five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta are called the Aṅguttara Nikāya. The Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, Cariyāpiṭaka, and the Vinaya Piṭaka and Abhidhamma Piṭaka are called the Khuddaka Nikāya. Alternatively, all the remaining words of the Buddha, excluding the four Nikāyas, are called the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Why is this Nikāya called the Khuddaka Nikāya? It is called the Khuddaka Nikāya because it is a collection of many minor units of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) and because it is their dwelling place. Indeed, a collection and a dwelling place are called "Nikāya". "Monks, I do not see any other single group (nikāya) so diverse as the animals of the animal kingdom"—this statement from the Dispensation and worldly usage such as "the dwelling of the Poṇika kings" or "the dwelling of the Cikkhallika kings" are evidence for this word "Nikāya". This Khuddakapāṭha text is a portion of the Khuddaka Nikāya. It is intended to explain, analyze, and clarify the meaning of these texts of the Khuddaka Nikāya included in the Suttanta Piṭaka. Among such texts of the Khuddaka Nikāya, the Khuddakapāṭha, which has nine divisions by way of the Refuges, the Training Rules, the Thirty-two Parts, the Boy's Questions, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Ratana Sutta, the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, and the Metta Sutta, is the beginning by way of being placed in the lineage of recitation of successive teachers. It is not the beginning by way of being spoken by the Blessed One.

By way of being spoken by the Blessed One—
"Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered in vain, seeking the builder of this house. Repeated birth is suffering.
O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters (defilements) are broken, the ridge-pole (ignorance) of the house is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned Nibbāna. It has attained the destruction of craving." These two verses are the beginning of all the Buddha's words. And that is the beginning by way of being spoken only by the mind, not by way of being spoken by breaking into speech. By way of being spoken by breaking into speech—"When indeed things (dhammas) become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin (arahant)..."
3:
“O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again.
All your rafters (defilements) are broken, the ridge-pole (ignorance) is shattered.
My mind has reached the unconditioned Nibbāna; it has attained the end of craving.”

These two verses are the beginning of all the Buddha's words. Such a beginning was uttered only by the mind and was not a spoken discourse. By way of being a spoken discourse—

“When indeed things (dhammas) become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin (arahant),
Then all his doubts vanish, since he understands things together with their causes.”

This verse is the beginning. Therefore, this Khuddakapāṭha text, which has nine divisions, is the beginning of these Khuddaka texts; I shall begin the commentary on its meaning from the very start of that text.

## Clarifying the Introduction

The beginning of that text is: “Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” The outline (mātikā) for that commentary is—

“By whom, where, when, and why were these Three Refuges spoken?
Why is it stated at the beginning here, even though it was not spoken at the beginning (by the Buddha)?

Having clarified the introduction, thereafter, one should explain the going for refuge to the Buddha and the person who goes.
One should also illustrate the distinction between the breach and non-breach (of refuge), the fruit, and the object to be approached.
In the next two, beginning with ‘Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ...’, this same method should be understood.

In the sequential determination, one should also point out the reason.
And one should manifest these Three Refuges by means of similes.”

Among those verses, according to the first verse—there are five questions: By whom were these Three Refuges spoken? Where were they spoken? When were they spoken? Why were they spoken? And why is it stated at the beginning here, even though it was not spoken at the beginning by the Blessed One?
4:
The answers to these five questions should be understood as follows: To the question 'Who taught it?', it was taught by the Blessed One alone; it was not taught by disciples, not by hermits, and not by deities. To the question 'Where?', it was taught at the Deer Park in Isipatana, near Bārāṇasī. To the question 'When?', it was taught when the Venerable Yasa, together with his companions, attained Arahantship, and when the sixty-one Arahants were teaching the Dhamma in the world for the benefit of the many. To the question 'Why?', it was taught for the purpose of the 'going forth' (pabbajjā) and for the purpose of 'higher ordination' (upasampadā).

As it was said:
"Monks, in this way one should be given the going forth and the higher ordination. First, having had the hair and beard shaved, having had him clothed in saffron robes, having had the upper robe arranged over one shoulder, having had him pay homage at the feet of the monks, and having had him sit in a squatting position with hands raised in salutation, he should be told: 'Say this,' and he should be made to say: 'Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi' (I go to the Buddha for refuge, I go to the Dhamma for refuge, I go to the Saṅgha for refuge)."

To the question 'Why is it stated at the beginning of this text?', it should be understood that the ancient teachers, who compiled the nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher into the three Piṭakas and established the path of oral tradition, placed it at the beginning of this Khuddakapāṭha because it is the path through which deities and humans enter the Dispensation, either as lay followers or as monastics; thus, it is the gateway to the Dispensation.

## The purification of the introduction is finished.

## 1. Explanation of the Triple Refuge

## Explanation of the Buddha

Now, regarding the statement "One should explain the going for refuge to the Buddha, and the one who goes," the 'Buddha' is the supreme being among all creatures, designated either based on the continuum of aggregates permeated by the attainment of unsurpassed liberation—the object of unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena—or designated based on the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, which is the foundation of omniscience. As it was said:
5:
"The Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-become, without a teacher, who himself penetrated the Truths among doctrines not heard before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers."

This is first the explanation of the Buddha according to the meaning.

According to the phrasing (expression), however, he should be understood in such ways as: "He is the Buddha because he knows (bujjhitā); he is the Buddha because he awakens others (bodhetā)." And this was also said:

"In what sense is he the Buddha? He is the Buddha because he has known the Truths; he is the Buddha because he awakens the generation (of beings); he is the Buddha because of omniscience; he is the Buddha because of all-seeing; he is the Buddha because he is not led by others; he is the Buddha because he has blossomed (with virtues); he is the Buddha because he has destroyed the taints (āsavas); he is the Buddha because he is free from defilements; he is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from lust; he is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from hatred; he is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from delusion; he is the Buddha because he is absolutely free from defilements; he is the Buddha because he has gone on the one-way path (the Path); he is the Buddha because he alone has fully awakened to the unsurpassed right self-enlightenment; he is the Buddha because he has destroyed non-knowledge (abuddhi) and attained knowledge (buddhi). This name 'Buddha' was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brothers, nor by his sisters, nor by his friends and colleagues, nor by his kinsmen and relatives, nor by ascetics and brahmins, nor by deities. This name 'Buddha' is a realization-based designation of the Blessed Buddhas, which is attained at the end of liberation, upon the acquisition of omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree."

And here, just as in the world one who knows is called 'avagata,' so he is the 'Buddha' because he has known the Truths. Just as the winds that dry leaves are called 'paṇṇasusa,' so he is the 'Buddha' because he awakens the generation of beings. 'He is the Buddha because of omniscience' means he is the Buddha because of the wisdom capable of knowing all phenomena. 'He is the Buddha because of all-seeing' means he is the Buddha because of the wisdom capable of making all phenomena known. 'He is the Buddha because he is not led by others' means he is the Buddha because he himself, without being awakened by another, is the Buddha. 'He is the Buddha because he has blossomed' means he is the Buddha in the sense of blossoming like a lotus due to the blossoming of various virtues. (It should be understood) in such ways as: "He is the Buddha because he has destroyed the taints," and so on.
6:
He is called 'Buddha' because, by abandoning the states that cause the mind to shrink, he has awakened from the sleep of all defilements, like a man who has awakened from sleep. The word 'Buddha', which has the meaning of 'knowing', is also used in the sense of 'going' (attaining) by way of synonym; just as a man who has gone on a journey is called 'one who has gone' (gata), so too he is called 'Buddha' because he has gone to the One Way (Ekāyana-magga). He is called 'Buddha' because he alone has realized the peerless Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). This means he is called 'Buddha' not because he was made to know by others, but because he himself realized the peerless Supreme Enlightenment. He is called 'Buddha' because he has destroyed ignorance (avijjā) and attained wisdom (buddhi). 'Buddhi', 'Buddha', and 'Bodha' are merely synonymous terms. In this context, just as one says 'blue cloth' or 'red cloth' because of its connection with the quality of blueness or redness, so too he is called 'Buddha' because of his connection with the quality of wisdom (buddhi). Furthermore, it should be understood that this designation 'Buddha' is not a name (given by parents), but a title that follows the meaning, as stated in the text. In this way, the meaning that accomplishes the derivation of all terms of the word 'Buddha' should be understood.

This is the explanation of the word 'Buddha' by way of its syllables.

## Saranagamanagamakavibhāvanā

Now, in terms such as 'taking refuge' (saraṇagamana), it is called 'refuge' (saraṇa) because it kills or destroys danger. For those who have gone for refuge, it is called 'refuge' because by that very act of taking refuge, it kills, dispels, removes, and ceases fear, trepidation, suffering, the miserable states (duggati), and defilements. Alternatively, the Buddha is the refuge because he kills danger by promoting the welfare of beings and preventing harm. The Dhamma is the refuge because it leads out from the wilderness of existence (bhava-kantāra) and provides relief. The Saṅgha is the refuge because it causes the attainment of great fruit even from small offerings. Therefore, by this method also, the Triple Gem is the refuge. 'Taking refuge' (saraṇagamana) is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that has destroyed defilements through faith and respect in the Triple Gem, which takes those gems as the final resort and does not depend on others. The being who possesses such consciousness goes to that refuge. By the arising of such consciousness as described, he approaches the Triple Gem, thinking, 'This is my refuge, this is my resort.' One who so approaches says, 'Venerable Sir, we go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma; may the Blessed One accept us as lay followers (upāsakas)...'
7:
...by way of undertaking, like the merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika; or by way of approaching as a disciple, like the Venerable Mahākassapa and others who said, 'Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am a disciple'; or by way of humble devotion, like the Brahmin Brahmāyu and others, of whom it is said, 'When this was said, the Brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, thrice uttered this inspired exclamation: "Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One! Homage to the Blessed One..."'; or by way of self-dedication, like monks devoted to meditation; or by way of the total eradication of the defilements of taking refuge, like the Noble Ones (Ariyas). Thus, they go for refuge in various ways according to the object and the function.

This is the explanation of taking refuge and the one who takes refuge.

## Bhedābhedaphaladīpanā

Now, I shall explain the meaning of the terms mentioned as 'the breach, the non-breach, the fruit, and that which should be approached.' For a person who has gone for refuge, the breach of taking refuge is twofold: blameworthy (sāvajja) and blameless (anavajja). Among these, the breach due to death is the blameless breach. The breach due to approaching other teachers besides the Triple Gem through self-dedication and so on, as mentioned before, or due to having wrong views that deviate from the undertaking of self-dedication, prostration, and so on within the Triple Gem, is the blameworthy breach. Both types of breach occur only to worldlings (puthujjanas). The refuge of those worldlings becomes soiled through the occurrence of ignorance, doubt, and wrong knowledge regarding the qualities of the Buddha, as well as through disrespect and so on. Noble Ones (Ariyas), however, have a refuge that is both unbroken and unsoiled. As it is said: 'It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that a person possessed of right view should designate another teacher.' Worldlings, however, have an unbroken refuge only as long as they do not reach a breach of refuge. For them, the blameworthy breach of refuge is a soiling and brings undesirable bad results. The blameless breach of refuge, having no result to ripen, bears no fruit. The unbroken refuge, however, brings only desirable good results as its fruit.
8: It is stated: "Whoever goes to the Buddha for refuge, they will not go to the plane of misery. Having abandoned the human body, they will fill the host of devas" (in the Dīgha Nikāya and Saṃyutta Nikāya). In that taught passage on going for refuge, those who have reached the undertaking by completely cutting off the defilements of the going for refuge will not go to the plane of misery. It should be understood that the meaning in this verse is that others, who merely go for refuge, will not go to the plane of misery simply by the act of going for refuge. This which has been stated is the explanation of the fruits of breach and non-breach (bhedābhedaphaladīpanā). ## Explanation of the Object of Refuge (Gamaniyadīpanā) In explaining the object of refuge, the objector says: In the Pali phrase "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi" (I go to the Buddha for refuge), he who goes to the Buddha for refuge might go to the Buddha or go to the refuge. In both cases, the use of a single verb (gacchāmi) is redundant. Why? Because in the action of going, there is no double object. Here, the grammarians do not accept it as a double-accusative verb (dvikammaka) like in "He leads the goat to the village" (ajaṃ gါmaṃ neti). Should it be said that it is meaningful, like in "He goes to the eastern direction, he goes to the western direction"? No, because the state of being in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) of the words "Buddha" and "refuge" (saraṇa) is not intended. This is true; if the appositional state of "Buddha" and "refuge" were intended, even a person with a hostile mind approaching the Buddha would be "one who has gone to the Buddha for refuge." The meaning is that he has gone to that refuge which is specifically designated as "the Buddha." Should it be said that it should only be in apposition because of the statement, "This refuge is secure, this refuge is supreme"? No, because that state exists only in that verse. For in that very verse-foot, the appositional state is intended as "the secure and supreme refuge" because the Triple Gem, starting with the Buddha, is unfailing in its nature as a refuge, which is defined as the removal of fear for those who have gone for refuge. Elsewhere, however, when there is a connection with the root gam (to go), the usage "going for refuge" (saraṇagamana) is not well-established in an appositional sense, so it is not intended. Therefore, this argument for apposition is inconclusive.
9:
If it is argued that even in the connection with the verb ‘to go’ (gami), the state of apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) should indeed be the case because the taking of refuge is well-established in the passage: “Having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering”? No, because it would lead to the same flaw previously mentioned. For even there, if there were a state of apposition, then even a person with a hostile mind, by coming to this refuge of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, would be released from all suffering; thus the same flaw mentioned before would indeed occur. And since we do not desire a statement that contains such a flaw, this argument is not proven.

For example, in the passage: “By relying on me, Ānanda, as a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta), beings subject to birth are released from birth” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.129), beings who are being released through the power of the Blessed One as a noble friend are described as “released by relying on a noble friend.” Similarly, here too, a being who is released through the power of the refuge of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha is described as “Having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.” Thus should the meaning be understood in this context.

In this way, in every respect, it is not appropriate for the word ‘Buddha’ alone, nor the word ‘refuge’ (saraṇa) alone, nor both together, to be the direct object (kamma) of the verb ‘to go’ (gami). However, since an object is required for the act of going (resorting to) indicated by “gacchāmi,” the appropriate reasoning will be stated here.

It is said—In this sentence “Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi,” the Buddha alone is the object to be resorted to (gamanīya). The word ‘refuge’ (saraṇa) is used to show the manner of going. It means: “I resort to the Buddha as a refuge.” With the intention that “This Buddha is my refuge, this Buddha is my final resort, the remover of harm, and the provider of welfare,” I go to, resort to, serve, and honor Him. Or, I know and understand Him in this way. For verbs that have the meaning of motion (gati) also have the meaning of knowledge (buddhi).

If it is argued that this is inappropriate because the particle ‘iti’ is not employed? That is not so. It might be that—if such were the meaning here, then the particle ‘iti’ should have been employed as in passages such as: “He understands as it really is: ‘Form is impermanent, form is impermanent’” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.55, 85). But since it is not employed, this is inappropriate. That is also not so. Why? Because that meaning is possible. Just as in passages like: “He who has gone to the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha as refuge” (Dhammapada 190), the meaning of the particle ‘iti’ is possible here as well. The particle ‘iti’ need not be employed in every instance just because its meaning is present. Even where it is not employed, the meaning of the particle ‘iti’ should be understood as if it were employed, both here and in other similar cases. Therefore, there is no flaw in that statement.

If it is argued that the statement “the word ‘refuge’ is to show the manner of going” is inappropriate because the refuge itself is the object to be resorted to in passages such as: “I allow, O bhikkhus, the going forth by the three takings of refuge” (Mahāvagga 34)?
10:
That statement is not appropriate. Why? Because that meaning is indeed possible. In that case too, the meaning (of the word *iti*) is possible; therefore, it is similar to what was said before, and even if it is not directly connected, it should be understood as if it were connected. Otherwise, the fault mentioned previously would occur; therefore, it should be taken exactly as instructed.

This is the explanation of the object to be approached (*gamanīya*).

## Explanation of the Dhamma Refuge and the Saṅgha Refuge

Now, regarding what was said: "In the words beginning with *Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ*, this same method is to be understood in both cases," I shall explain here—the method of explaining the meaning in the phrase "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi" should be understood in the same way for these two phrases: "Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi" and "Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." In those phrases, only the explanation of the meaning and the classification of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are different; the rest is just as previously stated. Therefore, I shall only state what is different here—some teachers say that the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna are "Dhamma." Our view is that only the Path and *Virāga* (Nibbāna) are "Dhamma" in this context, because they uphold those who have developed the Path and those who have realized Nibbāna so that they do not fall into the lower realms, and because they provide the supreme relief. The *Aggappasāda Sutta* is also evidence. In that Sutta, it was said: "Monks, as far as there are conditioned things (*saṅkhata dhammā*), the Noble Eightfold Path is said to be the best of them," and so forth.

The assembly of persons endowed with the four Noble Paths and those whose continuity of aggregates is suffused with the four Fruits of Recluseship is called the "Saṅgha," because they are united by the bond of [right] view (*diṭṭhi*) and virtue (*sīla*). This was said by the Blessed One:

"Ānanda, what do you think? These teachings which I have taught you having known them with direct knowledge—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path—do you see, Ānanda, even two monks who hold different views regarding these teachings?"

Indeed, only this Ultimate Saṅgha (*Paramattha Saṅgha*) is to be approached as a refuge. In the Suttas, it is also said: "He is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world." For a person who has taken refuge in this Saṅgha, even if they perform acts such as paying homage to the community of monks (*Bhikkhu-saṅgha*) other than that, or the community of nuns (*Bhikkhunī-saṅgha*)...
11:
...it is said: "He is like the unsurpassed field of merit for the world." For a person who has taken refuge in this Ultimate Saṅgha, the taking of refuge is neither broken nor defiled by performing acts such as paying homage to other communities of monks, or communities of nuns, or the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, or the conventional Saṅgha (*Sammuti-saṅgha*), or groups of four and so on, or even a single individual who has gone forth intending the Blessed One. This is the distinction here. As for the remaining points and the procedure regarding the breaking or non-breaking of this second refuge, it should be understood in the same way as the method previously stated. This is the commentary on the verse beginning with "Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ."

## The Reason for the Sequential Designation

Now, I shall explain the sequential designation and its reason. Among these three refuges, the Buddha is shown first because he is supreme among all beings. The Dhamma is shown immediately after the Buddha because it arises from that Blessed One and was taught by him. The Saṅgha is shown at the end because it is the support of that Dhamma and because it practices that Dhamma repeatedly. Alternatively, the Buddha is shown first because he directs all beings toward their welfare. The Dhamma is shown next because it arises from the Buddha and constitutes the welfare of all beings. The Saṅgha is shown at the end as a refuge because it consists of those who practice to attain welfare and those who have attained welfare. Thus, the sequential designation and its reason are explained.

## Explanation through Similes

Now, as it was said, "These three refuges should be explained through similes," I shall explain. Here, the Buddha is like the full moon. The Dhamma taught by him is like the mass of moonlight. The world, delighted and gladdened by the light of the full moon, is like the Saṅgha. The Buddha is like the young sun. The aforementioned Dhamma is like the network of the sun's rays. The world, whose darkness is dispelled by that sunlight, is like the Saṅgha. The Buddha is like a man who burns a forest. The Dhamma, which burns the forest of defilements, is like the forest fire. The Saṅgha, which is the field of merit because defilements have been burnt away, is like the ground that has become a field after the forest was burnt. The Buddha is like a great rain cloud. The Dhamma is like the flow of rainwater. The Saṅgha, whose dust of defilements has been settled, is like a countryside where the dust is settled by the falling rain.
12:
The Blessed One is like a skilled charioteer; the Dhamma is like the skillful method for training thoroughbred horses; the Saṅgha is like the group of well-trained thoroughbred horses. The Blessed One is like a surgeon because he extracts the thorn of all wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi); the Dhamma is like the surgical instrument or means for extracting the thorn; the Saṅgha is like the people from whom the thorn of wrong view has been well extracted.

Alternatively, the Blessed One is like an ophthalmic surgeon because he skillfully removes the film of delusion from the eyes; the Dhamma is like the medicine that skillfully removes the film; the Saṅgha is like the people whose film of delusion has been well removed and who possess the clear eye of wisdom. Alternatively, the Blessed One is like a skilled physician because he is able to remove the disease of defilements along with their latent tendencies (anusaya); the Dhamma is like a well-prepared medicine; the Saṅgha is like the group of people whose disease of defilements and latent tendencies has been well-quelled through the application of the medicine.

Alternatively, the Blessed One is like a good guide; the Dhamma is like a good path and a safe land; the Saṅgha is like the traveler who, having journeyed along the path, has reached the safe land. The Blessed One is like a skilled captain; the Dhamma is like a boat; the Saṅgha is like the people who have reached the other shore and attained happiness. The Blessed One is like the king of the Himavant mountains; the Dhamma is like the medicine produced on that mountain; the Saṅgha is like the people who are free from disease and delighted by using the medicine. The Blessed One is like a giver of wealth; the Dhamma is like the wealth; the Saṅgha is like the people who have well-obtained the Noble Wealth (ariyadhana) as they desired. The Blessed One is like one who shows a hidden treasure; the Dhamma is like the hidden treasure; the Saṅgha is like the people who have obtained the hidden treasure.

Furthermore, the Blessed One is like a brave man who grants safety; the Dhamma is like safety itself; the Saṅgha is like the people who are peaceful, having been freed from all fears without exception. The Blessed One is like one who gives comfort; the Dhamma is like the attainment of comfort; the Saṅgha is like the multitude of people who have attained comfort. The Blessed One is like a good friend; the Dhamma is like the instruction for welfare; the Saṅgha is like the people who have reached their own benefit by following the instruction for welfare. The Blessed One is like a mine of wealth; the Dhamma is like the essence of wealth; the Saṅgha is like the people who enjoy the essence of wealth. The Blessed One is like one who bathes a prince; the Dhamma is like the water for washing the head; the Saṅgha is like the group of princes who have been well-bathed with the water of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). The Blessed One is like one who adorns; the Dhamma is like the ornament; the Saṅgha is like the group of princes adorned with the ornament of the True Dhamma. The Blessed One is like a sandalwood tree; the Dhamma is like the scent of sandalwood produced from it; the Saṅgha is like the people whose fever of defilements has been quenched by using the True Dhamma. The Blessed One is like a father who gives an inheritance; the Dhamma is like the inheritance; the Saṅgha is like the group of sons who receive the inheritance of the True Dhamma.
14:
Furthermore, in the latter five training rules, what is appropriate should be applied. The specific teaching should also be mentioned. The state of being inferior and so forth should also be known.

In this matrix (mātikā), the decision should be known as follows: These ten training rules, beginning with 'abstaining from taking life' (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī), were spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by disciples or others. They were spoken in Sāvatthī, at Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, for the purpose of establishing the training rules for novices (sāmaṇeras) after the Venerable Rāhula was ordained in Kapilavatthu and [the Buddha] arrived in Sāvatthī from Kapilavatthu. Was it not spoken thus:

"Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Kapilavatthu as long as he liked, set out on a journey towards Sāvatthī. As he was traveling in due course, he arrived at Sāvatthī. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī, at Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. At that time, the novices thought: 'How many training rules do we have? Where should we train?' They reported this matter to the Blessed One. (The Blessed One said:) 'Monks, I allow ten training rules for novices, and the novices should train in them. They are: abstaining from taking life... (up to) abstaining from accepting gold and silver.'"

These ten training rules should be known as being placed into the mode of recitation as "I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life" (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī-sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi), following the sequence in the Suttas such as "he trains by undertaking the training rules" and following the sequence of the text shown in the Refuges (saraṇagamana). Thus, the method of "By whom, where, when, and why these were spoken" should be regarded as having been stated.

## Determination of Common and Specific [Precepts]

Among these ten training rules, the first two and the fourth and fifth are common to both lay devotees (upāsakas) and novices (sāmaṇeras) in terms of permanent virtue (nicca-sīla). In terms of Uposatha virtue, for lay devotees, the seventh and eighth are made into a single factor, and excluding the very last one, all are common with novices. The last training rule, however, is specific only to novices. Thus, the determination should be made by way of commonality and specificity. Among these ten, the first five training rules are called things to be avoided because they arise from an absolutely unwholesome mind and are natural misdeeds (pakati-vajja) like taking life, etc.
15: The training rules other than the one against taking life are things to be avoided by way of prescription. Where there is a training rule that is an offense by nature (pakati) and a training rule that is an offense by prescription (paṇṇatti), that training rule should be distinguished. ## General Explanation (Sādhāraṇavibhāvanā) In these ten training rules, the words "veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi" are common to all training rules. Therefore, this general explanation should be understood regarding these words, both by way of phrasing (byañjana) and by way of meaning (attha). Between those two, it should first be understood by way of phrasing as follows: It is called "veramaṇī" because it destroys the enemy that is unwholesome (akusala). It means it abandons, removes, eliminates, and leads to the non-existence of the enemy that is unwholesome. Alternatively, by the fact of performing that undertaking, a person abstains from the enemy that is unwholesome. Because of such abstaining, by changing the vowel 'vi' to 've', it is called "veramaṇī." For that reason, in this context, they recite it in two ways: as "veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ" and as "viramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ." It is called "sikkhā" because it should be trained in. It is called "pada" because one reaches the training by means of this factor. The factor of training is "sikkhāpada." It means the means for attaining the training. Alternatively, it means the root, the support, or the foundation. Since the abstinence itself is the training rule, it is called "veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ." According to the second method, it is also called "viramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ." It is called "samādiyāmi" because it is taken up well. It means one takes up and undertakes it with the intention of not transgressing the training rule, by performing it without breaking, without piercing, and without spotting it. By way of meaning, "veramaṇī" is the mental factor of abstinence (virati) associated with a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (kāmāvacarakusala-citta). That abstinence is taught in the Vibhaṅga Pali for one who abstains from taking life in this way: "The avoidance, abstinence, refraining, abstaining, non-action, non-performance, non-transgression, non-passing of the boundary, the destruction of the cause of taking life at that time," and so on. This so-called "veramaṇī" indeed exists in the supramundane (lokuttara) as well. However, because it is taught here as "samādiyāmi" (I undertake), it is only the abstinence that occurs by way of undertaking; therefore, that supramundane abstinence cannot occur here. Thus, it is stated that it is the mental factor of abstinence associated with a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere. Regarding "sikkhā," there are three: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). In this context, however, abstinence as virtue that is encountered (sampatta-virati-sīla), mundane insight (lokiya-vipassanā), the fine-material and immaterial sphere jhānas, and the noble path are intended as "sikkhā." Thus it is also taught: "Which states are sikkhā? At a time when a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge... at that time..."
16: When a wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge arises, contact occurs... non-distraction (avikkhepa) occurs. These states are called training (sikkhā). Which states are called training? At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material sphere, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states... enters and dwells in the first jhāna... the fifth jhāna... non-distraction occurs. These states are called training. Which states are called training? At whatever time for rebirth in the immaterial sphere... accompanied by the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... non-distraction occurs. These states are called training. Which states are called training? At whatever time one develops the supramundane jhāna, which leads out [of the round of rebirths]... non-distraction occurs. These states are called training (as taught in the Vibhaṅga). Among those trainings, it is called a training rule (sikkhāpada) because it is the means of attainment (pada) of any one of those trainings, or because it is the root (mūla), the support (nissaya), and the foundation (patiṭṭhā). This is indeed true: "Depending on virtue, established in virtue, one who develops and frequently practices the seven factors of enlightenment," and so forth has been taught. Thus, in this context, the clarification of the common terms should be made by way of their common characteristics, their phrasing (byañjana), and their meaning (attha). ## Commentary on the First Five Training Rules Now, regarding what was stated: "Furthermore, in the first five, by the explanation of the specific meaning... the decision should be known," in those verses, the following is said: In the term 'pāṇātipāta' (taking life), first, 'pāṇa' (life) refers to the continuity of the aggregates bound up with the life-faculty, or a being designated based on those aggregates. The volition to kill, occurring through either the door of body or speech, which originates the effort to cut off the life-faculty of that being, while perceiving it as a living being, is called pāṇātipāta. In the term 'adinnādāna' (taking what is not given), 'adinna' refers to property possessed by another. Where another person, in exercising their will, is not liable to punishment or blame. The volition to steal, occurring through either the door of body or speech, which originates the effort to take that property, while perceiving it as another's property, is called adinnādāna. Abrahmacariya (unchastity) means an ignoble practice. The volition to transgress, occurring through the body-door, due to indulging in the ignoble practice of sexual intercourse, which is the practice of two people...
17:
Abrahmacariya means ignoble conduct. The volition of transgression occurring at the body-door due to the practice of sexual intercourse, which is the practice of two people, and due to the practice of the ignoble, is called abrahmacariya.

In the term musāvāda, 'musā' refers to a verbal or bodily intimation of one who intends to deceive, which destroys the welfare of others. The wrong volition occurring at either the body-door or the speech-door, which originates the bodily or verbal intimation that deceives others with the intent to deceive, is called musāvāda.

In the term surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna, 'surā' is of five kinds: (1) liquor made from flour, (2) liquor made from cakes, (3) liquor made from rice, (4) liquor with yeast added, and (5) liquor mixed with ingredients (sambhāra). 'Meraya' is also of five kinds: (1) extract from flowers, (2) extract from fruits, (3) extract from molasses, (4) extract from honey, and (5) extract from a combination of flowers, fruits, etc. 'Majja' refers to both surā and meraya because of their intoxicating nature; or whatever else is intoxicating, which when drunk makes one intoxicated and heedless, is called majja. 'Pamādaṭṭhāna' (the occasion of heedlessness) refers to the volition with which one drinks or swallows it; that volition is called pamādaṭṭhāna because it is the cause of intoxication and heedlessness. Therefore, the volition to swallow intoxicants like surā and meraya occurring at the body-door with the intent to swallow should be understood as 'surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna'. Thus, the decision regarding pāṇātipāta and so on should first be understood here.

## Decision on Oneness, Multiplicity, etc.

Regarding the term "oneness, multiplicity, etc.," the question is raised: Does pāṇātipāta or others like adinnādāna become one because of the oneness of the victim, the killer, the effort, the volition, etc., or does it become many because of their multiplicity? Why is this said?

If it were one because of oneness, then when many killers kill a single victim, or one killer kills many victims, or many victims are killed by a single effort such as one's own hand (sāhatthika), or a single volition originates the effort that cuts off the life-faculty of many victims, then there would be only one act of pāṇātipāta.

If it were many because of multiplicity, then when one killer kills many victims while making a single effort for the sake of one person, or many killers kill only one person (Devadatta, Yajñadatta, or Somadatta) while making many efforts for the sake of many people like Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Somadatta, or one victim is killed by many efforts such as one's own hand, or many volitions originate the effort that cuts off the life-faculty of a single victim, then there would be many acts of pāṇātipāta.

Both of these are inappropriate. Therefore, it is not one because of the oneness of the victim, etc., nor is it many because of multiplicity; rather, oneness and multiplicity occur in another way. That (way of oneness and multiplicity) of pāṇātipāta is stated; likewise, it is stated for the remaining adinnādāna and so on.
18:
The decision is stated: In that context, first, the unity of the act of killing (pāṇātipāta) is not because the victim and the killer are individually one, nor is its diversity because they are diverse. Rather, unity exists only because of the simultaneous conjunction of the victim and the killer. Diversity exists because of the diversity of both or either of them. 

How so? Even if there are many killers, if they kill many victims through a single effort (payoga) such as shooting arrows or digging a pit, there are many acts of killing. Even if there is only one killer, if he kills many victims through one effort or many efforts, and through one volition (cetanā) or many volitions that produce those efforts, there are many acts of killing. Even if there are many killers, if they kill a single victim through many efforts or one effort in the ways mentioned above, there are many acts of killing. This method also applies to theft (adinnādāna) and so forth. Thus, in this matter, the decision should be understood by way of unity, diversity, and so on.

By way of object (ārammaṇa): In this matter, the act of killing has the life faculty (jīvitindriya) as its object. The precepts of refraining from theft, sexual misconduct, and intoxicants (adinnādāna, abrahmacariya, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna) have as their object one of the formations (saṅkhāra) among material phenomena, such as the visible-data base (rūpāyatana). False speech (musāvāda) has a being (satta) as its object because it occurs in reference to the person to whom one speaks falsely. Some teachers say that sexual misconduct also has a being as its object. They also say that theft has a being as its object when a being is to be stolen or carried away. In fact, in this case, the taking of a being as an object occurs only through the power of formations, not through the power of concepts (paññatti). Thus, in this matter, the decision should also be understood by way of object.

By way of undertaking (ādāna): These precepts, such as refraining from killing, are well-undertaken by a novice (sāmanera) only when undertaken in the presence of a monk. For a lay follower (upāsaka), however, they are well-undertaken whether undertaken by oneself or in the presence of another. They are well-undertaken whether undertaken together or individually. However, for one who undertakes them together, there is only one abstinence (virati) and only one volition (cetanā). The fivefold nature of these abstinences and volitions is understood only by way of their function. For one who undertakes them individually, it should be understood that there are five abstinences and five volitions. Thus, in this matter, the decision should also be understood by way of undertaking.

By way of breaking (bheda): In this matter, for novices, if one precept is broken, all precepts are broken. This is because those precepts are equivalent to the Pārājika offenses for them. Whichever precept is transgressed, one is bound by kamma through that act alone. For laypeople, however, when one precept is broken, only that one is broken,
19:
because for those laypeople, the virtue endowed with five factors becomes complete again only by re-undertaking the broken precept. Other teachers, however, say: "Among virtues undertaken separately, if one is broken, only one is broken. But among virtues undertaken together as 'I undertake the virtue endowed with five factors,' if one is broken, all the remaining ones are also broken." Why? Because the volition of undertaking (samādāna-cetanā) is not interrupted. Whichever precept is transgressed, one is bound by kamma through that transgression alone. Thus, in this matter, the decision by way of the variety of breaking precepts should also be understood.

Regarding the greatness of blame (mahāsāvajja): Among beings such as animals devoid of virtue, killing a small-bodied being is of little blame, while killing a large-bodied being is of great blame. Why? Because the effort (payoga) is great. Even if the effort is equal, the blame is great because the object (the being) is large. Among beings such as humans who possess virtue, killing a being with little virtue is of little blame, while killing one with great virtue is of great blame. When the body size and virtue are equal, it should be understood that the blame is little due to the mildness of defilements and effort, and great due to their intensity. The same method applies to the remaining precepts. In fact, among these five precepts, only the precept of refraining from intoxicants (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna) is extremely blameworthy; the precepts of killing and so forth are not like that. Why? Because it causes one to become insane even while being human, and because it creates an obstacle to the Noble Dhamma of the Path and Fruit. Thus, in this matter, the decision by way of the greatness of blame should also be understood.

By way of effort (payoga): In this case, there are six types of effort for the act of killing: manual (sāhatthika), by command (āṇattika), by missile (nissaggiya), permanent (thāvara), by sorcery (vijjāmaya), and by psychic power (iddhimaya). Among these six, striking by oneself or with an object connected to one's body is called manual effort (sāhatthika-payoga). That effort is of two types: specific (uddisaka) and non-specific (anuddisaka). Between these two, in specific killing, one strikes with a specific person in mind; one is bound by kamma only by the death of that person. In non-specific killing, with the thought 'Let whoever may die,' one is bound by kamma by the death of anyone resulting from the strike. In both cases, whether death occurs at the moment of striking or later due to that wound, one is bound by kamma at the very moment of striking. When one strikes with the intent to kill and the person does not die, and then strikes again with a different mind, if death occurs only because of the first strike, then one is bound by kamma at that time. If death occurs because of the second strike, the act of killing (pāṇātipāta) is not completed. Even if death occurs due to both strikes, one is bound by kamma only by the first strike. If death does not occur despite both strikes, there is no act of killing at all. This is the method.
20:
Even when many people surround and beat a single person, the karmic binding (kammabaddha) occurs only for the one whose blow causes the death.

Commanding another with a determined mind is called commanding effort (āṇattika-payoga). In this commanding effort, the karmic binding should be noted in the same way as described for personal effort (sāhatthika-payoga). In this command, six restrictions (niyama) should be known:

'The object, the time, the location, the weapon, the posture, and the specific action—these six are the factors that restrict a command.'

Among these six, 'object' (vatthu) refers to the living being to be killed. 'Time' (kāla) refers to times such as morning or evening, and stages of life such as youth or old age. 'Location' (okāsa) refers to a village, a market town, a forest, a main road, or a crossroads, and so on. 'Weapon' (āvudha) refers to a sword, an arrow, or a spear, and so on. 'Posture' (iriyāpatha) refers to the standing or sitting posture, etc., of both the victim and the killer. 'Specific action' (kiriyāvisesa) refers to stabbing, cutting, splitting, or making the head bald like a conch shell, and so on.

If the object is mistaken—for instance, if one commands, 'Kill that person,' but the commanded person kills someone else—there is no karmic binding for the commander. However, if the person is killed without mistaking the object, karmic binding occurs for both: for the commander at the moment of command, and for the one commanded at the moment of killing. This same principle applies to time and the other factors.

The act of throwing or discharging a weapon with the body or something connected to the body with the intent to kill is called missile effort (nissaggiya-payoga). This effort is also of two types: intentional and unintentional. Here, the karmic binding should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned.

Digging a pit, placing a trapdoor, or preparing medicine, poison, or mantras with the intent to kill is called permanent effort (thāvara-payoga). This effort is also of two types: intentional and unintentional. Therefore, in this case as well, the karmic binding should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned.

This is the distinction: if the person who initiated the act provides the pit, etc., to others, whether for a fee or for free, and someone dies because of that pit, the karmic binding occurs only for the initiator. Even if that person or another person destroys the pit and levels it with the ground, if those who clear the dust take the soil, or those who dig for roots dig up the roots, and [re-open] the pit...
21:
...[and re-open the pit], or if mud forms when it rains, and someone dies there by falling or getting stuck, the karmic binding occurs only for the original initiator. However, if the person who acquired the pit or another person makes it wider or deeper, and someone dies because of that effort, the karmic binding occurs for both. Just as roots are connected to the base, if the ground is made level (the pit is filled), one is released from the karma. In this way, regarding trapdoors and so on, the karmic binding should be understood as it may occur as long as they remain in existence.

Reciting spells or mantras for the purpose of killing is called effort through science (vijjāmaya-payoga). Performing a transformation of psychic power resulting from the fruition of karma for the purpose of killing—such as causing the striking of fangs of creatures with fangs—is called effort through psychic power (iddhimaya-payoga). In the case of taking what is not given (adinnādāna), there are efforts such as stealing by using false weights or measures, stealing by coercion, stealing by concealment, stealing by plotting, or stealing by substituting labels; these include personal effort and commanding effort. The divisions of these types of theft should be understood according to the method already mentioned. In the three precepts beginning with unchastity (abrahmacariya), only personal effort is applicable. Thus, in this matter, the decision should be understood by way of effort.

Regarding the factors (anga), there are five factors of killing living beings (pāṇātipāta): it must be a living being, there must be the perception that it is a living being, there must be the intent to kill, there must be the effort, and death must result from that effort. There are also five factors of taking what is not given (adinnādāna): it must be the property of another, there must be the perception that it is the property of another, there must be the intent to steal, there must be the effort, and there must be the taking of the object through that effort. There are four factors of unchastity (abrahmacariya): there must be an object of transgression, there must be the intent to indulge in that object, there must be the effort to indulge because of that intent, and there must be the enjoyment. Similarly, the remaining two precepts also have four factors each. Among those two, the factors of false speech (musāvāda) are: the matter must be false, there must be the intent to deceive, there must be the corresponding effort, and there must be the communication (vaci-viññatti) that makes another understand the deception; thus, these four factors should be known. The factors of the state of intoxication through liquor and drugs (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna) are: it must be one of the types of liquor, etc., there must be the intent to drink the intoxicating substance, there must be the corresponding effort, and it must enter the throat when drunk; thus, these four are the factors. In this way, in this matter, the decision should be understood by way of factors.

Regarding the origins (samuṭṭhāna): among these precepts, killing living beings, taking what is not given, and false speech have three origins, as they arise from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. Unchastity has only one origin, by way of body and mind. The state of intoxication through liquor and drugs has two origins, as it arises from the body and from body and mind. In this way, in this matter, the decision should be understood by way of origins.
22:
The decision should also be understood by way of feeling (vedanā). In this context of the five precepts, taking life (pāṇātipāta) is associated only with painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Taking what is not given (adinnādāna) is associated with any one of the three feelings; likewise, false speech (musāvāda) is associated with any one of the three feelings. The remaining two precepts (sexual misconduct and taking intoxicants) are associated with either pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā). Thus, the decision in these five precepts should be understood by way of feeling.

The decision should also be understood by way of root (mūla). In these five precepts, taking life has the roots of hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). Taking what is not given and false speech have the roots of either greed (lobha) and delusion, or hatred and delusion. The remaining two precepts have the roots of greed and delusion. Thus, the decision in these five precepts should be understood by way of root.

The decision should also be understood by way of action (kamma). In these five precepts, taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct (abrahmacariya) are bodily actions (kāyakamma) only and reach the path of action (kammapatha). False speech is verbal action (vacīkamma) only. That false speech which destroys the benefit of others reaches the path of action. Other types of false speech are merely verbal action. The occasion of distilled and fermented intoxicants which causes heedlessness (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna) is bodily action only. Thus, the decision in these five precepts should be understood by way of action.

Regarding abstinence (virati), there is a question: "From what does one who abstains from taking life and so forth abstain?" The answer is: One who abstains by way of undertaking (samādāna) first abstains from the unwholesome act of taking life and so forth, whether of one's own or of others. With what as the object does one abstain? One abstains by taking that very unwholesome act from which one is abstaining as the object. One who abstains by way of what is encountered (sampatta) also abstains only from the aforementioned types of unwholesome acts. With what as the object does one abstain? One abstains by taking the aforementioned objects of taking life and so forth as the object.

However, some teachers say: "One abstains from the occasion of distilled and fermented intoxicants which causes heedlessness by taking the formations (saṅkhāra) known as distilled and fermented intoxicants as the object. Among the formations of beings, one abstains from taking what is not given and false speech by taking as the object those formations of beings which are to be stolen or destroyed. One abstains from taking life and sexual misconduct by taking only beings as the object."

Other teachers, however, do not accept this, holding the view that: "If it were so, one would be doing one thing while thinking of another, and one would not know the unwholesome act that is being abandoned." They say that one abstains by taking one's own unwholesome act of taking life and so forth as the object. That statement is not appropriate. Why? Because that abstinence (virati) does not have a present object, nor is it an external (bahiddhā) object. In the text of the Vibhaṅga of the precepts, after asking, "Among the five precepts, how many are wholesome... how many are without conflict (araṇa)?", the answer is given: "They are only wholesome, sometimes associated with pleasant feeling." In that explanation, it is stated that they have a present object (paccuppannārammaṇa) and an external object (bahiddhārammaṇa). Such having of a present and external object is not appropriate for one who abstains by taking one's own unwholesome act of taking life and so forth as the object. As for the statement that was made:
23:
"One who thinks of one thing would be doing another, and would not know the unwholesome state that he abandons." Regarding that statement, the meaning is: when it occurs by way of accomplishing a function, it cannot be said that one who thinks of one unwholesome state does another unwholesome state different from what was thought, or that one abandons an unwholesome state without knowing the state being abandoned.

"Taking the Deathless (Nibbāna) as the object,
Abandoning all evils,
The noble person (ariya) established in the Path,
Would be the evidence in this case."

Thus, the decision in this precept should be understood by way of abstinence. Regarding the result (phala): all these unwholesome states such as taking life and so forth produce results in woeful states (duggati). Even in happy states (sugati), they produce undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasant results. They produce results such as lack of confidence (avesārajja) and so forth in the life to come as well as in the present life. Furthermore, in such ways as, "The lightest result of taking life, when it ripens for one who has become a human, leads to a short lifespan," the decision in this precept should also be understood by way of result.

Furthermore, in these five precepts, the decision regarding the abstinence from taking life and so forth should be understood by way of origin (samuṭṭhāna), feeling (vedanā), root (mūla), action (kamma), and result (phala). In that decision, what is to be made known is: all those abstinences (virati) arise from four origins—from the body, from the body and mind, from speech and mind, and from the body, speech, and mind. All abstinences are associated with either pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. They have the roots of non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa), or the roots of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion (amoha). Among these five abstinences, four are bodily actions. Abstinence from false speech is verbal action. At the moment of the Path, however, they arise only from the mind; all abstinences are then mental action (manokamma).

Among these five abstinences, through abstinence from taking life, the following results should be understood: completeness of limbs and organs, perfection of height and girth, perfection of speed, well-placed feet, being beautiful to look at, softness, purity, courage, great strength, clear and distinct speech, being loved by people, pure speech, having an undivided assembly, fearlessness, being invincible, not dying by the efforts of others, having an infinite retinue, good appearance, good figure, freedom from illness, freedom from sorrow, not being separated from loved and pleasant ones, and long life.

Through abstinence from taking what is not given, the following results should be understood: having great wealth, having abundant wealth and grain, having infinite possessions, the arising of possessions not yet arisen, the stability of possessions already arisen, the quick attainment of desired possessions, having possessions that are not shared with kings, thieves, water, fire, and unloved heirs, being superior to other people, never knowing the state of 'not having', and living happily.
24:
Possessing belongings that are not shared with [the five enemies:] kings, thieves, water, fire, and unpleasant heirs (exclusive ownership); obtaining extraordinary wealth; being superior to common people; the absence of poverty; and living in comfort, and so forth [are the fruits of abstaining from stealing].

By abstaining from unchastity (abrahmacariya): freedom from enemies; being loved by all people; ease in obtaining alms-food, water, clothing, and bedding; sleeping peacefully; waking peacefully; freedom from the fear of woeful states; not being reborn as a woman or a eunuch (napuṃsaka); absence of anger; being observant; absence of physical defects; not being downcast; mutual affection between men and women; having complete sense faculties; possessing complete physical marks; freedom from suspicion; freedom from anxiety; living in comfort; being free from danger; and not being separated from loved ones, and so forth.

By abstaining from false speech (musāvāda): clear sense faculties; speaking with distinct and sweet tones; having even and white teeth; being neither too fat, too thin, too short, nor too tall; having a pleasant touch; breath like the scent of a lotus; having a retinue that listens to one's words; having credible speech; having a soft, red, and thin tongue like a red or blue lotus; not being restless; and not being frivolous, and so forth.

By abstaining from intoxicants which cause negligence (surāmerayamajja...): quick understanding in all matters of the past, future, and present; constant presence of mindfulness; not being insane; possessing wisdom; not being lazy; not being dull; not being mute; not being intoxicated; not being negligent; not being confused; being undaunted; not being aggressive; being free from suspicion; speaking the truth; abstaining from slander, harsh speech, and frivolous talk; being diligent day and night; gratitude; reciprocating kindness; lack of stinginess; being generous; being virtuous; uprightness; absence of anger; possessing moral shame (hiri); possessing moral dread (ottappa); having upright view; great wisdom; penetrative insight; being a scholar; and skill in knowing what is beneficial and what is not, and so forth. Thus, the decision regarding the abstinences from killing and so forth should also be understood through origin (samuṭṭhāna), feeling (vedanā), root (mūla), action (kamma), and fruit (phala).

## Description of the Last Five Precepts

Now, regarding the verse that was stated:
"What is appropriate from that [the first five] should be applied to the last five as well;
the specific [features] should be stated, and the inferior [nature] etc. should also be known."
25:
## The commentary on the meaning of that verse is as follows:

Taking the appropriate words from the explanation of the first five precepts, they should be applied to the last five precepts as well. The application is as follows: Just as in the previous precepts, the precept on intoxicants (surāmeraya...) has as its object one of the formations (saṅkhāra) such as visible objects, so too does this precept on untimely eating (vikālabhojana). In this way, the variety of objects for all precepts should be understood. Regarding undertaking (samādāna), just as the previous ones are undertaken by a novice (sāmaṇera) or a lay devotee (upāsaka), so too are these latter precepts.

Regarding the factors (aṅga), just as the variety of factors for killing and so forth was stated in the previous precepts, here too, there are four factors for untimely eating: (1) the time being 'untimely' (after noon), (2) the food being 'temporary' (yāvakālika), (3) the act of swallowing, and (4) not being insane. Following this method, the classification of factors for the remaining precepts should also be understood. Regarding origin (samuṭṭhāna), just as the precept on intoxicants has two origins—from the body and from both body and mind—so too does untimely eating. In this way, the origin of all should be understood.

Regarding feeling (vedanā), just as the precept on taking what is not given (adinnādāna) is associated with any one of the three feelings, so too is untimely eating. In this way, the association with feeling for all should be understood. Regarding the root (mūla), just as the precept on unchastity (abrahmacariya) has greed and delusion as its roots, so too does untimely eating. The next two [precepts on dancing/singing and garlands/perfumes] should also be understood to have greed and delusion as their roots in this same way.

Regarding action (kamma), just as killing and so forth are bodily actions, so too are untimely eating and so forth. However, receiving gold and silver (jātarūparajatapaṭiggrahaṇa) may be either bodily action or vocal action according to the manner of occurrence through the body-door etc., but not by way of 'course of action' (kammapatha). Regarding the word 'viramato' (abstaining): just as in the previous precepts one abstains from the unwholesome acts of killing etc. of oneself or others, here too, one abstains from the unwholesome acts of untimely eating etc., or from both [unwholesome and wholesome] together. Just as the first five abstinences have four origins—body, body-and-mind, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind; and just as all precepts are associated with either pleasant feeling or neutral feeling; and have roots of non-greed and non-hatred, or non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; and produce various desirable fruits; so too it is in these latter precepts.

## "What is appropriate from the first five precepts should be applied to the last five; the specific (āveṇika) should be stated, and the inferior (hīna) etc. should also be known."

In this context, 'untimely eating' (vikālabhojana) means eating when the noon has passed. Because it is eating when the permitted time has passed, it is called 'untimely eating'. Regarding that eating after noon, and in the phrase 'dancing, singing, music, and seeing spectacles' (naccagītavāditavisūkadassana), dancing, singing, and music refer to any unspecified instance of dancing, singing, or music. 'Seeing spectacles' (visūkadassana) means watching performances that are a hindrance because they support the arising of defilements or because they destroy the wholesome portion. Or, it is watching performances that cause the increase of defilements. The characteristic of this 'visūkadassana' should be taken as stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta. In that Sutta, it is said: "Some recluses and brahmins, having consumed the food given in faith, remain addicted to such spectacles (visūkadassana)."
26:
Because it is eating after the time allowed for eating has passed, which is after noon, it is called *vikālabhojana*.

In this phrase '*nacca-gīta-vādita-visūkadassana*', dancing (*nacca*) means any kind of dancing. Singing (*gīta*) means any kind of singing. Instrumental music (*vādita*) means any kind of instrumental music. Unseemly shows (*visūkadassana*) means viewing performances that destroy the side of merit because they are conditions for the arising of defilements, or it means viewing what is an unseemly show. Dancing, singing, instrumental music, and viewing unseemly shows are collectively called *nacca-gīta-vādita-visūkadassana*. The meaning of *visūkadassana* here should be taken as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.

Indeed, it is said there: "Whereas some recluses and brahmins, while living on food provided by the faithful, continue to be addicted to such unseemly shows as: dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical shows, ballad recitations, hand-clapping, cymbals, pot-drums, fairy shows, iron-ball acrobatics, bamboo-pole acrobatics, bone-washing, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, staff-fights, boxing, wrestling, sham fights, roll-calls, battle arrays, and seeing troops—the recluse Gotama abstains from such unseemly shows." (DN 1).

Alternatively, by the aforementioned meaning, dancing, singing, and instrumental music themselves are unseemly (*visūka*). The viewing of these unseemly things—dancing, singing, and instrumental music—is *nacca-gīta-vādita-visūkadassana*. Although it should be said "viewing and hearing," just as in passages such as "He is one of wrong view, of perverted vision (*viparītadassana*)" (AN 1.308), the grasping of an object that does not occur at the eye-door is also called "vision" (*dassana*); so here, hearing is also called "vision" (*dassana*). A transgression of the precept occurs only for one who approaches and views with the desire to see. However, if one sees or hears what comes to the place where one is standing, sitting, or lying, or what becomes apparent while traveling, there may be defilement of mind, but there is no transgression. It should be understood that while a song associated with the Dhamma is not allowable, the Dhamma recited with a song-like intonation is allowable.

Garlands and so forth should be applied respectively to wearing and so forth. Therein, garland (*mālā*) means any kind of flower. Unguent (*vilepana*) means any perfume prepared by grinding for the purpose of anointing. All other types of scents such as scented powder and incense are perfume (*gandha*). All of these are not allowable for the purpose of decoration and adornment, but they are allowable for the purpose of medicine. For one who accepts flowers and perfumes brought for the purpose of offering, it is not the case that it is not allowable by any means; it is indeed allowable. High bed (*uccāsayana*) refers to a couch or stool with legs exceeding the standard measurement. Large bed (*mahāsayana*) refers to unallowable beds and unallowable bed-coverings. For one who finds pleasure in both of these, it is not allowable by any means. *Jātarūpa* is gold. *Rajata* is a kahāpaṇa (coin). All *māsakas* made of copper, wood, or lac that are used for trade in various places are also called *jātarūpa-rajata*. Finding pleasure in those gold and silver items in any way is called "accepting" (*paṭiggahaṇa*). It is specifically stated that such pleasure is not allowable by any means, distinguishing it from previous precepts. If these ten precepts are undertaken with inferior desire (*chanda*), mind (*citta*), energy (*viriya*), or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*), they are inferior merit. If undertaken with medium desire etc., they are medium merit. If undertaken with superior desire etc., they are superior merit. Alternatively, if they are defiled by the latent tendencies of craving, views, and conceit, they are inferior merit; if not defiled, they are medium merit. In those various precepts, if supported by wisdom...
27:
For one who finds pleasure [in gold and silver], it is not allowable by any means. *Jātarūpa* is gold. *Rajata* is a kahāpaṇa (coin). Whatever *māsaka* made of copper, *māsaka* made of wood, or *māsaka* made of lac is used for trade in various places, both are called *jātarūpa-rajata*. For that person, finding pleasure in them in any way is called "accepting" (*paṭiggahaṇa*). It should be stated as a specific rule that such pleasure is not allowable by any means, distinguishing it from previous precepts.

These ten precepts are inferior if undertaken with inferior desire (*chanda*), mind (*citta*), energy (*viriya*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*); they are medium if undertaken with medium ones; and they are superior if undertaken with superior ones. Alternatively, the precepts defiled and smeared by craving (*taṇhā*), views (*diṭṭhi*), and conceit (*māna*) are inferior; those not defiled are medium; and those precepts in various instances that are supported by wisdom are superior. Furthermore, those undertaken with a wholesome mind dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*) are inferior; those associated with prompted knowledge (*sasaṅkhārika-ñāṇasampayutta*) are medium; and those with unprompted knowledge (*asaṅkhārika*) are superior. In this way, the states of being inferior, medium, and superior should be understood.

By this much of the discourse, the matrix (*mātikā*) that was set forth previously for the purpose of explaining the text of the precepts through the six verses beginning with "By whom, where, when, why..." has been revealed in terms of its meaning.

## The Explanation of the Precepts in the Paramatthajotikā,
## the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, is finished.
## 3. Explanation of the Thirty-two Parts
## Explanation of the Connection of Words

Now, for the purpose of purifying the inclination and for the purpose of mental development of a clansman who, through these ten precepts, has purified his practice and is established in virtue—a practice which does not occur before the arising of a Buddha and is outside the scope of all sectarians—it is said in various Suttas:

"Monks, one thing, when developed and cultivated, leads to great spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). It leads to great benefit. It leads to great security from bondage (*yogakkhema*). It leads to great mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*). It leads to the attainment of the vision of knowledge. It leads to a happy dwelling in this very life. It leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation (*vijjā-vimutti-phala*)."
28:
What is the one thing? It is mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). Monks, those who do not enjoy mindfulness directed to the body do not enjoy the Deathless (amata). Monks, those who enjoy mindfulness directed to the body enjoy the Deathless. Monks, for those who have not yet enjoyed mindfulness directed to the body, the Deathless is not yet enjoyed; if it is enjoyed, the Deathless is enjoyed; if it is neglected, the Deathless is neglected; if it is not neglected, the Deathless is not neglected; if it is missed, the Deathless is missed; if it is undertaken, the Deathless is undertaken. Why is that? Because they have undertaken mindfulness directed to the body.

Thus, the Blessed One, having praised it in various ways, said: "Monks, how is mindfulness directed to the body developed? How is it frequently practiced so that it is of great fruit and great benefit? Here, monks, a monk having gone to the forest..." By such means, the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body is pointed out through these fourteen sections: the section on breathing (ānāpānapabba), the section on postures (iriyāpathapabba), the section on fourfold clear comprehension (catusampajaññapabba), the section on reflection on repulsiveness (paṭikūlamanasikārapabba), the section on reflection on elements (dhātumanasikārapabba), and the nine cemetery sections (nava sivathikapabba). Now we have reached the explanation of the development of that meditation subject. Among those fourteen, these three—the section on postures, the section on fourfold clear comprehension, and the section on reflection on elements—are taught by way of insight (vipassanā). The nine cemetery sections are taught by way of the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā) only within insight knowledges. In this context, if one desires concentration meditation (samādhibhāvanā) among the bloated corpses and so forth, that concentration meditation has already been explained in detail in the "Explanation of the Meditation on Foulness" (asubhabhāvanāniddesa) in the Visuddhimagga. However, these two—the section on breathing and the section on reflection on repulsiveness—are taught here by way of concentration (samādhi). Among those two, the section on breathing is a separate meditation subject by way of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati).

"Furthermore, monks, a monk reflects on this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the tips of the hair downwards, enclosed by skin and full of various kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are hairs of the head, hairs of the body... urine.'" Thus it is taught. In this way, in various Pali texts, the meditation on the thirty-two parts, which is the sequence of teaching the development of the collection of mindfulness directed to the body, including the brain within the bone marrow (aṭṭhimiñja), is begun. The following is the explanation of the meaning of that meditation subject:

Therein, "Atthi" means they exist. "Imasmiṃ" means in this body, which is said to be from the soles of the feet upwards, from the tips of the hair downwards, enclosed by skin, and full of various kinds of impurities. Let me further explain the word "body" (kāya). It is called kāya because it is a collection of filth and because it is the place where repulsive things such as hair and so forth arise. There are thirty-two parts such as hair, urine, and so forth. These thirty-two parts exist in this fathom-long physical body; this should be understood in every respect. What collection is taught by these thirty-two parts? In this fathom-long body, from the soles of the feet upwards, from the tips of the hair downwards, and within the boundary of the skin, one who searches through the entire internal collection will not see even an atom's worth of purity such as pearls, rubies, gems, conch shells, sandalwood, aloe wood, camphor, or perfumes.
