Instead, one sees only various kinds of impurities such as hair and body hair, which are extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and devoid of beauty...
29:
In that body (the collection of these thirty-two parts). "Kāya" refers to the physical body. Indeed, it is called "kāya" because it is an accumulation of impurities and because it is the source of hundreds of diseases, such as eye diseases and so forth, as well as repulsive things like hair and so forth. There are these thirty-two parts starting from hair... up to... urine. Regarding these thirty-two parts, the connection should be understood as: "In this body there are hairs of the head, there are hairs of the body." What is intended by saying this? In this fathom-long carcass, from the soles of the feet upwards, from the tips of the hair downwards, and all around within the skin, if one searches in every way, one does not see even an atom's worth of purity such as pearls, rubies, gems, aloe wood, sandalwood, tagara, camphor, or scented powders. Instead, one sees only various kinds of impurities such as hair and body hair, which are extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and devoid of beauty.

This is the explanation by way of the connection of words.

## Asubhabhāvanā
By way of the meditation on foulness (asubhabhāvanā), the explanation should be understood as follows: A son of good family who is established in virtue (sīla), such as the precept of refraining from taking life and so forth, who has pure effort, and whose primary task is the practice of meditation, wishing to engage in the development of the meditation on the thirty-two parts for the sake of attaining the paths and fruits through purity of intention, first has ten impediments (palibodha): dwelling (āvāsa), family (kula), gain (lābha), group (gaṇa), work (kamma), travel (addhāna), kin (ñāti), books (gantha), illness (roga), and supernormal powers (iddhi) or fame (kitti). Then, he should cut off those ten impediments by abandoning attachment to dwelling, family, gain, group, kin, and fame; by being free from concern regarding work, travel, and books; and by treating illness. Having thus cut off the impediments, with an uninterrupted desire for renunciation, undertaking a life of extreme effacement (sallekha), and not abandoning even the minor and lesser rules of Vinaya conduct, he should approach, in accordance with the Vinaya, a teacher (ācariya) who provides meditation subjects and who is endowed with the scriptures and attainments, or at least one of these. Having pleased the teacher's mind through the fulfillment of duties, he should inform him of his intention. That teacher, knowing the differences in his signs, intentions, temperament, and inclination, if this meditation subject is suitable...
30:
At that time, if the pupil wishes to reside in the same monastery where the teacher himself resides, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is given in brief. If he wishes to reside elsewhere, it should be explained in detail, including what should be abandoned and what should be undertaken, and with specific discourse suitable for one of lustful temperament (rāga-carita). Having learned that meditation subject in detail and having taken leave of the teacher—

“A large monastery, a new monastery, an old monastery, one by a road,
one with a pond, one dependent on vegetables, one dependent on flowers, one dependent on fruits, one that is famous,
one dependent on a city, one dependent on wood or bamboo, one dependent on fields, one with incompatible monks, one near a port or market,
one in a border region, an unsuitable one, and one where a friend cannot be found—
a wise man, knowing these eighteen places,
should avoid them from afar, just as one avoids a dangerous path.” (This is found in Visuddhimagga, 1, 52).

Thus, these are called the eighteen dwellings to be avoided. Having avoided those places, a monastery which—

“Monks, in what way is a dwelling endowed with five factors? Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a dwelling is not too far, not too near, and is well-provided with routes for coming and going; by day it is not crowded with people, and by night it is quiet and has little noise; it is free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, snakes, scorpions, and lice. For one residing in that dwelling, robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites are easily obtained without difficulty. In that dwelling, there reside elder monks who are learned, masters of the scriptures, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā. From time to time, he approaches those elders and asks: ‘Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones then open up what was not open, clarify what was not clear, and dispel doubts in various matters that give rise to doubt. Thus, monks, a dwelling is endowed with five factors.” (This is found in Aṅguttara Nikāya, 10, 11).

Thus, a dwelling endowed with five factors is described. Having approached such a dwelling and performed all duties, one should reflect on the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation...
31:
...and having gladdened the mind by recollecting the Buddha’s state of being well-awakened, the Dhamma’s state of being well-proclaimed, and the Saṅgha’s state of having practiced well—

“The wise should know the sevenfold skill in learning: by word, by mind, and by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation.”

Thus, the sevenfold skill in learning (uggahakosalla) and the tenfold skill in attention (manasikārakosalla)—by way of sequence, not too fast, not too slow, warding off distraction, transcending concepts, dropping the parts in sequence, reaching attainment (appanā), and the three suttas—are described. Without abandoning these skills, one should begin the meditation on the thirty-two parts (dvattiṃsākāra). For one who begins in this way, the meditation on the thirty-two parts succeeds in every way, and not otherwise.

In that meditation, first taking the skin-pentad (taca-pañcaka), a person who bears the Tipiṭaka should meditate for half a month, both verbally and mentally, in forward order (anuloma) such as “kesā, lomā,” etc. When proficient in forward order, one meditates in reverse order (paṭiloma) such as “taco, dantā,” etc. When proficient in reverse order, one meditates in both forward and reverse orders to cut off thoughts that wander outside, to become proficient in the Pali text, and to grasp the nature of the parts. Indeed, verbal recitation is a condition for cutting off wandering thoughts and for mental meditation and proficiency in the Pali text. Mental meditation is a condition for grasping the parts by way of either the foulness, color, or characteristics. Then, in the same manner, the kidney-pentad (vakka-pañcaka) for half a month; then both groups for half a month; then the lung-pentad (papphāsa-pañcaka) for half a month; then all three pentads for half a month. Then, although not mentioned at the end, the brain (matthaluṅga) is included here to be meditated upon together with the elements of the earth-property; thus the brain-pentad (matthaluṅga-pañcaka) for half a month; then all four pentads for half a month; then the fat-sextet (meda-chakka) for half a month; then the four pentads together with the fat-sextet for half a month; then the urine-sextet (mutta-chakka) for half a month; and finally, all thirty-two parts for half a month. In this way, for six months, one should meditate by defining them by color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation. This decision is stated with reference to a person of medium wisdom. One of dull wisdom should meditate for as long as he lives. For one of sharp wisdom, the meditation succeeds in no long time.
32:
Here it is asked: "How does this practitioner (yogāvacara) define this meditation subject of the thirty-two parts by way of color and so on?" When this practitioner develops the thirty-two parts analyzed by the skin-pentad (tacapañcaka) and so on in the manner "There are in this body hairs of the head," he first defines the hairs of the head by color as "they are black." Or he defines them as being of such a nature as they are seen by him. By shape, he defines them as "they are long and round like a spindle." By direction, since in this body the part above the navel is called the upper direction and the part below the navel is called the lower direction, he defines them as "they grow in the upper direction of this person." By location, he defines them as "they grow in the skin of the head bounded by the forehead, the ear-roots, and the nape of the neck."

In defining them thus, just as kusa grass growing on top of an anthill does not know "We grow on top of an anthill," nor does the anthill know "Kusa grass grows on me," so too the hairs of the head do not know "We grow in the skin of the head," nor does the skin of the head know "Hairs of the head grow in me." Indeed, these things are devoid of attention and reflection; they are non-sentient, indeterminate (abyākata), empty of self, extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive. He defines them as "not a being, not a person."

By way of delimitation (pariccheda), defining is of two kinds: by way of the similar (sabhāga) and the dissimilar (visabhāga). Among these, he defines them by similar delimitation thus: "The hairs of the head are delimited below by the surface of the skin where they are fixed, having entered to the extent of a grain of paddy, and by their own roots; above by space; and transversely by each other." He defines them by dissimilar delimitation thus: "Hairs of the head are not the remaining thirty-one parts; the remaining thirty-one parts are not hairs of the head." Thus he first defines the hairs of the head by color and so on.

Among the remaining parts, he defines the body hairs (lomā) by color as "mostly blue-black in color." Or he defines them as being of such a nature as they are seen by him. By shape, they are "bent like a bow" or "shaped like a palm-leaf midrib curved at the top." By direction, "they grow in both directions (upper and lower body)." By location, he defines them as "they grow mostly in the skin of the remaining body, excluding the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet."

In those body hairs, just as dabba grass growing in an old village site does not know "We grow in an old village site," nor does the old village site know "Dabba grass grows in me," so too the body hairs do not know "We grow in the skin of the body," nor does the skin of the body know "Body hairs grow in me." Indeed, these things are devoid of attention and reflection; they are non-sentient, indeterminate (abyākata)...
33:
(Those body hairs) are void of self, extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive. He must define them as neither a being nor a person. By delimitation, he must define them as being delimited below by the surface of the skin, by its own roots which enter that skin to the depth of a louse's egg (likkhā), above by space, and transversely by one another. This is the similar delimitation of those body hairs. The dissimilar delimitation is just the same as that of the hair of the head. Thus, he must define the body hair by color and so forth.

Next, the nails. For one who is complete, there are twenty. He must define all those nails by color as being white where they are free from flesh, and copper-colored where they are attached to flesh. By shape, they have the shape of their own location; mostly, he must define them as having a shape like a madhuka seed or like a fish scale. By direction, they grow in both directions (upper and lower). By location, they are situated on the tips of the fingers and toes.

Regarding those nails, for example, just as madhuka seeds placed on the ends of sticks by village children do not know "We are placed on the ends of sticks," nor do the sticks know "Madhuka seeds are placed on us," so too the nails do not know "We are situated on the tips of the fingers and toes," nor do the fingers and toes know "Nails are situated on our tips." This is because these things are devoid of attention and reflection; they are non-sentient. He must define them as not a person. By delimitation, he must define them as being delimited below and at the base by the flesh of the fingers and toes, or by the surface situated on those fingers and toes, above and at the tip by space, and on both sides by the skin at the two edges of the fingers and toes. This is the similar delimitation of those nails. The dissimilar delimitation is just the same as that of the hair of the head. Thus, he must define the nails by color and so forth.

Next, the teeth. For one who is complete, there are thirty-two. He must define all those teeth by color as being white. If they are set evenly for someone, they appear like a row of conch shells cut with a saw, or like a string of white jasmine buds set evenly. If they are set unevenly for someone, he must define them by shape as having various shapes like a row of benches placed in an old rest-house. Among those thirty-two teeth, at the ends of both rows of teeth, there are eight teeth, two each above and below, which have four points and four roots, shaped like a small bench. Outside of those eight molar teeth...
34:
The eight teeth situated in that order have three points at the top and three roots at the bottom, and are shaped like a junction (siṅghāṭaka). Outside of those, also in that order, there are four teeth, one below and one above, which have two points and two roots, and are shaped like a cart-prop (yānakūpatthambhinī). Outside of those, also in that order, the four canine teeth (dāṭhādantā) have only one point and one root, and are shaped like a jasmine bud (mallikāmakuḷa). Furthermore, in the middle of the two rows of teeth, there are eight teeth, four below and four above, which have only one point and one root, and are shaped like a gourd seed (tumbabīja). In terms of direction, they are located in the upper direction. In terms of location, the upper teeth are fixed in the upper jawbone with their points facing downwards, and the lower teeth are fixed in the lower jawbone with their points facing upwards.

In those teeth, just as the pillars fixed on a lower stone slab and inserted into an upper slab by a man doing new construction work do not know, 'We are fixed on a lower stone slab and inserted into an upper slab,' nor does the lower stone slab know, 'Pillars are fixed in me,' nor does the upper slab know, 'Pillars have entered me'; even so, the teeth do not know, 'We are fixed in the lower jawbone and have entered the upper jawbone,' nor does the lower jawbone know, 'Teeth are fixed in me,' nor does the upper jawbone know, 'Teeth have entered me.' These things are devoid of thought and reflection... they should be defined as 'not a person'. By way of delimitation, they are delimited by their own root-surfaces which are fixed by entering the jawbone through the lower jaw-socket, by the space above, and transversely by each other. This is their delimitation of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). As for the delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda), it is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines the teeth by way of color and so on.

After that, one defines the skin (taca), which covers various heaps of corpses inside the body, as white by way of color. Although that skin appears to be of various colors such as black or white due to the influence of the colors of the outer skin (chavi) being stained by dyes (chavirāga), it is actually white in its natural color. The whiteness of that skin becomes apparent when the outer skin (chavi) is destroyed by the impact of flames, blows, or injuries. By way of shape, briefly, it has the shape of a jacket (kañcuka), and in detail, it has various shapes. For instance, the skin of the toes has the shape of a silkworm's cocoon; the skin of the instep has the shape of a leather sandal covering the foot; the skin of the calf has the shape of a palm leaf used for wrapping rice.
35:
The skin of the calf has the shape of a palm leaf. The skin of the thigh has the shape of a long bag filled with rice. The skin of the buttocks has the shape of a cloth water-filter filled with water. The skin of the back has the shape of leather stretched over a wooden board. The skin of the belly has the shape of leather stretched over the body of a lute. The skin of the chest is mostly square in shape. The skin of the two arms has the shape of a leather-covered quiver. The skin of the back of the hand has the shape of a razor case, or the shape of a comb case. The skin of the fingers has the shape of a key case. The skin of the neck has the shape of a neck-wrap (collar). The skin of the face has the shape of an insect nest full of holes and crevices. The skin of the head has the shape of an alms-bowl bag.

A practitioner (yogāvacara) who defines the skin should send the mind between the skin and the flesh, starting from the upper lip, and first define the skin of the face. Then the skin of the head, then the outer skin of the neck, then the skin of the right arm in forward and reverse order. In the same way, the skin of the left arm, then the skin of the back, then the skin of the buttocks, then the skin of the right leg in forward and reverse order, then the skin of the left leg, then the skin of the bladder, belly, heart, and inner neck, then the skin of the lower jaw, then the skin of the lower lip. In this way, one defines it again up to the skin of the upper lip. In terms of direction, the skin exists in both directions. In terms of location, it stands enveloping the entire body.

In that regard, just as a box wrapped with wet leather does not know, 'I have wrapped the box,' nor does the box know, 'I am wrapped with wet leather'; even so, the skin does not know, 'I have wrapped this body made of the four great elements,' nor does this body made of the four great elements know, 'I am wrapped by the skin.' For these things are devoid of thought and reflection... they are not a person. Indeed—

'Covered with wet leather, this great wound with nine openings leaks from all sides, being impure and foul-smelling.'

By way of delimitation, it is defined as being delimited below by the flesh or by the surface fixed upon that flesh, and above by the outer skin (chavi). This is the delimitation of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda) for that skin. As for the delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda), it is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines the skin by way of color and so on.
36:
Furthermore, in this body, the flesh, which consists of nine hundred pieces, should be defined by color as being red, like the color of a Pālibhaddaka flower. By shape, it has various shapes. To explain: among those pieces of flesh, the flesh of the calves has the shape of a bundle of rice wrapped in a palm leaf; some teachers say it has the shape of an unblossomed Ketakī bud. The flesh of the thighs has the shape of a small grinding stone for mortar. The flesh of the buttocks has the shape of the edge of an oven. The flesh of the back has the shape of a half-split palm seed. The flesh of the two sides of the ribs has the shape of a thin layer of soft clay smeared on the belly of a bamboo basket. The flesh of the breasts has the shape of a half-lump of clay that has been rounded and set down. The flesh of the two arms has the shape of a large skinned rat with its tail, head, and feet cut off; some say it has the shape of a piece of meat placed on a butcher's block. The flesh of the cheeks has the shape of a Karañja seed placed on the cheek area; some say it has the shape of a frog. The flesh of the tongue has the shape of a Nuhī leaf. The flesh of the nose has the shape of a leaf basket placed face down. The flesh of the eye sockets has the shape of a half-ripe Udumbara fig. The flesh of the head has the shape of a thin layer of soft clay smeared on a bowl-baking pot. A practitioner (yogāvacara) who defines the flesh should define these gross pieces of flesh by their shape. For one who defines them in this way, the subtle pieces of flesh will appear to the knowledge. By direction, it occurs in both the upper and lower directions. By location, it stands smearing the more than three hundred bones. 

In this regard, just as a wall smeared with thick clay does not know, 'The wall is smeared by me,' nor does the wall know, 'I am smeared with thick clay,' even so, the flesh consisting of nine hundred pieces does not know, 'The three hundred bones are smeared by me,' nor do the three hundred bones know, 'I am smeared with the flesh consisting of nine hundred pieces.' For these things are devoid of concern and reflection... they are not a person. Rather: 

'Nine hundred pieces of flesh smear the carcass, 
Which is crowded with various kinds of worms, 
And is foul like a cesspit.' 

By boundary, it should be defined as being bounded below by the collection of bones or the surface on which it rests, above by the skin, and transversely by each other. This is its similar boundary (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its dissimilar boundary (visabhāga-pariccheda) is the same as that of the hair. Thus, the flesh is defined by color and so on. 

Furthermore, in this body, the sinews (nhāru), which consist of nine hundred divisions, should be defined by color as being white; some say they are the color of honey. By shape, they have various shapes.
37:
Therefore, among those sinews, the large sinews have the shape of Kandala buds. The sinews more subtle than those have the shape of ropes for binding pigs. The sinews smaller than those have the shape of rotten creepers. The sinews smaller than those have the shape of the strings of a great Sihala lute. The sinews smaller than those have the shape of thick threads. The sinews on the backs of the hands and the backs of the feet have the shape of birds' feet. The sinews on the head have the shape of a sparse net placed on the heads of village children. The sinews on the back have the shape of a fishing net moistened and spread out in the sun. The remaining sinews that follow the various major and minor limbs in this body have the shape of a net-jacket worn on the body.

By direction, they should be defined as occurring in both the upper and lower directions. Among those sinews, starting from the base of the right ear, five large sinews called kaṇḍara go to the left side, winding around the front and the back. Starting from the base of the left ear, five go to the right side, winding around the front and the back. Starting from the right side of the neck, five go to the left side, winding around the front and the back. Starting from the left side of the neck, five go to the right side, winding around the front and the back. Winding around the right arm, ten large sinews called kaṇḍara—five in front and five in back—ascend. In the same way, they ascend in the left arm, the right leg, and the left leg. Thus, they should be defined as these sixty large sinews that support the body and are the regulators of the body. By location, they stand binding the bones together in the whole body, between the bones and the skin, and between the bones and the flesh.

In this regard, just as in the case of wall-timbers bound with creepers, the creepers do not know, 'The wall-timbers are bound by us,' nor do the wall-timbers know, 'We are bound by creepers,' even so, the sinews do not know, 'The three hundred bones are bound by us,' nor do the three hundred bones know, 'We are bound by sinews.' For these things are devoid of concern and reflection... they are not a person. Rather:

'There are nine hundred sinews in this fathom-long foul carcass; 
They bind the collection of bones together, 
Just as creepers bind a house.'

By boundary, they should be defined as being bounded below by the three hundred bones or the surfaces on which they rest, above by the skin and flesh, and transversely by each other. This is their similar boundary (sabhāga-pariccheda). Their dissimilar boundary (visabhāga-pariccheda) is the same as that of the hair. Thus, the sinews are defined by color and so on.
38:
After that, since the thirty-two teeth have been taken separately, he defines all the remaining bones—sixty-four hand bones, sixty-four foot bones, sixty-four soft bones (nails) associated with flesh, two heel bones, two ankle bones in each foot, two shin bones, one knee bone, one thigh bone, two hip bones, eighteen spinal bones, twenty-four ribs, fourteen chest bones, one breastbone, two collarbones, two shoulder blade bones, two upper arm bones, two forearm bones, seven neck bones, two jawbones, one nose bone, two eye socket bones, two ear bones, one forehead bone, one crown bone, and nine skull bones—as being white in color.

In terms of shape, they have various forms. For instance, among those bones, the tip bones of the toes are like kataka seeds. The middle bones of the toes next to them are like immature jackfruit seeds. The base bones are like panava drums; some teachers say they are like peacock neck joints. The metatarsal bones are like a bundle of crushed white vine. The heel bones are like a single-seeded palmyra fruit. The ankle bones are like bound play-balls. Among the shin bones, the smaller one is like a bow-staff, and the larger one is like the back of a python withered by hunger. The part of the shin bone resting on the ankle bones is like a peeled date palm shoot. The part of the shin bone resting on the knee bone is like the top of a mridangam drum. The knee bone, when viewed from one side, is like a pot-beater. The thigh bones are like roughly hewn axe handles. The part of the thigh bone resting in the hip bone is like a goldsmith's tongs. The hip socket where the thigh bone rests is like a cut-off punnaga fruit. The two hip bones, being joined together, are like a potter's kiln; some teachers say they are like an ascetic's seat (bhisi). The pelvic bones are like a cobra's hood facing downwards. The eighteen spinal bones, which have small holes in seven or eight places, are like stacked lead sheets from the inside, and like a row of round bamboo joints from the outside. Between those bones, there are two or three spikes like saw teeth.
39:
Among the twenty-four ribs, the complete ones are like complete Sinhalese sickles, and the incomplete ones are like incomplete Sinhalese sickles. Some teachers say all the ribs are like the two outspread wings of a white chicken. The fourteen chest bones are like a row of planks from an old palanquin. The heart bone is like the head of a ladle (or like the leaf of a certain tree). The collarbones are like small iron axe handles. The bone below the collarbones is like a half-moon. The shoulder blades are like axe blades; some teachers say they are like half-cut Sinhalese hoes. The upper arm bones are like mirror handles; some say they are like large axe handles. The forearm bones are like twin palmyra trunks. The wrist bones are like stacked lead sheets joined on one side. The metacarpal bones are like crushed banana stems. The base bones of the fingers are like panava drums. The middle bones are like immature jackfruit seeds. The tip bones are like kataka seeds. The seven neck bones are like bamboo shoots placed in order on a spit. The lower jawbone is like a blacksmith's iron pincers. The upper jawbone is like a small paring knife. The eye and nose socket bones are like young palmyra fruit with the kernel removed. The forehead bone is like an overturned broken conch shell. The ear bones are like a barber's razor case. The bone above the forehead and ears, where the headband is tied, is like a piece of rag on a thick water pot. The crown bone is like a cut coconut. The skull bones are like a sewn-together rotten gourd. Thus, the bones should be defined by their shape. In terms of direction, they occur in two directions: the upper and lower body.

In terms of location, they are generally situated throughout the whole body. Specifically, the skull bones rest on the neck bones, the neck bones on the spinal bones, the spinal bones on the hip bones, the hip bones on the thigh bones, the thigh bones on the knee bones, the knee bones on the shin bones, the shin bones on the ankle bones, and the ankle bones on the metatarsal bones. The metatarsal bones support the ankle bones, the ankle bones support the shin bones... and so on... the neck bones support the skull bones. The remaining bones should be understood in this manner.

Just as in a stack of bricks or rafters, the upper bricks do not know, 'We rest on the lower bricks,' nor do the lower bricks know, 'We support the upper bricks,' even so, the skull bones do not know, 'We rest on the neck bones.' The ankle bones do not know, 'We rest on the metatarsal bones.' The metatarsal bones do not know, 'We support the ankle bones.' Why is this? Because these things are devoid of attention and reflection. They should be defined as not-self (anatta). In reality, these 300 bones, 900 tendons, and 900 pieces of flesh exist bound and smeared together. They are wrapped in 111 layers of skin and moistened by fluids. This collection, which is the source of sweat flowing from 990 million pores and the dwelling place of 80 types of parasites, is called the 'body.' This body is naturally filled with parasites.
40:
The skull bones situated on the neck bones do not know, 'We are situated on the neck bones.' The ankle bones do not know, 'We are situated on the bones of the top of the foot.' The bones of the top of the foot also do not know, 'We are situated supporting the ankle bones.' This is because these things are devoid of attention and reflection. These are merely material phenomena, not a person. In truth, these three hundred bones are bound and smeared together by nine hundred tendons and nine hundred pieces of flesh. They are covered by a single layer of thick skin. They are moistened by seventeen thousand vessels (of sap). They are filled with sweat and grime flowing from ninety-nine thousand pores, and with eighty families of worms, reaching the designation of 'body'. When a meditator (yogāvacara) investigates this body according to its nature, he sees nothing to be grasped, but sees only a heap of bones bound by tendons and cluttered with various impurities. Seeing this, he attains the state of being a son of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha). As it is said:

"Bones are situated in order, end to end,
Compared with many joints,
Not bound by any string, but bound by tendons,
Driven by old age,
Unconscious, like a wooden log."

"Impurity is born in impurity, in an impure and foul body,
In a foul-smelling body, it is foul-smelling, of a nature to break and perish."

"A bone-case is born in a bone-case, in a foul body,
Dispel the desire for that body,
Then you will become sons of the Ten-Powered One."

By delimitation, they are delimited internally by the bone marrow, externally by the flesh, and at the tips and bases by each other. This is their similar delimitation. Their dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair. Thus, bones are defined by color and so on.

Furthermore, the bone marrow situated inside the various bones in the body is defined by color as being white. By shape, it has the shape of its own location. For example, the marrow inside large bones has the shape of a large cane shoot that has been steamed, rolled, and placed inside a large bamboo joint.
41:
This is the similar delimitation of those three hundred bones. The dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair. Thus, bones are defined by color and so on. After that, the bone marrow situated inside the various bones in the body is defined by color as being white. By shape, it follows the shape of its location. For example: the marrow inside large bones has the shape of a large cane shoot that has been steamed, rolled, and placed inside a large bamboo joint. The marrow inside small bones has the shape of a small cane shoot that has been steamed, rolled, and placed inside a small bamboo joint. By direction, it occurs in two directions. By location, it is situated inside the bones.

In that marrow, for example, the curd or molasses inside bamboo and the like do not know, 'We are inside the bamboo,' nor does the bamboo know, 'Curd and molasses are inside us.' Even so, the bone marrow does not know, 'I am inside the bones,' nor do the bones know, 'Bone marrow is inside us.' In truth, these things are devoid of attention and reflection... not a person. By delimitation, it is delimited by the inner surfaces of the bones and by the portion called marrow. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair. Thus, bone marrow is defined by color and so on.

After that, the kidneys (vakka) inside the body, which consist of two round pieces, are defined by color as being slightly red, like the color of a Palibhadraka (Butea monosperma) seed. By shape, they have the shape of a pair of play-balls tied with string by village children, or according to some teachers, the shape of twin mangoes on a single stalk. By direction, they occur in the upper direction. By location, they are bound by a thick tendon that comes from the throat, goes a little way with a single base, and then splits into two, surrounding the heart-flesh.

In those kidneys, for example, a cluster of twin mangoes bound by a stalk does not know, 'The stalk binds me,' nor does the stalk know, 'I bind the cluster of twin mangoes.' Even so, the kidneys do not know, 'The thick tendon binds me,' nor does the thick tendon know, 'I bind the kidneys.' In truth, these things are devoid of attention and reflection... not a person. By delimitation, the kidneys are delimited by the portion called kidneys. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair. Thus, kidneys are defined by color and so on.

After that, the heart (hadaya) inside the body is defined by color as being red, like the color of the outer side of a red lotus petal. By shape, it is defined as having the shape of a lotus bud with the outer petals removed and placed upside down. That heart is open on one side like a Punnāga fruit with its tip cut off; it is smooth on the outside and like the inside of a loofah (kosātakī) fruit on the inside. For those with much wisdom...
42:
The heart of wise persons is slightly expanded; the heart of those with weak wisdom is merely a bud. Setting aside the heart-base (rūpa) upon which the mind-element (manodhātu) and mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) depend, within the interior of the heart—which is described as a lump of flesh—there exists about half a handful of blood. That heart-blood is red for one of lustful temperament (rāgacarita), black for one of hateful temperament (dosacarita), like the water from washing meat for one of deluded temperament (mohacarita), the color of bean soup (kulattha) for one of speculative temperament (vitakkacarita), the color of a kaṇikāra flower for one of faithful temperament (saddhācarita), and for one of wise temperament (paññācarita), it appears clear, exceptionally pure, untroubled, and radiant like a polished genuine gem. In terms of direction, it is in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated in the middle of the two breasts within the body.

In regard to that heart, for example, just as a doorpost (aggaḷatthambhaka) situated between two shutters (vātāpanakavāṭaka) does not know, "I am situated between two shutters," and the shutters do not know, "A doorpost is situated between us," even so, the heart does not know, "I am situated in the middle of the two breasts," and the breasts do not know, "The heart is situated between us." Indeed, these phenomena are devoid of reflection and consideration ... one should define them as "not a person." In terms of delimitation, one defines the heart as being delimited by the portion of the heart itself. This is its similar delimitation (sabhāgapariccheda); its dissimilar delimitation (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines the heart by color and so on.

After that, one defines the twin lump of flesh within the body called the liver (yakana) as being red in color, like the color of the outer petals of a red lotus (kumuda). In terms of shape, it has a single root and is twin-lobed at the tip, like the shape of a kovilāra leaf. For those with weak wisdom, it is just a single large piece; for those with wisdom, it consists of two or three small pieces. In terms of direction, it is in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated on the right side within the two breasts.

In regard to that liver, for example, just as a lump of meat stuck to the side of a pot (piṭharaka) does not know, "I am stuck to the side of a pot," and the side of the pot does not know, "A lump of meat is stuck to me," even so, the liver does not know, "I am situated on the right side within the two breasts," and the right side within the breasts does not know, "The liver is situated depending on me." Indeed, these phenomena are devoid of reflection and consideration ... one should define them as "not a person." As for delimitation, the liver...
43:
...one defines the liver as being delimited by the portion of the liver itself. This is the similar delimitation (sabhāgapariccheda) of the liver. Its dissimilar delimitation (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines the liver by color and so on.

After that, one defines the pleura (kilomaka), which is of two kinds—concealed and unconcealed—as being white in color, like the color of a fine cloth (dukūlapilotika). In terms of shape, it has the shape of its own location. In terms of direction, it occurs in both directions. In terms of location, the concealed pleura stands surrounding the heart and the kidneys (vakka), while the unconcealed pleura stands wrapping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the whole body.

In regard to that pleura, for example, when meat is wrapped in a worn cloth (pilotika), the worn cloth does not know, "I am wrapping the meat," and the meat does not know, "I am wrapped by a worn cloth," even so, the pleura does not know, "I am wrapping the heart, the kidneys, and the flesh beneath the skin throughout the whole body." The heart, the kidneys, and the flesh throughout the whole body do not know, "I am wrapped by the pleura." This is because these phenomena are devoid of reflection and consideration ... one should define them as "not a person." In terms of delimitation, it is delimited below by the flesh, above by the skin, and transversely by the portion of the pleura itself. This is the similar delimitation of that pleura. Its dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines the pleura by color and so on.

After that, one defines the spleen (pihaka) within the body as being dark blue in color, like the color of a faded nigguṇḍī flower. In terms of shape, it is mostly seven finger-breadths in size and has the shape of a black calf's tongue without attachments. In terms of direction, it is in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated on the left side of the heart, depending on the upper part of the stomach lining (udarapaṭala). If that spleen is struck by a weapon and protrudes outside, the life of beings comes to an end.

In regard to that spleen, for example, just as a lump of cow dung (gomayapiṇḍi) situated depending on the outside of a granary wall (koṭṭhaka) does not know, "I am situated depending on the outside of a granary wall," and the outside of the granary wall does not know, "A lump of cow dung is situated depending on me," even so, the spleen does not know, "I am situated depending on the upper part of the stomach lining," and the upper part of the stomach lining does not know, "The spleen is situated depending on me." This is because these phenomena are devoid of reflection and consideration ... one should define them as "not a person." In terms of delimitation, one defines it as being delimited by the portion of the spleen itself. This is the similar delimitation of that spleen. Its dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair. Thus, the spleen...
44:
By way of boundary, the spleen is defined as being delimited by its own portion. This is its similar boundary (sabhāga-pariccheda). As for its dissimilar boundary (visabhāga-pariccheda), it is just like hair. Thus, the spleen is defined by way of color and so on.

After that, the lungs, which consist of thirty-two pieces of flesh inside the body, are defined by way of color as being red, like the color of a not-too-ripe fig (udumbara). By way of shape, they have the shape of an unevenly cut cake; some teachers say they have the shape of a heap of roof tiles. Because of the absence of swallowed and drunk nutriment and so on inside the body, and because of being oppressed by the heat of the karma-born fire element (kammaja-tejo) that has arisen, those lungs are dry and without essence, like a trampled heap of straw. By way of direction, they are in the upper direction. By way of location, they are situated inside the body between the two breasts, covering the heart and liver from above and hanging down.

In this regard, just as a bird's nest hanging inside an old granary does not know, 'I am hanging inside an old granary,' nor does the interior of the old granary know, 'A bird's nest is hanging in me,' so too the lungs do not know, 'I am hanging inside the body between the two breasts,' nor does the space between the two breasts inside the body know, 'The lungs are hanging in me.' Indeed, these things are void of volition and reflection... [etc.]... not a person. By way of boundary, the lungs are defined as being delimited by their own portion. This is their similar boundary. As for the dissimilar boundary, it is just like hair. Thus, the lungs are defined by way of color and so on.

After that, the large intestine, which is thirty-two cubits long in a man and twenty-eight cubits long in a woman, and which is coiled in twenty-one places inside the body, is defined by way of color as being white, like the color of lime-plaster or sugar-gravel. By way of shape, it has the shape of a python's body that has been decapitated and placed coiled in a trough of blood. By way of direction, it is in both directions (upper and lower). By way of location, because it is bound at the throat-hole above and the anus below, it is situated inside the body between the throat-hole and the anus.

In this regard, just as the body of a decapitated python placed in a trough of blood does not know, 'I am in a trough of blood,' nor does the trough of blood know, 'The body of a decapitated python is in me,' so too the large intestine does not know, 'I am inside the body,' nor does the interior of the body know, 'The large intestine is in me.'
45:
Indeed, these things are void of volition and reflection... [etc.]... not a person. By way of boundary, the large intestine is defined as being delimited by its own portion. This is its similar boundary. As for the dissimilar boundary, it is just like hair. Thus, the large intestine is defined by way of color and so on.

After that, the small intestine (mesentery) inside the body is defined by way of color as having a color like the root of a water-lily (dakāsītalika). By way of shape, it has the shape of the root of a water-lily; some teachers say it has the shape of a cow's urine stream. By way of direction, it is in both directions. By way of location, it stays between the twenty-one coils of the large intestine, like the machine-string when those who work with axes and so on pull a machine, or like the rope that stays sewn between the coils of a rope-ring for wiping the feet, binding the coils of the intestine together at the edges.

In this regard, just as the rope that stays sewn through a foot-wiping rope-ring does not know, 'The foot-wiping rope-ring is sewn by me,' nor does the foot-wiping rope-ring know, 'The rope stays sewing me,' so too the small intestine does not know, 'I stay binding the large intestine between its twenty-one coils,' nor does the large intestine know, 'The small intestine stays binding me.' For these things are void of volition and reflection... [etc.]... not a person. By way of boundary, the small intestine is defined as being delimited by its own portion. This is its similar boundary. As for the dissimilar boundary, it is just like hair. Thus, the small intestine is defined by way of color and so on.

After that, the gorged food (undigested food) inside the body is defined by way of color as having the color of swallowed nutriment. By way of shape, it has the shape of a bag of rice loosely tied in a water-strainer. By way of direction, it is in the upper direction. By way of location, it stays in the stomach. What is called the 'stomach' is like a swelling produced in the middle of a wet cloth being squeezed from both ends. The intestinal membrane is smooth on the outside and smeared with pieces of flesh on the inside; some teachers say it is like a dirty woolen flower or like the inside of a rotten jackfruit. In that gorged food, thirty-two species of worms, such as takkolaka, gaṇḍuppādaka, palm-leaf-like worms, needle-mouthed worms, and thread-like worms, live in swarms, moving about in confusion. When there is no drink or food, those worms leap up and peck the heart. When drink or food arrives, they face upwards...
46: (The worms) cry out and peck at the heart. When drinks, food, and so on are swallowed, they face upwards and quickly snatch the first two or three mouthfuls that are swallowed. This undigested food is the birth-house, the latrine, the infirmary, and the cemetery for those species of worms. For example, just as in a cesspool at the gate of a Caṇḍāla village, when it rains with heavy drops in the autumn season (Sarada), various kinds of carcasses such as urine, excrement, skin, bones, sinew-fragments, spittle, nasal mucus, and blood, washed away by the water, fall in and become turbid with muddy water, swarming with various kinds of worms; after two or three days, it seethes with the heat of the sun's rays, releasing bubbles and foam on top, becoming dark blue in color, utterly foul-smelling and loathsome, reaching a state unfit even to approach or look at, let alone to smell or taste. In the very same way, various kinds of drinks, food, and so on, crushed by the pestle of the teeth, turned over by the hand of the tongue, smeared with spittle and phlegm, instantly lose their excellence of color, smell, and taste, becoming like dog vomit. Falling in, they are enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind, seething with the heat of the stomach fire, swarming with species of worms, releasing bubbles and foam on top, reaching a state as loathsome as a rotten oyster. Even hearing about it, a sense of disagreeableness towards drinks, food, and so on is established; how much more so if one were to look with the eye of wisdom? And the drinks, food, and so on that fall into that stomach go to five destinations: the worms eat one part, the stomach fire burns one part, one part becomes urine, one part becomes feces, and one part, having reached the state of essence, nourishes the blood, flesh, and so on. In that undigested food, for example, just as dog vomit in a loathsome dog-trough does not know, "I am in a dog-trough," nor does the dog-trough know, "Dog vomit is in me," even so, the undigested food does not know, "I am in this utterly foul-smelling and loathsome stomach," nor does the stomach know, "Undigested food is in me." For these things are devoid of thought and reflection... they are not a person. By delimitation, one defines undigested food by its own portion. This is its delimitation by similar parts (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation by dissimilar parts (visabhāga-pariccheda) is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines undigested food by color and so on.
47:
Thereafter, one defines the feces (karīsa) within the body: by color, it generally has the color of the food swallowed. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is produced in the lower direction. By location, it stays in the receptacle for ripe food (pakkāsaya). The "receptacle for ripe food" is the place between the navel and the base of the spine, at the end of the large intestine, about eight finger-breadths in height, resembling the interior of a bamboo tube. Just as rainwater falling on the upper ground flows down and fills the lower ground, even so, whatever drinks, food, and so on fall into the receptacle for undigested food (āmāsaya), being cooked by the stomach fire until they seethe with foam, reach a soft state like flour-paste, slide down through the intestinal opening, and stay accumulated like white clay packed into a bamboo tube.

In that feces, just as the white clay packed into a bamboo tube does not know, "I am in a bamboo tube," nor does the bamboo tube know, "White clay is in me," even so, the feces does not know, "I am in the receptacle for ripe food," nor does the receptacle for ripe food know, "Feces is in me." For these things are devoid of thought and reflection... they are not a person. By delimitation, one defines feces by its own portion. This is its delimitation by similar parts (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation by dissimilar parts (visabhāga-pariccheda) is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines feces by color and so on.

Thereafter, one defines the brain (matthaluṅga) inside the skull of the body: by color, it is white, having the color of a cluster of mushrooms. Some teachers say it has the color of cooked milk. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By location, it stays inside the skull, following the four sutures, like four lumps of dough placed together, existing as four distinct masses of brain.

In that brain, just as a lump of dough or cooked milk placed in an old gourd shell does not know, "I am in an old gourd shell," nor does the old gourd shell know, "A lump of dough or cooked milk is in me," even so, the brain does not know, "I am inside the skull," nor does the interior of the skull know, "The brain is in me." For these things are devoid of thought and reflection...
48:
These states [are devoid of attention and reflection] ... (p) ... one defines them as 'not a person'. By delimitation, one defines the brain by its own portion. This is its similar delimitation; its dissimilar delimitation is like hair. Thus, one defines the brain by color and so on.

Next, one defines the two kinds of bile in the body, local bile (baddha-pitta) and free bile (abaddha-pitta), by color as being like the color of thick oil of the Madhuca tree. Some teachers say free bile is like the color of a withered bakula flower. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is born in both directions (upper and lower). By location, free bile stays pervading the whole body like a drop of oil in water, excluding hair, body hair, nails, teeth, areas free of flesh, and hard dry skin. When it is disturbed, the eyes become yellow and revolve, and the body trembles and itches. Local bile is situated in the gallbladder (pittakosaka), which resembles a large kosātakī fruit, depending on the liver between the heart and lungs. When it is disturbed, beings become mad, their minds are deranged, and casting away shame and fear, they do what should not be done, speak what should not be spoken, and think what should not be thought.

In that regard, for example, just as oil pervading water does not know 'I stay pervading the water,' and the water does not know 'The oil stays pervading me,' so too free bile does not know 'I stay pervading the body,' and the body does not know 'Free bile stays pervading me.' For example, just as rainwater in a kosātakī fruit shell does not know 'I stay in the kosātakī fruit shell,' and the kosātakī fruit shell does not know 'Rainwater stays in me,' so too local bile does not know 'I stay in the gallbladder,' and the gallbladder does not know 'Local bile stays in me.' For these states are devoid of attention and reflection ... (p) ... one defines them as 'not a person'. By delimitation, one defines the bile by its own portion. This is its similar delimitation; its dissimilar delimitation is like hair. Thus, one defines the bile by color and so on.

Next, one defines the phlegm (semha) inside the body, about a bowlful in quantity, as white in color, like the color of the juice of kacchaka leaves. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is born in the upper direction. By location, it stays on the stomach lining (udarapaṭala).
49:
When swallowing drinks and food, just as pond-scum (sevāla-paṇaka) on water splits in two when a stick or a potsherd falls on it and then covers it again, so too when drinks and food fall, it splits in two and then covers it again. When it is weak, the stomach lining becomes like a ripe boil or a rotten hen's egg, having a very repulsive smell of a corpse. From the smell rising from it, the belch and the mouth also become foul-smelling like a rotten corpse. That man comes to be told, 'Go away, you smell foul.' When it is excessive and becomes thick, it stays inside the stomach lining like a lid on a latrine, suppressing and confining the smell of a corpse.

In that regard, for example, just as the layer of foam on a cesspool (candanikā) does not know 'I stay on the cesspool,' and the cesspool does not know 'The layer of foam stays on me,' so too phlegm does not know 'I stay on the stomach lining,' and the stomach lining does not know 'Phlegm stays on me.' For these states are devoid of attention and reflection ... one defines them as 'not a person'. By delimitation, one defines the phlegm by its own portion. This is its similar delimitation; its dissimilar delimitation is like hair. Thus, one defines the phlegm by color and so on.

Next, one defines the pus (pubba) inside the body as having the color of a faded leaf. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is born in both directions (upper and lower). By location, there is no fixed place for pus. Wherever blood stagnates and festers in a part of the body struck by stumps, thorns, fire, etc., or where boils and pimples arise, there it stays.

In that regard, for example, just as the resin that stays oozing from a place on a tree struck by an axe and so on does not know 'I stay in the struck place of the tree,' and the struck place of the tree does not know 'Resin stays in me,' so too pus does not know 'I stay in a part of the body struck by stumps, thorns, etc., or where boils and pimples have arisen,' and the part of the body does not know 'Pus stays in me.'
50:
In truth, these things are devoid of reflection and consideration... they are not a person; thus one should define them. By way of delimitation, pus is delimited by the portion consisting of pus. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. As for its delimitation by way of different kinds, it is just like that of the hair of the head. Thus, one should define pus by way of color and so forth.

After that, regarding the blood in the body, there are two kinds: accumulated blood and circulating blood. Among these, one should first define accumulated blood by way of color as being like the color of thick, cooked lac juice. Circulating blood should be defined as being like the color of clear lac juice. By way of shape, all blood has the shape of its own location. By way of direction, accumulated blood arises in the upper direction. Circulating blood arises in both directions; thus one should define it. By way of location, circulating blood, excluding the hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, the areas free of flesh, and the hard dry skin, pervades the entire kamma-born body, following the network of veins. Accumulated blood fills the lower part of the liver and, in a quantity of about a bowlful, remains moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs, letting drops fall slightly upon the kidneys, heart, and lungs. When that blood does not moisten the kidneys, heart, and so forth, beings become thirsty.

In that regard, just as water in a broken potsherd, though it moistens the clods of earth and so forth below, does not know, "I am in a broken potsherd and am moistening the clods of earth below," and neither the broken potsherd nor the clods of earth below know, "Water is in me" or "It is moistening us"; even so, the blood does not know, "I am in the lower part of the liver, moistening the kidneys, heart, and so forth," and neither the lower part of the liver nor the kidneys, heart, and so forth know, "Blood is in me" or "It is moistening us." In truth, these things are devoid of reflection and consideration... they are not a person; thus one should define them. By way of delimitation, blood is delimited by the portion consisting of blood. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. As for its delimitation by way of different kinds, it is just like that of the hair of the head. Thus, one should define blood by way of color and so forth.

After that, regarding the sweat in the body, one should define it by way of color as being like the color of clear sesame oil. By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it arises in both directions. By way of location, there is no fixed place for sweat where it might always remain like blood. For when...
51:
The body is heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, changes of weather, and so forth. At that time, it oozes from all the pores of the hair and body hair, like water from a bundle of lotus fibers, roots, joints, and stalks that have just been pulled from the water and are unevenly cut. Therefore, one should define sweat by way of shape according to the openings of those pores of the hair and body hair. The former teachers said, "The practitioner who grasps sweat should reflect upon it by way of its filling and remaining in the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair."

In that regard, just as water oozing from the openings of a bundle of lotus fibers, roots, and stalks does not know, "I am oozing from the openings of the bundle of lotus fibers, roots, and stalks," and neither do the openings of the bundle of lotus fibers, roots, and stalks know, "Water is oozing from us"; even so, sweat does not know, "I am oozing from the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair," and neither do the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair know, "Sweat is oozing from us." In truth, these things are devoid of reflection and consideration... they are not a person. By way of delimitation, sweat is delimited by its own portion. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind. As for its delimitation by way of different kinds, it is just like that of the hair of the head. Thus, one should define sweat by way of color and so forth.

After that, regarding the fat (adipose tissue) within the body between the skin and the flesh, one should define it by way of color as being like the color of sliced turmeric. By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. Thus, in a person with a stout body, the fat that pervades the space between the skin and flesh has the shape of a soiled cloth dyed with turmeric. In a person with a thin body, it has the shape of scraps of turmeric-dyed cloth that remain folded, depending on the flesh of the calves, the flesh of the thighs, the flesh of the back near the backbone, and the flesh of the abdominal membrane. By way of direction, it arises in both directions, upper and lower. By way of location, in a stout person, it pervades the entire body; in a thin person, it remains depending on the flesh of the calves and so forth. Although it is called 'grease' (sineha), because it is extremely repulsive, it is not taken for the purpose of hair oil, nor for mouthwash oil, nor for lighting lamps. 

In that regard, just as a soiled turmeric-dyed cloth depending on a heap of meat does not know, "I am depending on a heap of meat," and neither does the heap of meat know, "A soiled turmeric-dyed cloth is depending on me"; even so, the fat does not know, "I am depending on the whole body or on the flesh of the calves and so forth," and neither the whole body nor the flesh of the calves and so forth knows, "Fat is depending on me." In truth, these things are devoid of reflection and consideration... they are not a person; thus one should define it. By way of delimitation, fat is delimited below by the flesh, above by the skin, and all around by...
52:
One defines it as bounded by the portion of fat. This is its similar boundary. Its dissimilar boundary is just like hair. Thus, one defines fat by its color and so on.

After that, one defines tears in the body by color as having the color of clear sesame oil. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By location, it stays in the eye sockets. These tears do not always remain accumulated in the eye sockets like bile in the gallbladder. How then? When beings are joyful and laugh loudly, or when they are sorrowful and weep and lament, or when they partake of such unsuitable food, or when their eyes are struck by smoke, grit, dust, and so on, then, arising from such joy, sorrow, or unsuitable food, the tears fill the eye sockets and stay there or flow out. The ancient teachers explain: "The practitioner (yogāvacara) who grasps the tears should contemplate them only as they fill the eye sockets."

In this regard, just as water staying in the holes of a young palmyra nut with its stalk cut off does not know, "I am staying in the holes of a young palmyra nut with its stalk cut off," nor do the holes of the young palmyra nut know, "Water is staying in us"; even so, the tears do not know, "I am staying in the eye sockets," nor do the eye sockets know, "Tears are staying in us." For these things are devoid of concern and reflection... they are not a person. By boundary, one defines it as bounded by the portion of tears. This is its similar boundary. Its dissimilar boundary is just like hair. Thus, one defines tears by color and so on.

After that, one defines grease (melted fat) in the body by color as having the color of oil poured on rice-scum. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is produced in both directions. By location, it stays on the palms, the backs of the hands, the soles, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the points of the shoulders. This grease does not always remain melted in those locations. How then? When those parts become heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, or by an imbalance of the seasons or elements, then it melts in those places and flows like mist on pools of clear water.
53:
In this regard, just as the mist that stays covering the pools does not know, "I am staying covering the pools," nor do the pools know, "The mist is staying covering us"; even so, the grease does not know, "I am staying covering the palms and so on," nor do the palms and so on know, "The grease is staying covering us." For these things are devoid of concern and reflection... they are not a person. By boundary, one defines it as bounded by the portion of grease. This is its similar boundary. Its dissimilar boundary is just like hair. Thus, one defines grease by color and so on.

After that, one defines saliva inside the mouth in the body by color as having the color of white foam. By shape, it has the shape of its location; some teachers say it has a shape like sea foam. By direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By location, it stays on the tongue, having descended from both sides of the cheeks. This saliva does not always remain accumulated there. How then? When beings see or remember such food, or when they place something hot, bitter, pungent, salty, or sour in the mouth, or when their heart is distressed, or when disgust arises for some reason, then saliva arises and, descending from both sides of the cheeks, stays on the tongue. This saliva is thin at the tip of the tongue and thick at the root of the tongue. It is always able to moisten flaked rice, rice, or any other eatable placed in the mouth, without being exhausted, like the water in a hole dug in a river sandbank.

In this regard, just as the water staying in a hole dug in a river sandbank does not know, "I am staying in the bottom of the hole," nor does the bottom of the hole know, "Water is staying in me"; even so, the saliva does not know, "I am staying on the surface of the tongue, having descended from both sides of the cheeks," nor does the surface of the tongue know, "Saliva is staying on me, having descended from both sides of the cheeks." For these things are devoid of concern and reflection... they are not a person. By boundary, one defines it as bounded by the portion of saliva. This is its similar boundary. Its dissimilar boundary is just like hair. Thus, one defines saliva by color and so on.
54:
After that, one defines snot (siṅghāṇikā) in the body by color as being white, like the color of the pith of a young palm nut. By shape, it has the shape of its location. Some teachers say it has the shape of a rattan shoot or bud constantly inserted into the nose. By direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By location, it stays filling the nostrils. This snot does not always remain collected in the nose. How then? For example, if a man were to wrap curd in a lotus leaf and pierce the bottom of the leaf with a thorn, the mass of curd would then leak out through that hole and fall outside. In the same way, when beings cry, or when there is a disturbance of the elements due to incompatible food or climate, the brain matter inside the head, having turned into putrid phlegm, leaks out and descends through the opening above the palate, staying and filling the nostrils.

In this regard, just as putrid curd placed in a mother-of-pearl shell does not know, "I am in a mother-of-pearl shell," nor does the mother-of-pearl shell know, "Putrid curd is in me"; in the same way, the snot does not know, "I am in the nostrils," nor do the nostrils know, "Snot is in us." For these things are devoid of intention and reflection... one defines it as not a person. By delimitation, snot is delimited by its own portion of snot. This is its delimitation of similar parts (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation of dissimilar parts (visabhāga-pariccheda), however, is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines snot by color and so on.

After that, synovial fluid (lasikā) inside the body is the viscous putrid matter inside the joints of the body. One defines that synovial fluid by color as having a color like the resin of the kaṇikāra tree. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is produced in both directions (upper and lower). By location, it stays inside the one hundred and eighty joints, performing the function of lubricating the bone joints. For a person in whom this synovial fluid is scarce, when getting up, sitting down, moving forward, moving backward, bending, or stretching, the bones creak. Such a person wanders about as if making the sound of snapping fingers. When traveling a distance of even one or two leagues (yojana), the wind element (vāyodhātu) becomes disturbed, and the limbs ache. For a person in whom this synovial fluid is abundant, the bones do not creak during activities such as getting up or sitting down. Even when traveling a long distance, the wind element is not disturbed, and the limbs do not ache.
55:
Regarding that synovial fluid (lasikā), to use an analogy, just as the lubricating oil does not know, "I stay lubricating the axle (akkha)," nor does the axle know, "The oil stays lubricating me"; in the same way, the synovial fluid does not know, "I stay lubricating the one hundred and eighty joints," nor do the one hundred and eighty joints know, "The synovial fluid stays lubricating us." Indeed, these things are devoid of intention and reflection... one defines it as not a person. By delimitation, synovial fluid is delimited by its own portion of synovial fluid. This is its delimitation of similar parts (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation of dissimilar parts (visabhāga-pariccheda), however, is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines synovial fluid by color and so on.

After that, one defines urine (mutta) inside the body by color as having the color of bean-broth or lye-water. By shape, it has the shape of water inside a water-pot that has been filled and placed upside down. By direction, it is produced in the lower direction. By location, it stays inside the bladder (vatthi). The bladder refers to the bladder-bag. For example, just as cesspool water enters a mouthless pot placed in a cesspool without the path of entry being apparent, in the same way, urine from the body enters the bladder without the path of entry being apparent. Only the path of exit is apparent. When the bladder is full of urine, the effort of beings to "pass urine" arises. In that case, just as the cesspool water staying in the mouthless pot placed in the cesspool does not know, "I stay in the mouthless pot," nor does the pot know, "Cesspool water stays in me"; in the same way, the urine does not know, "I stay in the bladder," nor does the bladder know, "Urine stays in me." Indeed, these things are devoid of intention and reflection... one defines it as not a person. By delimitation, it is delimited by the interior of the bladder and by its own portion of urine. This is its delimitation of similar parts. Its delimitation of dissimilar parts, however, is just like that of the hair. Thus, one defines urine by color and so on. In this way, this practitioner defines these thirty-two parts by color and so on.

For that practitioner who thus defines these thirty-two parts by way of color and so on, through the practice of those respective meditations, the hairs and so forth become familiar and appear as distinct groups (koṭṭhāsa). From then on, just as when a man with good eyesight looks at a garland of thirty-two kinds of flowers strung on a single thread, all the flowers appear clearly to him as if without before or after; in the same way, [the thought arises], "In this body..."
56:
For one who observes this body with mindfulness, thinking, "In this body there are head hairs," all those things become manifest as if they were all together without priority or posteriority. When contemplating the head hairs, mindfulness does not remain continuously but occurs only to the extent of the urine. From that time on, for that practitioner, beings such as humans and animals wandering here and there lose their appearance as beings and appear only as a heap of parts. The drinks, food, and so forth consumed by those beings also appear as if they were being thrown into a heap of parts.

In this regard, it may be asked: "What should that practitioner do after the sign has appeared in such a way?" The answer is: That very sign which has appeared should be frequented, developed, practiced frequently, and well-defined. How does that practitioner frequent, develop, practice frequently, and well-define that sign? This practitioner frequents that sign which appears as a heap of parts such as head hairs; he adheres to it with mindfulness, associates with it, approaches it, and causes the "womb of mindfulness" to be taken. Developing the mindfulness obtained therein is called "developing" (bhāveti). "Practicing frequently" (bahulīkaroti) means repeatedly performing it, accompanied by mindfulness and driven by initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra). "Well-defining" (suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapeti) means defining it with mindfulness so that it is well-established and does not disappear again, upholding it and binding it.

Alternatively, it refers to the ten kinds of skill in attention (manasikāra-kosalla) mentioned previously: (1) in successive order, (2) not too fast, (3) not too slow, (4) by warding off distraction, (5) by surmounting the concept, (6) by successive letting go, (7) by way of characteristics, and (8, 9, 10) the three Suttantas. Among these ten, one frequents (āsevati) by attending in successive order. One develops (bhāveti) by attending neither too fast nor too slow. One practices frequently (bahulīkaroti) by attending while warding off distraction. One well-defines (suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapeeti) by attending through surmounting the concept and so forth.

In this regard, it may be asked: "How does this practitioner attend to these things by way of successive order and so forth?" The answer is: This practitioner, after attending to the head hairs, immediately attends to the body hairs, not the nails. Similarly, after attending to the body hairs, he immediately attends to the nails, not the teeth. This is the method in all cases. Why? Because if one attends out of order, like an unskilled man climbing a thirty-two-step ladder out of order, his body becomes exhausted and from there...
57:
...he falls from the ladder and cannot complete the ascent. Even so, because of not attaining the satisfaction (of the fruit of Arahantship) that should be reached through the power of the fulfillment of meditation, he becomes weary in mind and falls away from the meditation on the thirty-two parts, unable to complete the meditation.

One who attends in successive order also attends to "head hairs, body hairs" without being too fast. For one who attends too fast is like a man traveling who cannot notice the landmarks of the road such as even and uneven ground, trees, hills, valleys, and forks in the road; thus, he is not skilled in the journey and merely exhausts the journey in vain. Even so, he cannot notice the signs of the thirty-two parts such as color and shape; thus, he is not skilled in the thirty-two parts and merely exhausts the meditation subject in vain.

Just as one should not be too fast, so too one should attend without being too slow. For one who attends too slowly is like a man on a journey who lingers at trees, mountains, lakes, and so forth along the way, failing to reach his desired destination and meeting with ruin and disaster due to lions, tigers, and so forth right in the middle of the road. Even so, failing to reach the fulfillment of the meditation on the thirty-two parts, he meets with ruin and disaster due to sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) and so forth right in the middle because of the interruption of meditation.

One who attends without being too slow should also attend by warding off distraction. Warding off distraction means attending in such a way that the mind does not wander to other new tasks and so forth. For one whose mind is distracted outwardly has unsteady thoughts regarding head hairs and so forth; failing to reach the fulfillment of meditation, he meets with ruin right in the middle, like the companions of the Bodhisatta when going to Takkasilā. But one whose mind is not distracted and has steady thoughts regarding head hairs and so forth reaches the fulfillment of meditation, like the Bodhisatta obtaining the kingship of Takkasilā. For one who attends by warding off distraction in this way, through the power of application, practice, and attention, those things become manifest either as foul (asubha), or by way of color, or by way of voidness (suññata) from self.

Then, he attends to those things by surmounting the concept. Surmounting the concept means surmounting and letting go of the designations such as "head hairs, body hairs" and attending only by way of the foulness and so forth that have become manifest.
58:
How? Just as people living in a forest, being unfamiliar with the terrain, make signs such as breaking branches to recognize the location of water, and go there following those signs to use the water; but when they become familiar with the terrain, they discard those signs and, without even attending to them, approach the water and use it; in the same way, this practitioner (yogāvacara) first attends to these things by way of their respective verbal designations such as 'hair of the head, hair of the body,' and so on. When one of these things appears to him by way of foulness (asubha) or other qualities, he transcends and discards that verbal designation and attends only by way of foulness and so forth.

In this matter, it may be asked: "How do these things appear to this person as foul and so forth? How by way of color? Or how by way of voidness? And how does this person attend to these things as foul? How by way of color? Or how by way of voidness?" Hair of the head appears to him as foul in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, habitat, and location. He also attends to these hairs as foul in these same five ways.

For example: These hairs are foul by way of color, being extremely loathsome and disgusting. For this very reason, if people see a fiber or thread the color of hair in their food or drink during the day, they discard or loathe even delicious food and drink due to the perception of 'hair'. They are foul by way of shape as well. For this very reason, if people touch a fiber or thread the shape of hair in their food or drink at night, they discard or loathe even delicious food and drink due to the perception of 'hair'. They are foul by way of smell as well. For this very reason, the smell of hair when devoid of preparations such as oiling, wearing flowers, and perfuming is extremely disgusting; when smelling the scent of hair thrown into a fire, beings close their noses and even twist their mouths. They are foul by way of habitat (āsaya) as well. For just as various plants like taṇḍuleyyaka grow in a rubbish heap through the moisture of human filth, so do these hairs grow, increase, and flourish through the moisture of bile, phlegm, pus, and blood. They are foul by way of location (okāsa) as well. For just as taṇḍuleyyaka plants grow in a rubbish heap, they grow on the wet skin wrapped around the human head, on top of the heap of thirty-one rotting parts such as body hair, which is extremely disgusting. This method should be understood for body hair and so on. Thus, first, when these things appear to this person as foul, he attends to them as foul.

If they appear to him by way of color, then the hair of the head appears by way of the blue/black kasina (nīla-kasiṇa). Similarly, body hair and teeth appear by way of the white kasina (odāta-kasiṇa). This is the method.
59:
This method should be understood for all meditation subjects. The practitioner attends to that meditation subject only by way of the respective kasina. Thus, when it appears by way of color, he attends by way of color. If it appears to him by way of voidness, then the hairs appear as a group of 'nutritive essence as the eighth' (ojāṭṭhamaka) through the resolution of the perception of compactness, which cannot be further analyzed. Likewise for body hair and so on, in whatever way they appear. He attends to them in that very way. Thus, when they appear by way of voidness, he attends by way of voidness.

Attending in this way, he attends to these things by way of sequential relinquishing (anupubbamuñcana).
