'Sequential relinquishing' means: when letting go of the hair of the head which has appeared by way of foulness and so forth, and attending to the hair of the body—just as a leech, while still concerned with the spot it holds with its tail, grips another spot with its mouth, and only when it has gripped that spot firmly does it let go of the other—even so, while still concerned with the hair of the head, he attends to the hair of the body, and only when the attention is established on the hair of the body does he let go of the hair of the head. This method should be understood for all parts (koṭṭhāsa). For when he attends by way of sequential relinquishing, those things appearing by way of foulness and so forth appear without remainder and become more clearly manifest as a collection.

Then, for the person to whom those things appear as foul and become clearly manifest: just as a monkey in a palm grove of thirty-two palms, being harassed by a hunter, unable to stay on a single tree, runs about, and when it becomes tired and stops, it stays relying on a single palm spike enveloped in thick palm leaves; even so, the mind-monkey in this body of thirty-two parts, being harassed by that yogi, unable to stay in a single part, runs about, and when it no longer desires to run towards many objects and becomes tired and stops, it stays by way of access concentration (upacāra) relying on that part among the hair and so forth which is more familiar, more suitable to his temperament, or in which he has made a prior effort. Then, making that very sign the object of repeated thought and reflection (vitakka), he produces the first jhana in due order. Established in that first jhana, he begins insight (vipassanā) and reaches the Noble Plane (ariya-bhūmi).

For the person to whom those things appear by way of color, for him too, just as a monkey... (and so on) ... then, for that person, whichever part among the hair and so forth is more familiar...
60:
Or it is particularly suitable to one's temperament; or if there was effort made in a previous life, it remains by the power of access concentration (upacāra) based on that previous effort. Then, by repeatedly striking that very sign (nimitta) with thought and applied thought (vitakka), one produces the five fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara jhāna) in due order by way of the blue kasiṇa or the yellow kasiṇa. Establishing oneself in any one of those fine-material sphere jhānas, one begins insight (vipassanā) and reaches the noble plane (ariya-bhūmi).

For the person to whom those phenomena appear as void of self, they attend to them by way of characteristics (lakkhaṇa). The person attending by way of characteristics reaches access concentration (upacāra jhāna) in those thirty-two parts by way of the definition of the four elements (catudhātu-vavatthāna). Then, that person attending to those phenomena does so by way of the three discourses (suttas) on impermanence, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anatta). This is their method of insight. It is said that this person, having undertaken this insight and practiced in due order, reaches the noble plane.

With this much explanation, the question "How does this person attend to these phenomena by way of sequence, etc.?" has been answered. The meaning of the statement "The explanation should be understood by way of development (bhāvanā)" has also been shown.

## Miscellaneous Method
Now, in order to become proficient in studying the explanation of these very thirty-two parts, this miscellaneous method (pakiṇṇakanaya) should be understood:
"The determination of the thirty-two parts should be understood by way of sign (nimitta), characteristic (lakkhaṇa), element (dhātu), emptiness (suññata), and aggregates (khandha), etc."

Among those five, "by way of sign" means that in these thirty-two parts of various kinds as mentioned, there are one hundred and sixty signs, by means of which the practitioner (yogāvacara) grasps the thirty-two parts by way of groups (koṭṭhāsa). They are: the sign of color, the sign of shape, the sign of direction, the sign of location, and the sign of delimitation of the hair. These are the five signs. The same applies to body hair and so on.

"By way of characteristic" means that in the thirty-two parts, there are one hundred and twenty-eight characteristics, by means of which the practitioner attends to the thirty-two parts by way of characteristics...
61:
...performs the act of attention. What are those characteristics? They are the four characteristics: the characteristic of hardness of the hair, the characteristic of cohesion, the characteristic of heat, and the characteristic of motion. Likewise, there are four characteristics for body hair and so on. "By way of element" means that among the elements mentioned in this Sutta, "Monks, this person consists of six elements," there are one hundred and twenty-eight elements in the thirty-two parts. By means of those elements, the practitioner (yogāvacara) grasps the thirty-two parts by way of elements. What are those elements? The quality of hardness in the hair is the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), the quality of cohesion is the water element (āpo-dhātu), the quality of ripening is the fire element (tejo-dhātu), and the quality of supporting is the air element (vāyo-dhātu). These are the four elements. Likewise, there are four elements for body hair and so on. "By way of emptiness (suññata)" means that in the thirty-two parts, there are one hundred and twenty-eight kinds of emptiness. By means of those kinds of emptiness, the practitioner views the thirty-two parts as void of self. What is this insight into emptiness? Firstly, in the hair, the earth element is void of the water element and so on. Likewise, the water element and others are void of the earth element and so on. Thus, there are four kinds of emptiness. Likewise, there are four kinds of emptiness for body hair and so on. "By way of aggregates, etc." means that when the thirty-two parts such as hair are grasped by way of aggregates and so on, the determination should be understood in this manner: "How many aggregates are the hairs? How many bases (āyatana)? How many elements (dhātu)? How many truths (sacca)? How many foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)?" To the person who knows thus, the body appears like a heap of grass and wood. Therefore, it is said:

"There is no being, no man, no person, no individual to be found.
This body is void and is like a heap of grass and wood."

Then, for that person who has entered an empty place, who has a peaceful mind, who is endowed with suchness (tādi), and who clearly sees the Dhamma through insight, there arises a joy that is not of humans (amānusī rati). This joy that is not of humans, as taught, becomes very close to that person. Then, it is said:

"Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
one attains joy and gladness. To those who know,
that very joy and gladness is the Deathless (Nibbāna)."
62:
Thus, the deathless [nectar] of joy and rapture consisting of insight has been spoken of. One who experiences this through the object [of meditation] will, before long, realize the deathless Nibbāna, which is frequented by the Noble Ones and is free from aging and death.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Thirty-two Parts of the Body is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Boy's Questions (Kumārapañha)
## The Origin Story (Atthuppatti)
Now, the sequence for explaining the meaning of the Boy's Questions, beginning with "What is one?" (Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ), has arrived. Having stated the origin story of these questions and the purpose of their placement here, I shall provide the explanation.

Regarding the origin story: There was a great disciple of the Blessed One named Sopāka. That venerable one attained the fruit of Arahantship at only seven years of age. The Blessed One, wishing to grant him higher ordination (upasampadā) by means of answering questions, and seeing his ability to answer questions of the intended meaning, asked him questions beginning with "What is one?". Sopāka answered them. By those answers, he satisfied the Blessed One's mind, and that very answering became the higher ordination for that venerable one. This is the origin story of those Boy's Questions.

## The Purpose of Placement (Nikkhepappayojana)
Because the development of the mind (citta-bhāvanā) was shown through the recollections of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha by means of the Refuges; the development of virtue (sīla-bhāvanā) through the training rules; and the development of the body (kāya-bhāvanā) through the thirty-two parts of the body; therefore, these questions and answers are placed here now to show the introduction to the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā) in various ways.

Alternatively, since virtue is the proximate cause of concentration, and concentration is the proximate cause of wisdom—as it is said: "A wise man, established in virtue, should develop the mind and wisdom"—virtue was shown through the training rules, concentration was shown through the thirty-two parts of the body by taking them as objects, and then, to show the variety of wisdom through various dhammas for one with a concentrated mind, they are placed in this text. This is the purpose of placing those questions in this text. Now, I shall speak the explanation of the meaning of those questions. "What is one?" means: The Blessed One, regarding that one cause in which a monk, through the cause, becomes weary and gradually...
63:
As it is said, "should develop the mind and wisdom" (cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ), therefore, after showing virtue through the training rules and concentration through the thirty-two parts of the body by taking them as an object, it should be understood that these questions and answers are placed here to show the divisions of wisdom with its various requisites for one with a concentrated mind.

This is the purpose of placing those questions in this text.

## Commentary on the Questions (Pañha-vaṇṇanā)

## Commentary on the Question "What is One?" (Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ)

Now, the explanation of the meaning of those questions follows. In the question "What is one?" (Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ), the Blessed One asked the question referring to that one Dhamma in which a monk, when rightly weary of it, can gradually make an end of suffering, and in which this venerable one (Sopāka), being weary of it, has gradually made an end of suffering. The Elder answered with a teaching in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna): "All beings subsist on nutriment" (Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā). Suttas such as "Monks, what is Right Mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body..." are the supporting evidence for the validity of answering in this manner. In this context, it should be understood that the Elder, when asked "What is one?", pointed out either that nutriment by which all beings are said to be "subsisting on nutriment," or the state of their subsisting on nutriment. For only that Dhamma was intended by the Blessed One here as "one"; it was not said to make known that there is no other thing called "one" in the Teaching or in the world. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, when a monk is rightly weary of one Dhamma, rightly dispassionate, rightly liberated, rightly seeing the end, and having fully realized the state of perfection, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which one Dhamma? In the Dhamma that 'all beings subsist on nutriment.' Monks, when a monk is rightly weary of this one Dhamma... (pe)... he makes an end of suffering. That which was said by the Blessed One as 'One question, one summary, one explanation,' was said in reference to this."

In the phrase "subsisting on nutriment" (āhāraṭṭhitikā), nutriment is said to be a condition (paccaya), as in such passages as: "Monks, there is the sign of the beautiful (subha-nimitta). Therein, making much of inappropriate attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is the nutriment (āhāra) for the arising of unarisen sensual desire."
64:
In this way, by taking the supporting cause through the word 'nutriment' (āhāra), those things that exist due to a cause are called 'things that subsist through nutriment.' If it were said that they 'subsist through nutriment' with reference to the four types of nutriment, then the word 'all' (sabbē) would be inappropriate, because of the statement (from the Vibhaṅga): 'The devas dwelling in the Asaññasatta realm are without root-causes, without nutriment, without contact, and without feeling.'

In that statement, an objector's challenge might be as follows: If it is said thus, 'Which things are those with conditions? The five aggregates—the aggregate of form... etc... the aggregate of consciousness,' then it is appropriate for only the aggregates to have the state of subsisting through conditions. For beings, however, the statement 'they subsist through nutriment' would be inappropriate (so it might be thought). But this should not be regarded in that way. Why? Because the metaphorical designation (upacāra) of the aggregates is established in beings. Indeed, the metaphorical designation of the aggregates in beings is established. Why? Because they are designated and described depending on the five aggregates. How? It is like the metaphorical use of 'village' for 'houses.' Just as a village is described depending on houses, and even if one, two, or three houses are burnt, the metaphorical designation of 'village' for 'houses' is established as 'The village is on fire'; in the same way, while the five aggregates subsist through nutriment in the sense of being a cause, this metaphor 'Beings subsist through nutriment' should be understood as established. In the ultimate sense, also, while the aggregates are being born, aging, and dying, it should be understood that the Blessed One, by saying, 'Monk, moment by moment you are born, you age, and you die,' has already shown that the metaphorical designation of the aggregates is established in those beings.

Therefore, the nutriment by which all beings subsist in the sense of a condition, or their state of subsisting through that nutriment, should be known as a certainty (truth). Indeed, nutriment, or the state of subsisting through nutriment, becomes a basis for revulsion (nibbidā) because of its nature of impermanence. Then, a person who, seeing impermanence in those formations (saṅkhāra) called 'all beings,' becomes disenchanted, gradually makes an end of the suffering of the round of rebirth and reaches ultimate purity.

As the Blessed One said:
'When one sees with wisdom that all formations are impermanent,
then one becomes disenchanted with suffering;
this is the path to purity.'

In this context, there are two readings: 'Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ' and 'Kihā.' Among them, the reading of the Sri Lankans is 'Kihā.' They say 'Kihā' where 'Kiṃ' should be said. Some teachers say that 'ha' is an indeclinable (nipāta), and this same reading exists in the verses of the Elder Nuns (Therīgāthā). In both cases, the meaning is the same. It should be recited as one prefers. For example, as in 'A person touched by pleasure, or indeed by pain (dukhena), experiences painful mental feeling (domanassa)...'
65:
Just as in such passages, it is said 'dukha' in some places and 'dukkha' in others, so too it is said 'ekaṃ' in some places and 'ekkaṃ' in others. In this context, however, the reading 'Ekaṃ nāma' is the original.

## Explanation of the Question: What is Two?
Thus, with a mind delighted by the answering of this question, the Teacher asks the further question in the same manner as before: 'What is two?' The Elder, having repeated 'Two,' answers with a discourse defining the phenomena as 'Name and Form' (nāma-rūpa). In that answer, all that is non-material is called 'Name' (nāma) because of its bending (namana) towards the object and because of its being the cause of the mind's bending. In this context, however, because it is the cause of revulsion, only mundane phenomena subject to taints (sāsava) are intended. All the four great elements and the matter derived from those four great elements are called 'Form' (rūpa) in the sense of being deformed (ruppana); all such form is intended here. It is only by the power of the intended meaning in this context that it is said 'Two is name and form,' not because there are no other pairs of phenomena.

As the Blessed One said: 'Monks, when a monk is rightly disenchanted with two things... etc... he makes an end of suffering. With which two? With name and with form. Monks, when a monk is rightly disenchanted with these two things... etc... he makes an end of suffering. "Two questions, two recitations, two expositions"—that which was said was said in reference to this question' (as found in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

In this question, it should be understood that by seeing mere name and form, one abandons the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi) and, through the door of the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), becomes disenchanted and gradually makes an end of suffering, reaching ultimate purity. As the Blessed One said:
'When one sees with wisdom that all phenomena are non-self,
then one becomes disenchanted with suffering;
this is the path to purity.'

## Explanation of the Question: What is Three?
Now, with a mind delighted also by the answering of this question, the Teacher asks the further question in the same manner as before: 'What is three?' The Elder, having repeated 'Three,' and wishing to show the number in accordance with the grammatical gender of the meaning to be explained, answers: 'Three feelings' (tisso vedanā). Alternatively, 'Those which were called "three feelings" by the Blessed One...'
66:
It should be understood that the meaning in this context is: "I, the Buddha, believe this meaning to be three." For the teachings of the Buddhas, who have attained the grace of teaching through the divisions of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), have many methods. Some teachers, however, say that the word "tīṇi" (three) is an additional word (adhikapada). In the view of these teachers as well, following the previous method, it is said to be "the three feelings" (tisso vedanā). It is mentioned as "the three feelings" because there are no other three things [intended here].

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of three things... can make an end of suffering. In which three? In the three feelings. Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of these three things... can make an end of suffering. What was said as 'three questions, three summaries, three explanations (veyyākaraṇa),' was said in reference to this question." (A. Ni. 10.27)

In this regard, it should be understood according to the Sutta which says: "Whatever is felt, all that I declare to be suffering" (Saṃ. Ni. 4.259). Or:

"He who saw pleasure as suffering,
Saw suffering as a dart,
And saw the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling
As impermanent."
(Itivuttaka 53)

Thus, by seeing the nature of suffering in the three feelings according to the sequence of suffering as pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā), and suffering inherent in formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā), one abandons the perception of pleasure. Being weary through the method of contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), one gradually makes an end of suffering and attains ultimate purity (paramattha-visuddhi). As the Blessed One taught:

"When one sees with wisdom that all formations are suffering,
Then one becomes weary of suffering;
This is the path to purity."
(Dh. P. 278)

## The Explanation of the Question 'What is Four?'

Thus, the Teacher, whose mind was pleased by the answering of this question, asks the further question according to the previous method: "What is four?" In the context of answering this question, for some, the four nutriments (āhāra) are intended according to the previous method. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of four things... can make an end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). In which four? In the four nutriments. Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of these four things... can make an end of the suffering of the round. What was said as 'four questions, four summaries, four explanations,' was said in reference to this question."

For some others, one whose mind is well-developed in certain four things can gradually make an end of the suffering of the round; those four things are the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). As the Blessed One said: "Friends, a nun living in the region of Kajangalā, or a monk..."
67:
"Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of four things... can make an end of the suffering of the round. In which four? In the four nutriments. Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of these four things... can make an end of the suffering of the round. What was said as 'four questions, four summaries, four explanations (veyyākaraṇa),' was said in reference to this question."

For some individuals, by well-developing the mind in certain four things, one can gradually make an end of the suffering of the round; those things are the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). The nun of Kajangalā taught thus: "Friends, a monk who has well-developed his mind in four things, who is one who sees the limit [of the round] rightly, and having realized the peaceful Nibbāna, can make an end of the suffering of the round in this very life. In which four? In the four foundations of mindfulness. Friends, a monk who has well-developed his mind in these four things... can make an end of the suffering of the round. What was said by the Blessed One as 'four questions, four summaries, four explanations,' was said in reference to this question." (A. Ni. 10.28)

In this context, however, because the cutting off of the craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) occurs through the sequential understanding and penetration of certain four things, those Four Noble Truths (ariya-sacca) are intended. Or, because answering in this manner is indeed a good explanation, the Elder Sumana Sāmaṇera, after repeating "four", answered "the Noble Truths". In that statement, "four" is the delimitation of the number. "Noble Truths" means the truths that are noble, truths that are not false, and truths that are unerring. The Blessed One taught thus: "Monks, these Four Noble Truths are real, unerring, and not otherwise; therefore, they are called Noble Truths." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1097)

Alternatively, they are called so because they are to be known and approached by the world including the devas. Or, they are called "noble" (ariya) because they cause the arising of happiness, which is recognized as the state to be striven for. Or, they are called "noble" because they do not cause the arising of things that lack happiness. Or, because the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha, who are regarded as noble ones, penetrate these four truths through their perfect union with the noble qualities of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), they are also called "Noble Truths". The Blessed One taught thus: "Monks, the Noble Truths are these four... Monks, these four Noble Truths are of the Noble Ones..."
68:
“Monks, these Noble Truths are four. ... Monks, these Noble Truths are four; the Noble Ones penetrate these truths, therefore they are called ‘Noble Truths’,” so He said.

Alternatively, they are called Noble Truths because they are the truths of the Noble Blessed One. As it is said: “Monks, in the world with its devas ... among the host of devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the Noble One, therefore they are called Noble Truths.”

Or else, they are called Noble Truths because by fully awakening to them, one achieves the state of a Noble One. As it is said: “Monks, because of fully awakening to these four Noble Truths as they really are, the Tathāgata is called the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”

This is the word-meaning of these truths. Furthermore, through the successive understanding and penetration of these Noble Truths, the cutting off of craving for existence occurs. As it is said: “Monks, this suffering Noble Truth has been understood, has been penetrated. ... The Noble Truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering has been understood, has been penetrated; craving for existence is cut off, the conduit to existence is exhausted, now there is no more renewed existence.”

## Explanation of the Question “What is Five?”

The Teacher, whose mind was delighted by the answering of this question, asked the further question in the same manner as before: “What is five?” The Elder Sopāka, having repeated “Five”, answered: “They are the aggregates of clinging.” In that question, “five” is the delimitation of the number. The aggregates that are produced by clinging or that produce clinging are the “aggregates of clinging” (upādānakkhandhā). Whatever form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are accompanied by taints (āsavas) and are objects of clinging—this is a designation for them. Here too, as in the previous method, it is said “five aggregates of clinging” because there is no other group of five. As it is said:

“Monks, a monk who feels proper revulsion towards five things ... becomes one who makes an end of suffering. Which five? The five aggregates of clinging. Monks, a monk who feels proper revulsion towards these five things ... becomes one who makes an end of suffering. ‘Five questions, five...
69:
“...five summaries, five expositions”—this which was said, was said in reference to this question.

And here, one who contemplates the five aggregates by way of their rise and fall, having obtained the essence of insight, successively realizes the deathless Nibbāna. As it is said:
“Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
one obtains joy and gladness;
for those who know, that is the Deathless Nibbāna.”

## Explanation of the Question “What is Six?”

Thus, the Teacher, whose mind was satisfied by the answering of this question, asked the further question in the same manner as before: “What is six?” The Venerable Sopāka, having repeated “Six”, answered: “They are the six internal sense bases.” In that statement, “six” is a term delimiting the number. They are called “internal” (ajjhattika) because they are constantly associated with one’s own internal continuity, or because they occur with oneself as the primary focus. They are called “bases” (āyatana) because they cause the round of rebirth to flourish, or because they lead to the long suffering of the round of rebirth. This is a designation for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Here too, it is said “six internal sense bases” as in the previous method, not because there are no other groups of six. As it is said:

“Monks, a monk who feels proper revulsion towards six things ... becomes one who makes an end of suffering. Towards which six? Towards the six internal sense bases. Monks, a monk who feels proper revulsion towards these six things ... becomes one who makes an end of suffering. ‘Six questions, six summaries, six expositions’—this which was said, was said in reference to this question.”

In this context, regarding the six internal sense bases, because it was said: “Monks, ‘empty village’ is a designation for the six internal sense bases,” one who clearly sees them as empty, as not lasting long like bubbles or mirages, as hollow, and as deceptive, and thus feels revulsion, successively makes an end of suffering and reaches Nibbāna, where the King of Death cannot see. As it is said:
70:
“Just as one would look upon a bubble, just as one would look upon a mirage, the King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world in this way.” (Dhammapada, 170).

## Explanation of the Question "What is Seven?"

The Blessed One, whose mind was pleased by this answering of the question, asked the further question, “What is seven?” Although the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti) were mentioned in the explanation of the Great Questions (Mahāpañha), the Elder Sopāka, wishing to show those dhammas in which a monk with a well-developed mind can make an end of suffering, answered, “They are the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).” This meaning was also approved by the Blessed One. As He said—

“Lay followers, the nun living in Kajangalā is wise; she is of great wisdom. Lay followers, if you were to approach me and ask about this matter, I would answer it in the same way as the nun of Kajangalā has answered.”

And it was answered by that nun in this way—

“Friends, a monk whose mind is well-developed in seven dhammas... [pe]... can make an end of suffering. In which seven? In the seven factors of enlightenment. Friends, a monk whose mind is well-developed in these seven dhammas... [pe]... can make an end of suffering. That which was spoken by the Blessed One as ‘seven questions, seven recitations, seven explanations’ was spoken in reference to these seven factors of enlightenment.”

Thus, it should be understood that this meaning was indeed approved by the Blessed One.

In that passage, “seven” (satta) is a numerical limit that excludes less or more. “Factors of enlightenment” (bojjhaṅga) is a designation for the dhammas beginning with mindfulness (sati). The meaning of the term therein is: the Noble Disciple awakens (bujjhati) through the harmony of dhammas known as mindfulness (sati), investigation of dhammas (dhammavicaya), energy (viriya), rapture (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā), which arise at the moment of the mundane and supramundane paths and are the opposites of many dangers such as the basis of sloth and restlessness, striving, indulgence in sensual pleasures, devotion to self-mortification, and the adherence to the views of annihilation and eternalism; thus it is called “Bodhi.” It means that one rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself. As He said: “Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, the peerless...”
71:
“...He fully awakened to the peerless Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi).” Or, because he awakens through that harmony of dhammas of the kind already described, the Noble Disciple is also called “Bodhi.” Thus, because they are factors of that Bodhi known as the harmony of dhammas, they are called factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), like the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅga) and the factors of the path (maggaṅga). Or, because they are factors of that Noble Disciple who has acquired the designation “Bodhi,” they are called bojjhaṅga, like the limbs of an army (senaṅga) or the parts of a chariot (rathaṅga).

Furthermore, “In what sense are they factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)? They are bojjhaṅga because they lead to awakening (bodhāya saṃvattanti), they are bojjhaṅga because they awaken (bujjhanti), they are bojjhaṅga because they awaken subsequently (anubujjhanti), they are bojjhaṅga because they awaken thoroughly (paṭibujjhanti), they are bojjhaṅga because they awaken fully (sambujjhanti).” In this way, the meaning of bojjhaṅga should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Thus, one who develops and frequently practices these seven factors of enlightenment will, before long, certainly become one who attains qualities such as disenchantment (nibbidā); because of such attainment, he is said to be one who makes an end of suffering in this very life. This was spoken by the Blessed One—

“Monks, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and frequently practiced, lead to absolute disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.”

## Explanation of the Question “What is Eight?”

The Teacher, whose mind was pleased by this answering of the question, asked the further question, “What is eight?” Although the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma) were mentioned in the explanation of the Great Questions (Mahāpañha), the Elder Sopāka, wishing to show those dhammas in which a monk with a well-developed mind makes an end of suffering, did not say directly “the eight noble path-factors,” but because there is no such thing as a path free from the eight factors, and because the collection of the eight factors itself is the path, he answered “the Noble Eightfold Path” (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga) with the elegance of instruction to fulfill that meaning. The Blessed One also approved of this meaning and this method of instruction. As He said: “Wise lay followers, the nun living in Kajangalā... [pe]... I would answer it in the same way as the nun of Kajangalā has answered.”
72:
That nun also replied thus: "Friends, a monk whose mind is well-developed in the eight things... becomes one who makes an end of suffering. That which was spoken by the Blessed One as 'eight questions, eight summaries, eight explanations,' was spoken in reference to this very thing."

Thus, it should be understood that both this meaning and the method of teaching were approved by the Blessed One.

In that term "Noble Eightfold Path" (ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga), "Noble" (ariya) should be understood as such because it is to be approached by those desiring Nibbāna; or alternatively, because it is far from defilements, because it makes one noble, and because it leads to the attainment of the noble fruit. It is called "Eightfold" (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it has eight factors. This Eightfold Path should be understood as a mere collection of factors, like an army with four divisions or music with five instruments, because its nature cannot be found by separating the factors. It is called "Path" (magga) because Nibbāna is sought by it, or because it seeks Nibbāna itself, or because it goes along killing the defilements.

Thus, a monk who develops this Eightfold Path with its eight divisions destroys ignorance, gives rise to knowledge, realizes Nibbāna, and by that path is said to be one who makes an end of suffering in this very life. For this has been said:

"Monks, just as if an awn of hill-paddy or an awn of barley is rightly placed and is trodden upon by the hand or foot, there is the possibility that it will pierce the hand or foot and cause blood to flow. Why is that? Monks, because the awn is rightly placed. Even so, monks, there is the possibility that a monk, with rightly placed view and with rightly placed development of the path, will destroy ignorance, give rise to knowledge, and realize Nibbāna."

## Explanation of the Question "What is Nine?" (Nava Nāma Kinti-pañha-vaṇṇanā)

The Teacher, whose mind was satisfied by this answering of the question, asked the further question: "What is nine?" The Elder, having repeated "Nine," answered: "The nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa)." In that [question], "nine" is the delimitation of the number. "Beings" (satta) refers to [beings designated based on the aggregates] connected with the life-faculty.
73: They are beings designated based on the five aggregates connected with the life faculty, or it is a designation. 'Āvāsa' (abodes) means they dwell in these places; because they are places of dwelling, they are called abodes. The dwelling places of beings are called 'sattāvāsa' (abodes of beings). This is the sequence of the teaching. In terms of meaning, this name 'sattāvāsa' is just a designation for the nine types of beings. As the Blessed One said: "Friends, there are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans, some devas, and some fallen beings (vinipātika). This is the first abode of beings. Friends, there are beings with diverse bodies and uniform perception, such as the Brahmakāyika devas who are first reborn. This is the second abode of beings. Friends, there are beings with uniform bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the Ābhassara devas. This is the third abode of beings. Friends, there are beings with uniform bodies and uniform perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas. This is the fourth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings who are non-percipient and without feeling, such as the Asaññasatta devas. This is the fifth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings who, having completely transcended perceptions of form ... have reached the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). This is the sixth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings ... who have reached the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). This is the seventh abode of beings. Friends, there are beings ... who have reached the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). This is the eighth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings ... who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). This is the ninth abode of beings." Here too, as in the previous method, it is said "nine abodes of beings," not because there are no other nine things. As the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is rightly weary of nine things ... makes an end of suffering. Which nine? The nine abodes of beings. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is rightly weary of these nine things ... makes an end of suffering. 'Nine questions, nine summaries, nine expositions'—this which was spoken was spoken with reference to this."
74:
In this context as well, according to the words: "Nine things should be fully understood. Which nine? The nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa)," one who, through the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā), abandons the view of the nine abodes of beings as permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and self, and sees them as merely a mass of pure formations (saṅkhāra), becomes weary. Through the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), being dispassionate through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), being liberated through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), and clearly seeing the end through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), one realizes the peaceful Nibbāna through the full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā) and makes an end of suffering in this very life. Therefore, it is said:

"Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of nine things... (pe)... makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which nine? In the nine abodes of beings."

## Explanation of the question "What is ten?"

The Teacher, whose mind was pleased by this answering of the questions, asked a further question: "What is ten?" Among the answers to this question, in other explanations besides this one, the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha) are mentioned. As it is said:

"Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of ten things... (pe)... makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which ten? In the ten unwholesome courses of action. Monks, a monk who is rightly weary of these ten things... (pe)... makes an end of suffering in this very life. That which was said: 'Ten questions, ten subjects, ten answers,' was said in reference to this."

In this context, however, because this venerable one (the Elder Sopāka) wished to explain the fruit of Arahantship without referring to himself, or because explaining in this manner is indeed a good explanation, he answered with a discourse based on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), showing the attainment (adhigama) of those ten qualities possessed by one who is called an Arahant, saying: "One who is possessed of ten qualities is called an Arahant." Therefore, in this statement, it should be understood that the ten qualities possessed by one who is called an Arahant were pointed out by the Elder when asked "What is ten?" Those ten are:

"Venerable sir, it is said, 'an asekha, an asekha'; to what extent, venerable sir, is a monk an asekha? Here, monks, a monk is possessed of the Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Speech (sammā-vācā) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Action (sammā-kammanta) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) belonging to an asekha. He is possessed of the Right Knowledge (sammā-ñāṇa) belonging to..."
75:
...He is possessed of the Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Speech (sammā-vācā) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Action (sammā-kammanta) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) belonging to an asekha, he is possessed of the Right Knowledge (sammā-ñāṇa) belonging to an asekha, and he is possessed of the Right Liberation (sammā-vimutti) belonging to an asekha. Thus, monks, a monk is called an asekha," (as taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, 10.111).

It should be understood in the same manner as stated in such suttas.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Boy's Questions is concluded.

## 5. Maṅgala Sutta Vaṇṇanā
## The Purpose of the Arrangement

Now, having reached the sequence of the explanation of the meaning of the Maṅgala Sutta placed immediately after the Kumārapañha, I shall provide the explanation after stating the purpose of placing the Maṅgala Sutta here in this text. What is that reason? Although this Maṅgala Sutta was not taught by the Blessed One in this specific order, the way of entering the Dispensation (sāsana) through the Refuges (saraṇagamana), and the method of the divisions of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) through the Precepts (sikkhāpada), the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), and the Boy's Questions (kumārapañha) have been shown. All that has been shown is the highest blessing (maṅgala); therefore, one who desires blessings should especially apply themselves to this Maṅgala Sutta. It is placed (by the commentators) to show that the nature of the blessing of this Maṅgala Sutta should be understood according to this sequence of suttas.

This is the purpose of the arrangement of the Maṅgala Sutta in this text.
76:
## Account of the First Great Council

For the purpose of explaining the meaning of this Mangala Sutta thus set forth, this is the mātikā (matrix):

“By whom, when, and for what reason it was spoken; having stated this procedure, and the meaning of the text beginning with ‘Evaṃ me sutaṃ’ in various ways; the teacher, explaining the origin and stating what auspiciousness is in which Mangala Sutta, having defined that, should clarify its status as a blessing.”

In that mātikā, this half-verse, “By whom, when, and for what reason it was spoken; having stated this procedure,” is spoken with reference to these words: “Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One... [pe]... addressed the Blessed One with a verse.” Indeed, these words were spoken by way of oral tradition. The Blessed One, however, is the Self-Enlightened One (Swayambhū) without a teacher; therefore, these words are not the words of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Thus, the question “By whom, when, and for what reason were these words spoken?” should be answered. They were spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council.

That First Great Council should be understood from the very beginning for the sake of proficiency in the origin (nidāna) of all the discourses. Starting from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma until the discipline of the wanderer Subhadda, the Lord of the World, having performed the Buddha’s duties, attained parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) at the break of dawn on the full moon day of Visākha, between the twin Sāla trees in the Sāla grove of the Malla princes near the city of Kusinārā. Among the seven hundred thousand monks who gathered due to the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, the Elder of the Saṅgha, Venerable Mahākassapa, seven days after the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, recalled the words spoken by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age: “Enough, friends, do not sorrow, do not lament; we are well-freed from that Great Ascetic. We were oppressed by him saying ‘This is allowable for you, this is not allowable for you.’ Now we shall do whatever we wish, and we shall not do what we do not wish.” Recalling these words repeatedly, he thought: “It is possible that evil monks, thinking ‘The teaching has its teacher passed away,’ might gain a following and before long cause the True Dhamma to disappear. As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya remain, the teaching is not one whose teacher has passed away. As the Blessed One said—”
77:
“Ānanda, whatever Dhamma I have taught and Vinaya I have prescribed for you, that Dhamma and Vinaya shall be your teacher after my passing.” (Thus the Blessed One had said).

“It would be well if I were to chant the Dhamma and Vinaya so that this Dispensation may be long-lasting and endure for a long time.”

The Blessed One favored me by saying, “Kassapa, you should wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes,” thereby sharing his own robes. Also, by placing me on equal footing with himself in terms of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) consisting of the nine successive attainments and the six higher powers, saying: “Monks, just as I, as much as I desire, secluded from sensual pleasures... [pe]... enter and dwell in the first jhāna, so too Kassapa, as much as he desires, secluded from sensual pleasures... [pe]... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.” Thinking, “What other duty could there be for me to be free from debt (to the Sasana)? Did not the Blessed One favor me with this extraordinary favor, just as a king hands over his royal regalia to his son who will continue the lineage, thinking ‘This one will be the establisher of my lineage of the True Dhamma’?” he inspired the monks to chant the Dhamma and Vinaya. As he said:

“Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks: ‘Once, friends, I was traveling on the road from Pāvā to Kusinārā with a large community of monks, about five hundred monks...’” Thus, the entire Subhadda section should be understood in detail.

Furthermore, he said: “Come, friends, let us chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya. Before what is not Dhamma shines and Dhamma is set aside, before what is not Vinaya shines and Vinaya is set aside; before those who speak what is not Dhamma become powerful and those who speak Dhamma become weak; before those who speak what is not Vinaya become powerful and those who speak Vinaya become weak (let us chant).”
78:
The monks said, "Venerable sir, in that case, let the Elder select the monks."

The Elder Mahākassapa, setting aside many hundreds and thousands of monks—including worldlings (puthujjana), stream-enterers (sotāpanna), once-returners (sakadāgāmi), non-returners (anāgāmi), and dry-insight arahants (sukkhavipassaka) who were bearers of the ninefold pariyatti of the Teacher’s dispensation—selected only four hundred and ninety-nine arahant monks who were masters of all the divisions of the Tipitaka, had attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), possessed great psychic power, and for the most part had been designated as foremost (etadagga) by the Blessed One in various categories such as the three knowledges (tevijjā). Regarding those monks, it is said (in the Cullavagga): "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected five hundred arahants less one."

Why did the Elder make it one less? It was to make a place for the Venerable Ānanda. For without that Venerable one, as well as with him, it was not possible to perform the rehearsal of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgīti). Since that Venerable one was a trainee (sekha) with tasks still to be done, it was not appropriate to select him together [with the arahants]. However, because there was no discourse such as Sutta or Geyya taught by the One of Ten Powers that he had not received, even in the absence of the Blessed One, it was not possible to perform the rehearsal without him. If he was to be selected by the Elder because of his great helpfulness in the Dhamma rehearsal despite being a trainee, why was he not selected [initially]? It was to avoid the reproach of others. For the Elder Mahākassapa was very intimate with the Venerable Ānanda. Indeed, even when gray hairs had appeared on Ānanda's head, the Elder would still admonish him as a youth, saying, "This youth does not know his measure." Furthermore, this Venerable one was born of the Sakyan clan and was the son of the Blessed One's younger uncle (a cousin). In that selection, monks might think he was acting out of favoritism (chandāgati) and reproach him, saying, "The Elder has set aside many arahants who are non-trainees (asekha) and have attained analytical insights, and has selected Ānanda, a trainee who has attained analytical insights, because of their intimacy." Avoiding such reproach from others, he thought, "The rehearsal cannot be done without Ānanda; I will take him only with the consent of the monks," and thus did not select him.

Then the monks themselves, of their own accord, requested the Elder for the sake of Ānanda. As it is said: "The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa—'Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is a trainee, he is incapable of going to a wrong course (agati) through favoritism, hatred, delusion, or fear. Moreover, he has mastered much Dhamma and Vinaya in the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, Venerable sir...'"
79:
"...let the Elder select the Venerable Ānanda as well." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected the Venerable Ānanda as well (Cullavagga, 437). Thus, with that Venerable one selected by the consent of the monks, there were five hundred elders.

Then the elder monks thought: "Where should we rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya?" Then the elder monks thought: "The city of Rājagaha has a wide area for alms-resort and abundant lodgings. What if we, staying for the rains retreat in Rājagaha, were to rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya? Let no other monks enter the rains retreat in Rājagaha." Why did they think so? [They thought:] "This is our permanent work; we fear that some incompatible person might enter the midst of the Saṅgha and disrupt it." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñatti-dutiya kamma). This should be understood in the manner stated in the Saṅgītikhandhaka (Cullavagga, 437).

Then, after the passing of the seven days of the funeral celebrations and the seven days of the relic worship following the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata, the Elder Mahākassapa, considering that "Half a month has passed; now only one and a half months of the summer remain; the time for entering the rains (vassūpanāyikā) is near," said, "Friends, let us go to Rājagaha." Taking half of the community of monks, he set out on one route. The Venerable Anuruddha also took half of the community and set out on another route. The Venerable Ānanda, however, taking the bowl and robes of the Blessed One and surrounded by a community of monks, went to Sāvatthī, intending to go to Rājagaha after visiting Sāvatthī. Wherever the Venerable Ānanda went, there was great lamentation: "Venerable Ānanda, where have you left the Teacher and come?" When the Elder eventually reached Sāvatthī, there was great lamentation just as at the time of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna.

There, the Venerable Ānanda, having convinced the great multitude with a Dhamma talk connected with impermanence and so forth, entered the Jetavana monastery. He opened the door of the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) where the One of Ten Powers had resided, took out the couch and chair, dusted them, swept the Perfumed Chamber, discarded the withered flowers and rubbish, brought back the couch and chair and placed them in their original positions, and performed all the major and minor duties that were to be done during the Blessed One's lifetime.
80:
At that time, Venerable Ānanda, since the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, had spent much time standing and sitting, causing an imbalance in his physical elements. To soothe his body, on the second day, he drank a milk-purgative and remained within the Jetavana monastery. Referring to this medicinal intake, he said to the youth sent by Subha Māṇava:

“Young man, it is not the right time; today I have taken a dose of medicine. Perhaps we may meet tomorrow.”

On the second day, accompanied by Venerable Cetaka as his attendant monk, he went and, being questioned by Subha Māṇava, preached the tenth discourse in the Dīgha Nikāya, known as the Subha Sutta.

Then, the Elder, having arranged for the repair of the broken and dilapidated parts of the Jetavana monastery, went to Rājagaha as the time for the commencement of the rains retreat approached. Likewise, Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Anuruddha, taking the entire Saṅgha of monks, also went to Rājagaha.

At that time, there were eighteen great monasteries in Rājagaha. All of them were neglected, fallen into ruin, and covered in refuse. For upon the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, all the monks had taken their own bowls and robes, abandoned the monasteries and precincts, and departed. There, the Elders, for the sake of honoring the words of the Blessed One and to avoid the accusations of sectarians, thought: “Let us first repair the broken and dilapidated parts during the first month.” For the sectarians might say: “The disciples of the Ascetic Gotama looked after the monasteries only while their Teacher was alive; now that he has attained Parinibbāna, they have abandoned them.” It is said that they thought this to avoid such accusations.

And this has also been stated:

“Then it occurred to the Elder monks: ‘Friends, the Blessed One praised the repair of broken and dilapidated parts. Come, friends, let us repair the broken and dilapidated parts in the first month; in the middle month, having assembled, we shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya.’”

On the second day, they went and stood at the palace gate. King Ajātasattu came, paid homage, and made an invitation, saying: “Venerable sirs, what shall I do? What is required?” The Elders informed him of the need for manual labor to repair the eighteen great monasteries. “Very well, venerable sirs,” the King replied, and provided men to perform the manual labor. The Elders had all the monasteries repaired during the first month.
81:
Then the Elders informed the King: “Great King, the repair of the monasteries is complete. Now we shall perform the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.” The King replied: “Very well, venerable sirs, proceed with confidence. Let my wheel of command (āṇācakka) be; let your wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) be. Command me, venerable sirs, what shall I do?” The Elders said: “Great King, provide a place of assembly for the monks who will be compiling the Dhamma.” “Where shall I build it, venerable sirs?” “Great King, it is fitting to build it at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the side of Mount Vebhāra.”

“Very well, venerable sirs,” King Ajātasattu replied. He had a great pavilion constructed, resembling the creation of Vissakamma, with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and stairs, adorned with various floral and creeper designs. It was decorated with beautiful canopies hanging with various flower garlands, and the floor was like a jeweled pavement of precious gems, strewn with various flowers. Having prepared this pavilion, which resembled a celestial mansion of Brahma, he arranged five hundred priceless rugs for the five hundred monks. He placed the Elders' seats on the southern side facing north, and in the center of the pavilion, he prepared a Dhamma-seat facing east, worthy of the Blessed Buddha. Placing a fan decorated with ivory there, he informed the Saṅgha: “Venerable sirs, the task is complete.”

The monks said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, tomorrow is the assembly of the Saṅgha. You are still a trainee (sekha) with tasks yet to be done. Therefore, it is not fitting for you to go to the assembly. Be heedful.” Then Venerable Ānanda thought: “Tomorrow is the assembly. It is not proper for me to go to the assembly while still being a trainee.” He spent much of the night in mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). At the time of dawn, he descended from the walking path, entered the monastery, and thought, “I will lie down,” inclining his body. His two feet were off the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow; in this interval, his mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging.

For this venerable one, having spent much time outside on the walking path without being able to attain distinction, thought: “Did not the Blessed One say to me: ‘Ānanda, you have performed merit; apply yourself to striving, and you will soon be free of taints’? There is no such thing as a flaw in the speech of the Buddhas. But my energy is over-exerted, and because of that, my mind tends toward restlessness. Now, let me balance my energy and concentration.” He descended from the walking path, stood at the place for washing feet, and after washing his feet, entered the monastery and sat on the couch. Thinking, “I will rest for a moment,” he inclined his body toward the couch. His two...
82:
While his two feet were lifted from the ground and before his head had reached the pillow, in that very interval, his mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging. The Elder’s attainment of Arahantship was an occurrence free from the four postures. Therefore, if it were asked, "Which monk in this Dispensation attained Arahantship without sitting, lying down, standing, or walking?" it would be appropriate to answer, "The Venerable Ānanda."

Then, on the second day, the Elder monks, having finished their meal and put away their bowls and robes, assembled in the Dhamma Hall. The Venerable Ānanda, however, wishing to make known his attainment of Arahantship, did not go together with the monks. While the monks were sitting in their respective seats according to seniority, they sat leaving a seat for the Venerable Ānanda. In that assembly, some asked, "For whom is this seat?" and they answered, "It is for Ānanda." They asked again, "Where has Ānanda gone?" At that time, the Elder thought, "Now is the time for me to go." Then, wishing to display his psychic power, he dived into the earth and manifested himself right in his own seat. Some teachers say he came through the air and sat down.

When the Venerable Ānanda was thus seated, the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks, "Friends, shall we recite the Dhamma first or the Vinaya?" The monks replied, "Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is the very life of the Buddha’s Dispensation; as long as the Vinaya endures, the Dispensation endures. Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya first." "Who shall be made the leader to recite the Vinaya?" "The Venerable Upāli should be made the leader." "Is Ānanda not capable?" "It is not that he is not capable. However, while the Blessed One was still alive, he placed the Venerable Upāli in the pre-eminent position (etadagga) regarding the mastery of the Vinaya, saying: 'Monks, among my monk disciples who are bearers of the Vinaya, Upāli is the foremost.' (A. Ni. 1.228). Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya by questioning the Elder Upāli." Then the Elder [Mahākassapa] formally moved a motion for himself to question the Vinaya. The Elder Upāli also formally moved a motion for himself to answer. In doing so, it was according to this Pali text:

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:
"Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I would question Upāli on the Vinaya."
83:
The Venerable Upāli also informed the Saṅgha: "Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Vinaya by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer."

Having thus formally moved the motion for himself, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the senior Elders, and sat upon the Dhamma-seat holding a fan adorned with ivory. Then the Elder Mahākassapa questioned the Elder Upāli on the entire Vinaya, starting from the first Pārājika, and the Elder Upāli answered. All five hundred monks together recited the first Pārājika training rule along with its origin (nidāna). In this manner, all the remaining training rules should be understood as they appear in the Vinaya Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). Having thus recited the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, including the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra, the Elder Upāli laid down the ivory fan, descended from the Dhamma-seat, paid homage to the senior monks, and sat in his appropriate seat.

After reciting the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa, wishing to recite the Dhamma, asked the monks: "In reciting the Dhamma, who should be made the leader to recite the Dhamma?" The monks replied: "The Elder Ānanda should be made the leader." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I would question Ānanda on the Dhamma." The Venerable Ānanda also informed the Saṅgha: "Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Dhamma by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer."

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the senior Elders, and sat upon the Dhamma-seat holding an ivory fan. Then the Elder Mahākassapa questioned the Elder Ānanda on the Dhamma: "Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta preached?" "Venerable Sir, it was preached at the royal rest-house in Ambalaṭṭhikā, between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā." "On account of whom?" "On account of the wanderer Suppiya and the youth Brahmadatta." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda on the origin (nidāna) of the Brahmajāla Sutta and the persons involved. "Friend Ānanda, where was the Sāmaññaphala Sutta preached?" "Venerable Sir, it was preached at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove in Rājagaha." "With whom [was it preached]?"
84:
"Together with King Ajātasattu, the son of the Videha Queen," he answered. Then, Venerable Mahākassapa questioned Venerable Ānanda regarding the origin (nidāna) of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and also regarding the person (puggala) involved. In this manner, he questioned him on all five Nikāyas, and to each question, Venerable Ānanda gave his answer. This First Great Council was conducted by five hundred elders—

"Because it was conducted by five hundred, it is called 'Pañcasata';
Because it was conducted only by the elders, it is called 'Therika'."

While this First Great Council was in progress, after questioning the entire Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, and so forth, and then questioning the Khuddaka Nikāya in due order, Venerable Mahākassapa asked, "Friend Ānanda, where was the Maṅgala Sutta spoken?" and so on. At the end of such words, in the context of "He asked the origin and the person," when the origin was asked, Venerable Ānanda, wishing to explain that origin in detail—how it was spoken, who heard it, when it was heard, who spoke it, where it was spoken, and to whom it was spoken—and desiring to show this meaning, said: "Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery... addressed the Blessed One with a verse." It should be understood that these words spoken by Venerable Ānanda were uttered at the time of the First Great Council.

Now, as to the point "Why was it spoken?": Because this Venerable Ānanda was questioned about the origin by the Elder Mahākassapa, he spoke to explain that origin in detail from the very beginning. Alternatively, seeing Venerable Ānanda seated on the Dhamma-seat surrounded by a group of those who had attained mastery (arahants), the thought occurred to some deities: "This Venerable Videhamuni is by nature of the Sakyan lineage and an heir of the Blessed One. The Blessed One also designated this Venerable Ānanda as foremost (etadagga) five times. He is endowed with the four wonderful and marvelous qualities and is beloved and pleasing to the four assemblies. Now, having received the inheritance of the Blessed One's Dhamma-kingdom, he has perhaps become a Buddha." Therefore, Venerable Ānanda, knowing the thoughts of those deities and not wishing to accept praise for qualities he did not possess, but wanting to show only his status as a disciple (sāvaka), said: "Thus have I heard, at one time..."
85:
"The Blessed One... spoke"—it should be understood that this was also spoken at the time of the First Great Council. Between these two statements, the five hundred Arahants and many thousands of deities rejoiced greatly, saying "Sādhu! Sādhu!" to Venerable Ānanda. A great earthquake occurred. Various kinds of flower rain fell from the sky. Many other wonders appeared. Many deities also felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking: "This Sutta which we heard in the presence of the Blessed One has now become something heard indirectly (parokkha)." Thus, it should be understood that although Venerable Ānanda recited this at the time of the First Great Council, it was spoken for this reason. By this sequence of words, the meaning of this half-verse is clarified: "By whom, when, and for what reason it was spoken, having stated this, [one should state] this method."

## Commentary on the text beginning with "Evaṃ"

Now, to explain the meaning collected in the mnemonic (mātikā) beginning with "The meaning of the text beginning with 'Evaṃ' in various ways," it is said: The word "Evaṃ" (thus) should be understood in the senses of simile (upamā), instruction (upadesa), praise (sampahaṃsana), blame (garahaṇa), acceptance of words (vacanasampaṭiggaha), manner (ākāra), illustration (nidassana), limitation (avadhāraṇa), and so forth.

Indeed, this word "Evaṃ" is seen in the sense of simile (upamā) in such passages as: "As (evaṃ) a mortal born should do much good..." (Dhammapada 53). In the sense of instruction (upadesa) in: "Thus (evaṃ) you should advance, thus you should retreat." In the sense of praise (sampahaṃsana) in: "So it is (evametaṃ), Blessed One; so it is, Sugata." In the sense of blame (garahaṇa) in: "Indeed, thus (evamevaṃ) this low woman speaks the praise of that shaven-headed wretched ascetic, whether there is a reason or not." In the sense of acceptance of words (vacanasampaṭiggaha) in: "'Yes (evaṃ), Bhante,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One." In the sense of manner (ākāra) in: "Bhante, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this manner (evaṃ)."

In the sense of illustration (nidassana) in: "Come, young man, go to where the ascetic Ānanda is. Having approached, ask in my name if the ascetic Ānanda is free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and living in comfort. Say: 'The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, asks the venerable Ānanda if he is free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and living in comfort.' And say thus (evañca): 'It would be good if the venerable Ānanda would come to the house of the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, out of compassion.'"

In the sense of [limitation/avadhāraṇa] in: "What do you think, Kālāmas, are these things wholesome or unwholesome?" "Unwholesome, Bhante." "Are these things blameworthy or blameless?" "Blameworthy, Bhante." "Are they censured by the wise..."
86:
When asked, "Are they praised by the wise or blamed by the wise?", they replied, "Venerable Sir, they are blamed by the wise." When asked, "When fulfilled and undertaken, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? What do you think in this matter?", they replied, "Venerable Sir, when fulfilled and undertaken, they lead to harm and suffering; thus it appears to us in this matter." In such passages (from the Aṅguttara Nikāya), the word 'evaṃ' is used in the sense of certainty (avadhāraṇa). However, in this context (of 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ'), it should be understood in the senses of manner (ākāra), indication (nidassana), and certainty (avadhāraṇa).

Among these three, the word 'evaṃ' in the sense of manner shows this meaning: Who is capable of knowing in every aspect the words of the Blessed One—which are subtle through various methods, arisen from many intentions, endowed with meaning and phrasing, possessed of various miracles, deep in Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration, and which reach the ear-path of all beings according to their respective languages? Nevertheless, by generating the desire to hear with all one's strength, it is shown as: "Thus I heard; I too heard in one particular manner."

In the sense of indication, by exempting himself, saying, "I am not self-enlightened (Sayambhū); I have not realized this Dhamma by myself," he indicates the entire sutta now to be spoken, saying, "Thus I heard; I too heard in this way."

In the sense of certainty, in accordance with the Blessed One's praise, "Monks, among my monk disciples who are of great learning, Ānanda is the foremost; among those who possess a good course (of knowledge), mindfulness, resoluteness, and who are attendants, Ānanda is the foremost," he shows his own power of retention and generates the desire to hear in beings, showing: "Thus I heard; and that hearing was neither deficient nor excessive in terms of meaning or phrasing; it is just so, and not otherwise."

The word 'me' is seen in three meanings. Thus, in such passages as "Food over which verses have been chanted is not to be eaten by me (me)," it has the meaning of 'mayā' (by me). In such passages as "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to me (me) in brief," it has the meaning of 'mayhaṃ' (to me). In such passages as "Monks, be heirs of my (me) Dhamma," it has the meaning of 'mama' (my/of me). In this context, however, it is appropriate in both meanings: "I heard" (mayā sutaṃ) and "my hearing" (mama sutaṃ).

The word 'suta', whether with a prefix or without, has many different meanings such as going, the taught Dhamma, being overcome by lust, accumulation, practice, being cognized by ear-consciousness, being known through the ear-door, and so on. Thus, in such passages as "He has gone (pasuto) to the army"...
87:
(In some passages, the word 'suta' has) the meaning of going. In such passages as "For one who sees the taught Dhamma (sutadhamma)," it has the meaning of the Dhamma that has been taught. In such passages as "An oozing woman (avassutā) for an oozing man (avassutassa)," it has the meaning of one overcome by lust. In such passages as "Much merit has been accumulated (pasutaṃ) by you," it has the meaning of accumulated. In such passages as "Those wise ones devoted to meditation (jhānappasutā)," it has the meaning of being repeatedly devoted to meditation. In such passages as "Seen, heard (sutaṃ), sensed," it has the meaning of being cognized by ear-consciousness. In such passages as "One who remembers what is heard (sutadharo), a storer of what is heard," it has the meaning of one who bears the Dhamma known through the sequence of the ear-door.

In this context (of 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ'), 'suta' means that which is apprehended by the cognitive process (viññāṇavīthi) preceded by ear-consciousness, or the act of apprehending. In that phrase, when the word 'me' has the meaning of 'mayā' (by me), then "Thus was it heard by me, apprehended by the cognitive process preceded by ear-consciousness" is appropriate. When the word 'me' has the meaning of 'mama' (my), then "Thus my hearing was the apprehending by the cognitive process preceded by ear-consciousness" is appropriate.

Thus, among these three words, 'Evaṃ' is the indication of the function of ear-consciousness. 'Me' is the indication of the person endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. 'Sutaṃ' is the indication of the accurate reception, neither deficient nor excessive nor perverted, by rejecting non-hearing. Furthermore, 'Evaṃ' is the indication of the occurrence of the consciousnesses of hearing, etc., in various ways upon the object. 'Me' is the indication of the self. 'Sutaṃ' is the indication of the Dhamma.

Furthermore, 'Evaṃ' is the indication of the Dhamma to be pointed out. 'Me' is the indication of the person. 'Sutaṃ' is the indication of the person's function.

Furthermore, 'Evaṃ' is the indication of the various ways of the cognitive processes by way of the designation of manner. 'Me' is the indication of the agent. 'Sutaṃ' is the indication of the object.

Furthermore, 'Evaṃ' is the indication of the person's function. 'Sutaṃ' is the indication of the consciousness's function. 'Me' is the indication of the person endowed with both functions.

Furthermore, 'Evaṃ' is the indication of the state (bhāva). 'Me' is the indication of the person. 'Sutaṃ' is the indication of that person's function.

Among those three words, the words 'Evaṃ' and 'Me' are designations of the non-existent (avijjamāna-paññatti) by way of ultimate reality (paramattha) as it truly is. 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of the existent (vijjamāna-paññatti). Furthermore, the words 'Evaṃ' and 'Me', depending on those respective aspects...
88: The words "Evaṃ" and "Me" are called derivative designations (upādā-paññatti) because they are spoken in reference to various modes. The word "Sutaṃ" is called a comparative designation (upanidhā-paññatti) because it is spoken in comparison with seeing and so forth. Here, by the word "Evaṃ," non-confusion is shown; by the word "Sutaṃ," non-confusion in hearing is shown. Likewise, by the word "Evaṃ," wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is shown, because for one who attends unwisely, there is no penetration of various states. By the word "Sutaṃ," non-distraction (avikkhepa) is shown, because for one whose mind is distracted, there is no act of listening. Indeed, a distracted person, even when being taught with all excellence, says, "I did not hear; please say it again." Through wise attention here, one fulfills the right direction of oneself and the possession of merit performed in the past. Through non-distraction, one fulfills the hearing of the True Dhamma and the association with good people. By this excellent mode of "Evaṃ," he shows his own endowment with the last two "wheels" (cakka); by the connection with hearing in "Sutaṃ," he shows endowment with the first two wheels. Likewise, he shows the purity of intention and the purity of effort; through that purity of intention, proficiency in attainment (magga-phala), and through purity of effort, proficiency in the scriptures (āgama). By this word "Evaṃ," which shows various penetrations, he shows his own perfection in the analytical knowledges of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) and of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). By this word "Sutaṃ," which shows the penetration of the varieties of what is to be heard, he shows perfection in the analytical knowledges of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā). Speaking this word "Evaṃ," which shows wise attention, he makes it known: "These teachings have been reflected upon by my mind and well-penetrated by wisdom." Speaking this word "Sutaṃ," which shows the connection with hearing, he makes it known: "Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and practiced verbally." By both these words, showing the fulfillment of meaning and phrasing, he inspires respect in hearing the Dhamma. By this entire phrase "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," the Venerable Ānanda, not claiming the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the level of the unworthy and, professing the state of a disciple, enters the level of the virtuous. Likewise, he raises the mind from the false Dhamma and establishes it in the True Dhamma. By showing, "This was merely heard by me; it is the word of that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One," he frees himself, points to the Teacher, entrusts the word of the Conqueror, and establishes the guide of the Dhamma. Furthermore, by saying "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," not claiming it as something originated by himself but revealing what was previously heard, he indicates: "From the Blessed One, who is courageous due to the four knowledges of fearlessness, who possesses the ten powers, who stands in the station of the leader like a lion without fear, who roars the lion's roar, who is the most excellent of all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma, the Lamp of Dhamma, the Heir to the Dhamma, the one who sets in motion the noble wheel of the True Dhamma..."
89:
...who is courageous due to the four knowledges of fearlessness, who possesses the ten powers, who stands without fear, who roars an outcry like the lion's roar of the king of lions, who is the most excellent of all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Great Master of Dhamma, who has lit the lamp of Dhamma, who inherits only the Dhamma, who sets in motion the noble wheel of authority which is the True Dhamma, the Fully Enlightened One who knows by himself without distortion—in this Dhamma of that Blessed One, one should know that by destroying lack of faith and producing the perfection of faith in all devas and humans, it is shown that one should not harbor doubt or uncertainty regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the word, or the syllable.

In this regard, there is a summary verse: "The disciple of the Buddha Gotama, speaking the words 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth, destroys lack of faith in the Dispensation and increases faith."

"Ekaṃ" is an indication of numerical limitation. "Samayaṃ" is an indication of a defined period. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" is an indefinite indication. The word "Samaya" is seen in the senses of: concurrence of causes, opportunity, time, group, cause, view, attainment, abandonment, and penetration.

Accordingly, in such passages as "Perhaps tomorrow we might approach, depending on the time and the concurrence of conditions," it expresses the meaning of concurrence (samavāya). In such passages as "Monks, there is a single opportunity and time for living the holy life," it expresses the meaning of opportunity (khana). In such passages as "the hot season, the sweltering season," it expresses the meaning of time (kāla). In such passages as "a great assembly of devas in the Mahāvana forest," it expresses the meaning of group (samūha). In such passages as "Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate this cause either; the Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī, and he will know me thus: 'The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher's Dispensation'; Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate this cause either," it expresses the meaning of cause (hetu). In such passages as "At that time, the wanderer Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta, who was learning, was staying in the Mallikā Queen's park with a single Sal tree, the Tindukācīra, which was a place for discussing views," it expresses the meaning of view (diṭṭhi).

"Because of attaining the benefit that is in the present life and the benefit that is in the future life, the wise one is called a Pandit," in such passages it expresses the meaning of attainment (paṭilābha). "Because of rightly abandoning conceit, he made an end of suffering," in such passages it expresses the meaning of abandonment (pahāna).
