"The sense of oppression of the Truth of Suffering, the sense of being conditioned..."
90:
In the passage from the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, "Santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho," etc., the word 'samaya' signifies the sense of 'penetration' (paṭivedha). However, in this Maṅgala Sutta, the meaning of the word 'samaya' is 'time' (kāla). Therefore, "ekaṃ samayaṃ" indicates one particular time among various designations of time such as year, season, month, fortnight, night, day, morning, noon, evening, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, and a moment (muhutta).

Alternatively, there are many times (samaya) well-known among devas and humans regarding the Blessed One, such as: the time of His conception, the time of His birth, the time of His spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the time of His great renunciation, the time of His practicing austerities (dukkara-cariyā), the time of His victory over Māra, the time of His attainment of omniscience, the time of His dwelling in the bliss of the present life, the time of His teaching the Dhamma, and the time of His Parinibbāna. Among these times, "ekaṃ samayaṃ" refers to the single occasion known as the time of teaching the Dhamma. Furthermore, among the times of the functions of wisdom and the functions of compassion, it refers to the time of the function of compassion; among the times of practicing for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others, it refers to the time of practicing for the benefit of others; among the two duties of the assembled audience, it refers to the time of Dhamma talk; and among the times of teaching (desanā) and practice (paṭipatti), it refers to the time of teaching. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" is said with reference to any such appropriate occasion.

Here, a question is raised: Why is it that in the Abhidhamma, it is stated as "yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ," and in other Sutta passages, it is stated as "Bhikkhus, here a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... yasmiṃ samaye," using the locative case (bhumma-vacana); and in the Vinaya, it is stated as "tena samayena buddho bhagavā," using the instrumental case (karaṇa-vacana); yet here in this Maṅgala Sutta, it is stated as "ekaṃ samayaṃ" using the accusative case (upayoga-vacana)? This is because while those cases (locative and instrumental) are appropriate in the Abhidhamma and Vinaya, a different sense is intended here. In the Abhidhamma and other Sutta passages, the sense of location (adhikaraṇa) and the sense of a state characterized by another state (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa) are appropriate. The 'samaya' which has the meaning of time and collection is the location (adhikaraṇa); by the occurrence of that 'samaya'—defined as the cause of the momentary coincidence of the states such as contact (phassa) taught therein—the occurrence of those states is marked. Therefore, to clarify that meaning, the locative case is used there.

In the Vinaya, however, the sense of cause (hetu) and the sense of instrument (karaṇa) are appropriate. There is that time of prescribing training rules (sikkhāpada) which is difficult to be known even by such persons as the Venerable Sāriputta. With that time as the cause and as the instrument, the Blessed One, while prescribing the training rules and considering the reason for their prescription, dwelt in various places. Therefore, to clarify that meaning, the instrumental case is used there.
92:
In this context, taking the linguistic definition of "vaṇṇāgama" (augmentation of a letter) or "vaṇṇavipariyāya" (transposition of letters), or following the grammatical method of inserting letters as in the case of "pisodara" etc., it should be understood that because this Blessed One possesses fortune (bhāgya) consisting of the perfections such as giving and virtue which bring about mundane and supramundane happiness, He is called "Bhagavā" although He should be called "Bhāgyavā."

Furthermore, because He has broken greed, hatred, delusion, wrong attention, shamelessness, fearlessness of sin, anger, enmity, disparaging, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, hypocrisy, stubbornness, impetuosity, pride, excessive pride, intoxication, negligence, craving, ignorance, the three unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, stains, uneven perceptions, thoughts, the obstacles (papañca), the fourfold perversions, taints (āsava), ties (gantha), floods (ogha), bonds (yoga), wrong paths (agati), grasping (upādāna) through craving, the five mental barrennesses, shackles, hindrances, delight, the six roots of contention, the body of craving, the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya), the eight wrongnesses (micchatta), the nine roots of craving, the ten courses of unwholesome action, the sixty-two views, the hundred and eight varieties of craving, and all the hundreds of thousands of defilements that cause distress and fever; or in brief, because He has broken the five Maras, namely: Kilesamāra, Khandhamāra, Abhisaṅkhāramāra, Maccumāra, and Devaputtamāra, He is called "Bhagavā" although He should be called "Bhaggavā" (the breaker) because He has broken all these dangers. In this regard, it is said:

"He has broken greed, He has broken hatred,
He has broken delusion, He is free from taints;
Evil states have been broken by Him,
Therefore He is called 'Bhagavā'."

By His possession of fortune, the perfection of His form-body (rūpakāya), which bears the marks of a hundred merits, is illustrated; by His breaking of defilements, the perfection of His Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) is illustrated. Likewise, it shows His state of being highly esteemed by those comparable in the world, and His state of being approachable by householders and monastics. It also shows His ability to remove the physical and mental suffering of those who approach Him, His helpfulness through the gift of material things and the gift of Dhamma, and His power to connect them with mundane and supramundane happiness.

Furthermore, because in the world the word "bhaga" is applied to the six qualities of lordship (issariya), doctrine (dhamma), fame (yasa), glory (siri), wish (kāma), and effort (payatta); and since He possesses supreme lordship over His own mind, or the mundane powers such as the ability to become minute (aṇimā) or light (laghimā) which are complete in every aspect; likewise, He possesses the supramundane Dhamma; He possesses fame that is extremely pure, attained through true virtues and pervading the three worlds; He possesses glory in all His major and minor limbs, complete in every aspect and capable of inspiring clarity in the eyes and minds of people occupied with seeing His form-body; He possesses the fulfillment of His wishes (kāma) in the sense that whatever He desired or longed for, whether for His own benefit or the benefit of others, was accomplished exactly so; and He possesses effort (payatta) known as right endeavor, which is the cause of His being honored by the entire world; therefore, because He is endowed with these six glories, He is called "Bhagavā" in the sense of "the Possessor of the Six Glories."
93:
Furthermore, because He has analyzed (vibhattavā) all phenomena into categories such as wholesome and so on; or analyzed wholesome and other phenomena into aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), truths (sacca), faculties (indriya), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and so on; or because He has analyzed the Noble Truth of Suffering in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and changing; the Truth of Origin in the sense of accumulation, source, connection, and impediment; the Truth of Cessation in the sense of escape, seclusion, being unconditioned, and deathlessness; and the Noble Truth of the Path in the sense of leading out, being a cause, seeing, and predominance; it means He has analyzed, opened up, and taught them. Therefore, He is called "Bhagavā" although He should be called "Vibhattavā."

And because He has frequented (bhaji), resorted to, and practiced extensively the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra), the brahma abidings (brahma-vihāra), the noble abidings (ariya-vihāra), the seclusions of body, mind, and substratum (kāya-citta-upadhi-viveka), the void, undirected, and signless liberations (suññata-appaṇihita-animitta-vimokkha), and other mundane and supramundane higher human states (uttarimanussadhamma), He is called "Bhagavā" although He should be called "Bhattavā."

Furthermore, because He has vomited out (vanta) the going (gamana) known as craving in the three planes of existence (bhava) through the Noble Path, He is called "Bhagavā" by taking the letter "Bha" from the word "bhava," the letter "Ga" from "gamana," and the letter "Vā" from "vanta," and lengthening the vowel. This is like the word "mekhalā" in the world, which is used instead of "mehanassa khassa mālā."

By this much, with the words "Thus have I heard" (Evaṃ me sutaṃ), the Venerable Ānanda, while teaching the Dhamma exactly as he had heard and learned it, makes the Dhamma-body (dhammasarīra) of the Blessed One manifest as if before one's eyes. By doing so, he consoles the people who are distressed by not seeing the Blessed One, saying, "This teaching is not one whose teacher is gone; this is your teacher."

By the words "At one time the Blessed One" (Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā), the Venerable Ānanda, showing the non-existence of the Blessed One at that time, shows the parinibbāna of the form-body (rūpakāya). By doing so, he stirs spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in those intoxicated with the pride of life, saying, "Even that Blessed One, the teacher of such a Noble Dhamma, the possessor of the ten powers, whose body was like a mass of diamonds, has attained parinibbāna; who else then should cherish a desire for life?" and he inspires them to strive in the True Dhamma.

By saying "Evaṃ" (Thus), he indicates the perfection of the teaching (desanā-sampatti); by "me sutaṃ" (heard by me), the perfection of the disciple (sāvaka-sampatti); by "ekaṃ samayaṃ" (at one time), the perfection of time (kāla-sampatti); and by "bhagavā" (the Blessed One), the perfection of the teacher (desaka-sampatti).

In the phrase "was staying at Sāvatthī" (Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati), Sāvatthī is the city that was the dwelling place of the sage named Savattha. Just as in the words "Kākandī" and "Mākandī," it is called "Sāvatthī" by way of the feminine gender; so say the grammarians. However, the teachers of the Commentaries say...
94:
It is called Sāvatthī because it is said, "Everything (sabba) that is for the use and enjoyment of humans is here (atthi)." Also, in the gathering of merchants, when asked, "What goods are there?", the answer given was "Everything is here (sabbamatthi)"; hence it is called Sāvatthī.

"All items of use are always gathered in the city of Sāvatthī;
Therefore, because of having everything required, it is called Sāvatthī.
The capital of the Kosalans is delightful, beautiful to behold, and gladdens the heart;
It is never silent from the ten sounds and is replete with food and drink.
Having reached growth and abundance, prosperous, wealthy, and delightful,
The supreme city of Sāvatthī is like Āḷakamandā, the city of the gods."

In that Sāvatthī (He was dwelling). Here, the locative case expresses the sense of proximity.

"Viharati" (dwells) means, without specific distinction, being endowed with one of the dwellings: the postures (iriyāpatha), the divine dwelling (dibba-vihāra), the Brahma dwelling (brahma-vihāra), or the noble dwelling (ariya-vihāra). Here, however, it indicates being engaged in one of the postures such as standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. Therefore, whether the Blessed One is standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, it should be understood simply as "viharati" (He dwells). Indeed, the Blessed One carries on and maintains the physical body (attabhāva) without letting it collapse by interrupting the discomfort of one posture with another posture. Therefore, it is said "viharati".

In the word "Jetavane", he is called "Jeta" because he conquers his enemies; or he is called "Jeta" because he was born when the king had conquered his enemies; or he is called "Jeta" because he was given this name for the sake of auspiciousness. It is called "Vana" (forest/grove) because it causes beings to resort to it; it means it makes beings resort to it through its own perfection and produces affection in them. Or it is called "Vana" because it is requested; it is as if it is requesting beings, "Come here and enjoy me," by means of the fragrance of various flowers, the songs of birds such as the intoxicated cuckoos, and the branches, blossoms, fruits, shoots, and leaves swaying in the gentle breeze. The forest of Prince Jeta is Jetavana. That forest was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner; therefore, it is called Jetavana. In that Jetavana (He was dwelling).

In the phrase "Anāthapiṇḍikassa Ārāme", that householder was named "Sudatta" by his parents. However, because of the fulfillment of all his desires, his freedom from the stain of stinginess, and his being endowed with virtues such as compassion, he always gave alms-food (piṇḍa) to the helpless (anātha). Therefore, he came to be known as "Anāthapiṇḍika". In the word "Ārāma", beings come and delight there; or specifically, monks come and delight there. Because it is a place of delight, it is called "Ārāma". Of that householder...
95:
...because he always gave alms-food to the helpless, he reached fame by the name Anāthapiṇḍika. It is called "Ārāma" because beings come and delight here, or especially because renunciants come and delight here. This means that because of its beauty with flowers, fruits, and shoots, and its possession of the five qualities of a resting place, such as being neither too far nor too near, they come from various places and reside there delightfully without weariness. Or, because of the aforementioned perfections, it is called "Ārāma" because it draws even those going to other places into itself and makes them delight. That monastery was purchased by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from the hand of Prince Jeta by spreading eighteen koṭis of gold; he then spent eighteen koṭis to have the dwellings built, and eighteen koṭis to complete the dedication ceremony of the monastery. Thus, by relinquishing fifty-four koṭis of gold, it was offered to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha; therefore, it is called "Anāthapiṇḍika’s Ārāma". In that Anāthapiṇḍika’s Ārāma (He was dwelling).

In this context, the phrase "in Jetavana" mentions the former owner, and "in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Ārāma" mentions the later owner. What is the purpose of mentioning both? The answer is: as a matter of authority, to establish the answer to the question "Where was it spoken?" and to urge other seekers of merit to follow their example. In that monastery, the eighteen koṭis of gold received from selling the land where the gate-towers and pinnacled houses were built, and the trees worth many koṭis, were the donation of Jeta; fifty-four koṭis were the donation of Anāthapiṇḍika. Since the Venerable Ānanda, by mentioning them, shows that "Thus do seekers of merit perform meritorious deeds," he urges other seekers of merit to follow their example. Thus, it should be understood that the purpose here is to urge seekers of merit to follow their example.

Here, an objection is raised: "If the Blessed One dwells in Sāvatthī, it should not be said 'in Jetavana Monastery.' If He dwells in Jetavana Monastery, it should not be said 'in Sāvatthī.' For it is not possible to dwell in two places at the same time." The answer is: Was it not said before that "the locative case expresses the sense of proximity"? Just as herds of cattle grazing near rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā are said to be "grazing in the Gaṅgā" or "grazing in the Yamunā," so too, when He dwells in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery, which is near Sāvatthī, it is said "He dwells in Sāvatthī".
96: It should be understood that the Blessed One was staying in Jeta's Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. Indeed, the word 'Sāvatthī' is mentioned to show the village for alms-resort, and the remaining words 'Jetavane Anāthapiṇḍikassa Ārāme' are mentioned to show a dwelling place suitable for those who have gone forth. Among those words, by mentioning Sāvatthī, it shows the Blessed One's favor toward householders, and by mentioning Jeta's Grove and so on, it shows His favor toward those who have gone forth. Similarly, by the former (Sāvatthī), because of the acceptance of the four requisites, it shows the avoidance of the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga); by the latter (Jeta's Grove), because of the abandonment of the objects of sensual desire, it shows the means of avoiding the practice of devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga). By the former, it shows the devotion to teaching the Dhamma; by the latter, it shows the mind's inclination toward seclusion. By the former, it shows the approach to the alms-village out of compassion; by the latter, it shows the departure from the alms-village out of wisdom. By the former, it shows the intention to fulfill the welfare and happiness of beings; by the latter, it shows the state of being unstained by defilements while performing the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, it shows the comfortable dwelling which is the cause for not abandoning righteous happiness; by the latter, it shows the cause for repeatedly engaging in superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). By the former, it shows being of great benefit to humans; by the latter, it shows being of great benefit to devas. By the former, it shows the growth in the world of the Buddha who was born in the world; by the latter, it shows the state of being unstained by worldly conditions. Thus it should be understood in this way and so forth. The word 'Atha' is a particle in the sense of non-interruption, and the word 'kho' is a particle showing a specific new topic. By that word 'kho', it shows that while the Blessed One was staying in that monastery without interruption, this specific topic arose. What is that specific topic? It is 'Aññatarā devatā' (a certain deity) and so on. In that phrase, 'Aññatarā' is an indefinite reference. Because that deity was not well-known by name or clan, he is called 'Aññatarā' (a certain one). A deva is indeed a 'devatā'; this term 'devatā' is common to both females and males. However, here it refers only to a male deity (devaputta); that male deity is called 'devatā' by virtue of the common name. In this phrase 'Abhikkantāya rattiyā', the word 'abhikkanta' is found in the senses of exhaustion (end), excellence, beauty, great approval, and so on. Among those meanings, in such passages as 'Venerable Sir, the night is exhausted (ended), the first watch has passed, the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting for a long time; Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks,' it is found in the sense of exhaustion (khaya). In such passages as 'This person, among these four persons, is more excellent and more sublime,' it is found in the sense of excellence (sundara). Who is this, shining with psychic power and retinue, illuminating all directions with a most beautiful appearance, who is worshipping my feet?
97:
In meanings such as "abhirūpa," it denotes being extremely beautiful. In passages such as "Abhikkantaṃ, bho Gotama; abhikkantaṃ, bho Gotama," it denotes great rejoicing (approval). Here, however, it is used in the sense of "exhaustion" (ending). Therefore, "abhikkantāya rattiyā" means "when the night had passed."

In the term "abhikkantavaṇṇā," the word "abhikkanta" denotes being extremely beautiful, while the word "vaṇṇa" is found in meanings such as complexion, praise, caste (class), cause, shape, measure, and visual object (rūpāyatana). Among these, in passages such as "The Blessed One is of golden complexion" (suvaṇṇavaṇṇosi Bhagavā), it denotes complexion. In passages such as "Householder, when will these praises of the ascetic Gotama be well-founded?" (samaṇassa Gotamassa vaṇṇā), it denotes praise. In passages such as "Master Gotama, there are these four castes" (cattāro vaṇṇā), it denotes caste. In passages such as "For what cause is he called a scent-thief?" (kena vaṇṇena), it denotes cause. In passages such as "Having created the shape of a great elephant king" (hatthirājavaṇṇaṃ), it denotes shape. In passages such as "There are three measures for a bowl" (tayo pattassa vaṇṇā), it denotes measure. In passages such as "Color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence" (vaṇṇော gandho raso ojā), it denotes visual object. Here, however, the word "vaṇṇa" should be understood as complexion. Therefore, "abhikkantavaṇṇā" means "having an extremely beautiful complexion."

In the term "kevalakappaṃ," the word "kevala" exists in many meanings such as without remainder, majority, unmixed, not exceeding, firm meaning, and detachment from defilements. Accordingly, in passages such as "The holy life that is entirely complete and pure" (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ), it denotes being without remainder. In passages such as "The entire populations of Aṅga and Magadha will approach, taking many kinds of food" (kevalakappā ca Aṅgamagadhā), it denotes majority. In passages such as "There is the arising of this entire mass of suffering [unmixed with happiness]" (kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa), it denotes being unmixed. In passages such as "This venerable one will surely have nothing more than mere faith" (kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ), it denotes not exceeding. In passages such as "Venerable sir, Anuruddha’s pupil named Bāhiya stands firmly for the sake of creating a schism in the Saṅgha" (kevalakappaṃ saṅghabhedāya), it denotes a firm meaning. In passages such as "One who is detached [from defilements] and has lived the life is called a supreme person" (kevalī vusitavā), it denotes detachment. Here, however, only the meaning of "without remainder" of this word "kevala" is intended.

This word "kappa" also exists in many meanings such as faith, usage (convention), time, designation, cutting, distinction (vikappa), hint (lesa), and entirety (surrounding). Accordingly, in passages such as "Master Gotama, this faith is according to the truth" (okappanīyaṃ), it denotes great faith. In passages such as "Monks, I allow the enjoyment of fruit through the five usages of ascetics" (samaṇakappehī), it denotes usage. In passages such as "By which he dwells for a permanent time" (niccakappaṃ), it denotes time. In passages such as "Venerable Kappa" (āyasmā Kappo), it denotes designation. In passages such as "Having hair and beard removed and cut, and being adorned" (katakesamassu), it denotes cutting. In passages such as "Eating when the sun has passed two finger-breadths is allowable [as a distinction]" (dvaṅgulakappo), it denotes distinction (vikappa). In passages such as "To eat what is produced from an old hint" (allikanipphannaṃ), it denotes a hint (lesa). In passages such as "Having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana monastery all around" (kevalakappaṃ Veḷuvanaṃ), it denotes entirety.
98:
In passages such as "Master Gotama, such faith in the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is indeed true," the word kappa denotes the meaning of great faith. In passages such as "Monks, I allow the enjoyment of fruit through the five usages (vikappa) of ascetics," it denotes the meaning of usage (vohāra). In passages such as "By which he dwells for an entire permanent time," it denotes the meaning of time. In passages such as "Venerable Kappa is thus," it denotes the meaning of designation. In passages such as "Having hair and beard removed and cut, he is adorned," it denotes the meaning of cutting (chedana). In passages such as "Eating when the sun has passed two finger-breadths is allowable," it denotes the meaning of distinction (vikappa). In passages such as "There is a pretext (hint) for sleeping," it denotes the meaning of hint (lesa). In passages such as "Having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana monastery all around with radiance," it denotes the meaning of entirety (samantabhāva). In this Maṅgala Sutta, however, the meaning of entirety of the word kappa is intended. Therefore, in the phrase "kevalakappaṃ Jetavanaṃ," the meaning should be understood as "the entire Jetavana monastery without remainder."

"Obhāsetvā" means spreading with radiance, making a single glow or a single illumination like the moon or the sun.

In the phrase "yena Bhagavā tenupasaṅkami," the instrumental case (yena, tena) is used in the sense of the locative (place). Therefore, it should be understood in this context as "approached the place where the Blessed One was." Alternatively, it should be understood as "approached for the very reason that devas and humans should approach the Blessed One." For what reason should one approach the Blessed One? Just as flocks of birds approach a great tree that is always fruiting with the desire to enjoy sweet-tasting fruit, one approaches with the desire to attain various special qualities. "Upasaṅkami" means they went. "Upasaṅkamitvā" indicates the completion of the approach. Or, it means that after arriving in this way, they went to a very close place known as the presence of the Blessed One.

"Bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā" means having saluted, bowed down, and paid homage to the Blessed One.

"Ekamantaṃ" is an adverbial neuter (bhāvanapuṃsaka) usage, meaning in one place or to one side. Alternatively, it is the accusative case (upayogavacana) used in the sense of the locative. "Aṭṭhāsi" excludes sitting and so on, and indicates the posture of standing; it means he remained standing.
99:
In what way did that deity stand so that she was said to be "standing to one side"?

"Not behind, not in front, nor too near or too far; not directly to the side, nor upwind; neither too low nor too high. Having avoided these eight faults, she stood to one side."

Why did this deity only stand and not sit? Because of her desire to return quickly. Deities come to the human world for a specific purpose, just as a clean man might go to a latrine. By nature, the human world is repulsive to them due to its foul odor from a distance of a hundred yojanas; they do not delight in it. Therefore, having performed the task for which she came, she did not sit because she wished to return quickly. Furthermore, people sit to dispel the fatigue of postures such as walking, but deities have no such fatigue; for this reason also, she did not sit. She also did not sit out of respect for the Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka) who stood surrounding the Blessed One. Moreover, she did not sit solely out of reverence for the Blessed One. When deities wish to sit, a seat appears for them; not desiring one and not even forming the thought of sitting, she stood in a suitable place.

"That deity, standing to one side" means that for these aforementioned reasons, that deity stood in a suitable place. "Addressed the Blessed One in verse" means she spoke to the Blessed One with words composed and bound by syllables and feet. In what way? "Many deities and humans... tell me the supreme blessing."

## Account of the Origin of the Question on Blessings

In this Mangala Sutta, since the teacher who wished to explain the meaning of the text beginning with "Evaṃ" in various ways has set down the table of contents (mātikā) saying, "having stated the origin (samuṭṭhāna)," and since this is the opportunity to state that origin, I shall first state the origin of the question on blessings and afterwards explain the meaning of these verse-parts. What is the origin of the question on blessings? It is said that in Jambudīpa, a great multitude of people would gather at various city gates, rest houses, assembly halls, and so on, and having given gold and silver, they would have various stories told, such as the abduction of Sītā (Sītāharaṇa). Each story would conclude after four months. At that time, one day, a discussion on blessings arose: "What indeed is a blessing? Is a blessing something seen (diṭṭha), something heard (suta), or something sensed (muta)? Who knows what a blessing is?"
100:
Then, a man named Diṭṭhamaṅgalika (one who believes in seen blessings) said, "I know what a blessing is. In the world, a seen blessing is a form (rūpa) that is regarded as highly auspicious." What is that seen blessing? In this world, some person, having risen early, sees a cātaka bird, or a bael-wood staff (beluva-laṭṭhi), or a pregnant woman, or children who are adorned and prepared, or full pots (puṇṇaghaṭa), or a fresh red fish (allarohatamaccha), or a thoroughbred horse, or a thoroughbred chariot, or a bull, or a cow, or a monkey (kapila), or whatever other such form that is regarded as highly auspicious; this is called a "seen blessing" (diṭṭhamaṅgala). Some people accepted his words, while others did not. Those who did not accept them argued with him.

Then, a man named Sutamaṅgalika (one who believes in heard blessings) said, "Sirs, the eye sees both what is pure and what is impure. Likewise, it sees both the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant. If a blessing were merely what is seen, then everything would be a blessing. Therefore, what is seen is not a blessing; rather, what is heard is a blessing. A heard blessing is a sound (sadda) regarded as highly auspicious." What is that sound? In this world, some person, having risen early, hears such words as "prosper" (vaḍḍhati), or "full" (puṇṇā), or "Phussa" (an asterism), or "Sumanā", or "Sirī", or "Sirivaḍḍhā", or "Today is a good constellation, a good moment, a good day, a good blessing," or whatever other such sound that is regarded as highly auspicious; this is called a "heard blessing" (sutamaṅgala). Some people accepted his words, while others did not. Those who did not accept them argued with him.

Then, a man named Mutamaṅgalika (one who believes in sensed blessings) said, "Sirs, the ear also hears both good and bad sounds, both pleasant and unpleasant. If a blessing were merely what is heard, then everything would be a blessing. Therefore, what is heard is not a blessing; rather, what is sensed (muta) is a blessing. A sensed blessing is an odor, a taste, or a touch regarded as highly auspicious." What is that sensed object? In this world, some person, having risen early, smells the scent of flowers such as the scent of the lotus, or chews a tooth-stick (dantakaṭṭha) associated with the Phussa asterism, or touches the earth, or touches green crops, or fresh cow dung, or a tortoise, or sesame, or flowers, or fruit, or anoints himself well with Phussa-clay, or wears a new cloth, or wears a turban, or smells any other such odor, tastes any taste, or touches any touch regarded as highly auspicious; this is called a "sensed blessing" (mutamaṅgala). Some people accepted his words, while others did not.
101: Regarding these blessings, those who held the view that what is seen is a blessing were unable to convince those who held the view that what is heard or what is sensed is a blessing. None among them could convince the other two groups. Among those people, those who accepted the words of the one who held "seen" as a blessing believed that "only the visible object seen is a blessing." Those who accepted the words of those who held "heard" and "sensed" as blessings believed that "only the sound heard and the object sensed are blessings." Thus, this talk of blessings became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Then, the people throughout Jambudīpa gathered in groups and pondered over the blessings, asking, "What indeed is a blessing?" The guardian deities of those people, having heard that talk, likewise pondered over the blessings. The earth-dwelling deities (Bhumma devas), who were friends of those guardian deities, heard it from them and likewise pondered over the blessings. The space-dwelling deities (Ākāsaṭṭha devas), who were friends of the earth-dwelling deities; the Cātumahārājikā devas, who were friends of the space-dwelling deities; and in this manner, step by step up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmas, who were friends of the Sudassī devas—having heard it, even the Akaniṭṭha Brahmas gathered in groups and pondered over the blessings. Thus, the pondering over blessings arose everywhere, up to the ten thousand world systems. Although they deliberated, saying, "This is a blessing, that is a blessing," they could not reach a conclusion for twelve years. Excluding the noble disciples (Ariya-sāvakas), all humans, devas, and Brahmas were divided into three groups based on the views of what is seen, heard, and sensed. Not even a single person could reach a conclusion according to the truth, saying, "This alone is a blessing." Thus, the "Blessing Tumult" (Maṅgala-kolāhala) arose in the world. There are five kinds of tumults (kolāhala): the Tumult of the Aeon (Kappa-kolāhala), the Tumult of the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti-kolāhala), the Tumult of the Buddha (Buddha-kolāhala), the Tumult of the Blessing (Maṅgala-kolāhala), and the Tumult of the Sage (Moneyya-kolāhala). Among these five, the devas of the sense sphere (Kāmāvacara devas), with disheveled hair, weeping faces, wiping tears with their hands, wearing red garments, and assuming a very unsightly appearance, wander through the paths of humans and announce: "After a hundred thousand years, the destruction of the aeon will occur. This world will perish. The great ocean will dry up. This great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be burnt up and destroyed. The destruction of the world will occur up to the Brahma realm. Friends, develop loving-kindness (mettā). Friends, develop compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā). Attend to your mother. Attend to your father. Respect the elders in the family. Be vigilant, do not be negligent!" This is called the Tumult of the Aeon. The same devas of the sense sphere wander through the paths of humans and announce: "After a hundred years, a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) will appear in the world." This is called the Tumult of the Universal Monarch. However, the Brahmas of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), having adorned themselves with Brahma ornaments...
102: ...and wound Brahma turbans around their heads, being filled with joy and happiness and speaking of the Buddha's virtues, wander through the paths of humans and announce: "After a thousand years, a Buddha will appear in the world." This is called the Tumult of the Buddha (Buddha-kolāhala). The devas living in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), knowing the minds of devas and humans, wander through the paths of humans and announce: "After twelve years, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) will preach the Blessing Dhamma." This is called the Tumult of the Blessing (Maṅgala-kolāhala). The devas living in the Pure Abodes wander through the paths of humans and announce: "After seven years, a certain monk, having met with the Blessed One, will ask about the practice of the Sage (Moneyya-paṭipadā)." This is called the Tumult of the Sage (Moneyya-kolāhala). Among these five tumults, this Tumult of the Blessing arose in the world for devas and humans. Then, when devas and humans searched and searched but could not find the blessings, after twelve years had passed, the devas living in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven gathered together and pondered thus: "Just as a householder [thinks] for the people in the house, a village headman for the villagers, and a king for all people, so too this Sakka, the Lord of Devas, is our chief and superior. He is the lord of the two deva realms by virtue of merit, power, sovereignty, and wisdom. What if we were to ask Sakka, the Lord of Devas, about this matter?" They went to Sakka and, having prostrated before him—who had a body radiant with ornaments suitable for that moment, was surrounded by twenty-five million celestial nymphs, and was seated on the noble Paṇḍukambala stone throne at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree—stood at a respectful distance and said: "O Lord, please know that currently, a problem concerning blessings has arisen. Some say 'what is seen' is a blessing, some say 'what is heard' is a blessing, and some say 'what is sensed' is a blessing. Among these three views, we and other devas cannot reach a conclusion. It would be good if you, O Lord Sakka, would explain it to us according to the truth." The King of Devas, being wise by nature, asked, "Where did this talk of blessings first arise?" The devas replied, "Lord, we heard it from the Cātumahārājikā devas." From there, the Cātumahārājikā devas said they heard it from the space-dwelling deities, the space-dwelling deities from the earth-dwelling deities, and the earth-dwelling deities from the guardian deities of humans. The guardian deities of humans said, "It arose in the human world." Then Sakka, the Lord of Devas, asked, "Where is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) residing?" They replied, "O King of Devas, He is residing in the human world." He then asked if anyone had already asked the Blessed One, and [they replied] that no one...
103:
Sakka, the Lord of Devas, said: "Friends, why do you discard a bright, genuine fire and light a firefly? Why do you think that I am the one to be questioned, bypassing the Blessed One who teaches the complete blessings? Come, friends, let us go and question the Blessed One. By questioning Him, we will surely obtain a glorious answer to the problem." He then commanded a certain devaputta, saying, "Go and question the Blessed One." That devaputta, adorning himself with attire suitable for that moment, shining like a streak of lightning and surrounded by a host of devas, went to the Jetavana Monastery. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and standing at a respectful distance, desiring to ask the question regarding blessings, he addressed Him with the verse beginning with "Bahu devā manussā ca."

This is the origin of the question on blessings.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Bahu Devā"

Now follows the commentary on the meanings of the words of the verse. The word 'Bahu' is a term indicating an indefinite number; by this, it means not just hundreds, but thousands and hundreds of thousands. They are called 'Devā' (devas) because they play with the five cords of sensual pleasure, or because they shine with their own glory. Furthermore, there are three types of devas: devas by convention (sammuti), devas by rebirth (upapatti), and devas by purity (visuddhi). As it is said: "There are three kinds of devas: sammuti-deva, upapatti-deva, and visuddhi-deva. Therein, kings, queens, and princes are called sammuti-deva. Celestial beings starting from the Four Great Kings and those above them are called upapatti-deva. Arahants are called visuddhi-deva."

In this context, upapatti-devas are intended. They are called 'Manussā' (humans) because they are the offspring of Manu. However, ancient teachers say they are called 'manussā' because of the loftiness of their minds. These humans are of four types: those of Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha. In this context, those of Jambudīpa are intended. They are called 'Maṅgala' (blessings) because beings reach greatness through these practices; it means they attain prosperity and growth. 'Acintayuṃ' means they thought about them, desiring, longing for, and yearning for them. 'Ākaṅkhamānā' means desiring, longing for, and being thirsty for. 'Sotthānaṃ' means the state of well-being (Nibbāna), or the existence of all beautiful, good, and noble qualities associated with benefits in the present life and the hereafter. 'Brūhi' means preach, reveal, or tell.
104:
"Open it, analyze it, and make it clear." 'Maṅgala' means the cause of prosperity, the cause of growth, and the cause of all attainments. 'Uttama' means distinguished, noble, and that which brings welfare and happiness to all the world. This is the word-by-word commentary of the verse.

This is the summary of the meaning: That devaputta, seeing that devas from the ten thousand world systems had gathered in this world system out of a desire to hear the question on blessings, and had created subtle bodies so that ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, or even eighty devas stood in a space no larger than the tip of a single hair, and seeing the Blessed One sitting on the appointed noble Buddha-seat, outshining all devas, Māras, and Brahmās with His glory and power, and knowing through His own mind the thoughts of the humans living throughout the entire Jambudīpa who had not yet arrived, he spoke thus to remove the dart of doubt from all devas and humans:

"Many devas and humans,
Desiring well-being, have thought about blessings;
Tell us the supreme blessing."

"Being questioned by me with the consent of those devas and out of a desire to favor humans, O Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please tell us that blessing which is supreme because it brings absolute welfare and happiness to all of us."

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Asevanā Ca"

Having thus heard the words of the devaputta, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ." In that verse, "Asevanā" means not associating, not attending upon. "Bālānaṃ" refers to fools, meaning those who live merely by breathing and not by the life of wisdom. "Paṇḍitānaṃ" refers to the wise, meaning those who possess wisdom and proceed by the way of knowledge regarding benefits in the present and the hereafter. "Sevanā" means associating, attending upon, being a companion to them, being intimate with them, and being united with them. "Pūjā" refers to honor, respect, reverence, and salutation. "Pūjaneyyānaṃ" means those worthy of honor. "Etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ": combining all those—not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor—He said, "This is the supreme blessing." Regarding the point you, devaputta, asked, "Tell us the supreme blessing," He said, "Understand this very thing as the supreme blessing." This is the word-by-word commentary of this verse. The meaning of this verse should be understood. Thus, having heard the words of the devaputta, the Blessed One spoke this verse "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ." In this regard, what is called a verse (gāthā) is of four kinds: there are single verses and multiple verses. Among those four types of verses, a verse spoken such as "O Gotama, wise as the earth, what kind of disciple is such a one?" or "Friend, how did you cross the flood?" is called a Pucchita-gāthā (a questioned verse).
105:
The explanation of the meaning of this verse should be understood as follows: Having heard the words of the deity in this manner, the Blessed One spoke this verse beginning with "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ."

In this regard, there are four types of verses: asked verses (pucchita-gāthā), unasked verses (apucchita-gāthā), verses with a sequential connection (sānusandhika-gāthā), and verses without a sequential connection (ananusandhika-gāthā).

Among these four, a verse spoken when asked by others, such as: "O Gotama of vast wisdom like the earth, I ask you: what kind of conduct makes a disciple good?" and "Friend, how did you cross the flood?", is called an asked verse. A verse spoken of his own accord according to his own inclination without being asked by others, such as: "What others call happiness, that the Noble Ones call suffering," is called an unasked verse. Because the Blessed One said, "Monks, I will teach the Dhamma with its causes and reasons," all verses spoken by the Buddhas are verses with a sequential connection. Verses without a sequential connection do not exist in this Dispensation. Among these types of verses, this verse is called an asked verse because it was spoken by the Blessed One when asked by the deity.

This is like, for example, a man skilled in paths who, when asked about a route, first describes the path to be abandoned and then describes the path to be taken. Just as he says, "In such a place there is a fork in the road; there, leave the left path and take the right path," so too, among those who should be associated with and those who should not, the Buddha first describes the one who should not be associated with and then describes the one who should be associated with. The Blessed One is like the man skilled in paths. As he said:

"Tissa, 'a man skilled in paths' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. For he is skilled in this world, skilled in the world beyond, skilled in the realm of Death, skilled in the realm beyond Death, skilled in the realm of Māra, and skilled in the realm beyond Māra."

Therefore, wishing to first speak of the one who should not be associated with, he said: "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ, paṇḍitānañca sevanā" (Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise). Just like the path to be abandoned, first, fools should not be associated with or attended upon. Then, like the path to be taken, the wise should be associated with and attended upon. Why did the Blessed One, when teaching the auspicious blessings, first teach non-association with fools and association with the wise? It is said: Because deities and humans, through associating with fools, held the view that auspiciousness consists in things seen and so forth, and that view is inauspicious. Therefore, wishing to condemn the association with bad friends (akalyāṇamitta) which destroys the welfare of both this world and the next, and to praise the association with good friends which accomplishes the welfare of both worlds...
106:
...praising the association with good friends, the Blessed One first taught non-association with fools and association with the wise.

In that context, those called 'fools' (bāla) are any beings possessed of unwholesome courses of action such as killing living beings; those fools should be known by three characteristics. As stated in the Bāla Sutta: "Monks, these three are the characteristics of a fool." Furthermore, the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa; Devadatta, Kokālika, Kaṭamodaka-Tissa, the son of Khaṇḍadevi, Samuddadatta, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others; and in the past, the brother of Dīghavida and other such beings are to be known as fools.

Like a house on fire, they destroy themselves and those who follow their words through their wrongly held views. For example, the brother of Dīghavida, with a body measuring sixty leagues, fell on his back and was cooked in the great hell for the interval between four Buddhas; and the five hundred families who delighted in his view were also reborn in his company and cooked in the great hell. This was spoken by the Blessed One:

"Monks, just as fire escaping from a reed-hut or a grass-hut burns even gabled houses that are plastered inside and out, draft-free, with well-fitted bolts and closed windows; even so, monks, whatever fears arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise. Whatever calamities arise... whatever obstacles (upasagga) arise... they arise from the fool, not from the wise. Thus, monks, the fool is dangerous, the wise is safe. The fool is calamitous, the wise is not. The fool is obstructive, the wise is not."

Furthermore, a fool is like a rotting fish, and one who associates with him is like the leaf-wrapper of that rotting fish; he reaches the state of being discarded and loathed by the wise. This also has been said:

"When a man wraps rotting fish with kusa grass,
The kusa grass also smells putrid; such is association with fools."

Akitti the Wise also said this when a boon was being granted by Sakka, the king of devas: "Sakka, I wish not to see a fool, not to hear a fool, and [not to dwell] with a fool..."
107:
One should not see a fool, nor hear a fool, nor live together with a fool. One should not engage in conversation with a fool, nor take delight in it.

"Kassapa, what has the fool done to you? Tell me the reason. Why do you not desire to see a fool?"

"The unwise fool leads one to ruin; he engages one in what is not the task. Even when led wrongly, he thinks himself superior; when well-advised, he becomes angry. He does not know discipline; it is better not to see such a fool."

Thus, the Blessed One, censuring the association with fools in every way, said, "Not associating with fools is a blessing." Now, wishing to praise the association with the wise, he said, "And associating with the wise is a blessing." In this context, the "wise" refers to those beings endowed with the ten courses of wholesome action, starting with abstaining from taking life. These wise persons are to be known by three characteristics. As it is said in the Sutta: "Monks, these three are the characteristics of a wise man." Alternatively, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the eighty great disciples, and other disciples of the Tathāgata, as well as Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Vidhura, Sarabhaṅga, Mahosadha, Sutasoma, King Nimi, Prince Ayoghara, Akitti Paṇḍita, and others, should be known as the wise.

These wise ones are like protectors in times of fear, like lamps in the darkness, and like the attainment of food and drink when oppressed by the suffering of hunger and thirst; they are capable of destroying all fears, calamities, and misfortunes for those who follow their words. Accordingly, depending on the Tathāgata, countless and immeasurable devas and humans have reached the destruction of the taints (āsavas), have been established in the Brahma world, established in the deva worlds, or reborn in happy realms. By gladdening their minds towards the Elder Sāriputta and serving him with the four requisites, eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven. Likewise, it was so with all the great disciples such as Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākassapa. Some of the teacher Sunetta's disciples were reborn in the Brahma world, some reached the company of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas... and some were reborn in the company of wealthy householders. It has also been said: "Monks, there is no fear arising from the wise, no calamity arising from the wise, no misfortune arising from the wise."
108:
Furthermore, a wise person is like a bouquet of fragrant flowers such as the Tagara. One who associates with such a wise person is like the leaf used to wrap that fragrant bouquet; thus, they become worthy of association, beloved, and pleasing to the wise. Regarding this:

"If a person wraps Tagara flowers with a Palāsa leaf, the leaf itself becomes fragrant. In the same way, those who associate with the wise become fragrant, as if imbued with the scent of pure virtue."

The wise Akitti also said this when Sakka, the king of devas, offered him boons:

"May I see the wise, may I hear the wise, may I live together with the wise. May I engage in conversation with the wise, and may I take delight in that wise person."

"Kassapa, what has the wise person done for you? Tell me the reason. Kassapa, why do you desire to see the wise?"

"The wise person leads one on the right path; he engages one only in what is correct. Through good guidance, one becomes more noble step by step; when well-advised, he does not become angry. Such a wise person knows discipline well; therefore, association with such a wise person is truly excellent."

Thus, the Blessed One, praising the association with the wise in every way, said, "Associating with the wise is a blessing." Now, wishing to praise the honoring of those who have gradually become worthy of honor through not associating with fools and associating with the wise, he said, "And honoring those worthy of honor is a blessing."

Among them, those worthy of honor are the Blessed Buddhas, who are free from all faults and endowed with all virtues. Next are the Paccekabuddhas and the noble disciples (ariya-sāvakas). Honoring such noble persons, even in a small way, leads to welfare and happiness for a long time. In this regard, the florist Sumana, Queen Mallikā, and others are examples.

I shall relate one such example. One morning, the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, entered the city of Rājagaha for alms. At that time, the florist Sumana, while carrying flowers for King Bimbisāra of Magadha, saw the Blessed One who had reached the city gate—inspiring in appearance, pleasing to behold, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, and shining with the glory of a Buddha. Upon seeing him, the florist thought: "The King, taking these flowers, might give me a hundred or a thousand coins..."
109:
(The flowers) should be given (to the King); the money received from such giving would only result in happiness in this world. However, making an offering to the Blessed One has immeasurable and incalculable fruits, bringing welfare and happiness for a long time. Thinking, "Now I shall worship the Blessed One with these flowers," and with a heart full of faith, he took a handful of flowers and threw them towards the Blessed One. The flowers traveled through the air and remained as a floral canopy above the Blessed One. Seeing that miracle, the florist, with even greater faith, threw another handful of flowers; those too traveled and remained as a floral garment. In this way, he threw eight handfuls of flowers, and they traveled and remained as a floral gabled pavilion.

The Blessed One was inside that floral pavilion, and a great multitude of people gathered. Looking at the florist, the Blessed One manifested a smile. The Venerable Ānanda, thinking, "The Buddhas do not smile without a cause or reason," asked the reason for the smile. The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, because of the power of this offering, this florist, after wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, will finally become a Paccekabuddha named Sumaniissara." At the conclusion of his words, he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma:

"That deed is well done, which, having been done, one does not repent;
The fruit of which one experiences with a delighted and happy mind."

At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. Thus, it should be understood that even a small offering to those worthy of offerings leads to welfare and happiness for a long time. That was merely an offering of material things (āmisa-pūjā); what then need be said about the offering of practice (paṭipatti-pūjā)? Those clansmen who worship the Blessed One with their own virtues, such as taking refuge, undertaking the precepts, observing the Uposatha, and the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla)—who could ever finish praising the benefits of their worship? It is said that they worship the Tathāgata with the highest form of worship. As the Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, whatever monk or nun, or lay follower (upāsaka) or lay woman follower (upāsikā), dwells practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing dutifully, and living according to the Dhamma, such a person honors, respects, reveres, worships, and venerates the Tathāgata with the highest worship." Following this method, it should be understood that worshipping Paccekabuddhas and Noble Disciples (ariyasāvakas) also brings welfare and happiness.
110:
Furthermore, in the context of laypeople, a younger brother should honor his elder brother and elder sister. A son should honor his parents. Daughters-in-law should honor their husband's parents (parents-in-law). In this way, those worthy of honor should be understood in this context. Honoring these individuals is indeed a blessing (mangala), because it is a wholesome deed and a cause for the increase of life span and other forms of prosperity.

For this was said by the Blessed One:
"They will be those who honor their mothers, honor their fathers, honor recluses, honor brahmins, and respect the elders in the family. They will live undertaking this wholesome Dhamma. Because of undertaking these wholesome Dhammas, they will increase in life span and also in beauty," and so forth.

Now, since the table of contents (mātikā) was laid down as: "In whatever place a blessing exists, having defined it, one should clarify its status as a blessing," therefore this is said: Thus, in this verse, three blessings have been taught: not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor. Among them, not associating with fools is to be understood as a blessing because it is a cause for the benefit of both worlds by protecting against the dangers arising from associating with fools. Associating with the wise and honoring those worthy of honor are blessings because they are causes for Nibbāna and happy states (sugati), as mentioned in the description of their glorious fruits. Hereafter, without showing the mātikā, I shall define whatever blessing exists in whatever place and clarify its status as a blessing.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning with "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ" is finished.

## Explanation of the Verse Beginning with "Patirūpadesavāso ca"

Thus, although the Blessed One was requested only once, "Tell me the highest blessing," like a noble man who gives much when asked for little, he taught three blessings in one verse. Beyond that, because of the devas' desire to listen, because of the existence of blessings, and because of the desire to engage various beings in various blessings that are suitable for them, he began to speak many more blessings with the verses beginning with "Patirūpadesavāso ca." In those verses, first, "patirūpa" means suitable. "Desa" means a village, a market town, a city, or a country—any place or location where beings reside. "Vāsa" means...
111:
Dwelling in that place is called 'nivāsa'. 'Pubbe' means in the past, in previous past existences. 'Katapuññatā' means the state of being one who has accumulated merit. 'Atta' refers to the mind, or it refers to the entire self (the physical body). 'Sammāpaṇidhi' means the right directing or establishing of that self. The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already described. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā) here.

The commentary on the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā), however, should be understood as follows: 'Patirūpadesavāsa' (dwelling in a suitable locality) refers to a place where the fourfold assembly travels, where the bases of meritorious action such as giving (dāna) and so on occur, and where the ninefold dispensation of the Teacher shines. Dwelling in such a place is called a blessing (maṅgala) because it is a condition for beings to perform merit. The fishermen and others who entered the island of Sīhaḷa are examples of this.

Alternatively: 'Patirūpadesavāsa' refers to the place of the Blessed One's Seat of Enlightenment (bodhimanda), the place where the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion, the place at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree where the Twin Miracle was performed—defeating the doctrines of all heretics in the midst of an assembly spanning twelve yojanas—the place of the descent from the deva world, or any other place where the Buddha resided, such as Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, and so on. Dwelling in such places is called a blessing because it is a condition for beings to attain the six unsurpassable things (anuttariya).

Alternatively (Mahāvagga, 259): In the east is the market town named Gajaṅgala; beyond that is Mahāsālā; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country (majjhimadesa). In the south-east is the river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country. In the south is the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country. In the west is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country. In the north is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country. This Middle Country is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in breadth, and nine hundred in circumference. This is what is called a 'suitable locality' (patirūpadesa).

In this region, Universal Monarchs (cakkavatti) arise, who rule over the four great islands and the two thousand surrounding small islands. Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) for one asaṅkhyeyya and a hundred thousand aeons, Great Disciples (mahāsāvaka) such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna arise. Having fulfilled the perfections for two asaṅkhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, Silent Buddhas (paccekabuddha) arise. Having fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen asaṅkhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons...
112:
The central core within the border regions is called the Middle Country (majjhimadesa). In the north is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; the outer side of that mountain is the border region, and the inner side is the Middle Country. This Middle Country is 300 yojanas in length, 250 yojanas in breadth, and 900 yojanas in circumference. This very region is called a 'suitable locality' (patirūpadesa).

In this Middle Country, Universal Monarchs (cakkavatti) who rule over the four great islands and two thousand small islands appear. Great disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna also appear in this very region after fulfilling perfections for one asaṅkhyeyya and a hundred thousand aeons. Silent Buddhas (paccekabuddha) also appear after fulfilling perfections for two asaṅkhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons. The Buddhas also appear in this very region after fulfilling the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen asaṅkhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons. Beings living in that Middle Country, having accepted the advice of the Universal Monarch and established themselves in the five precepts, become heaven-bound. Likewise, by establishing themselves in the advice of Silent Buddhas, or by establishing themselves in the advice of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas, they become heaven-bound and Nibbāna-bound. Therefore, dwelling in such a place is called a blessing because it is a condition for these attainments.

'Pubbe-katapuññatā' means having accumulated merit in a past life in relation to Buddhas, Silent Buddhas, and Arahants (khīṇāsava). Such merit is also a blessing. Why? Because after seeing a Buddha or a Silent Buddha, or in the presence of a Buddha or a disciple of a Buddha, even at the conclusion of a four-line verse heard, it can lead one to the fruit of Arahantship. A person who has made a resolution in a past life and has an abundance of root-merit can, by using that root-merit, develop insight and reach the state of an Arahant with the destruction of taints, just like King Mahākappina and his Chief Queen. Therefore, it is said: 'Having performed merit in the past is a blessing.'

'Attasammāpaṇidhi' means that in this world, a certain person establishes their immoral self in virtue, establishes their faithless self in the accomplishment of faith, and establishes their stingy self in the accomplishment of generosity. This right directing of oneself is also a blessing. Why? Because it is the cause for abandoning enmity in the present and future lives and for attaining special benefits.

Thus, in this verse, three blessings are stated: dwelling in a suitable locality, having performed merit in the past, and rightly directing oneself. The nature of these as blessings has been clarified in their respective places.

The commentary on the meaning of the verse beginning with 'Patirūpadesavāsa' is finished.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with Bāhusaccañca

Now, the verse beginning with 'Bāhusaccañca' will be explained. There, 'bāhusacca' means the state of being one of great learning. 'Sippa' means any kind of manual skill. 'Vinaya' means the discipline of body, speech, and mind. 'Susikkhita' means well-trained. 'Subhāsita' means well-spoken. The word 'yā' is an indefinite designation. 'Vācā' means speech. The remaining words are to be understood in the manner already described. This is the word-by-word commentary here.

The commentary on the meaning should be understood as follows: One of 'great learning' (bahussuta) is one who bears and accumulates the heard teachings of the Dhamma. In this Dispensation, it refers to one who has much learning in the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, and so on, and who upholds the Dispensation of the Blessed One. Such great learning is called a blessing because it is a cause for abandoning the unwholesome and acquiring the wholesome, and because it is a cause for realizing the Ultimate Truth. This is true; therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, the noble disciple who is possessed of great learning abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity.' Another reason is...
113:
The explanation of the meaning should be understood as follows: 'Great learning' (bāhusacca) is praised as the state of bearing the Teacher's Dispensation in such ways as "he is a bearer of what is heard, an accumulator of what is heard" and "here, someone has heard much, (having heard) the Suttas, Geyyas, and Veyyākaraṇas." This great learning is called a blessing because it is the cause for abandoning the unwholesome and attaining the wholesome, and for gradually realizing the ultimate truth. For the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who is possessed of great learning abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity."

In another discourse, it is said: "He examines the meaning of the teachings he has remembered. When he examines the meaning, the teachings are accepted through reflection. When the teachings are accepted through reflection, desire arises. One who has desire makes an effort. One who makes an effort compares and weighs. One who compares and weighs strives. One who strives realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it penetratingly with wisdom."

Furthermore, the great learning of householders, if it is blameless, should be understood as a blessing because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds.

'Art' (sippa) is of two kinds: the art of householders and the art of non-householders (monastics). Among these, the art of householders refers to crafts such as gem-cutting and goldsmithing that are free from harming others and devoid of the unwholesome. This is a blessing because it brings about welfare in this world. The art of non-householders refers to the preparation of a monk's requisites, such as managing and sewing robes. This blameless art, praised in various discourses as "here, bhikkhus, a monk is skillful in the various duties to be done for his fellow practitioners" and called "a quality that makes for a protector," should be understood as a blessing because it brings about welfare and happiness for both oneself and others in both worlds.

'Discipline' (vinaya) is also of two kinds: the discipline of householders and the discipline of non-householders. Among these, the discipline of householders is the abstinence from the ten unwholesome courses of action. When a person is well-trained in that discipline, it is called a blessing because it brings about welfare in both worlds through the absence of defilement and the establishment of the quality of conduct. (The discipline of non-householders) is the restraint from falling into the seven classes of offenses. When a monk is well-trained in the same manner, it is called a blessing because it brings about happiness in both lives. Alternatively, the fourfold purification of virtue is the discipline of non-householders. Established in that virtue, the monk...
114:
...brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds, and thus it is called a blessing. The discipline of non-householders is the non-committing of the seven classes of offenses. When well-practiced in the manner already stated, or when the fourfold purification of virtue is called the discipline of non-householders, it should be understood as a blessing because, by training in this way, one can reach Arahantship, and thus it is the cause for attaining mundane and supramundane happiness.

'Well-spoken speech' (subhāsitā vācā) is speech free from faults such as lying. As it is said (in the Subhāsita Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta): "Bhikkhus, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken." Or, only speech that is not useless chatter is called well-spoken speech. It is said:

"The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is the best.
One should speak Dhamma, not non-Dhamma; that is the second factor.
One should speak what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant; that is the third factor.
One should speak the truth, not what is false; that is the fourth factor."

This speech should also be understood as a blessing because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds. Although this speech is already included within 'discipline' (vinaya), it should be taken separately without being subsumed under the concept of discipline (or it should be incorporated into discipline). Alternatively, instead of such effort, the speech of teaching Dhamma to others and so forth should be understood here as well-spoken speech. Like living in a suitable locality, that speech is called a blessing because it is a condition for beings to attain welfare in both worlds and Nibbāna. It is said:

"The speech that the Buddha speaks,
For the attainment of secure Nibbāna,
And for making an end of suffering,
That indeed is the most excellent of speeches."

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are taught: great learning, proficiency in arts, well-trained discipline, and well-spoken speech. Their nature as blessings has been clearly explained in their respective places.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with 'Bāhusaccañca' is finished.
115:
## Commentary on the Verse on Supporting Parents

Now, in the phrase "mātāpitu-upaṭṭhānaṃ," the mother and father are referred to as "mātāpitu." "Upaṭṭhānaṃ" means supporting or ministering. Cherishing and supporting sons and wives is called "puttadārassa saṅgaho." Occupations that are not tangled or confused are called "anākulā kammantā." The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā).

As for the explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā), it should be understood thus: She who gives birth to children is called the mother; likewise, he is called the father. Supporting (upaṭṭhānaṃ) means providing assistance by washing their feet, massaging their limbs, bathing them, and by offering the four requisites. In this regard, because parents are of great benefit to their children, desiring their welfare and being compassionate, they are worthy of support. When parents see their young children returning from playing outside with their bodies covered in dust, they wipe away the dust, kiss their heads, embrace them, and feel great affection. Even if children were to carry their parents on their heads for a hundred years and serve them, they would not be able to repay their debt of gratitude. Because parents are the ones who bring up and nourish their children, show them this world, are regarded as Brahma, and are regarded as the first teachers (pubbācariya), supporting them brings praise in this life and the happiness of heaven in the life hereafter. Therefore, it is called a blessing (maṅgala).

For the Blessed One has said:
"Mother and father are called 'Brahma' and 'first teachers';
They are worthy of offerings (āhuneyya) from their children, for they are compassionate toward their offspring.
Therefore, a wise person should pay homage to them and honor them
With food and drink, with clothing and bedding,
By anointing and bathing them, and by washing their feet.
Because of such service to one's parents, the wise
Praise that person in this very life, and after death, he rejoices in heaven."

Another way: Supporting (upaṭṭhānaṃ) consists of five duties, such as maintenance, performing their affairs, and maintaining the family lineage. This should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause of welfare and happiness in the present life through five ways, such as restraining them from evil. For the Blessed One has said:

"Young householder, a child should minister to his parents, who are the eastern direction, in five ways: 'Having been supported by them, I will support them; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage; I will conduct myself in a way worthy of my inheritance; and I will make offerings on behalf of my parents who have passed away.' Young householder, parents thus ministered to by their children in these five ways, show their compassion to their children in five ways: they restrain them from evil, they encourage them in good, they have them trained in arts and sciences, they provide them with a suitable spouse, and at the proper time, they hand over the inheritance."
116:
"...I shall perform their duties, I shall maintain the family lineage, I shall conduct myself in a way worthy of my inheritance, or otherwise, I shall make offerings on behalf of my parents who have passed away." (Thus one should support them). Young householder, when a child ministers to his parents, who are called the eastern direction, in these five ways, the parents show their compassion to the child in five ways: they restrain him from evil, they exhort him to do good, they have him trained in arts and sciences, they provide him with a suitable spouse, and at the proper time, they hand over the inheritance.

Furthermore, he who supports his parents by establishing them in the faith of the Triple Gem, by establishing them in virtue (sīla), or by causing them to go forth into the monkhood, is the foremost among those who support their parents. Such support of one's parents is the repayment of the gratitude for what the parents have done, and because it is the proximate cause for many benefits in the present life and in the life hereafter, it is called a blessing.

In the term "puttadārassa," both sons and daughters born of oneself are counted under the name "putta" (children). "Dārā" refers to any of the twenty types of wives. Children and wife are called "puttadāra." Supporting them through honoring and so forth is called "saṅgaha." This support (saṅgaha) should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause of welfare and happiness in the present life, such as well-organized work. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "The western direction should be known as wife and children." Taking the wife and children mentioned here under the term "bhariyā" (wife), He said: "Young householder, a husband should minister to his wife, who is the western direction, in five ways: by honoring her, by not despising her, by being faithful to her, by handing over authority to her, and by providing her with ornaments. Young householder, a wife thus ministered to by her husband in these five ways, shows her compassion to her husband in five ways: she performs her duties well, she is hospitable to the retinue and household, she is faithful to him, she protects the wealth he has earned, and she is skillful and diligent in all her duties."

Another way: Support (saṅgaha) means cherishing through righteous giving (dāna), pleasant speech (piyavācā), and beneficial conduct (atthacariyā). These include: providing maintenance on Uposatha days, allowing them to see festivals on festival days, performing auspicious ceremonies on auspicious days, and giving advice and instruction regarding welfare in the present life and the hereafter. That blessing of support (saṅgaha-maṅgala) should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause of welfare in the present and the hereafter according to the method already stated, and because it is a state to be honored even by the devas. As Sakka, the king of devas, said: "Mātali, those humans who perform meritorious deeds, who are virtuous, who are lay followers (upāsaka), and who support a wife righteously—to those humans, I pay homage."
117:
Sakka, the king of devas, said to the deva Mātali: 'Those householders who perform merit, are virtuous, are lay followers (upāsakas) who have taken refuge in the Triple Gem, and support their wives righteously—to them I pay homage.'

'Unconfused occupations' (anākulā kammantā) refers to occupations such as farming, cattle-rearing, and trade that are free from confusion—such as acting at the wrong time, acting inappropriately, or acting sluggishly—due to knowing the right time, acting appropriately, being diligent, possessing energetic effort, and acting without failure. These, when practiced skillfully by oneself, one's children and wife, or one's servants and workers, are called blessings because they are the cause for the increase of wealth and grain in this very life. As the Blessed One said:
'One who acts appropriately, is diligent, and energetic gains wealth.'

And:
'One who is habituated to sleeping by day, who hates rising at night, who is constantly intoxicated and addicted to drink, is unable to maintain a household.'

'Saying "It is too cold, it is too hot, it is too late (late at night)," the young man who abandons his work lets opportunities pass him by.'

'But he who regards neither cold nor heat as more than a blade of grass, and performs his duties as a man, does not fall away from happiness.'

'To one who gathers wealth as a bee [collects nectar], wealth accumulates like an anthill.'

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: support for mother, support for father, cherishing wife and children, and unconfused occupations. Or, by splitting the cherishing of wife and children into two, there are five; or by combining the support for mother and father into one, there are three. Their status as blessings has been explained in various places.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with 'Mātāpitu-upaṭṭhānaṃ' is finished.

## Explanation of the Verse Beginning with Dānañca

Now, the meaning of the word 'Dānañca' should be understood. It is called 'dāna' (giving) because it is given by means of this [gift]; it means offering one's own property to another. 'Dhamma-cariyā' means the practice of Dhamma, or conduct not departing from the Dhamma. They are called 'ñātakā' (relatives) because they are known as 'these are our relatives.' 'Anavajjāni kammāni' (blameless actions) refers to actions that are not censurable either in private or in public. The rest of the words are as previously explained. The explanation of the meaning should be understood thus: 'Dāna' is one's own property well-prepared for the sake of another...
118:
Righteous conduct is called 'dhamma-cariyā.' They are called 'ñātakā' (relatives) because they are known as 'these are ours.' 'Anavajjāni' (blameless) means those that are not censurable and are faultless. The rest is as previously explained; this concludes the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā).

The explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā) should be understood as follows: 'Dāna' is the volition (cetanā) of relinquishing the ten kinds of gifts, such as food, preceded by right understanding for the sake of another; or it is the non-greed (alobha) associated with that volition. Indeed, through non-greed, one offers that object to another; therefore it is said, 'It is called dāna because it is given by means of this.' It is called a blessing because it is the cause for attaining special fruits in the present life and in the future, such as being dear and pleasing to many people. In this context, suttas such as 'The donor, Sīha the general, is dear and pleasing to many people' should be remembered.

Another way: Dāna is of two kinds—material gift (āmisa-dāna) and the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna). Among them, material gift is as already described.
