The teaching of the Dhamma proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One, which brings about the end of suffering and happiness in this world and the next, out of a desire for the welfare of others, is called the gift of Dhamma. Of these two kinds of gifts, this gift of Dhamma is supreme. As it is said: 'The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of Dhamma excels all tastes; the delight in Dhamma excels all delights; the destruction of craving overcomes all suffering.'

Among those two, the status of material gift as a blessing has already been stated. As for the gift of Dhamma, it is called a blessing because it is the proximate cause for qualities such as experiencing the meaning. As the Blessed One said: 'Monks, in whatever way a monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and mastered it, in that very way he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.'

'Dhamma-cariyā' means the practice of the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kamma-patha). As the Blessed One said: 'Householders, there are three kinds of righteous conduct and even conduct by way of the body,' and so on. This righteous conduct should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for rebirth in the heavenly world. As the Blessed One said: 'Householders, by reason of righteous conduct and even conduct, some beings here, after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.'

'Relatives' (ñātakā) refers to those connected up to the seventh generation of ancestors, whether from the mother's side or the father's side. Supporting those relatives who come to one when they are afflicted by the loss of wealth or the loss of relatives, with food, water, snacks, grain, etc., as much as one is able, is called a blessing because it is the cause for attaining special present benefits such as praise, and future benefits such as reaching a good destination.

'Blameless actions' (anavajjāni kammāni) refers to observing the Uposatha, performing service (veyyāvacca), planting gardens, building bridges, and so on. These actions are called blessings because they bring about various forms of welfare and happiness.
119:
Relatives are those connected up to the seventh generation of ancestors on both the mother's and father's sides. Supporting such relatives who have come to one's presence, being afflicted by the loss of wealth or by disease, with food, clothing, provisions, grain, and so forth according to one's ability, is called a blessing (maṅgala) because it is a cause for attaining special benefits such as praise in the present life and reaching a happy destination (sugati) in the future life.

Blameless actions refer to wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, such as observing the Uposatha, rendering service (veyyāvacca), planting gardens and groves, and building bridges. These are called blessings because they are causes for attaining various kinds of welfare and happiness. In this context, one should remember such discourses as: "Visākhā, it is possible that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, upon the breakup of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā)."

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are spoken of: giving (dāna), practicing the Dhamma (dhammacariyā), supporting relatives (ñātakānañca saṅgaho), and blameless actions (anavajjāni kammāni). The nature of these as blessings has already been clearly explained in their respective places.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Dānañca" is finished.

## Explanation of the Verse Beginning with Āratī

Now, regarding the terms "āratī" and "viratī": "āratī" means abstaining; "viratī" means refraining particularly, or it is called "virati" because beings particularly refrain from unwholesome states through this restraint. "Pāpa" refers to unwholesome states. Because of the sense of being intoxicating (madanīya), liquor is called "majja"; the drinking of that liquor is "majjapāna"; restraint from that drinking of liquor is "saṃyama". "Appamāda" is non-negligence in wholesome states. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated; this is the word-by-word explanation.

The explanation of the meaning should be understood as follows: "Āratī" is the lack of delight in evil by the mind of one who habitually sees the danger in it. "Viratī" is the refraining by way of body and speech through the doors of action. That "viratī" is of three kinds: situational abstinence (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati). Among these, when a clansman, considering his own birth, family, or lineage, refrains from an object that has come before him, thinking, "This is not fit for me; should I kill this living being? Should I take what is not given?", this is called situational abstinence (sampatta-virati). Abstinence that occurs by the power of undertaking training rules such as "I refrain from taking life" is called abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati). The abstinence associated with the Noble Path (Ariyamagga), from which point onward the clansman no longer commits acts such as taking life, is called abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati). From the moment abstinence by eradication occurs, the five fears and enmities for the Noble Disciple are stilled. Whatever evil there is... in the city of Kusināra, the son of a wealthy man from taking life...
120:
Considering one's birth, family, and lineage, and reflecting, "If I were to kill this living being or take what is not given by another, such an act would not be fit for me," and thus refraining from an object that has come before one, is called situational abstinence (sampatta-virati). Abstinence that proceeds by the power of undertaking training rules is called abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati). From the time of such undertaking, the clansman no longer commits acts such as taking life. Abstinence associated with the Noble Path (Ariyamagga) is called abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati). From the moment this abstinence occurs, the five fears and enmities for the Noble Disciple are stilled. Evil (pāpa) refers to the four unwholesome acts described in detail as: "Young householder, taking life is a defilement of action (kamma-kilesa), taking what is not given... misconduct in sensual pleasures... false speech..." These are the four unwholesome acts. In the verse also, it is summarized: "Taking life, taking what is not given, false speech, and going to another's wife—these the wise do not praise." This refers to refraining from the four unwholesome acts known as defilements of action. Repeatedly abstaining (āratī) and particularly refraining (viratī) from those evils are called blessings because they lead to the attainment of various special benefits, such as the abandonment of fears and enmities in the present life and the future life. In this context, one should remember such discourses as: "Young householder, the Noble Disciple particularly refrains from taking life."

Restraint from drinking intoxicants (majjapāna saṃyama) is a synonym for the previously mentioned abstinence from the training rule of fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence. This is because one who drinks intoxicants does not know what is beneficial or what is the Dhamma; he may cause harm to his mother, father, the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata. In the present life, he receives blame; in the future life, he reaches a miserable destination; and in subsequent lives, he suffers from madness. Restraint from drinking intoxicants stills those faults and brings about the fulfillment of the opposite virtues; therefore, this restraint should be understood as a blessing.

Heedfulness in wholesome states (appamāda) is the opposite of negligence (pamāda), which is described in the Vibhaṅga as: "Lack of thoroughness in the development of wholesome states, lack of persistence, lack of steadfastness, sluggishness, lack of desire, laying down the burden, lack of cultivation, lack of development, lack of frequent practice, lack of resolution, lack of application—this is negligence. Such negligence, being negligent, the state of being negligent, is called negligence." Thus, in terms of meaning, heedfulness should be understood as the non-separation from mindfulness (sati) in wholesome states. Because that heedfulness is the cause for attaining various wholesome states and for attaining the Deathless (Amata), it is called a blessing.
121:
It is said. Regarding this heedfulness (appamāda), one should repeatedly reflect on the Teacher's instruction, such as: "Of one who is heedful and ardent [in burning away defilements]," and "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless," and so forth. Thus, in this verse, three blessings are spoken of: avoidance of evil, restraint from intoxicating drink, and heedfulness in wholesome states. Their nature as blessings has already been clearly explained in their respective places. The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Āratī" is finished.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Gāravo ca"

Now, in this context of "Gāravo ca," etc., "Gāravo" means the state of being respectful. "Nivāto" means the habit of humility. "Santuṭṭhī" means contentment. Knowing the favors done by others is called "Kataññutā" (gratitude). "Kālena" means at the proper time. Listening to the Dhamma is called "Dhammassavana." The remaining words are to be understood in the manner already stated. This is the explanation of the words.

The explanation of the meaning should be understood as follows: Respect (Gārava) is the act of showing reverence, esteem, and the state of being respectful toward those worthy of being treated with esteem, such as the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, the disciples (sāvakas) of the Buddha, teachers, preceptors (upajjhāyas), mother, father, elder brothers, elder sisters, and so forth, as is appropriate. This respect is called a blessing because it is a cause for going to a happy destination (sugati) and so forth. The Blessed One also taught: "He shows respect to those worthy of respect, honors those worthy of honor, and worships those worthy of worship. Because of that kamma thus performed and undertaken, after the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. If he comes to the human world, wherever he is reborn, he is of high birth."

He also taught: "Monks, these seven things lead to non-decline. Which seven? Respect for the Teacher..." Therefore, it is called a blessing.

Humility (Nivāta) means having a humble mind and a humble habit. A person endowed with that humility, having abandoned pride and conceit, humbles himself like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with broken horns, or like a snake with its fangs removed, becoming gentle and mild...
122:
...he is one who speaks pleasantly; this is called humility (nivāta). This humility is called a blessing because it is the cause for obtaining qualities such as retinue and fame. As it is said: "One who is humble in practice and not stubborn, such a person of patient nature gains fame" (D. Ni. 3.273).

Contentment (Santuṭṭhi) means being satisfied with whatever requisites one receives. That contentment is of twelve types. They are: three types regarding robes—contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi), contentment according to one's strength (yathābala-santuṭṭhi), and contentment according to what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi). The same applies to alms-food and the other requisites.

To explain the divisions of that contentment: In this Dispensation, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether it is of good quality or poor quality. He is satisfied with only that which he has received; he does not long for another, and even if he could obtain another, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding robes. However, if a bhikkhu is ill and, when wearing a heavy robe, he stoops or becomes exhausted, and he exchanges it with a compatible bhikkhu and is satisfied even while making do with a light robe, this is his contentment according to his strength regarding robes. Another bhikkhu may be a recipient of refined requisites. When he receives an expensive robe, such as one made of silk, he thinks, "This is suitable for senior elders who have been long ordained and are very learned," and having given it to them, he himself collects old rags from a dust-heap or elsewhere, makes a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi), and is satisfied even while wearing it. This is his contentment according to what is appropriate regarding robes.

In this Dispensation, a bhikkhu receives alms-food, whether it is coarse or refined. He is satisfied with only that which he has received; he does not long for another, and even if he could obtain another, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding alms-food. However, if a bhikkhu is ill and, by eating coarse alms-food, he suffers severe illness or pain, and he gives that food to a compatible bhikkhu and, having eaten ghee, honey, milk, and so forth from that bhikkhu's hand, he performs his recluse duties and is satisfied, this is his contentment according to his strength regarding alms-food. Another bhikkhu receives refined alms-food. He thinks, "This alms-food is suitable for senior elders who have been long ordained and for other fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) who cannot manage without refined alms-food," and having given it to them, he himself goes on alms-round and is satisfied even while eating mixed food. This is his contentment according to what is appropriate regarding alms-food.
123: In this Dispensation, a monk obtains a lodging. He is content with that obtained lodging and does not accept another even if it is better. This is called 'contentment with whatever is obtained' (yathālābhasantosa) regarding lodging. If a monk is ill and, while staying in a windless lodging, is greatly oppressed by bile disorders and the like, he gives that lodging to a compatible monk and stays in a well-ventilated, cool lodging obtained from him. Even while practicing the Dhamma of a recluse there, he remains content. This is called 'contentment according to one's strength' (yathābalasantosa) regarding lodging. Another monk, even upon obtaining an excellent lodging, does not accept it, thinking: 'An excellent lodging is a ground for negligence; sloth and torpor overcome one sitting there, and for one overcome by sleep who then wakes up, sensual thoughts frequently arise.' Rejecting it, he stays anywhere—in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a leaf hut—and remains content. This is called 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding lodging. In this Dispensation, a monk obtains medicine, such as chebulic myrobalan or emblic myrobalan. He is satisfied with just that medicine and does not long for ghee, honey, molasses, and so on obtained by others; even if he receives them, he does not accept them. This is called 'contentment with whatever is obtained' (yathālābhasantosa) regarding medicinal requisites for the sick. If a monk is ill and needs oil but obtains only molasses, he gives that molasses to a compatible monk and, receiving oil from his hand to use as medicine, remains content while practicing the Dhamma of a recluse. This is called 'contentment according to one's strength' (yathābalasantosa) regarding medicinal requisites. Another monk is offered chebulic myrobalan soaked in fermented cow's urine in one vessel and the 'four sweets' (catumadhura) in another, with the words: 'Venerable sir, please take whichever you wish.' Although the illness could be cured by either of these two medicines, he thinks: 'Chebulic myrobalan in fermented urine has been praised by the Buddhas and others,' and 'It is said: "Going forth is based on medicine of fermented urine; therein you should endeavor for the rest of your life."' Thinking thus, he rejects the 'four sweets' and, even while using the fermented urine myrobalan as medicine, remains supremely content. This is called 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding medicinal requisites. All such various types of contentment are called santuṭṭhī. This contentment should be understood as a blessing (maṅgala) because it is the cause for attaining the abandonment of evil states such as great desire, excessive greed, and evil wishes; because it is a cause for a happy destination; because it is a requisite for the Noble Path; and because it is the cause for being unhindered in the four directions. The Buddha also said: ...
124:
"He is unobstructed in the four directions, and is content with whatever is available," and so forth (Sutta Nipāta, 42).

Gratitude (Kataññutā) means knowing a favor done by someone, whether small or great, by repeatedly reflecting on it. In fact, since they protect from sufferings such as hell, only wholesome deeds (puñña) are of great benefit to beings. Remembering the benefit of those wholesome deeds is also to be understood as gratitude. This gratitude is called a blessing because it is a cause for attaining various special qualities, such as being praised by the wise. The Blessed One also said: "Monks, these two persons are rare in the world. Which two? The one who is first to do a favor (pubbakārī) and the one who is grateful and appreciative (kataññū katavedī)." (A. Ni. 2.120).

Timely hearing of the Dhamma (Kālena dhammassavana) means hearing the Dhamma to dispel restlessness (uddhacca) when the mind is associated with it, or when it is overcome by any of the thoughts such as sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka). Other teachers say that hearing the Dhamma once every five days is called timely hearing of the Dhamma. As the Venerable Anuruddha said: "Venerable Sir, every five days we sit together throughout the night for Dhamma talk."

Furthermore, hearing the Dhamma at a time when one can approach good friends (kalyāṇamitta) and listen to the Dhamma that can dispel one's doubts is also to be understood as timely hearing of the Dhamma. As it was said: "They approach from time to time and ask questions..." and so forth. Such timely hearing of the Dhamma is to be understood as a blessing because it is a cause for attaining various special qualities, such as the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), the four advantages, and the destruction of the taints (āsava). For it was said:

"Monks, at the time when a noble disciple pays attention, applies his mind, concentrates his whole heart, and listens to the Dhamma with attentive ears, at that time the five hindrances do not exist in him."

"Monks, for those who have heard the Dhamma... and have well-penetrated it, four advantages are to be expected."

"Monks, these four things, when rightly developed and rightly practiced from time to time, lead gradually to the destruction of the taints. Which four? Timely hearing of the Dhamma is one of them," and so forth.
125:
Thus, in this verse, five blessings are spoken of: respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, and listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. Their nature as blessings has already been clearly explained in their respective places. The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Gāravo ca" is finished.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Khantī ca"

Now, in this verse "Khantī ca," patience is called "Khanti." Because he is easy to instruct with respect, he has speech that is easy to speak to; therefore, he is called "Suvaca" (amenable). The conduct of one who is easy to admonish is called "Sovacassa." The state of the conduct of one who is easy to admonish is called "Sovacassatā" (obedience/amenability). Because their defilements are stilled, they are called "Samaṇas" (ascetics/monks). "Dassana" means seeing or beholding. Discussing the Dhamma together is called "Dhammasākacchā." The remaining words are to be understood in the manner already stated. This is the explanation of the words.

The explanation of the meaning should be understood as follows: Patience (Khanti) is the patience of endurance (adhivāsana-khanti). A monk endowed with that patience, even when people abuse him with the ten grounds for abuse, or when they harass him by killing, binding, and so forth, remains without alteration, as if not hearing and as if not seeing, like the ascetic Khantivādī. Regarding this meaning, it was taught: "In the past, there was an ascetic who demonstrated only patience; the King of Kāsi mutilated him while he stood firm in that very patience."

Or else, like the Venerable Puṇṇa, he attends to it wisely because there is no fault beyond that. That Venerable Puṇṇa said: "Venerable Sir, if the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, then I will think: 'These people of Sunāparanta are truly good, they are very good, because they do not strike me with their hands,'" and so forth.

One who is endowed with such patience is worthy of praise even by virtuous ascetics. The ascetic Sarabhaṅga said this -
126:
"Having slain anger, one never sorrows;
the sages praise the abandoning of hypocrisy.
Endure the harsh speech of all;
the virtuous call this the supreme patience."

One endowed with patience is also praised by the devas. As Sakka, the lord of devas, said:
"When one who is strong endures one who is weak,
the virtuous call that the supreme patience;
the weak must always endure."

One endowed with patience is also praised by the Buddhas. As the Blessed One said:
"He who, without anger, endures abuse, beating, and binding,
him whose army is the strength of patience, I call a Brahmin."

That patience should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for attaining these praised virtues and other qualities mentioned here.

"Sovacassatā" (obedience) means that when one is addressed by fellow practitioners in accordance with the Dhamma, one does not resort to evasion, silence, or fault-finding, but instead follows the advice with great respect and reverence, saying, "It is well." This obedience is called a blessing because it is the cause for receiving advice and instruction from fellow practitioners, and because it is the cause for abandoning faults and attaining virtues.

"Seeing recluses" (samaṇānaṃ dassanaṃ) means approaching, attending to, recollecting, listening to, and beholding those recluses whose defilements are calmed, who have developed the body, speech, mind, and wisdom, and who are endowed with supreme restraint and tranquility. All these are collectively called "seeing" (dassana) in a concise sense. Such seeing should be understood as a blessing because it is of great benefit. Why? Because it brings much assistance. The Blessed One also said: "Monks, I say that seeing those monks is of great benefit," and so forth.

Therefore, a clansman who desires his welfare, upon seeing virtuous monks arriving at his door, should honor them with offerings to the best of his ability if he has them. If he has none, he should pay homage with the fivefold prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita). If he cannot do that, he should salute them with joined palms. If he cannot even do that, he should look upon them with a clear mind and affectionate eyes. Due to the merit based on such seeing, for many thousands of births, one will not suffer from eye diseases, inflammation, squinting, or blemishes, but will possess clear, five-colored, and glorious eyes. Those eyes will be like the blue sapphire shutters opened in a celestial mansion. For a hundred thousand eons, in the worlds of devas and humans, the pleasures and prosperity...
127:
Diseases, burning sensations, protrusions, or boils do not occur in the eyes. The eyes possess the splendor of the five clear colors and are magnificent, resembling sapphire door-leaves opened in a jewel mansion. One obtains prosperity in the celestial and human worlds for a duration of a hundred thousand aeons. It is not surprising that a wise human being should experience such a fulfillment of results due to the merit consisting of seeing a monk (samaṇadassana), which has been properly performed. For even in the case of those who have gone to the animal realm, the fulfillment of results from seeing a monk, performed with mere faith, is praised thus:

“This owl, with round eyes, a long-time resident of Vediyaka, this Kosiya is indeed happy; he sees the Excellent Buddha who has arisen in the morning.

Having gained confidence of heart in me and in the unsurpassed Saṅgha of monks, this owl will not go to a state of misery for a hundred thousand aeons.

Passing away from the celestial world, urged by his wholesome kamma, he will become a Paccekabuddha of infinite wisdom, renowned as Somanassa.” (Thus He said).

Timely discussion of the Dhamma (kālena dhammasākacchā) means that at the first watch of the night or at dawn, two monks who are bearers of the Suttas discuss a Sutta with each other; or those who know the Vinaya discuss the Vinaya, those who know the Abhidhamma discuss the Abhidhamma, those who know the Jātakas discuss the Jātakas, and those who know the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) discuss the Commentaries. Or they discuss at various times to purify the mind oppressed by sloth, distraction, or doubt. This is called timely discussion of the Dhamma. It is called a blessing because it is the cause of qualities such as proficiency in the scriptures (āgama-byatti).

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: patience (khantī), obedience (sovacassatā), seeing monks (samaṇadassanaṃ), and timely discussion of the Dhamma (kālena dhammasākacchā). Their nature as blessings has already been explained in their respective places.

## The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with 'Khantī ca' is finished.
128:
## Explanation of the Verse Beginning with 'Tapo ca'

Now, in this word 'tapo ca', it is called 'tapa' because it burns away (tapati) evil unwholesome states. 'Brahmacariya' means the sublime practice, or the practice of the sublime ones; it means the excellent practice. Seeing the Noble Truths is 'ariyasaccāna-dassana'. Some teachers recite it as 'ariyasaccāni dassanaṃ', but such a recitation is not good. It is called 'Nibbāna' because it has departed from the entanglement (vāna) of craving. Realization is 'sacchikiriyā'. Realizing Nibbāna is 'nibbāna-sacchikiriyā'. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. This is the word-by-word explanation (pada-vaṇṇanā).

The explanation of the meaning should be understood thus: 'Tapa' refers to the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara) because it burns away unwholesome states such as covetousness and grief. Or it is energy (vīriya) because it burns away laziness. A person endowed with these qualities is called 'ardent' (ātāpī). This 'tapa' should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for abandoning covetousness and so on, and for attaining states such as the jhānas.

'Brahmacariya' is a term for abstinence from sexual intercourse, the practice of a monk (samaṇa-dhamma), the Dispensation (Sāsana), and the Path (Magga). For instance, in passages such as 'Having abandoned unchastity, he is a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī)', abstinence from sexual intercourse is called 'brahmacariya'. In passages such as 'Friend, is the holy life (brahmacariya) lived under the Blessed One? Yes, friend', the practice of a monk is called 'brahmacariya'. In passages such as 'O Evil One, I shall not pass away into final Nibbāna until this holy life (brahmacariya) of mine is successful, prosperous, widespread, and known by many', the Dispensation is called 'brahmacariya'. In passages such as 'Monk, this Noble Eightfold Path itself is the holy life (brahmacariya), namely, Right View...', the Path is called 'brahmacariya'. Here, however, since the Path is included later by 'seeing the Noble Truths', all the remaining meanings of 'brahmacariya' are appropriate. This 'brahmacariya' should also be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for the progressive attainment of various specific distinctions.

'Ariyasaccāna-dassana' means seeing the Path through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths mentioned in the 'Questions of the Boy' (Kumārapañha). Seeing that Path is called a blessing because it is the cause for transcending the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra).

'Nibbāna-sacchikiriyā' here refers to the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) as Nibbāna. That Fruition of Arahantship is also called Nibbāna because it has departed from craving, which is called 'vāna' (entanglement) in the five destinations of rebirth.
129:
The attainment of that Fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala), or its reviewing, or its realization (sacchikiriyā) is so called. As for the other Nibbāna, its realization is accomplished simply by seeing the Noble Truths; therefore, that aspect of Nibbāna is not intended here. Thus, this realization of the Fruition of Arahantship should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for dwelling in happiness in the present life (diṭṭhadhammika-sukhavihāra) and so forth.

In this way, in this verse, four blessings are stated: austerity (tapo), the holy life (brahmacariya), seeing the Noble Truths, and the realization of Nibbāna. The nature of these as blessings has already been clearly explained in their respective places.

The commentary on the meaning of the verse beginning with "Tapo ca" is finished.

## Commentary on the Verse: Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi

Now, in the phrase "Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi", "phuṭṭhassa" means touched, contacted, or reached. "Lokadhammā" are the conditions that occur in the world; it means those things that are unavoidable as long as the process of the world exists. "Cittaṃ" means the mind or heart. "Yassa" refers to the mind of a monk, whether junior, middle-seated, or senior. "Na kampati" means it does not shake, it does not waver. "Asokaṃ" means without sorrow, having the thorn of sorrow pulled out. "Virajaṃ" means free from the dust of defilements, having the dust of defilements destroyed. "Khemaṃ" means without fear, free from danger. The rest is as previously explained. This is the word-by-word commentary.

The explanation of the meaning should be understood thus: "The mind of him which, when touched by worldly conditions, does not shake" means the mind of an Arahant which, when touched or overwhelmed by the eight worldly conditions such as gain and loss, does not shake, does not move, and does not waver. That mind of such a person should be understood as a blessing because it cannot be shaken by anything and because it brings about the state of the supreme supramundane.

Whose mind is it that does not shake when touched by these? Only the mind of an Arahant whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), and no one else's. For it is said:

"Just as a solid rock is not moved by the wind,
So also forms, tastes, sounds, smells, and all touches;
Desirable and undesirable things do not cause the mind of such a one to waver.
His mind is steady and liberated, and he contemplates their passing away."
130:
"Asokaṃ" (sorrowless) refers specifically to the mind of an Arahant. Because that mind is free from sorrow (soka), which is described as "sorrow, the act of sorrowing, the state of sorrowing, inner sorrow, inner deep sorrow, the state of the mind being consumed," and so forth, it is called "asokaṃ". Some teachers say "asokaṃ" refers to Nibbāna, but that does not connect well with the preceding phrase "the mind of him which, when touched by worldly conditions, does not shake". Just like "asokaṃ", "virajaṃ" (stainless) and "khemaṃ" (secure) also refer to the mind of an Arahant. That mind is "virajaṃ" because it is free from the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion. It is "khemaṃ" because it is secure from the four bonds (yoga). Therefore, these qualities should be understood as blessings because, when taken in their respective aspects at each moment of occurrence as pointed out, although they are threefold, they bring about the supreme supramundane state such as the non-occurrence of the aggregates, and they bring about the state of being worthy of offerings (āhuneyya) and so forth.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: a mind unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, a sorrowless mind, a stainless mind, and a secure mind. The nature of these as blessings has already been clearly shown in their respective places.

The commentary on the meaning of the verse "Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi" is finished.

## Commentary on the Verse: Etādisāni

Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the thirty-eight great blessings through the ten verses beginning with "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ", now spoke the final verse beginning with "Etādisāni katvāna", wishing to praise those very blessings he had taught.

The commentary on its meaning is as follows: "Etādisāni" means such as these blessings of the kind I have taught, such as not associating with fools. "Katvāna" means having done. The words "katvāna", "katvā", and "karitvā" are identical in meaning. "Sabbatthamaparājitā" means being unconquered in all places by even one of the four enemies known as the Maras: the Mara of the aggregates (khandha-māra), the Mara of defilements (kilesa-māra), the Mara of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-māra), and the Mara as a deity (devaputta-māra); it means they themselves have conquered these four Maras. Here, the letter "ma" should be understood as a mere euphonic junction (padasandhi).

"Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti" means that by performing such blessings, they become unconquered by the four Maras and reach well-being (sotthi) in all places, in this world and the next, and in all postures such as standing and walking. They reach well-being because the distresses that would arise from associating with fools and so forth no longer exist. It means they go without calamity, without blame, without fear, and without enmity. In the word "sotthiṃ", it should be understood that the niggahita is inserted for the sake of the metrical smoothness of the verse.
131:
It means that because there is no exhaustion or distress caused by the taints (āsavas), they reach safety, being free from danger, free from blame, secure, and without fear. In this word 'sotthiṃ', it should be understood that the nasal sound (anunāsika) is added for the sake of the metrical ease of the verse.

With the verse "Taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ", the Blessed One concluded the teaching. How? Thus: "O deity, those gods and humans who perform such blessings reach safety in all places. Therefore, consider these thirty-eight types of blessings, starting from not associating with fools, as the highest, most excellent, and noble for those who practice them."

When the Blessed One concluded the teaching in this way, one hundred thousand crores of deities attained the Fruit of Arahatship. The number of those who attained the Fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, and Non-returning was incalculable. Then, on the second day, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, last night a certain deity approached me and asked a question about blessings. Then I spoke the thirty-eight blessings to that deity. Ānanda, learn this discourse on blessings; having learned it, teach it to the monks." The Elder learned it and taught it to the monks. This Mangala Sutta has been handed down through the lineage of teachers until today. Thus, it should be known that this holy life (dispensation) is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.

Now, to gain proficiency in the practice of knowledge regarding these blessings, the connection from the beginning is as follows: Thus, these beings who desire happiness in this world, the next world, and the supramundane, having abandoned association with fools, relying on the wise, honoring those worthy of honor, living in a suitable locality, being prompted toward wholesome states due to having performed merit in the past, establish themselves rightly. Being adorned with great learning, skills, and discipline, they speak well-spoken words in accordance with the discipline. As long as they do not renounce the lay life, they clear their old debts by supporting their parents. They create new debts by supporting their wives and children. They achieve prosperity in wealth and grain by engaging in uncomplicated work. They take the essence of wealth through giving, and the essence of life through practicing the Dhamma. They benefit their own people by supporting relatives, and benefit others by doing blameless work. By abstaining from evil, they avoid harming others; by restraint from intoxicants, they avoid harming themselves. Being diligent in wholesome qualities, they increase the side of merit. Having increased merit, even if they renounce the lay appearance and remain in the state of a monk, they fulfill the completion of duties through respect and humility toward the Buddha, the Buddha's disciples, preceptors, teachers, and so on.
132:
By being easily contented, they abandon greed for requisites; by being grateful, they stand on the ground of the virtuous; by listening to the Dhamma, they abandon mental sluggishness; by patience, they overcome all dangers; by being easy to admonish, they make themselves ones who have a refuge; by seeing recluses, they observe the application of practice; by discussing the Dhamma, they dispel doubts regarding things that are grounds for doubt; by the practice of sense-restraint (indriya-saṃvara), they fulfill the purification of virtue; by the holy life of a recluse's practice, they fulfill the purification of mind; and thereafter, they fulfill the four higher purifications. Through this practice, reaching the purification of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi) which is the means of seeing the Noble Truths, they realize Nibbāna, known as the Fruit of Arahatship. Having realized that Fruit of Arahatship, just as the King of Mountains, Sineru, is unshaken by wind and rain, they have minds that are unshaken by the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma), being sorrowless, stainless, and secure. Those who are secure are undefeated by anyone in all places and go in safety everywhere. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Having performed such things, being undefeated everywhere,
They go in safety everywhere; that is their supreme blessing."

## In the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Explanation of the Mangala Sutta is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Ratana Sutta
## The Purpose of Placement

Now, the sequence for explaining the meaning of the Ratana Sutta, which is placed immediately after the Mangala Sutta starting with "Yānīdha bhūtāni", has arrived. Having stated the purpose of placing the Ratana Sutta here, and thereafter, in order to show the entry into the meaning of this Sutta with a well-purified origin, just as one enters and takes water from rivers and lakes through a well-purified landing place:

"By whom, when, where, and for what reason this was spoken—having shown this method, I shall perform the explanation of the meaning of this Ratana Sutta."
133:
In this context, because the Maṅgala Sutta demonstrates self-protection and the destruction of the āsavas (cankers) which have as their cause the performance of unwholesome and wholesome deeds, and this Ratana Sutta accomplishes the protection of others and the destruction of the āsavas which have as their cause non-human beings and so forth, therefore, the Ratana Sutta should be placed immediately after that Maṅgala Sutta. This is the first purpose for placing the Ratana Sutta here.

## The Story of Vesālī

Now, regarding the phrase "By whom was it spoken, when, where, and for what reason?", it is said: This Ratana Sutta was spoken by the Blessed One himself, and not by disciples or others. And it was spoken at that time when the city of Vesālī was oppressed by calamities such as famine, and the Licchavī princes invited the Blessed One from the city of Rājagaha to Vesālī; it was spoken then in Vesālī for the purpose of dispelling those calamities. This is the brief answer to those questions. In detail, however, the ancient teachers have commented starting from the story of Vesālī.

In that context, this is the detailed explanation: It is said that a fetus was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. The queen, knowing this, informed the king. The king provided the protection for the fetus. When the fetus was fully matured after being well-protected, she entered the maternity chamber. For meritorious women, childbirth usually occurs at the time of dawn. She was one of those meritorious women; therefore, at the time of dawn, she gave birth to a lump of flesh resembling the color of a Bandhujīvaka flower placed in a red lac solution. Then, thinking, "Other queens give birth to sons resembling golden statues, but I, the chief queen, have given birth to a lump of flesh; disgrace may come upon me in the presence of the king," and fearing that disgrace, she placed that lump of flesh in a vessel, covered it with another vessel, sealed it with the royal seal, and had it cast into the current of the Ganges. As soon as it was discarded by humans, the deities provided protection. They also tied a golden plate there, having written with cinnabar, "The offspring of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī." Then, that vessel traveled along the current of the Ganges, unmolested by dangers such as waves.

At that time, a certain ascetic lived on the bank of the Ganges, supported by a family of cowherds. As that ascetic was descending to the Ganges early in the morning, he saw the vessel coming...
134:
Upon seeing the vessel, he took it, thinking it was a discarded cloth (paṃsukūla). Then, seeing the inscribed plate and the royal seal on that vessel, he opened it and saw the lump of flesh. Seeing it, the thought occurred to him, "This might be a fetus, for it has no foul or putrid smell." He took it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean spot.

Then, after the lapse of half a month, it became two lumps of flesh. The ascetic saw this and kept them well. Then again, after the lapse of half a month, five buds appeared on each lump of flesh for the development of hands, feet, and head. The ascetic saw this and again kept them well. Then, after the lapse of half a month, one lump of flesh became a boy resembling a golden statue, and one lump of flesh became a girl. A parental affection for those children arose in the ascetic. Milk came out from the ascetic's thumb. From that time on, he obtained milk-rice; he himself ate the rice and poured the milk into the mouths of the children. Whatever food entered the stomachs of those children could be clearly seen from the outside, as if placed in a crystal bowl. In this way, they became the Licchavīs. Other teachers, however, say, "They had skin that was attached to each other as if it had been sewn together." Thus, they became known as 'Licchavī' either because of having no skin (nicchavi) or because of having attached skin (līnacchavi).

As the ascetic was busy nurturing the children, he entered the village for alms late in the morning and returned very late in the day. Knowing that preoccupation of the ascetic, the cowherds said, "Venerable sir, nurturing children is an obstacle for those who have gone forth. Give these children to us; we will nurture them. May you, venerable sir, strive only in your own ascetic practices." The ascetic consented, saying, "Very well." On the next day, the cowherds leveled the road, scattered flowers, raised banners and flags, and came to the hermitage playing various musical instruments. The ascetic said, "These children are of great merit; nurture them to grow without negligence. When they have grown up, perform marriages between them. Please the king with the five products of the cow, obtain a piece of land, and build a city. In that city, consecrate the prince and appoint him as king," and then he handed over the children. They also consented, saying, "Very well," and took the children away to nurture them.

When the children reached the proper age, while playing in places of dispute, they would strike other cowherd children with their hands and feet. Those children would cry. When asked by their parents, "Why are you crying?", they said, "These children, who have no parents and were raised by the ascetic, beat us excessively." Then the parents of those children said, "These children harass other children and cause them suffering; these children should not be associated with, they should be avoided (vajjitabba)." From that time on, that region...
135:
That region, measuring three hundred yojanas in circumference, is called 'Vajjī'. At that time, cowherds, having pleased the king, took possession of that region. Having founded a city there, they consecrated a sixteen-year-old prince and made him king. Having arranged a marriage for that prince with a certain maiden, they made a pact: 'No maiden shall be brought in from outside, and this maiden of ours shall not be given to anyone else.' From their first union, two children were born—a daughter and a son; in this manner, two were born each time for sixteen times. Then, as those children grew up in due course, that city became insufficient to accommodate their residences, gardens, and retinues. Therefore, they enclosed the city with walls three times, each at an interval of one gāvuta. Because that city was repeatedly made wide (visālī-kata), it came to be known as 'Vesālī'. This is the story of Vesālī.

## Inviting the Blessed One

This city of Vesālī was prosperous and reached the height of abundance at the time of the Buddha's appearance. In that city, there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings. Likewise, there were sub-kings, generals, treasurers, and so forth. As it is said:

'At that time, Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food. There were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven palaces; seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven gabled houses; seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven parks; and seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven lotus ponds.'

At a later time, that city of Vesālī suffered from famine due to drought and poor harvests. First, the poor people died, and their bodies were discarded outside the city. Due to the stench of the corpses, non-human beings (demons) entered the city, and then even more people died. Because of that loathsomeness, the ahivātaka disease (plague) broke out among living beings. Thus, the inhabitants of Vesālī, oppressed by these three fears—famine, non-human beings, and disease—approached the king and said, 'Great King, three kinds of fear have arisen in this city. Such fears have never occurred before in this city for seven generations of royal lineages. We think it is because you, the King, do not observe the Dhamma.' The King then assembled all the citizens at the royal pavilion and said, 'Investigate and reflect upon whether I have practiced unrighteously.' Although all those citizens investigated the entire lineage, they did not see even a single fault. Then, not seeing any fault in the king, they deliberated, 'How shall we appease this fear for ourselves?' At that time, some people pointed towards the six great heretical teachers.
136:
'This danger has arisen now because of your unrighteousness,' they submitted. The king assembled all the people in the assembly hall and said, 'Investigate my unrighteous conduct.' Those people investigated the entire tradition but did not see any fault.

Then, seeing no fault in the king, they deliberated, 'How shall we appease this danger for ourselves?' Among them, some pointed to the six teachers, saying, 'The danger will be appeased just by their arrival.' Others, however, said, 'It is heard that a Buddha has appeared in the world. That Blessed One preaches the Dhamma for the benefit of all beings; He possesses great psychic power and majesty. By the mere arrival of that Blessed One, all dangers would be appeased.' Because of those words, they were delighted and said, 'Where does that Blessed One dwell now? Even if sent for by us, He might not come.' Then others said, 'Buddhas are compassionate; why would He not come? However, that Blessed One is currently dwelling in the city of Rājagaha. King Bimbisāra is attending to Him, so that king might not allow Him to come.'

'In that case, let us inform the king and invite Him,' they planned. They sent two Licchavī kings to King Bimbisāra with a large army and many gifts, saying, 'Persuade King Bimbisāra and bring the Blessed One.' They went, presented the gifts to the king, informed him of the situation, and said, 'Great King, please send the Blessed One to our city.' King Bimbisāra did not give a direct promise but said, 'You yourselves should know [how to proceed].'

Those kings approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and submitted: 'Venerable Sir, three fears have arisen in our city. If the Blessed One were to come, it would be for our welfare.' The Blessed One, having reflected, accepted the invitation, perceiving: 'When the Ratana Sutta is recited in Vesālī, that protection will spread throughout a hundred thousand crores of world-systems. At the conclusion of the Sutta, eighty-four thousand beings will realize the Dhamma.'

Then King Bimbisāra, hearing that the Blessed One had accepted, had a proclamation made by beat of drum in the city: 'The Blessed One has accepted to go to Vesālī.' He approached the Blessed One and asked, 'Venerable Sir, do You accept the journey to Vesālī?' When the Buddha replied, 'Yes, Great King,' the king said, 'Venerable Sir, in that case, please wait for a while until I prepare the road.'

Then King Bimbisāra leveled the five-yojana stretch of land between Rājagaha and the Ganges River, built a monastery at every yojana, and informed the Blessed One of the time to depart. The Blessed One, with five hundred monks...
137:
The Blessed One set out, surrounded by five hundred monks. King Bimbisāra had the five-league road strewn knee-deep with flowers of five colors. He had banners, flags, full pots, plantain trees, and other decorations set up. He caused two white umbrellas to be held over the Blessed One and one white umbrella over each monk. Accompanied by his retinue, he made offerings of flowers, scents, and other requisites. He invited the Blessed One to stay at each monastery along the way, offered great alms, and in five days, escorted Him to the banks of the river Gaṅgā. There, while decorating a boat with all kinds of ornaments, he sent a message to the princes of Vesālī: "The Blessed One has arrived; prepare the way and come to welcome the Blessed One."

Those princes of Vesālī thought, "We shall perform double the honors." They leveled the three-league ground between Vesālī and the Gaṅgā. They prepared four white umbrellas for the Blessed One and two white umbrellas for each monk. Performing their offerings, they came to the banks of the river Gaṅgā and stood there.

Then, King Bimbisāra joined two boats together, constructed a pavilion, and decorated it with floral garlands and other ornaments. In that pavilion, he prepared a Buddha-seat made of all kinds of jewels, and the Blessed One sat there. The five hundred monks also boarded the boat and sat in their appropriate places. As the King followed the Blessed One, he waded into the water up to his neck and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall remain right here on the bank of the Gaṅgā until the Blessed One returns," and then he turned back. Above, the devas and brahmas performed offerings as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. Below, the Naga kings such as Kambala and Assatara, who dwelt in the Gaṅgā, performed their offerings. Thus, with great honor, the Blessed One traveled a distance of one league on the Gaṅgā and entered the territory of the Vesālī princes.

Then the Licchavī princes, performing double the honors compared to those of King Bimbisāra, came to welcome the Blessed One in the water up to their necks. At that very moment, at that very instant, a great rain cloud (Mahāmegha) arose from the four quarters, with its peak of dark clouds spreading and flashing with lightning, and it thundered loudly. Then, as soon as the Blessed One set His first foot on the bank of the Gaṅgā, the Pokkharavassa rain fell. Only those who wished to get wet became wet; those who did not wish to get wet did not. In all places, water flowed to the depth of the knees, the thighs, the waist, and the neck. The current of water swept all the carcasses into the Gaṅgā, and the surface of the earth became exceedingly pure.

The Licchavī princes invited the Blessed One to stay at every league along the way, offered great alms, and for three days, while performing double the honors, they proceeded toward the city of Vesālī...
138:
They escorted Him. When the Blessed One arrived at the city of Vesālī, Sakka, the king of devas, arrived surrounded by a host of devas. Due to the assembly of powerful devas, the non-human beings (amanussa) mostly fled. The Blessed One stood at the city gate and addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, learn this Ratana Sutta, take the materials for offerings, and together with the Licchavī princes, wander between the three walls of Vesālī and perform the protection (paritta)." He then recited the Ratana Sutta. The answers to the questions, "Who spoke this sutta, when, where, and why?" have been explained in detail by the ancient teachers starting from the story of Vesālī.

Thus, on the very day the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, the Venerable Ānanda learned this Ratana Sutta, which was spoken at the gate of Vesālī for the purpose of warding off those calamities. Reciting it for protection, he took water in the Blessed One's alms-bowl and went about sprinkling it throughout the entire city. As soon as the Elder began reciting "Yaṃ kiñci," those non-human beings who had not fled before and were clinging to heaps of rubbish, walls, and other places, fled through the four gates. The gates became congested. Then, some non-human beings, finding no room at the gates, broke through the walls and fled. As soon as the non-human beings had left, the diseases in the bodies of the humans were appeased. They came out and honored the Elder with all kinds of flowers, scents, and other offerings. The people smeared the Santhāgāra hall in the center of the city with all kinds of perfumes, hung a canopy, decorated it with all ornaments, prepared a Buddha-seat there, and invited the Blessed One.

The Blessed One entered the Santhāgāra and sat on the prepared seat. The community of monks, the kings, and the people also sat in their appropriate seats. Sakka, the king of devas, also sat down with the divine assembly from the two deva worlds, as did other devas. The Venerable Ānanda, having wandered through the whole of Vesālī and established protection, came with the inhabitants of Vesālī and sat on one side. There, the Blessed One recited that very same Ratana Sutta to the entire assembly.

By this much, the introductory outline (mātikā) that was set down as "Who spoke it, when, where, and why... having revealed this method," has been detailed in all its aspects.
139:
## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with Yānīdha

Now, as promised by the statement "I shall provide the commentary on its meaning," the commentary begins. Other teachers, however, say: "The Blessed One spoke only the first five verses, and the remaining verses were spoken by the Elder Ānanda at the time of performing the protection (paritta)." Be that as it may, what benefit is there for us in such investigation? In every way, I shall provide the commentary on the meaning of this Ratana Sutta.

"Yānīdha bhūtāni" is the first verse. In that verse, "yāni" refers to those deities, whether of low power or high power. "Idha" refers to this place, meaning the place of assembly at that moment. Regarding the word "bhūtāni," the term "bhūta" is used in various senses: in "bhūtasmiṃ pācittiyaṃ," etc., it means what is manifest; in "bhūtamidaṃ bhikkhave samanupassatha," etc., it refers to the five aggregates; in "cattāro kho bhikkhu mahābhūtā hetū," etc., it refers to the four great elements such as the earth element; in "yo ca kālaghaso bhūto," etc., it refers to an Arahant; in "sabbeva nikkhipissanti bhūtā loke samussayaṃ," etc., it refers to all sentient beings; in "bhūtagāmapātabyatāya," etc., it refers to plants and trees; in "bhūtaṃ bhūtato sañjānāti," etc., it refers to the collection of beings below the Cātumahārājikā realm. However, in this context, it should be understood specifically as non-human beings (amanussa).

"Samāgatāni" means assembled together. "Bhummāni" means those (deities) born on the earth. The word "vā" is used in the sense of an alternative (vikappa). By that word "vā," one alternative is made: "Whatever terrestrial beings are assembled here," and then to make a second alternative, it says "yāni ca antalikkhe." The meaning is: "Or whatever beings (deities) born in the sky are all assembled here."

In this verse, the beings born from the Yāma realm up to the Akanittha realm are to be understood as "beings in the sky" because they are born in celestial mansions manifest in the sky. Below the Yāma realm, from Mount Sineru down to the earth, there are deities residing in trees, vines, and so on, as well as deities born on the earth. All those are to be understood as "terrestrial beings" because they are born on the earth or on things connected to the earth, such as trees, vines, and mountains.
140:
Thus, the Blessed One, having distinguished all non-human beings with the two phrases "bhummāni vā yāni ca antalikkhe," spoke "sabbeva bhūtā sumanā bhavantu" to show them by including them again with a single phrase. "Sabbe" means all without exception. "Eva" is used for emphasis, meaning including everyone without excluding even one. "Bhūtā" means non-humans. "Sumanā bhavantu" means may they be happy-minded, possessing joy and gladness. "Athopi" is a combination of two particles used when transitioning from one matter to another. "Sakkacca suṇantu bhāsitaṃ" means listen respectfully to my teaching, which brings celestial fortune and supramundane happiness, by paying attention, reflecting, and focusing the mind entirely.

Thus, in this context, the Blessed One included the deities with the general statement "yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatāni," then distinguished them into two types with "bhummāni vā yāni ca antalikkhe," and then brought them together again with "sabbeva bhūtā." He concluded the verse by enjoining them in the perfection of disposition (āsayasampatti) with the words "sumanā bhavantu," and in the perfection of application (payogasampatti) with the words "sakkacca suṇantu bhāsitaṃ," as well as in the perfection of wise reflection (yonisomanasikārasampatti) and the perfection of hearing from others (paratoghosasampatti), and likewise in the perfection of right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi), the perfection of associating with the virtuous (sappurisūpanissaya), and the perfection of the causes of concentration and wisdom.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with Tasmā Hi

"Tasmā hi bhūtā" etc. is the second verse. In that verse, "tasmā" is a word indicating a reason. "Bhūtā" is a word of address (vocative). "Nisāmetha" means listen. "Sabbe" means all without exception. What is meant is: "Since you all have abandoned your celestial abodes and the abundance of enjoyments there and have assembled here for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, and not for the purpose of seeing dances and plays, etc., therefore, O beings, all of you listen and pay attention."

Alternatively, seeing their state of being happy-minded and their desire to listen respectfully through the words "sumanā bhavantu, sakkacca suṇantu," He said: "Because (yasmā) you are endowed with the purity of disposition through right self-direction, wise reflection, and happy-mindedness, and with the purity of application through the desire to listen respectfully, which has as its proximate cause the association with the virtuous and hearing from others, therefore (tasmā hi), O beings, all of you listen and pay attention." Or else...
141:
Referring to the word "spoken" (bhāsitaṃ) at the end of the previous verse, and wishing to show the reason, He said: "Therefore, O spirits, all of you, listen and attend." Why? Because what is called the utterance of the Buddha is extremely rare, as the moment of a Buddha's arising (buddhupāda), which is free from the eight inopportune moments (aṭṭhakkhaṇa), is difficult to obtain. Furthermore, it can bring about many benefits through the power of Great Compassion. Because I, the Buddha, wish to speak such a beneficial Dhamma, I said, "Listen to what is spoken." Therefore, He preached this verse-line: "Tasmā hi bhūtā nisāmetha sabbe" (Therefore, O spirits, all of you, listen).

Having established the reason in this way and urged them to listen to His words, He began to preach the subject to be reflected upon, saying: "Show loving-kindness to the human race." The meaning is: Show loving-kindness—which consists of affection and the desire for their welfare—towards these human beings who are being oppressed by the three calamities. Some teachers read "mānusikaṃ pajaṃ," but this is not appropriate as it does not fit the sense of "dwelling on the earth." The interpretations of other teachers are also not appropriate. The intention here is: I, the Buddha, do not speak with the authority of being a Buddha, but rather, I say, "Show loving-kindness to the human race" for your benefit and for the benefit of these human beings. In this regard:

"Those royal seers who, having conquered the earth with its many inhabitants,
Went about performing sacrifices:
Assamedha, Purisamedha,
Sammāpāsa, Vājapeyya, and Niraggaḷa.

They do not experience even a sixteenth part
Of the benefit of a well-developed heart of loving-kindness.
If a person, with a heart free from ill-will,
Develops loving-kindness even towards a single being,
He becomes meritorious because of that.

A virtuous person who feels compassion for all beings in his mind
Performs abundant merit."

It should be understood that for those who develop loving-kindness through the power of such Sutta discourses and the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, that loving-kindness brings welfare.

"A person who is protected by the devas always sees auspicious things." ...
142:
It should be understood that for those who develop loving-kindness through the power of such Sutta discourses, that loving-kindness brings welfare. Thus, wishing to show the benefit to both devas and humans, He said, "Show loving-kindness to the human race," and now, wishing to show the help rendered [by humans], He said: "Those who bring offerings (bali) day and night, therefore, protect them diligently."

The meaning of that verse is: Those humans who, having made images such as paintings or wood carvings, approach shrines, trees, and the like, and make offerings during the day dedicated to the devas. They also make offerings at night during the dark fortnight and so on. Or, by offering food-tickets (salākabhatta) and the like, they make offerings during the day by dedicating the merit (pattidāna) to the devas, starting from the guardian devas up to the Brahma world. By hoisting umbrellas, offering lamps, and arranging all-night Dhamma listening and the like, they make offerings at night by dedicating the merit. Why should such people not be protected? Since they thus make offerings dedicated to you devas day and night, therefore, protect those people. Because of those acts of offering, protect and guard those humans; remove what is harmful to them and bring what is beneficial. Being diligent, keep their gratitude in your heart and protect them by constantly remembering them.

## Explanation of the Verse "Yaṃ kiñci"

Having thus shown the helpfulness of humans towards devas, He began to utter an Asseveration of Truth (Saccavacana) in the manner of "Yaṃ kiñci vittaṃ" (Whatever wealth...), both for the purpose of allaying the calamities of those humans and for the purpose of enabling devas and humans to hear the Dhamma by proclaiming the virtues of the Buddha and so on. In that verse, the term "Yaṃ kiñci" (whatever) includes all wealth used in various places without exception or specification. "Vittaṃ" means wealth (dhana). It is called "vitta" because it produces joy (vitti). "Idha vā" (or here) refers to the human world. "Huraṃ vā" (or elsewhere) refers to the remaining worlds beyond that. Although this would include all worlds except the human world, since "saggesu vā" (or in the heavens) is mentioned later, it should be understood as referring to the abodes of Nagas, Garudas, and others, excluding the human and heavenly worlds.

Thus, by these two terms, He points out the wealth used by humans for trade, ornament, and enjoyment, such as gold, silver, pearls, gems, cat's eye, coral, rubies, musāragalla, and so on; as well as the wealth of Nagas, Garudas, and others that arises in jeweled mansions many hundreds of leagues wide, with grounds covered in pearl and gem sands. "Saggesu vā" (or in the heavens) refers to the Sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and Fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) celestial realms.
143:
They are called *sagga* (heavens) because they are brought into existence through happiness resulting from beautiful deeds. Alternatively, they are called *sagga* because they are supremely excellent. Whether possessed of an owner or ownerless, [a jewel] moves about. It is called *ratana* (jewel) because it brings, produces, and increases delight (*rati*). The meanings of being cherished in the mind, being of great value, being incomparable, being rare to see, and being used only by noble beings are the designations of that jewel. Thus it was said:

'Because it is cherished and revered, of great value, incomparable, rare to see, and used only by noble beings, it is called a jewel.'

*Paṇīta* means excellent, supreme, and of immeasurable worth. Thus, by this verse-foot, the following are indicated: the treasures with owners in the heavens—such as the celestial mansions (*vimāna*), the Sudhamma hall, and the Vejayanta palace, which measure many hundreds of leagues and are made of all kinds of jewels; the ownerless treasures associated with empty mansions because beings, in the absence of a Buddha's arising, only fill the four woeful states; and other ownerless treasures found in the earth, the great ocean, the Himavanta, and so forth.

In the phrase *Na no samaṃ atthi Tathāgatena*, the word '*na*' is used in the sense of negation (*paṭisedha*). The word '*no*' is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). '*Samaṃ*' means equal. '*Atthi*' means exists. '*Tathāgatena*' means with the Buddha. What is meant is this: among all these treasures and riches that have been described, there is not even a single jewel that is equal to the Buddha-jewel.

Indeed, it is called a jewel because it is cherished and revered. For example, when the Wheel-treasure and the Gem-treasure of a Universal Monarch appear, the multitude of people do not show such reverence to any other treasure. No one takes flowers and perfumes to go to the shrines of *yakkhas* or the abodes of earth-deities; instead, all people revere and honor only the Wheel-treasure and the Gem-treasure. They pray for various boons, and some of their prayers are fulfilled. Yet, even that treasure is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. If something is called a jewel because it is cherished and revered, then only the Tathāgata is the true jewel. For when the Tathāgata arises, those deities and humans of great power do not show reverence to anyone else, nor do they worship anyone else.

It was for this reason that the Great Brahmā Sahampati worshipped the Tathāgata with a garland of jewels as large as Mount Sineru. Other deities and humans, such as King Bimbisāra, King Kosala, and the merchant Anāthapiṇဍika, also worshipped according to their own capacity. Even after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the great King Asoka spent ninety-six crores of wealth to establish eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the whole of Jambudīpa in honor of the Buddha. What need is there to mention other acts of reverence? Furthermore, for whom else who has passed away are there such acts of reverence and honor shown toward the places of birth, enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and Parinibbāna, or toward images and stupas, as are shown to the Blessed One? Thus, even in the sense of being cherished and revered, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, it is called a jewel because of its great value. That noble distinction is as follows...
144:
Similarly, it is called a jewel because of its great value. An example of such a jewel is the cloth from the Kāsī country. As it was said: 'Monks, Kāsī cloth, even when worn out, is beautiful in color, pleasant to the touch, and of great value.' Just so, even that jewel of cloth is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. If something is called a jewel because of its great value, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel. For if the Tathāgata accepts even a handful of dust from some people, it brings them great fruit and great benefit, as in the case of King Asoka. This is due to the great value of the Tathāgata. In this regard, this passage from the Sutta should be understood as proving the absence of fault through the statement of great value: 'Monks, for those from whom he accepts robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, it brings them great fruit and great benefit. I say this is because of his great value. Monks, just as that Kāsī cloth is of great value, so too, monks, do I describe this person as being of great value.' Thus, even in the sense of being of great value, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Similarly, it is called a jewel because it is incomparable (*atula*). That incomparable jewel is the appearance of the Wheel-treasure of a Universal Monarch. That Wheel-treasure has a hub made of sapphire (*indanīla*), a thousand spokes made of the seven kinds of jewels, a rim made of coral, and joints made of red gold. Above every ten spokes, there is a small bell to catch the wind and make a sound. The sound coming from those bells is like the sound of a five-piece orchestra played by a highly skilled musician. On both sides of the hub of that Wheel-treasure, there are two lion-face shapes; the interior is hollow like a cartwheel. It has no maker or one who commissions its making; it arises through the influence of kamma and the physical environment (*utu*). When a Universal Monarch, having fulfilled the ten duties of a Universal Monarch, has washed his head on the full-moon Uposatha day, and sits purifying his virtue on the upper terrace of his palace while observing the Uposatha, he sees it rising like the full moon or the sun. The sound of that Wheel-treasure can be heard from twelve leagues away, and its color can be seen from one league away. While the multitude of people look on with great wonder, thinking, 'Is a second moon or sun rising?', it comes over the city and settles at a height neither too high nor too low on the eastern side of the King's inner palace, standing as if fixed by an axle so that the people may worship it with perfumes and flowers.
145:
Following that very Wheel Gem, the Elephant Gem (Hatthiratana) appears. That elephant is entirely white, with red feet, well-established in seven places, possessed of psychic power, capable of traveling through the air, and comes from either the Uposatha lineage or the Chaddanta lineage. If it comes from the Uposatha lineage, it is the eldest of all. If it comes from the Chaddanta lineage, it is the youngest of all, well-trained, disciplined, and perfected in self-control. Carrying a retinue of twelve yojanas and traveling around the entire Jambudīpa in succession, it can return to its royal capital even before the morning meal.

Following that very Elephant Gem, the Horse Gem (Assaratana) appears. That horse is entirely white, with red feet, a black head, and hair like muñja grass; it comes from the Valāhaka horse-king lineage. The remaining details are exactly the same as those of the Elephant Gem.

Following that very Horse Gem, the Jewel Gem (Maṇiratana) appears. That jewel is a beryl (veḷuriya), beautiful, of genuine quality, eight-faceted, well-polished, and in length, it is like the hub of a chariot wheel; it comes from Mount Vepulla. Even in the fourfold darkness, when placed at the top of the king's banner, that Jewel Gem illuminates for a distance of one yojana. By that light, people, thinking it is daytime, perform their tasks, and they can see even down to the smallest insects and ants.

Following that very Jewel Gem, the Woman Gem (Itthiratana) appears. That woman is either the king's original chief queen, or she comes from Uttarakuru or from the Madda royal family. She is free from the six defects, such as being too tall; she surpasses human beauty but has not yet reached divine beauty. The body of that woman is warm when it is cold and cool when it is hot. Her touch is like that of fine cotton-wool that has been beaten a hundred times. The scent of sandalwood wafts from her body, and the scent of blue lotus wafts from her mouth. She is also endowed with many virtues, such as rising before the king.

Following that very Woman Gem, the Treasurer Gem (Gahapatiratana) appears. That treasurer is the very merchant who usually performs the king's affairs. As soon as the Wheel Gem appears, the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) manifests in that treasurer. With that divine eye, he can see hidden treasures within a distance of one yojana all around, whether they have an owner or are ownerless. That Treasurer Gem approaches the king and invites him, saying, "O King, may you remain unconcerned; I shall perform the financial duties with your wealth."
146:
Following that Treasurer Gem, the Minister Gem (Pariṇာyaka-ratana), who is the king's own eldest son, appears. As soon as the Wheel Gem appears, that eldest son becomes endowed with extraordinary wisdom and skill. Because he can discern the minds of the retinue within twelve yojanas with his own mind, he is capable of restraining those who should be restrained and encouraging those who should be encouraged. That Minister Gem approaches the king and invites him, saying, "O King, may you remain unconcerned; I shall administer the affairs of the kingdom for you."

Furthermore, there is another such gem of incomparable value. It is not possible to value that gem by comparing or judging it, saying, "It is worth a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred billion." Among those gems, not even a single one is equal to the Buddha Gem. If a gem exists in the sense of being incomparable, only the Tathāgata is such a gem. For it is not possible for anyone to measure, judge, or define the Tathāgata by his virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), or wisdom (paññā), saying, "He has this much virtue," or "He is equal to this person," or "He is similar to this person."

Thus, in the sense of being incomparable, there is no gem equal to the Tathāgata. Likewise, a gem is so called in the sense of being rare to see. For instance, a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is a gem because he is rare to appear, and his Wheel Gem and so forth are also gems. Yet even that Universal Monarch gem is not equal to the Buddha Gem. If a gem exists in the sense of being rare to see, only the Tathāgata is such a gem. What need is there to mention the gem-status of the Universal Monarch and others? For they appear many times even in a single aeon (kappa). However, because the world is empty of a Tathāgata even for incalculable aeons, the Tathāgata is rare to see, appearing only once in a long while. This was also spoken by the Blessed One at the time of his Parinibbāna:

"Ānanda, the deities are complaining: 'We have come from afar to see the Tathāgata. Rarely do Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, appear in the world. Tonight, in the last watch of the night, the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna will take place. And this powerful monk stands in front of the Blessed One, blocking the view, so that we do not get the chance to see the Tathāgata in his final hour.'"

Thus, in the sense of being rare to see, there is no gem equal to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, a gem is so called in the sense of being used only by noble beings. For instance, the Wheel Gem and others of the Universal Monarch. Those Wheel Gems and others are worth more than a hundred billion in wealth...
147:
Even if they live on the top floor of a seven-storied palace, for those of low birth and base men such as the Caṇḍāla, Veṇa, Nesāda, Rathakāra, and Pukkusa, this jewel does not arise for their enjoyment even in a dream. It arises for the enjoyment only of a King of the Khattiya (warrior-noble) class, who is well-born from both parental sides and who has fully practiced the ten duties of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch). Therefore, it is a jewel to be enjoyed only by noble beings. Even that jewel cannot compare to the Buddha-jewel (Buddha-ratana). If a thing is called a jewel because it is enjoyed by noble beings, then only the Blessed One is truly a jewel. This is because the Blessed One is not to be enjoyed (encountered) even in a dream by the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others of their kind, who are regarded as base beings in the world, who lack supporting conditions (upanissaya), and who hold perverted views. However, he is to be enjoyed (encountered) by those who possess supporting conditions and are capable of attaining the Fruit of Arahantship even at the end of a single four-line verse, such as Bāhiya Dārucīriya and others, as well as the Great Disciples born of noble families. These Great Disciples enjoy (attend upon) the Blessed One while accomplishing the unsurpassed seeing (dassananuttariya), the unsurpassed hearing (savananuttariya), the unsurpassed service (pāricariyānuttariya), and so forth. Thus, in the sense of being enjoyed by noble beings, there is no jewel equal to the Buddha.

Furthermore, a thing is called a jewel because it generally produces delight (rati). For example, it is like the Wheel-jewel (Cakka-ratana) of a Cakkavatti King. Just by seeing that Wheel-jewel, the Cakkavatti King becomes delighted and joyful; thus, that jewel produces delight for the King. Furthermore, the Cakkavatti King, holding a golden ewer in his left hand and sprinkling (consecrating) the Wheel-jewel with his right hand, says: "May the noble Wheel-jewel turn; may the noble Wheel-jewel be victorious." Then the Wheel-jewel, emitting a melodious sound like a musical instrument with five components, travels through the air toward the eastern direction. The Cakkavatti King follows it with his fourfold army, twelve yojanas in width, by the power of the Wheel. It travels neither too high nor too low—below the upper parts of tall trees and above the lower parts of short trees. He travels while receiving gifts such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts from the trees, and accepting presents from the hands of those who come to offer them. He goes about admonishing the rival kings who come with great respect, saying "Come, Great King," with principles such as "Living beings should not be killed."
