When the Cakkavatti King wishes to eat or take a daytime rest, the Wheel-jewel descends from the sky and stays fixed as if its axle were struck into the ground, on a level piece of land suitable for all purposes such as bathing. Again, when the King's mind intends to travel, it moves again, making a sound as before. Hearing that sound, the retinue of twelve yojanas also follows through the air.
148:
(The Wheel-jewel) travels. The Wheel-jewel gradually enters the eastern ocean. When it enters, the water recedes for about one yojana and stands like a wall. The multitude of people take the seven kinds of jewels as much as they desire. Then the Cakkavatti King, holding a golden ewer, pours water and declares, "From this day forth, let this place be my kingdom," and then turns back. The army goes in front, the Wheel-jewel follows behind, and the King follows in the middle. In every place where the Wheel-jewel has receded, the water fills back as before. In this same manner, it travels to the southern, western, and northern oceans.

After thus wandering through the four directions, the Wheel-jewel ascends into the sky to a height of about three yojanas. Standing there in the sky, the Cakkavatti King, having achieved victory through the power of the Wheel-jewel, surveys the entire world-system (Cakkavāḷa) like a great forest of fully blossomed lotuses—the continent of Pubbavideha, seven thousand yojanas in circumference and surrounded by five hundred minor islands; the continent of Uttarakuru, eight thousand yojanas in circumference; the continent of Aparagoyāna, also seven thousand yojanas in circumference; and the continent of Jambudīpa, ten thousand yojanas in circumference—thus the four great continents and two thousand minor islands. As he surveys them, great delight and joy arise in that King. Thus, that Wheel-jewel produces delight for the King; however, even that Wheel-jewel cannot compare to the Buddha-jewel. If a thing is called a jewel because it produces delight, then only the Blessed One is truly a jewel. What can this Wheel-jewel do?

For the Blessed One produces a delight that is superior and more sublime than the delight of a Cakkavatti King—which, produced by all jewels such as the Wheel-jewel, does not equal even a fraction, a part, or a minute portion of the celestial delight. He produces the delight of the first jhāna, the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas; the delight of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana); the delight of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana); the delight of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala); and the delight of the Path and Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi), Non-returning (anāgāmi), and Arahantship for countless devas and humans who follow his instruction. Thus, in the sense of producing delight, there is no jewel equal to the Buddha.

Furthermore, what is called a jewel is of two kinds: conscious (saviññāṇaka) and unconscious (aviññāṇaka). Among them, the unconscious jewels are the Wheel-jewel and the Gem-jewel, or any other things not connected with the faculties (indriya) such as gold and silver. The conscious jewels are those from the Elephant-jewel to the Counselor-jewel (pariṇāyaka-ratana), or any other such things connected with the faculties. Between these two kinds of jewels, the conscious jewel...
149:
(Animate treasure) is said to be the most excellent. Why? Because inanimate treasures such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls are brought for the purpose of decorating animate treasures such as elephant-treasures.

Animate treasures are also of two kinds: animal-treasures and human-treasures. Among these, the human-treasure is said to be the most excellent. Why? Because the animal-treasure serves as a mount (vehicle) for the human-treasure. Human-treasures are also of two kinds: the woman-treasure and the man-treasure. Among these, the man-treasure is said to be the most excellent. Why? Because the woman-treasure comes to serve at the feet of the man-treasure. Man-treasures are also of two kinds: the householder (agārika) treasure and the homeless (anagārika) treasure. Among these, the homeless treasure is said to be the most excellent. Why? Because even a Wheel-turning Monarch, the most excellent among householder treasures, pays homage with the five-point prostration to a homeless treasure endowed with virtues such as morality, and by serving and attending upon him, attains celestial and human prosperity, and finally reaches the bliss of Nibbāna.

Thus, the homeless treasure is also of two kinds: the Noble One (Ariya) and the ordinary person (Puthujjana). The Noble treasure is of two kinds: the trainee (Sekha) and the non-trainee (Asekha). The non-trainee treasure is of two kinds: the dry-insight practitioner (Sukkhavipassaka) and the tranquility-vehicle practitioner (Samathayānika). The tranquility-vehicle treasure is of two kinds: those who have reached Disciple-perfection (Sāvakapāramī) and those who have not. Among these, the one who has reached Disciple-perfection is said to be the most excellent. Why? Because of the greatness of their qualities. Even more excellent than the treasure of one who has reached Disciple-perfection is the Paccekabuddha treasure. Why? Because of the greatness of their qualities. For even hundreds of disciples equal to Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna do not reach even a hundredth part of the qualities of a single Paccekabuddha. Even more excellent than the Paccekabuddha treasure is the Sammāsambuddha treasure. Why? Because of the greatness of their qualities. For even if Paccekabuddhas were to sit knee to knee, filling the entire Jambudīpa, they would not reach the number, the portion, or even a fraction of a portion of the qualities of a single Sammāsambuddha. For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, whatever beings there are, whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed, the Tathāgata is said to be the foremost among them," and so forth. Thus, in any way, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "There is no one equal to Us, other than the Tathāgata."

Having thus spoken of the peerless nature of the Buddha-treasure compared to other treasures, now, for the purpose of pacifying the calamities that have arisen for those beings, without relying on birth, lineage, status as a clansman, or beauty of appearance, but rather starting from the Avīci hell...
150:
In the world up to the highest plane of existence (Bhavagga), relying on the peerless nature of the Buddha-jewel through such qualities as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), one performs an act of truth: 'In the Buddha is this precious jewel; by this truth, may there be well-being.'

The meaning of that verse is: Whatever wealth or jewel there may be in this world, or in the other world of Nagas and Garudas, or in the heavens, none is equal to the Buddha-jewel in those respective qualities; thus, the jewel in the Buddha is supreme. If this statement of truth is true, then by this truth, may there be well-being, beauty, health, and freedom from danger for these living beings. Here, just as in sentences such as 'Ānanda, the eye is empty of self or what belongs to self,' it should be understood that it is empty of the nature of self or the nature of what belongs to self. Otherwise, it would not be denied that the eye is either the self or what belongs to self. Thus, 'ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ' means the state of being a jewel is supreme, or the nature of being a jewel is supreme. Otherwise, it would seem as if the Buddha himself is not the jewel. It is not that where a jewel exists, it cannot be called a jewel. However, a jewel is that which is connected by one means or another with the meaning of being honored and so forth; since it is designated as a jewel based on that state of being a jewel, the Buddha is established as a jewel by the existence of that jewel-like quality. Alternatively, by this method of 'this jewel in the Buddha,' it should be understood that the Buddha himself is the jewel. As soon as the Blessed One spoke this verse, well-being arose for the royal families and the fears were calmed. The authority of this verse was accepted by non-human beings across a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

## Commentary on the Verse 'Khayaṃ Virāgaṃ'

Having thus spoken the truth by the qualities of the Buddha, he now began to speak by the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna with the verse 'Khayaṃ virāgaṃ'. In that verse, because passions (rāga) and so forth are exhausted and utterly destroyed by the realization of Nibbāna, or because it is merely the destruction consisting of the non-arising and cessation of them, or because it is dissociated from passion and so forth both in terms of association and object, or because when that Nibbāna is realized, passion and so forth are absolutely detached, gone, and destroyed—therefore, it is called 'Destruction' (Khaya) and 'Detachment' (Virāga). Furthermore, because its arising, passing away, or alteration of what exists is not known, it is called the 'Deathless' (Amata), considering that it is not born, does not age, and does not die. It is called 'Supreme' (Paṇīta) in the sense of being the highest goal and in the sense of being free from the heat of defilements. 'Yadajjhagā' means that Nibbāna which he attained, found, and realized by the power of his own knowledge.
151:
'Sakyamuni' means he is called 'Sakya' because he was born into the Sakya clan, and 'Muni' because he is endowed with the qualities of a sage (moneyya-dhamma). Being a sage who is a Sakya prince, he is called Sakyamuni. 'Samāhito' means having a mind established through the concentration of the Noble Path (ariya-magga-samādhi). There is no state of dhamma equal to that Dhamma attained by the Sakyamuni Buddha, which is known by names such as 'destruction' (khaya) and so forth. Therefore, it was also said in another Sutta: "Monks, whatever dhammas there are, whether conditioned (saṅkhata) or unconditioned (asaṅkhata), detachment (virāga) is said to be the foremost among them," and so on.

Having thus spoken of the uniqueness of the Dhamma of Nibbāna compared to other dhammas, the Blessed One now utters the word of truth for the purpose of pacifying the dangers that have befallen beings, based on the incomparable nature of the Jewel of Nibbāna-Dhamma through its qualities of destruction (khaya), detachment (virāga), the deathless (amata), and the sublime (paṇīta): "This too is a precious jewel in the Dhamma; by this truth, may there be well-being." The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same manner as explained in the previous verse. The authority of this verse is also respectfully accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) throughout the hundred-thousand-million world systems.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with 'Yaṃ Buddhasseṭṭho'

After speaking the truth through the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna, he now begins the verse "Yaṃ buddhasseṭṭho" to describe the qualities of the Dhamma of the Path (magga-dhamma). In that verse, he is 'Buddha' because he has realized the [Four Noble] Truths; he is 'Seṭṭho' because he is supreme and praiseworthy. Being both Buddha and supreme, he is 'Buddhasseṭṭho'. Alternatively, he is 'Buddhasseṭṭho' because he is the most excellent among the Buddhas known as Anubuddha, Paccekabuddha, and Sutabuddha. That Supreme Buddha praised and revealed that concentration of the Noble Path in various discourses in this manner: "Of all paths, the Eightfold Path is the best, for it is the secure way to reach Nibbāna," and "Monks, I will teach you the Noble Right Concentration together with its supports and its requisites."

'Suci' (pure) means extremely purified because it causes the total eradication of the stains of defilements. 'Samādhimānantarikaññamāhu' means that the wise call that concentration of the Noble Path 'Ānantarika-samādhi' (the concentration with immediate result) because it definitely yields its fruit immediately after its own occurrence. Indeed, once the Path-concentration has arisen, there is no obstacle that can prevent the arising of its fruit. Regarding this, it was said: "If this person were practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), and it were the time for the world-aeon to burn up, the world-aeon would not burn as long as this person has not yet realized the fruit of Stream-entry."
152:
"...there is no such danger. How did I, the Buddha, preach? If this person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry and encounters the time of the world's destruction, the world will not burn as long as that person has not realized the fruit of Stream-entry. This person is called 'one who stays for an aeon' (ṭhitakappī). All persons possessed of the Path are also those who stay for an aeon" (Puggalapaññatti 17).

'There is no concentration equal to that concentration' means there is no concentration of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) that is equal to that pure Ānantarika-samādhi praised repeatedly by the Supreme Buddha. Why? Because for one who has developed those rūpāvacara and arūpāvacara concentrations and is reborn in those respective Brahma worlds, there is still the possibility of being reborn again in hell and other [woeful states]. However, for the Noble Person (ariya-puggala) who has developed this concentration of the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-samādhi), all rebirth is completely eradicated. Therefore, it was said in another Sutta: "Monks, among conditioned (saṅkhata) dhammas... the Noble Eightfold Path is said to be the foremost," and so on.

Thus, the Blessed One, having stated that the Ānantarika-samādhi is incomparable to other mundane concentrations, now applies the word of truth based on the incomparable nature of the Jewel of the Path-Dhamma, just as in the previous method: "This too is a precious jewel in the Dhamma; by this truth, may all beings be happy." The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as previously stated. The authority of this verse is also accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) in the hundred-thousand-million world systems.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with 'Ye Puggalā'

Having thus spoken the truth through the special qualities of the Path-Dhamma, he now begins [the verse] 'Ye puggalā' to speak also of the qualities of the Saṅgha. In that verse, the word 'Ye' is an indefinite pronoun. 'Puggalā' means beings. 'Aṭṭha' is the numerical limit of those persons. They are eight: four practicing for the Path and four established in the Fruit. 'Sataṃ pasatthā' means those praised by the virtuous—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the disciples of the Buddha, and other devas and humans. Why? Because they are endowed with qualities such as virtue (sīla) that arise simultaneously [with their state]. Just as the color and fragrance of flowers like the Campaka, Vakula, and clove arise together with the flower, so too the qualities of virtue, concentration, and so on arise together for these persons. Therefore, like flowers endowed with color and fragrance, these persons are dear, pleasing, and praiseworthy to devas, humans, and the virtuous. Thus it was said: 'Ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā'.

Alternatively, 'Ye' is an indefinite pronoun. 'Puggalā' means beings. 'Aṭṭhasataṃ' (one hundred and eight) is the numerical classification of those Noble Persons. To explain in detail: there are three types of Stream-enterers (sotāpanna)—the Ekabījī, the Kolaṃkola, and the Sattakkhattuparama. There are three types of Once-returners (sakadāgāmī) who attain the fruit of Once-returning in the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial realms. These three Stream-enterers and three Once-returners become twelve each (total 24) through the power of four types of persons [modes of progress]. There are five types of Non-returners (anāgāmī) in the Aviha realm: the Antarāparinibbāyī, the Upahaccaparinibbāyī, the Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī, the Asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī, and the Uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī. Similarly, there are five each in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, excluding the Stream-enterer and Non-returner [types mentioned], there are four types of Non-returners. Thus, there are twenty-four Non-returners. There are two types of Arahants: the Sukkhavipassaka and the Samathayānika. There are four persons on the Path (maggaṭṭha). Thus, there are fifty-four. All these persons become one hundred and eight (108) through the power of the 'Follower by Faith' (saddhānusārī) and 'Follower by Dhamma' (dhammānusārī). The remaining words are as previously explained.
153:
There are three types of Once-returners (Sakadāgāmin) who have attained the fruit in the sensual realm, the fine-material realm, and the immaterial realm. All these, by way of the four modes of progress (paṭipadā), become twenty-four. In the Aviha realm, there are five types of Non-returners (Anāgāmin): the one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna after landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), the one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), and the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī). Likewise, there are five in each of the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, there are four, excluding the one who goes upstream. Thus, there are twenty-four Non-returners. There are two types of Arahants: the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and the serenity-vehicle practitioner (samathayānika). Including the four standing in the paths (maggaṭṭha), there are fifty-four persons. When all these persons are doubled by way of the predominance of faith (saddhādhura) and the predominance of wisdom (paññādhura), they become one hundred and eight. The remaining explanation is as previously stated.

"Cattāri etāni yugāni honti" means that all those persons who are indicated in detail as eight or one hundred and eight, when taken in brief, form four pairs: the one standing in the path of Stream-entry and the one standing in its fruit form one pair, and in this manner, up to the one standing in the path of Arahantship and the one standing in its fruit, there are four pairs. In the phrase "te dakkhiṇeyyā," the word "te" (they) is a specification of the persons previously indicated without specification. All those persons who were said to be eight or one hundred and eight in detail, or four pairs in brief, are "dakkhiṇeyya" because they are worthy of noble offerings. An offering (dakkhiṇā) is a gift given with faith in kamma and its result, without expecting services such as medical treatment or running errands in return. Persons endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla) are worthy of such offerings. Since these persons possess such virtues, they are called "te dakkhiṇeyyā."

"Sugatassa sāvakā" means the Blessed One is called "Sugata" because He is endowed with an auspicious going, because He has gone to the auspicious state (Nibbāna), because He has gone well, and because He has spoken well. All those persons are called "sāvaka" (disciples) because they listen to the words of that Sugata. Although others also hear the words, they do not perform the duties that should be done after hearing. These noble members of the Saṅgha, however, having heard, practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma and attain the paths and fruits. Therefore, they are called "sāvaka." "Etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni" means that even small gifts given to these disciples of the Buddha yield great fruits because of the purity of the offering on the part of the recipients. Therefore, it is said in another Sutta: "Monks, as far as there are communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's disciples is declared the foremost, namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons. This is the Blessed One's Saṅgha of disciples... the result is supreme."

Thus, the Blessed One spoke of the virtues of the Saṅgha by way of all persons established in the paths and fruits, and now, relying on those very virtues, He utters the word of truth beginning with "Idampi saṅghe." The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as previously stated. The deities in ten thousand world systems accepted the authority of this verse. Having thus spoken the word of truth through the virtues of the Saṅgha by way of those standing in the paths and fruits, He now begins to speak through the virtues of certain Arahants (khīṇāsava) who are enjoying the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), with the verse beginning "Ye suppayuttā."
154:
Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Saṅgha-gem by way of all those standing in the paths and fruits, now utters the word of truth relying on those very virtues: "Idampi saṅghe." Its meaning should be understood in the same way as previously stated. The non-humans (deities) in a hundred thousand million world systems accepted the authority of this verse.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Ye Suppayuttā"

Having thus spoken the truth through the virtues of the Saṅgha by way of those standing in the paths and fruits, He now begins to speak through the virtues of only those Arahants (khīṇāsava) who are enjoying the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti): "Ye suppayuttā." In that verse, "ye" (those) is a term of indication without limitation. "Suppayuttā" means well-applied; it means those who, having abandoned various forms of wrong livelihood (anesanā) and relying on a pure livelihood, have begun to apply themselves to insight (vipassanā). Alternatively, "suppayuttā" means endowed with very pure bodily and vocal efforts; by this term, He shows their aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). "Manasā daḷhena" means with a firm mind, with a mind endowed with steady concentration; by this term, He shows their aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). "Nikkāmino" means those who, being without regard for body or life, have made their exit from all defilements through energy led by wisdom; by this term, He shows their aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) endowed with energy.

"Gotamasāsanamhi" means in the Dispensation of the Tathāgata, who is Gotama by lineage. By this term, He shows that those outside this Dispensation who perform various kinds of futile penance (amaratapa) cannot exit from defilements because they lack virtues such as right application. "Te" is a word referring back to the persons previously indicated. In the word "pattipattā," "patti" means the state to be attained; that which is to be attained means that which is worthy of being attained, which upon reaching, one becomes eternally secure from bonds (yogakkhema)—this is a designation for the fruit of Arahantship. Because they have reached that attainable fruit of Arahantship, they are called "pattipattā." "Amataṃ" refers to Nibbāna. "Vigayha" means having entered into it by way of making it an object. "Laddhā" means having obtained. "Mudhā" means without cost (without spending even a small coin like a kākaṇika). "Nibbutiṃ" means the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which is the cooling of the distress of defilements. "Bhuñjamānā" means enjoying or experiencing. What is meant is this: Those persons who are "suppayuttā" because they are endowed with virtue in this Dispensation of Gotama, who are "manasā daḷhena" because they are endowed with concentration, and who are "nikkāmino" because they are endowed with wisdom—they, by this right practice, having entered into Nibbāna and obtained for free the peace called the attainment of fruition, are called "pattipattā" (those who have reached the goal).
155:
In this way, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Jewel of the Saṅgha through the power of the Arahants (khīṇāsava) who enjoy the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), now applies the word of truth based on that very virtue: "This too is a precious jewel in the Saṅgha." The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same manner as previously explained. The authority of this verse is also accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Yathindakhīlo"

Having thus spoken the truth established in the Saṅgha through the virtues of Arahants, he now begins to speak through the virtues of the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), who is evident to the multitude, with the verse beginning "Yathindakhīlo." In that verse, "yathā" is a word of comparison. "Indakhīlo" is the name for a pillar made of heartwood, driven into the ground after digging eight or ten cubits deep inside the threshold for the purpose of securing the city gate. "Pathaviṃ" means the earth. "Sito" means entered into and established (supported). "Siyā" means would be. "Catubbhi vātehi" means by winds coming from the four directions. "Asampakampiyo" means unable to be shaken or moved. "Tathūpamaṃ" means having such a comparison. "Sappurisaṃ" means the noble man. "Vadāmi" means I, the Buddha, declare. "Yo ariyasaccāni avecca passati" means he who sees the Four Noble Truths by penetrating them with wisdom. Therein, the Noble Truths should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Kumārapañha.

The summary of the meaning here is: Just as a city pillar (indakhīla), because of its deep foundation, remains unshakeable by the winds coming from the four directions when established in the earth, so too do I declare this noble person to be like that pillar—the one who sees the Noble Truths with penetration. Why? Because that person, like the city pillar, is unshakeable by the winds of all sectarian doctrines; because of that vision, no one can shake or move them. Therefore, it is also stated in another Sutta:

"Bhikkhus, just as an iron pillar or a city pillar (indakhīla) with a deep foundation, well-planted, is steady and unshakeable; even if a fierce storm of wind and rain should come from the eastern direction, it would not shake it, would not make it tremble, would not move it. From the western... [etc.]... southern... northern... [etc.]... it would not move it. For what reason? Bhikkhus, because of the depth of its foundation..."
156:
...of the foundation, because the city pillar is well-planted. Even so, bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins understand as it really is: 'This is suffering... [etc.]... this is the path,' they do not look to the face of another recluse or brahmin, thinking, 'Surely this venerable one knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen.' For what reason? Bhikkhus, because the four Noble Truths have been well seen.

In this way, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Jewel of the Saṅgha through the power of the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) who is evident to the multitude, now applies the word of truth based on that very virtue: "This too is a precious jewel in the Saṅgha." The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same manner as previously explained. The authority of this verse is also accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Ye Ariyasaccāni"

Having thus spoken the truth established in the Saṅgha through the virtues of the Stream-enterer without distinction, he now intends to speak of those three types of Stream-enterers: the Ekabījī, the Kolaṅkola, and the Sattakkhattuparama. As it is said:

"Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, becomes a Stream-enterer... [etc.]... having been reborn only once more, he makes an end of suffering; this person is called an Ekabījī. Likewise, having wandered and transmigrated through two or three families, he makes an end of suffering; this person is called a Kolaṅkola. Likewise, having wandered and transmigrated among devas and humans for up to seven times, he makes an end of suffering; this person is called a Sattakkhattuparama."

Among those three types of Stream-enterers, he speaks the verse beginning "Ye ariyasaccāni" through the virtue of the Sattakkhattuparama, who is the youngest (least advanced). In that verse, the phrase "Ye ariyasaccāni" is just as previously explained. "Vibhāvayanti" means they make [the truths] manifest to themselves by destroying the darkness of defilements that shroud the truths with the light of wisdom. "Gambhīrapaññena" refers to the Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññū), who possesses incomparable wisdom, a wisdom whose foundation cannot be reached by the knowledge of the world including the devas. "Sudesitāni" means the teachings well-expounded through various methods such as in brief or in detail. Even if those Stream-enterers, depending on the causes of heedlessness such as being a king of devas or a wheel-turning monarch, should become greatly heedless, yet by the knowledge of the path of Stream-entry, the kammic consciousness (abhisaṅkhāravijñāna)...
157:
Those persons who have realized the Noble Truths, even if they become exceedingly negligent by relying on the causes of negligence such as the status of a king of gods or a universal monarch, do not take up an eighth birth. This is because the karmic-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāravijñāna) has ceased through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga-ñāṇa), and the mental and physical phenomena (nāma-rūpa) that would have arisen in the beginningless saṃsāra have ceased and disappeared, leaving only seven births. In the seventh birth itself, they undertake insight (vipassanā) and reach the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala).

In this way, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the Saṅgha Jewel by way of the person who is 'at most seven times' (sattakkhattuparama), now utters the word of truth, "Idampi saṅghe," based on those very virtues. The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The authority of this verse is also accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with 'Sahāvassa'

Thus, after speaking the truth based on the Saṅgha through the virtue of the sattakkhattuparama person not taking an eighth birth, the Buddha now begins to speak of the virtue that is superior to other persons who have not yet abandoned the taking of births, even though this person still takes seven births, with the verse beginning with "Sahāvassa."

In that verse, "sahāva" means together with. "Assa" refers to any one of the stream-enterers (sotāpanna) among those of whom it was said, "They do not take an eighth birth." "Dassanasampadāya" means due to the attainment of the path of stream-entry. For the path of stream-entry is called "dassana" (vision) because it is the very first vision of Nibbāna upon seeing Nibbāna and completing the necessary task. The manifestation of that path of stream-entry within oneself is called dassanasampadā. It occurs together with that very attainment of vision. In the phrase "tayassu dhammā jahitā bhavanti," the word "assu" is a mere particle used for completing the sentence (padapūraṇa), as in the passage, "Idaṃ su me, Sāriputta, mahāvikaṭabhojanasmiṃ hoti" (Sāriputta, this benefit occurred to me in the use of the great foul medicine). Therefore, the meaning here is that together with the attainment of the wisdom that sees Nibbāna, three things are abandoned, they are already relinquished by that stream-enterer.

Now, to show the abandoned things, he said: "Sakkāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, and whatever sīlabbataparāmāsa there may be." In that context, the view with twenty bases regarding the body, which is called the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) that are clearly present, is called sakkāyadiṭṭhi (self-identity view). Alternatively, the view that exists in that body is sakkāyadiṭṭhi; the meaning is the view existing in the body of the aforementioned nature. Or, the view that occurs only in the existing body is sakkāyadiṭṭhi, in the existing body of the aforementioned nature...
158:
...the meaning is the view that proceeds as 'self' regarding the existing body, such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so on. Because that sakkāyadiṭṭhi has been abandoned, all forms of wrong view (diṭṭhigata) are also abandoned. For that sakkāyadiṭṭhi is their root. Wisdom is called 'that which cures' (cikicchita) because it calms the diseases of all defilements; that which is devoid of this medicinal wisdom, or the mind that is devoid of that medicinal wisdom, is called vicikicchita (doubt). It is a designation for the eight-based doubt (vimati) spoken of in the manner beginning with "He doubts the Teacher." Because that vicikicchā is abandoned, all doubts are also abandoned. For that vicikicchā is their root. The morality (sīla) such as the cow-practice and dog-practice, and the observance (vata) such as the cow-observance and dog-observance, which appear in passages like "Outside of this dispensation, recluses and brahmins believe in purification through morality and purification through observances," are called sīlabbata. Because that sīlabbataparāmāsa is abandoned, all ascetic practices (amaratapa) such as nakedness and shaving the head are also abandoned. For that sīlabbata is their root. Therefore, at the end of all wrong views, he said, "yadatthi kiñci" (whatever there may be). It should be understood that here, sakkāyadiṭṭhi is abandoned by the attainment of the vision of the truth of suffering (dukkha), vicikicchā by the attainment of the vision of the truth of origin (samudaya), and sīlabbata by the attainment of the vision of the truth of the path (magga) and Nibbāna.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with 'Catūhapāyehi'

Having thus shown the abandonment of the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), he now says, "catūhapāyehi ca vippamutto" (and he is fully freed from the four states of misery), showing the abandonment of the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa) which would have existed if that round of defilements were present. In that verse, the four states of misery (apāya) are hell (niraya), the animal realm (tiracchāna), the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), and the host of asuras (asurakāya). The meaning is that although this person still takes seven births, he is fully freed from these four states of misery.

Having thus shown the abandonment of the round of results for that stream-enterer, he now says, "chaccābhiṭhānāni abhabba kātuṃ" (he is incapable of committing the six major crimes), showing the abandonment of the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) which is the root of that round of results. In that phrase, abhiṭhānāni means gross crimes; he is incapable of committing these six. These should be understood as the acts of matricide, patricide, killing an Arahat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and following another teacher, which were spoken of in the Ekakanipāta in the manner beginning with, "Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should deprive his mother of life." For even though a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) endowed with right view would not deprive even a small insect or ant of its life-faculty (life), he certainly would not commit those anantariya kammas.
159:
In fact, these words are spoken for the purpose of disparaging the state of a worldling (puthujjana). Indeed, because a worldling has not seen the Four Noble Truths, they may commit such heinous acts (abhithāna) that carry great blame. However, a person endowed with vision (dassana-sampanna) is incapable of committing them. The use of the term 'incapable' (abhabba) here is to show that they do not commit such acts even in future lives. Indeed, even if such a Sotāpanna does not know their own status as a Noble Disciple in a future life, by the very nature of things (dhammatā), they do not commit those heinous acts, nor the five enmities (pañca-verāni) such as killing, nor the six things including following another teacher. With reference to those six heinous acts, some teachers also recite "cha chābhithānāni."

In this context (regarding the non-committing of killing, etc.), the young daughters of householders who were Noble Disciples, such as Matamacchaggāha, serve as evidence.

In this way, although the Noble Disciple may still have to take up to seven more births, the Blessed One spoke of the virtues of the Saṅgha Jewel by way of their distinguished qualities over those who have not yet abandoned the taking of future births. Now, relying on that very virtue, He applies the word of truth: "Idampi saṅghe." The meaning of this should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The authority of this verse is accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

## Kiñcāpi Soti Gāthāvaṇṇanā

Thus, after speaking the truth based on the Saṅgha through the distinguished qualities of those who will take seven more births over other persons, the Blessed One now begins the verse "Kiñcāpi so kammaṃ karoti pāpakaṃ." This is to show that not only is one endowed with vision incapable of committing the six heinous acts, but even if they commit a slight evil deed, they are incapable of concealing it. This speaks to the virtue of the non-concealment of committed faults by a person endowed with vision, even if they live negligently.

The meaning of that verse is: That person endowed with vision, due to a lapse in mindfulness and living negligently, may commit an evil deed with the body. This excludes what the Blessed One said regarding worldly faults (loka-vajja) and the transgression of training rules: "My disciples do not transgress the training rules I have laid down even for the sake of their lives." Instead, it refers to other transgressions of regulations (paṇṇatti-vajja) such as those concerning building a hut (kuṭikāra) or sleeping in the same room (sahaseyya), which are deeds loathed by the Buddha. Or they may commit an evil deed by speech, such as teaching Dhamma word by word (padasodhamma), speaking more than five or six words to a woman (uttari-chappañcavācā), or frivolous talk (samphappalāpa) and harsh speech (pharusavācā). Or else, they may commit an evil deed by mind, such as the arising of greed or hatred at some time, taking pleasure in gold and silver, or lack of reflection when using requisites like robes.
160:
That person endowed with vision, knowing that 'this act is improper and should not be done,' is incapable of concealing that transgression, and thus does not hide it even for a moment. At that very moment, they reveal it to the Teacher or to wise fellow practitioners of the holy life and atone for it according to the Dhamma. They practice restraint, thinking, 'I will not do this again.' Why? Because it is stated that one who has seen the state (diṭṭhapada) is incapable (of concealment). The meaning is that it is stated to be impossible for a person endowed with vision, who has seen the state of Nibbāna, to conceal such an evil deed after committing it.

How so?

"Monks, just as a young, tender infant lying on his back, if he happens to touch a hot coal with his hand or foot, quickly draws it back; even so, monks, such is the nature of a person endowed with vision. Although he may commit such an offense, the emergence (atonement) from that offense is evident. Then he quickly reveals, uncovers, and makes it plain to the Teacher or to wise fellow practitioners of the holy life. Having revealed, uncovered, and made it plain, he arrives at restraint in the future." Thus it is taught (in the Majjhima Nikāya).

In this way, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtue of the Saṅgha Jewel through the quality of non-concealment of committed faults even by a negligent person endowed with vision, now relies on that very virtue to utter the word of truth: "Idampi saṅghe," and so on. The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. The authority of this verse is accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

## Vanappagumbe Ti Gāthāvaṇṇanā

Thus, after speaking the truth based on the Saṅgha through the various qualities of the persons included in the Saṅgha, the Blessed One now begins the verse "Vanappagumbe yathā phussitagge." This is to speak the truth based on the Buddha once again, relying on the Pariyatti Dhamma (the scriptural Dhamma) which was taught by the Blessed One—briefly in this sutta and in detail elsewhere—while illustrating the virtues of the Triple Gem. In that verse, a collection of trees situated close together is called 'vana' (forest). A thicket that has grown with roots, heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, branches, and leaves is called 'gumba' or 'pagumba.' A thicket of the forest or a thicket in the forest is 'vanappagumbe.' This very thicket is referred to as 'vanappagumbe.' It can also be said that "There is..."
161:
It is just as in the terms "savitakka savicāra" (with initial and sustained thought), "atthi avitakka vicāramatta" (there is only sustained thought without initial thought), "sukha" (pleasure), "dukkha" (pain), "jīva" (soul), and so forth. The word "yathā" is a term used for comparison. In that forest, there are flowering tips; therefore, it is called "phussitagga." It means that flowers have blossomed on all the large and small branches. That term is expressed as "phussitagge" in the same manner as previously mentioned. "Gimhāna-māse paṭhamasmiṃ" means in one of the four months of summer. If one asks in which month the summer first blossoms, it means in the month of Citta, the first month of summer. That month is called both "paṭhama-gimha" (the first of summer) and "bāla-vasanta" (early spring). What follows is clear according to the meaning of the words.

This is the summary of the meaning here: Just as in the early spring called the first month of summer, a grove of young trees and bushes with well-blossomed tips in a thicket of various trees is exceedingly beautiful, even so, the noble Pariyatti Dhamma—which leads to Nibbāna and points out the path to Nibbāna—is exceedingly glorious with flowers of various meanings such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense-bases (āyatana), the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and right efforts (sammappadhāna), and the groups of virtue (sīla-kkhandha) and concentration (samādhi-kkhandha). The Buddha did not teach this Dhamma for the sake of gain or for the sake of honor and offerings; rather, with a heart urged by Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā), He taught it for the sake of Nibbāna, the supreme benefit of beings. In this text "paramam hitāya," the nasal (niggahīta) is inserted for the sake of ease in reciting the verse. Its meaning is: He taught for the sake of Nibbāna, the supreme benefit.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of the Pariyatti Dhamma which is like a forest grove with well-blossomed tips, now performs an act of truth centered on the Buddha based on that very Pariyatti, saying "Idampi Buddhe." The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. However, it should be specifically applied as: "In the Buddha, there is this precious jewel known as the aforementioned Pariyatti Dhamma." The authority of this verse is accepted by the non-human beings in the hundred thousand crores of world-systems.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with Varo Varaññū

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken the truth centered on the Buddha through the Pariyatti Dhamma, now begins to speak by way of the Supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), starting with "Varo varaññū." Therein, "varo" means the Noble One or the Excellent One, because He is desired by those of noble inclination who think, "O, may we also become like this!" or because He is endowed with noble qualities. "Varaññū" means the knower of Nibbāna. Nibbāna is called "vara" (noble) because it is more excellent than all other dhammas. The Blessed One Himself realized that Nibbāna through penetration at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "Varado" means the giver of the noble Dhamma, which is the portion of Nibbāna, to the group of five monks (pañcavaggiya), the Bhaddavaggiya, Uruvela Kassapa, and others, as well as to other devas and humans. "Varāharo" means the bringer of the noble Path (magga).
162:
'Varaññū' means the knower of Nibbāna. Nibbāna is called 'vara' (the noble) because of its excellence over all dhammas. The Blessed One Himself penetrated and knew that Nibbāna at the foot of the Bodhi tree. 'Varado' means the giver of the noble Dhamma that is conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) and conducive to the development of dispositions (vāsanābhāgiya) to the group of five, the Bhaddavaggiya, the matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila), and other devas and humans. 'Varāharo' is so called because He brought the noble Path. The Blessed One, while fulfilling the thirty perfections (pāramī) starting from the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, brought the ancient noble Path that was followed by previous Buddhas; therefore, He is called 'Varāharo'.

Alternatively, He is 'Varo' because of the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa); 'Varaññū' because of the realization of Nibbāna; 'Varado' because of giving the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha) to beings; and 'Varāharo' because of bringing the supreme practice. He is 'Anuttaro' (the Peerless One) because there is no one with qualities superior to these supramundane qualities.

Another way: He is 'Varo' through the fulfillment of the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna); 'Varaññū' through the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna); 'Varado' through the fulfillment of the foundation of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna); and 'Varāharo' through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna). He brought the noble Truth of the Path (maggasacca). Furthermore, He is 'Varo' due to the accumulation of merit; 'Varaññū' due to the accumulation of wisdom; 'Varado' because He gives the means for attaining Buddhahood to those who desire it; and 'Varāharo' because He brings the means for attaining Paccekabuddhahood to those who desire it. He is 'Anuttaro' either because of being incomparable in those various qualities or because He is the teacher of others while having no teacher Himself. 'Dhamma-varaṃ adesayi' (He taught the noble Dhamma) is said because He taught the noble Dhamma endowed with qualities such as being well-expounded (svākkhātata) for the benefit of those who desire the state of a disciple (sāvaka). The rest is as previously explained.

Thus, the Blessed One, having stated His own qualities through the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, now relies on those very qualities to utter the word of truth based on the Buddha: 'Idampi buddhe'. Its meaning should be understood as before. Specifically, it should be connected as: 'That noble supramundane Dhamma which He knew, which He gave, which He brought, and which He taught—this too is a precious jewel in the Buddha.' The authority of this verse was also accepted by non-human beings (amanussa) in a hundred thousand crores of world-systems.

## Commentary on the Verse Beginning with 'Khīṇaṃ'

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken the truth based on the Buddha with two verses relying on the Pariyatti Dhamma and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, now wishes to speak the word of truth based on the Saṅgha. He does so by relying on the virtues of those individuals who, having heard that Pariyatti Dhamma and practiced accordingly, attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma and reached Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). Thus, He begins the verse 'Khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ'. In that verse, 'khīṇaṃ' means well-exhausted; 'purāṇaṃ' means old kamma; 'navaṃ' means that which arises in the present; 'natthi sambhavaṃ' means there is no manifestation. 'Viraṭṭacittā' means having a mind detached from a new existence; 'āyatike bhavasmiṃ' means in a future new existence. Those individuals whose old kamma is exhausted, whose new kamma does not arise, and who have minds detached from a future existence are the monks whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava). 'Khīṇabījā' means they have seeds that are destroyed; 'aviruḷhichandā' means they have no desire for rebirth...
163:
Having practiced in accordance with the Dhamma they heard and attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, based on the virtue of their attainment of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna), the Buddha began to speak the truth based on the Saṅgha once more with the verse beginning with "Khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ". In that verse, "khīṇaṃ" means well-severed. "Purāṇaṃ" refers to old kamma. "Navaṃ" refers to kamma currently arising in the present. "Natthi sambhavaṃ" means there is no more manifestation. "Virattacittā" means those with minds free from lust (rāga). "Āyatike bhavasmiṃ" means in a new existence in the future time. "Te" refers to those Khīṇāsava monks whose old kamma is exhausted, who have no new kamma, and who are detached from future existence. "Khīṇabījā" means those whose seeds of rebirth are severed. "Avirūḷhichandā" means those devoid of the desire for growth. "Nibbanti" means they are extinguished. "Dhīrā" means those endowed with wisdom. "Yathāyaṃ padīpo" means just like this lamp flame.

What does this mean? Even though the old kamma associated with the past has arisen and ceased for beings, because the moisture of craving (taṇhā) has not yet been abandoned, it is not yet exhausted due to its ability to bring about rebirth. That old kamma, because the moisture of craving has been dried up by the Path of Arahantship, is exhausted like a seed burnt by fire, being unable to produce results in the future. And the new kamma currently occurring for them through acts such as worshipping the Buddha is called "navaṃ"; because craving has been abandoned, it is like a flower from a tree with severed roots, unable to produce fruit in the future, and thus for them there is no more arising (natthi sambhavaṃ). Those Khīṇāsava monks, being detached from future existence because craving has been abandoned, are called "khīṇabījā" (those with exhausted seeds) because the rebirth-linking consciousness—stated in the passage "Kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed"—is exhausted due to the exhaustion of kamma. Although there was previously a desire for growth known as "renewed existence," because that desire has been abandoned by the abandonment of the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca), at the time of death, there is no more new existence as before; thus they are called "avirūḷhichandā". Those wise ones (dhīrā), being endowed with wisdom, are extinguished (nibbanti) through the cessation of the final consciousness, just as this lamp flame is extinguished. Furthermore, they transcend the pathways of designation such as "having form or being formless." It is said that at that time, among the lamps lit to worship the city deities, one lamp went out; referring to that, the Buddha said, "Yathāyaṃ padīpo."

In this way, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtue of attaining Nibbāna without remainder for those who heard the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) taught in the previous two verses and practiced accordingly to attain the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, now concluded the teaching with the verse "Idampi saṅghe," employing a word of truth based on the Saṅgha, relying on that very virtue.
164:
The meaning of this verse should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. However, this verse should be specifically applied as: "This jewel in the Saṅgha, known as Nibbāna within the continuum of the Khīṇāsava monks in the manner described, is sublime." The authority of this verse was also accepted by non-humans in a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

At the conclusion of the teaching, there was safety for the royal family, all dangers were subsided, and eighty-four thousand beings attained the Dhamma.

## Commentary on the Three Verses Beginning with Yānīdha

Then, Sakka, the king of devas, thought: "The Blessed One has brought safety to the citizens by uttering words of truth relying on the virtues of the Triple Gem. I, too, should say something relying on the virtues of the Triple Gem for the sake of the citizens' well-being." Having thought thus, he spoke the three verses at the end beginning with "Yānīdha bhūtāni." In those verses, the Buddha is called "Tathāgata" because he has come (āgata) in the same way as those who strive for the welfare of the world should come; because he has gone (gata) in the same way as the previous Buddhas have gone; because he has understood (ājānana) in the same way as things should be understood; because he has known (jānana) in the same way as things should be known; and because he speaks (gadana) that which is truly so. And because that Blessed One is greatly worshipped by devas and humans with external offerings such as flowers and scents, and with internal offerings such as practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, Sakka, the king of devas, joining all the assembly of devas with himself, said: "We revere the Buddha, the Tathāgata, worshipped by devas and humans. May there be well-being!"

Regarding the Dhamma, the Path-Dhamma is called "Tathāgata" because it has gone (gata) in such a way as to sever the host of defilements by the power of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) joined in union. The Nibbāna-Dhamma is also called "Tathāgata" because it is penetrated by wisdom as it truly is, is sufficient for the destruction of all suffering, and is thus understood by the Buddhas and others. Because the Saṅgha has also gone (gata) by various paths in the same way as those practicing for their own benefit should go, it is also called "Tathāgata." Therefore, in the remaining two verses, it is said: "We revere the Tathāgata-Dhamma, may there be well-being," and "We revere the Tathāgata-Saṅgha, may there be well-being." The rest is just as previously explained.
165:
He is called 'Tathāgata' because he has known through wisdom and because he is perfect in removing all suffering. He is also called 'Tathāgata' because he has gone truly (without deviation) like the Buddhas and other noble ones. Furthermore, just as individuals who practice for their own benefit reach the Saṅgha, he is called 'Tathāgata' because he goes truly through various paths of the Dhamma. Therefore, in the remaining two verses, the words 'We worship the supramundane Dhamma that is gone truly; may these beings be happy; we worship the Saṅgha; may these beings be happy' are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

After reciting these three verses, Sakka, the King of the Devas, circumambulated the Blessed One and returned to the celestial realm together with his divine retinue. The Blessed One preached the same Ratana Sutta on the second day as well. Once again, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. In this way, he preached for seven days, and every day, there was a similar realization of the Dhamma. After staying in the city of Vesālī for half a month (fifteen days), the Blessed One informed the kings, 'We shall depart.' Then, the kings escorted the Blessed One to the banks of the Gaṅgā River for three days with double the honors.

The Nāga kings living in the Gaṅgā thought, 'Humans are paying homage to the Tathāgata; why should we not do the same?' They created boats made of gold, silver, and jewels, arranged thrones also made of gold, silver, and jewels, and covered the water's surface with five kinds of lotuses. They entreated the Blessed One, saying, 'Please show us favor.' The Blessed One accepted and boarded the jeweled boat. He had the five hundred monks board five hundred boats, and the Nāga kings escorted the Blessed One along with the Saṅgha of monks to the Nāga realm. There, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the Nāga assembly throughout the night. On the second day, they offered a great alms-giving of celestial food and drinks. After giving the blessing (anumodanā), the Blessed One departed from the Nāga realm.

The earth-dwelling devas also thought, 'Humans and Nāgas are paying homage to the Blessed One; why should we not do the same?' and they raised tiered umbrellas over forests, thickets, trees, and mountains. In this manner, grand and special honors were manifested all the way up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. King Bimbisāra also offered honors double those performed by the Licchavī kings when they arrived. As previously mentioned, he escorted the Blessed One to the city of Rājagaha over five days.

When the Blessed One arrived at Rājagaha, after the meal, a discussion arose among the monks assembled in the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla): 'How wonderful is the power of the Blessed Buddha! For the sake of the Blessed One, the ground for eight yojanas on both this side and the other side of the Gaṅgā has been leveled, cleared of hollows and heights, strewn with white sand, and covered with flowers. The water of the Gaṅgā for the distance of one yojana is covered with lotuses of various colors. Tiered umbrellas have been raised all the way to the Akaniṭṭha realm.' Knowing this, the Blessed One emerged from the Gandhakuṭi, proceeded with a miracle suitable for the moment, and sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the circular pavilion. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' The monks...
166:
The monks reported everything, and the Blessed One said: 'Monks, this special honor did not arise through my power as a Buddha, nor through the power of Nāgas, devas, or Brahmas. Rather, it arose through the power of a small act of renunciation and giving in a past life.' The monks said: 'Venerable Sir, we do not know of that small act of giving. It would be good if the Blessed One would tell us about it so that we may know.'

The Blessed One said: 'Monks, in the past, there was a Brahmin named Saṅkha in the city of Takkasilā. He had a son, a young man named Susīma, who was about sixteen years of age. One day, the young man approached his father, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. Then his father asked, "Dear Susīma, what is it?" Susīma replied, "Father, I wish to go to the city of Vārāṇasī to study the arts." "In that case, dear Susīma, a certain Brahmin of such a name is my friend; go to him and learn," his father said, and gave him a thousand kahāpaṇas. Taking the thousand coins, he paid homage to his parents and eventually reached Vārāṇasī. He approached the teacher Brahmin in the proper manner, paid homage, and introduced himself. The teacher accepted the young man, thinking, "He is the son of my friend," and performed all the duties of hospitality. After Susīma had recovered from the fatigue of the journey, he placed the thousand coins at the teacher's feet and asked for permission to study the arts. The teacher granted permission and began the instruction.

The young man Susīma learned quickly and extensively. He retained everything he learned without loss, like oil poured into a golden vessel. Thus, he completed the arts that usually take twelve years to learn in just a few months. When he practiced recitation, he saw only the beginning and the middle, but not the end. So, he approached the teacher and said, "I see only the beginning and the middle of this art, but not the end." The teacher said, "Dear son, I too see it in the same way." "Teacher, then who knows the end of this art?" he asked. "Dear son, there are sages in Isipatana; they might know," the teacher replied. "Teacher, I shall approach them and ask," he said. "Ask as you wish, dear son," the teacher said. Susīma went to Isipatana, approached the Paccekabuddhas, and asked, "Venerable sirs, do you know the end?" "Yes, friend, we know," they replied. "Please teach it to me as well," he requested. "Friend, in that case, you must ordain; it is not possible to teach it to one who is not ordained," they said. "Very well, venerable sirs, please ordain me; I will do whatever you wish..."
167:
When he requested, "Please teach me the end [of the training]," those Pacceka-Buddhas, being unable to urge him in meditation subjects after ordaining him, taught him the training of conduct (abhisamācārika-sikkhāpada) in such a way as, "This is how you should dress, this is how you should robe yourself," and so forth. While training there, because he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), he realized Pacceka-enlightenment (paccekabodhi) before long. He became famous throughout the whole of Vārāṇasī as "Susīma Pacceka-Buddha," attaining the highest gain and fame, and possessing a great following. Because he had performed karma leading to a short life, he attained Parinibbāna not long after. The other Pacceka-Buddhas and the great multitude performed the funeral rites for his body, took the relics, and established a stupa at the city gate.

Then the brahmin Saṅkha, thinking, "It has been a long time since my son left, and I do not know any news of him," and wishing to see his son, departed from Takkasilā and in due course arrived at Vārāṇasī. Seeing a great multitude gathered, he thought, "Surely among these many people, at least one will know news of my son." He approached and asked, "Has a youth named Susīma come here? Do you know any news of him?" They replied, "Brahmin, we know. In this city, after mastering the three Vedas under a brahmin, he ordained in the presence of Pacceka-Buddhas, became a Pacceka-Buddha himself, and attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). This is the stupa established for that Susīma Pacceka-Buddha."

That brahmin struck the ground with his hands, wept and lamented, and then went to the courtyard of that shrine (cetiya). He pulled up the grass, brought sand in his upper garment and scattered it in the courtyard of the Pacceka-Buddha's shrine, sprinkled the ground all around with water from a water-pot, made an offering of wild flowers, raised a banner with his upper garment, tied his own umbrella above the stupa, and then departed.

The Blessed One, having thus taught this past story and connecting the birth-story with the present, gave a Dhamma talk to the monks. "Monks, it might occur to you that the brahmin Saṅkha at that time was someone else. It should not be seen thus. I myself was the brahmin Saṅkha at that time. I pulled up the grass in the courtyard of the shrine of Susīma Pacceka-Buddha; as a result of that deed, they made the eight-league road smooth and clean, free from stumps and thorns. I scattered sand at that shrine; as a result of that deed, they scattered sand on the eight-league road. I made an offering there with wild flowers; as a result of that deed, on the nine-league road, on both land and water, they laid out flower-carpets with various kinds of flowers. I sprinkled the ground with water from a water-pot at that shrine; as a result of that deed, it was made to rain the pokkharavassa (lotus-leaf rain) in the city of Vesālī. I raised a banner and also tied and offered an umbrella at that shrine; as a result of that deed, banners were raised as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, and tiers of umbrellas were erected. Monks, this extraordinary honor of mine did not arise through the power of a Buddha, nor through the power of Nagas, Devas, or Brahmas; rather, it arose solely through the power of a small act of renunciation and offering."

At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, he recited this verse:
"If by renouncing a small pleasure, one sees a great pleasure,
the wise person should renounce the small pleasure, seeing the great pleasure."

## The explanation of the Ratana Sutta in the Paramatthajotikā is finished.
168:
On the nine-league journey, they made flower-carpets with various flowers on both land and water. I sprinkled the ground with water from a water-pot at that shrine; as a result of that deed of mine, the rain called pokkharavassa fell in the city of Vesālī. I raised a banner at the shrine of that Susīma Pacceka-Buddha and tied an umbrella; as a result of that deed of mine, banners were raised as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, and umbrellas upon umbrellas were erected. Monks, thus this extraordinary honor of mine did not arise through the power of a Buddha, nor through the power of Nagas, Devas, or Brahmas; rather, it arose through the power of a small act of renunciation.

At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, he recited this verse:
"If by renouncing a small pleasure, one sees a great pleasure,
the wise person should renounce the small pleasure, seeing the great pleasure."

## The commentary on the Ratana Sutta
## in the Paramatthajotikā, the Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā, is finished.

## 7. Tirokuṭṭa Sutta Vaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta)
## Nikkhepappayojana (The Purpose of the Placement)

Now, the sequence for the explanation of the meaning of the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, which was placed immediately after the Ratana Sutta beginning with "They stand outside the walls" (Tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti), has arrived. Having stated the purpose of its placement here, we shall provide the explanation of its meaning.

In that regard, although this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta was not spoken by the Blessed One in this specific sequence, it was spoken to show that a person who becomes negligent in the practice of meritorious deeds—which were shown in various ways prior to this—might be born among such hungry ghosts (petas), even if they are born in a place superior to hell or the animal realm. Therefore, one should not be negligent in the practice of meritorious deeds. Alternatively, it was spoken to show that among the spirits (bhūtas) by whom Vesālī was oppressed, and for the quelling of whose affliction the Ratana Sutta was spoken, some were of this nature. This following statement should be understood as the purpose of placing the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta here.
169:
## Discourse on Appreciation

Now, the sequence of the commentary on the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, which is placed immediately after the Ratana Sutta, has arrived. I shall provide the commentary, stating the purpose of placing this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta in this Khuddakapāṭha scripture. Although the Blessed One did not speak in this sequence within the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta itself, it was spoken to demonstrate that a person who is negligent in the practice of meritorious deeds—which were shown in various ways prior to this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta—will, upon being reborn in a state distinct from hell or the animal kingdom, arise as a peta of such a nature. Therefore, it was spoken to show that one should not be negligent in the practice of meritorious deeds. The Ratana Sutta was spoken to appease the afflictions in the city of Vesālī; it was also spoken to show that among those groups of spirits (bhūta), some are of such a nature. This should be understood as the purpose of placing the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta in this scripture.

By whom, where, when, and for what reason the Tirokuṭṭa was proclaimed,
Having explained all that, if it is performed in due order,
It is well-done; therefore, I shall provide the commentary in that very manner.

By whom was this sutta proclaimed? Where, when, and for what reason? It is said: It was proclaimed by the Blessed One. It was spoken on the second day in the city of Rājagaha for the purpose of expressing appreciation (anumodanā) to the King of Magadha (King Bimbisāra). To clarify this meaning, this detailed account should be told:

Ninety-two aeons (kappas) ago, there was a city named Kāsi. In that city, there was a king named Jayasena. That king had a queen named Sirimā, and in her womb, the Bodhisatta named Phussa was conceived, who in due course attained the Peerless Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). King Jayasena, developing possessiveness thinking, "My son has renounced and become a Buddha; the Buddha is mine alone, the Dhamma is mine, the Saṅgha is mine," served the Buddha himself at all times and gave no opportunity to others.

The Blessed One's three younger half-brothers thought: "Buddhas arise for the benefit of the entire world, not for the sake of one person alone. Our father gives no opportunity to others. How might we obtain the chance to serve the Blessed One?" Then this thought occurred to those princes: "Come, let us employ a certain stratagem." They caused the border region to appear as if it had revolted. Then the King, hearing that the border was in revolt, sent his three sons to pacify the border. When they returned after pacifying it, the King, being pleased, granted them a boon, saying, "Take whatever you desire."

They said, "We wish to serve the Blessed One." The King said, "Except for this, take any other boon." They replied, "We have no need for any other." The King then said, "If so, take it by setting a time limit." They requested to serve for seven years, but the King did not grant it. In this way, they pleaded for six, five, four, three, two, and one year; then for seven months, six, five, and four months, until finally they requested for three months. The King granted it, saying, "Take it for three months."

Those princes, having obtained the boon and being extremely joyful, approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable Sir, we wish to serve the Blessed One for the three months of the rains retreat. May the Blessed One accept our invitation."

The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. From that time on, those princes sent word to the man in charge of their province, saying, "For these three months, we must serve the Blessed One. Starting with a monastery, prepare all the requisites for serving the Blessed One."
170:
"Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One spend the three months of the rains retreat here." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. Then those princes sent a letter to the man appointed in their province, saying, "For these three months, the Blessed One is to be served by us. Starting with a monastery, prepare all the necessary provisions for the service of the Blessed One." Having prepared everything, that man reported back to them. Those princes, wearing dye-stained robes and accompanied by two thousand five hundred men as attendants, respectfully served the Blessed One, led Him to the province, handed over the monastery, and invited Him to stay.

Among them, there was a treasurer's son, a householder, who together with his wife was faithful and devoted. He respectfully offered the gift of food to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. The man appointed in the province, taking that treasurer as the leader, also respectfully conducted the alms-giving together with eleven thousand men of the province. In that place, some people of the province had malicious minds. They created obstacles to the alms-giving, ate the offerings themselves, and set fire to the dining hall. When the retreat was over, the princes performed a great honor to the Blessed One and, escorting the Blessed One, returned to their father the King. Having arrived there, the Blessed One (Phussa) eventually attained Parinibbāna.

The King, the princes, the man appointed in the province, and the treasurer, in due course passed away and were reborn in heaven along with their retinues. However, the people with malicious minds were reborn in the hells. Thus, those two groups, being reborn from heaven to heaven and from hell to hell, passed ninety-two aeons. Furthermore, in this Auspicious Aeon (Bhadda Kappa), during the time of Kassapa Buddha, those people with malicious minds were reborn in the realm of petas. At that time, when people gave alms for the sake of their deceased relatives who were petas, they dedicated it, saying, "May this be for our relatives." Those petas then obtained prosperity. Then these petas, seeing that circumstance, approached Kassapa Buddha and asked, "Venerable Sir, might we also obtain such prosperity?"

The Blessed One said, "You cannot obtain it now. However, in the future, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. During the time of that Blessed One, there will be a king named Bimbisāra. He was your relative ninety-two aeons ago. He will give alms to the Buddha and dedicate it to you. At that time, you shall obtain it." When this was said, it is said that to those petas, those words were as if He had said, "You will obtain it tomorrow."

Furthermore, when the interval between one Buddha and another had passed, our Blessed One arose in the world. Those three princes, together with those two thousand five hundred men...
171:
Having passed away from the celestial world, they were reborn in a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha. In due course, they went forth as ascetics and became the three ascetics at Gayāsīsa. The man who was the worker in the district became King Bimbisāra. The treasurer became the great treasurer named Visākha. The treasurer's wife became the treasurer's daughter named Dhammadinnā. In this way, all the remaining retinue were reborn as the king's attendants.

Our Blessed One, having appeared in the world and passed seven weeks (forty-nine days), gradually went to the city of Vārāṇasī and preached the Discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. Beginning with the group of five monks, he disciplined the three ascetics who had two thousand five hundred followers and then went to the city of Rājagaha. On the very day of his arrival in Rājagaha, he established King Bimbisāra, along with one hundred and ten thousand Magadhan Brahmins and householders, in the fruit of Stream-entry. Then, the Blessed One accepted the king's invitation for the next day's meal. On the second day, Sakka, the king of gods, walked in front of the Blessed One, praising him with verses such as:

“The Tamed One, with the tamed former ascetics; the Liberated One, with the liberated Arahants;
With a complexion like the color of refined gold, the Blessed One enters the city of Rājagaha.”

Being thus praised with these verses, he entered the city of Rājagaha and accepted the great offering at the king's palace. Those petas stood around with the hope, “Now the king will dedicate the offering to us; now he will dedicate it.”

After giving the offering, the king thought only of the place where the Blessed One would reside, wondering, “Where should the Blessed One stay?” and did not dedicate that offering to anyone. The petas, their hopes shattered, made extremely terrifying screaming sounds in the king's palace during the night. The king was struck with fear, agitation, and trembling. When the night turned to dawn, he informed the Blessed One, saying, “Venerable Sir, I heard such a sound. What will happen to me?” The Blessed One said, “Great King, do not fear. No evil will happen to you. Rather, you have former relatives who have been reborn as petas. They have been wandering for an entire interval between Buddhas, hoping for this very thing, thinking, ‘Having given an offering to the Buddha, he will dedicate it to us.’”
172:
“They were wandering behind you, Great King, hoping, ‘He will dedicate the merit to us.’ Because you did not dedicate it to them yesterday, those petas, having lost hope, made such terrifying sounds.”

The king asked, “But Venerable Sir, if I give now, can they receive it?” “Yes, Great King,” he replied. “Then, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my offering for today; I will dedicate it to them.” The Blessed One accepted. The king returned to the palace, prepared a great offering, and had the time announced to the Blessed One. The Blessed One went into the inner palace and sat on the prepared seat together with the Saṅgha of monks. Those petas also stood outside the walls and other places, hoping, “Perhaps we will receive it today.” The Blessed One made it so that all of them were clearly visible to the king. While pouring the water of dedication, the king dedicated it, saying, “Let this merit be for my relatives.” At that very moment, lotus-covered ponds appeared for those petas. By bathing and drinking there, their distress, exhaustion, and thirst were appeased, and they became golden-hued. The king offered gruel, hard food, and soft food and dedicated it; at that moment, divine gruel, hard food, and soft food appeared for them. By consuming these, their faculties became vibrant. Then, he offered clothing and dwellings and dedicated them. Divine garments, divine vehicles, divine palaces, divine rugs, divine bedding, and other ornaments appeared for them. The Blessed One resolved that all their prosperity should be clearly visible to the king. The king was exceedingly delighted. Then, after the Blessed One had finished his meal and washed his hands, he spoke these verses beginning with “Tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti” to gladden the King of Magadha.

By this sequence of words, this mātikā (summary)—“By whom, where, when, and why was the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta preached”—has been analyzed both in brief and in detail.

## Commentary on the First Verse

Now, I shall explain the meaning of this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta in order. It is as follows: In the first verse, “tirokuṭṭā” means the outer side of the walls. “Tiṭṭhanti” is a word expressing the act of standing, excluding sitting and other postures. Therefore, just as people say of someone going to the other side of a wall or a mountain, “He goes past the wall or the mountain without obstruction,” so too in this context, regarding those standing on the outer side of the walls...
173:
"They stand outside the walls," He said. In the phrase "and at the junctions and crossroads," "sandhi" refers to four-way intersections, as well as the joints of a house, the joints of a wall, and the openings of windows. Three-way junctions are called "siṅghāṭaka." Combining these two terms with the preceding one, He said, "and at the junctions and crossroads." "They stand at the doorposts" means they stand leaning against the posts of city gates and house doors. In the phrase "having come to their own homes," "their own home" refers to either the home of relatives from a past life or a home where they themselves previously lived as owners. Because those petas come with the perception of it being their own home to both types of houses, He said, "having come to their own homes."

## Explanation of the Second Verse

In this way, the Blessed One, wishing to show King Bimbisāra the many petas who—though they had not lived there before—came to the palace of King Bimbisāra (the home of their past relatives) with the perception of it being their own home, and stood outside the walls, at junctions, crossroads, and doorposts, experiencing the results of their stinginess (macchariya); some having the appearance of long beards and hair, with dark faces, their black limbs emaciated and rough with loose, hanging sinews, standing here and there like palm trees burnt by a forest fire; some with bodies scorched by flames of fire rising from their bellies and emerging from their mouths due to the heat of hunger and thirst; some with throat-holes as small as the eye of a needle and bellies the size of a mountain, who, even when obtaining food and drink, are unable to eat as much as they desire and thus suffer from hunger and thirst, finding no other taste; some who, with bodies extremely hideous, deformed, and terrifying, lick the blood, pus, and discharge flowing from the mouths of their own or others' ruptured boils and pustules as if it were nectar—[the Blessed One] said:

"They stand outside the walls, and at the junctions and crossroads;
They stand at the doorposts, having come to their own homes."
