Having said this, wishing to show again the dreadful nature of the kamma committed by those petas, He spoke the second verse beginning with, "Though there is abundant food and drink."

In that verse, "pahūte" means not a little, but much; it means as much as desired. Indeed, the letter 'bh' is changed to 'h', as in "pahu santo na bharati" and so on. However, some teachers read it as "bahūte" or "bahūke." These readings are merely due to negligence.
174:
In that text, "annapāna" refers to food and drink. "Khajjabhojja" refers to hard food and soft food. By this, He shows the fourfold nutriment consisting of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. "Upaṭṭhite" means standing near, prepared, or gathered. Not a single person—mother, father, or child—remembers those beings who have arisen in the realm of the petas. For what reason? It is because of kamma. It is because of the kamma of stinginess (kadariya) of various kinds, such as not giving oneself and preventing others from giving, which they themselves had previously committed. Indeed, that kamma does not allow their relatives to remember them.

## Explanation of the Third Verse

The Blessed One, wishing to show those petas who, even when abundant food and drink are present, wander about hoping for their relatives, thinking, "May they give something dedicated to us," but who do not receive even a mere remembrance from their relatives due to the kamma that produces such extremely bitter results—said:

"Though there is abundant food and drink, and hard and soft food are prepared,
No one remembers those beings, because of their kamma."

Having said this, wishing to praise again the gift given by King Bimbisāra dedicated to his relatives who had reached the realm of the petas, He spoke the third verse beginning with "Evaṃ dadanti ñātīnaṃ."

In that verse, "evaṃ" (thus) is a word of comparison. It can be connected in two ways: First, although those beings are not remembered due to their kamma, [relatives] give for some reason; those relatives who are thus compassionate. Second, just as you, Great King, have given, so do those relatives who are compassionate give pure, choice, timely, and allowable drink and food to their relatives. "Dadanti" means they give, they dedicate, they hand over. "Ñātīnaṃ" refers to relatives connected from both the mother's and father's sides. "Ye" refers to anyone such as sons, daughters, or brothers. "Anukampakā" means those who desire one's welfare and seek one's benefit. "Suciṃ" means pure, beautiful, pleasing, righteous, and righteously obtained. "Paṇītaṃ" means excellent, superior. "Kālena" means at the time when the relative petas have come and stood outside the walls and so on. "Kappiyaṃ" means suitable, proper, and fit for the use of the Noble Ones. "Pānabhojanaṃ" means drink and food. Here, by the expression "drink and food," all gifts to be given are intended.
175:
## Commentary on the First Half of the Fourth Verse

In this way, the Blessed One, wishing to praise the food and drink given by the King of Magadha out of compassion for his relatives who had become petas (departed spirits), said:

“Thus they give to their relatives, those who are compassionate; pure, choice, timely, and allowable food and drink.”

Having said this, wishing to show again the manner in which the gift given becomes beneficial to those petas, he spoke the first half of the fourth verse: “May this be for your relatives.” This half-verse should be connected with the first half of the third verse as follows:

“Thus they give to their relatives, those who are compassionate: ‘May this be for your relatives, may the relatives be happy,’ thus they give.”

By this connection, it is shown that they give in this manner, “May this be for your relatives,” and not otherwise; thus, the word ‘evaṃ’ (thus), having the sense of ‘manner,’ illustrates the manner of giving.

In that passage, ‘idaṃ’ (this) refers to the gift (deyyadhamma). ‘Vo’ is a mere particle (nipāta), just as in “Kacci pana vo Anuruddhā samaggā sammodamānā” and “Yehi vo ariyā” etc., and is not a genitive case (denoting possession). ‘Ñātīnaṃ hotu’ (may it be for relatives) means may it be for the relatives who have been reborn in the realm of the departed (peta-visaya). ‘Sukhitā hontu ñātayo’ (may the relatives be happy) means may those relatives reborn in the realm of the departed, experiencing the benefit of this gift, reach happiness.

## Commentary on the Second Half of the Fourth Verse and the First Half of the Fifth Verse

4-5. In this way, the Blessed One, wishing to show the manner in which the gift is given to relatives reborn in the realm of the departed, said: “May this be for your relatives, may the relatives be happy.” Then, because even when it is said, “May this be for your relatives,” the karma performed by one person does not give results to another; rather, that object given with such a dedication becomes a condition (paccaya) for the wholesome karma of the peta relatives. Therefore, wishing to show how the wholesome karma that produces results at that very moment arises for those petas based on that very gift, he spoke the second half of the fourth verse, “And they there...”, and the first half of the fifth verse, “When there is abundant food and drink.”
176:
The meaning of those words is: those peta relatives come from all directions and gather together at the place where the gift is given, or it means they become united as one. “Sammā āgatā samāgatā” (well-come and gathered) means they have come properly for this purpose, thinking, “These relatives of ours will dedicate a gift for our sake.” “Pahūte annapānamhi” (in the presence of abundant food and drink) means when abundant rice, hard food, and soft food are given, being dedicated to them at that time. “Sakkaccaṃ anumodare” (they appreciate respectfully) means, having great faith in karma and its results without abandoning it, being respectful and having undistracted minds, they rejoice and appreciate, saying, “May this gift of ours be for our welfare and happiness”; they become filled with joy and gladness.

## Commentary on the Second Half of the Fifth Verse and the First Half of the Sixth Verse

5-6. In this way, the Blessed One, wishing to show how wholesome karma that produces results at that very moment arises for those reborn in the realm of the departed, said:

“And they, having gathered there, the peta relatives who have come together,
In the presence of abundant food and drink, appreciate respectfully.”

Having said this, wishing to show the manner of praise toward their relatives by those petas who are experiencing the results of the wholesome karma that arose depending on their relatives, he spoke the second half of the fifth verse, “May they live long,” and the first half of the sixth verse, “And honor has been paid to us.”

The meaning of those words: “Ciraṃ jīvantu” means may they live for a long time, may they be long-lived. “No ñātī” means our relatives. “Yesaṃ hetu” means depending on which relatives or because of which relatives. “Labhāmashe” means we receive. They speak this referring to the prosperity and happiness they have received at that moment. Indeed, an offering (dakkhiṇā) is successful and yields results at that very moment through three factors: the appreciation (anumodana) of the petas themselves, the dedication (uddesa) of the donors, and the perfection of the recipients (dakkhiṇeyya-sampadā). Among these, the donors are the special cause. Therefore, the petas say, “Yesaṃ hetu labhāmashe” (Because of whom we receive). “Amhākañca katā pūjā” (And honor has been paid to us) means that by those who dedicate this gift, saying “May this be for your relatives,” honor has also been paid to us. “Dāyakā ca anipphalā” (And the donors are not without fruit) means that in whichever person's continuity (santāna) the wholesome deed consisting of renunciation (pariccāga) is performed, it gives results to that person right there; therefore, the donors are also not without benefit.

In this matter, a questioner might ask: “Do only relatives reborn in the realm of the departed receive it, or do other petas receive it as well?”
177:
In this matter, [the objector] asked: "Do only relatives who have been reborn in the realm of the departed (petas) receive [the gift], or do other departed ones receive it as well?" To answer this question—since the Blessed One himself answered this when asked by the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, there is nothing further for us to say here. That answer was as follows:

"Master Gotama, we Brahmins give gifts and perform faith-offerings (saddhā), thinking, 'May this gift reach our departed kinsmen and relatives; may our departed kinsmen and relatives enjoy this gift.' Master Gotama, does that gift actually reach those departed kinsmen and relatives? Do those departed kinsmen and relatives enjoy that gift?" (he asked). "Brahmin, it reaches one who stands in a fitting place (ṭhāna), but not one who stands in an unfitting place (aṭṭhāna)," (the Buddha replied).

"Master Gotama, what is a fitting place, and what is an unfitting place?" (he asked again). "Brahmin, here, a certain person kills living beings... [etc.]... and holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in hell (niraya). He subsists there on the food of the beings in hell; he is sustained there by that. Brahmin, this is an unfitting place where the gift does not reach the one standing there.

Brahmin, here, a certain person kills living beings... [etc.]... and holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the animal realm. He subsists there on the food of the animals; he is sustained there by that. Brahmin, this is also an unfitting place where the gift does not reach the one standing there.

Brahmin, here, a certain person abstains from killing living beings... [etc.]... and holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of humans... [etc.]... or in the company of devas. He subsists there on the food of the devas; he is sustained there by that. Brahmin, this is also an unfitting place where the gift does not reach the one standing there.

Brahmin, here, a certain person kills living beings... [etc.]... and holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the realm of the departed (pettivisaya). The food of the beings born in the realm of the departed is such that..."
178:
That person subsists there in that realm of hungry ghosts (peta-loka) on that food; he remains there on that food. Or else, whatever gift friends and colleagues or kinsmen and relatives give from this world (by sharing merit), the hungry ghost subsists there on that; he remains there on that. Brahmin, this is indeed the condition where the gift is of benefit to one stationed there. "Master Gotama, if that deceased kinsman or relative has not been reborn in that place, who then enjoys that gift?" "Brahmin, other deceased kinsmen and relatives of that donor may be reborn in that place; they enjoy that gift." "Master Gotama, if that deceased kinsman or relative has not been reborn in that place, and other deceased kinsmen and relatives have also not been reborn in that place, who then enjoys that gift?" "Brahmin, it is impossible, there is no chance, that over this long period of time, this realm of hungry ghosts would be void of deceased kinsmen and relatives. Furthermore, Brahmin, the donor himself is not without fruit (the donor also benefits)." (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 10.177).

## Commentary on the Latter Half of the Sixth Verse and the Seventh Verse

6-7. In this way, the Blessed One, wishing to praise the attainment of the former relatives of the King of Magadha who had been reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, showed: "Great King, those relatives of yours, being delighted by this perfection of giving, praise it thus"—

"May our relatives live long, for whose sake we have received (this gift); an offering has been made to us, and the donors are not without fruit."

Having said this, wishing to show again that for those reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, there is no other means of obtaining wealth such as farming or cattle-rearing, and that they must subsist only on what is given from this world, He spoke the latter half of the sixth verse, "Na hi tattha kasī atthi," and this seventh verse beginning with "Vaṇijjā tādisī."

Therein, the commentary on the meaning is: Great King, in that realm of hungry ghosts, there is no farming depending on which those ghosts might obtain wealth. When it is said "cattle-rearing is not found here," it means not only is there no farming, but there is also no cattle-rearing in this realm of hungry ghosts depending on which they might obtain wealth.
179:
In that realm of the departed (peta), there is no such thing as farming by which those departed ones might obtain wealth. "Vaṇijjā tādisī natthi" means there is also no such trade that could be the cause for their obtaining wealth, which would be the cause for their prosperity (meaning such trade does not exist). "Hiraññena kayakayaṃ" means that in that realm of the departed, there is no buying and selling with gold and silver that could be the cause for their obtaining wealth. "Ito dinnena yāpenti, petā kālagatā tahiṃ" means that they actually subsist only on the offerings given from this human world by relatives or friends; they sustain their existence. "Petā" refers to beings born in the realm of the departed. "Kālagatā" refers to those who have gone to their time of death; there is also a variant reading "kālakatā," which means those who have completed their death. "Tahiṃ" means in that realm of the departed.

## Commentary on the Eighth and Ninth Verses
8-9. Having thus said, "They subsist on the offerings given from this world, the departed who have passed away there," now, wishing to clarify that meaning with similes, He spoke these two verses beginning with "Unname udakaṃ vuṭṭhaṃ."

The meaning of that verse is: Just as water rained by clouds on high ground flows to the low ground, reaching whatever part of the land is low or depressed, even so, the gift given from this world benefits the departed, brings results, and manifests. The meaning is that just as the place for the flow of water is the low ground, the place for the benefit of the gift to reach is the world of the departed. The Blessed One also said, "Brahmin, this is the place where the gift benefits one stationed there." Furthermore, just as the great rivers, being filled by the confluence of ponds, lakes, clefts, small channels, and large channels, fill the ocean, even so, the gift given from this world benefits the departed in the manner previously stated.

## Commentary on the Tenth Verse
Thus the Blessed One, having clarified this meaning with similes that "They subsist on the offerings given from this world, the departed who have passed away there," again, because those departed ones, overcome by the hope that "We might receive something from these relatives," come to the houses of their relatives but are unable to request, "Give us such and such a thing," therefore, these subjects of recollection for them...
180:
To show that a son of good family should give an offering by repeatedly recollecting the favors done in the past, the Buddha spoke this verse beginning with "Adāsi me". The meaning of that verse is: "He gave me such wealth or grain"; "He himself exerted effort and performed this task for me"; "This person is a relative related to me from my mother’s or father’s side"; "He is a friend (mitta) because he was a worthy refuge through the power of affection"; "This person is a companion (sakhā) who played in the dust with me"—thus, by repeatedly recollecting everything in this way, one should give an offering to the departed (petas); one should dedicate the gift. There is another variant reading: "Petānaṃ dakkhiṇā dajjā". The meaning of that reading is: "dajjā" means it should be given. What is it that should be given? It is the offering (dakkhiṇā) given to the departed. Therefore, it means that one who recollects the favors done in the past in the manner beginning with "Adāsi me" is repeatedly recollecting. It should be understood that the nominative case is used where the instrumental case would be expected.

## Commentary on the Eleventh Verse
In this way, the Blessed One, wishing to show the reasons for recollecting which are the causes for dedicating offerings to the departed, said:

"He gave to me, he worked for me, he was my relative, friend, and companion; one should give an offering to the departed, recollecting the favors done in the past."

Having said this, he then spoke this verse beginning with "Na hi ruṇṇaṃ vā" to show that for those who remain preoccupied only with weeping, sorrow, and so on due to the death of a relative, and do not give anything for the sake of the deceased, that weeping, sorrow, and so on only result in personal distress and do not achieve any benefit for the departed.

In that verse, "ruṇṇa" means weeping, the state of crying, or the shedding of tears. By this term, physical exertion (kāyapari-ssama) is shown. "Soka" means sorrow or the state of grieving. By this term, mental exertion (cittapari-ssama) is shown. "Yā caññā" means that which is other than weeping and sorrow. "Paridevanā" means the lamentation of one struck by the loss of a relative, wailing by recounting virtues in such a way as "O dear only son, where have you gone?" By this term, verbal exertion (vacīpari-ssama) is shown.
181:
## Commentary on the Twelfth Verse
In this way, the Blessed One showed the futility of weeping and so forth, saying: "Weeping, sorrow, or any other lamentation does not benefit the departed (petas); indeed, it only causes distress to oneself, while the relatives remain thus (without benefit)." Then, wishing to show the benefit of the offering (dakkhiṇā) given by the King of Magadha, he spoke this verse beginning with "Ayañca kho dakkhiṇā."

The meaning of that verse is: Great King, this offering given by you today, dedicated to your group of relatives, is well-established in the Saṅgha. Because the Saṅgha is the unrivaled field of merit (puññakkhetta) for the world, that offering benefits, fulfills, and bears fruit for those departed relatives for a long time. The word "upakappati" means it benefits at that very moment, or reaches them without delay. For example, just as it is said, "It occurred to the Tathāgata at that very moment," when something appears in his knowledge instantly, here too, "upakappati" is used to mean it benefits at that very moment. Alternatively, as it was said, "Brahmin, this is the place where the gift benefits one who stands there," it means it benefits those who reside in various states of the peta realm, such as those who are hungry and thirsty, those who eat vomit, those who live on what is given by others, or those consumed by craving. It is like in the world when giving coins, it is said, "He gives according to the coins." According to this interpretation, "upakappati" means it manifests or is produced.

## Commentary on the Thirteenth Verse
In this way, the Blessed One, showing the benefit of the offering given by the King, said:

"And this offering has been given, well-established in the Saṅgha;
It benefits that departed one for a long time, accruing at that very moment."

Having said this, [he continued]: Furthermore, by giving this offering, the duty to relatives (ñātidhamma) has been shown through performing what should be done by relatives for their kin; it has been made clear to many people. You too should fulfill the duty to relatives by performing what should be done for them, and not distress yourselves with futile weeping and so forth. By enabling the departed to obtain celestial splendor, a grand honor has been paid to them. By satisfying the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, with food, drink, and so forth, strength has been given to the monks. By generating the volition of generosity (cāga-cetanā) accompanied by qualities such as compassion, immeasurable merit has been accumulated.

Therefore, the Blessed One, gladdening the King with these true qualities, instructed him well with the Dhamma through this verse: "And this duty to relatives has been shown." Indeed, showing the duty to relatives is itself "instruction" (sandassana). With the words, "And a grand honor has been paid to the departed," he incited him. Indeed, praising it as "grand" is itself "inciting" (samādapana) to perform the honor repeatedly. With the words, "And strength has been given to the monks," he roused him. Indeed, such an offering is the giving of strength; by increasing his enthusiasm through the giving of strength, it is "rousing" (samuttejana). With the words, "Immeasurable merit has been accumulated by you," he gladdened him. Indeed, the proclamation of the accumulation of merit, by way of praising his true qualities, generates joy and is thus to be understood as "gladdening" (sampahaṃsana).
182:
Merit has been accumulated; therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to gladden King Bimbisāra with these true qualities, said:

"And this duty to relatives has been shown,
And a grand honor has been paid to the departed,
And strength has been given to the monks,
Immeasurable merit has been accumulated by you."

With this verse, he concluded the teaching.

Alternatively, with the verse-line "And this duty to relatives has been shown," the Blessed One well-instructed King Bimbisāra with a Dhamma talk. In this context, showing the duty to relatives is itself "instruction" (sandassana). With the words "And a grand honor has been paid to the departed," he incited him. In this context, praising it as "grand" is itself "inciting" (samādapana) to perform the honor repeatedly. With the words "And strength has been given to the monks," he roused him. In this context, such an offering is the giving of strength; by increasing the King's enthusiasm through the giving of strength, it is "rousing" (samuttejana). With the words "Immeasurable merit has been accumulated by you," he gladdened him. In this context, the proclamation of the accumulation of merit, by way of praising the King's true qualities, generates joy and is thus to be understood as "gladdening" (sampahaṃsana).

At the conclusion of the teaching, because the disadvantages of being reborn in the peta realm were explained, eighty-four thousand beings who were moved and strove with wise reflection attained Dhamma realization. On the second day as well, the Blessed One preached this same Tirokuṭṭa Sutta to devas and humans; it is said that such Dhamma realizations occurred in this way for seven days.

## The Commentary on the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta
## in the Khuddakapāṭha-Aṭṭhakathā named Paramatthajotikā is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta
## Occasion for the Discourse (Nikkhepakāraṇa)

Now, the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, which begins with "Nidhiṃ nidheti puriso" (A man buries a treasure), is placed immediately after the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta. Of that Sutta—
183:
It should be understood as giving joy. At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma, having become stirred and having practiced with wise reflection after the faults of being reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas) were shown. On the second day as well, the Blessed One preached this same Tirokuṭṭa Sutta to devas and humans. In this manner, such realization of the Dhamma occurred for seven days. Thus ends the commentary on the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta in the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary named Paramatthajotikā.

Commentary on the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta. Now, the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, which begins with "Nidhiṃ nidheti puriso," is placed immediately after the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta. Having stated the reason for its placement here and having shown the circumstances of its origin (atthuppatti), I shall provide the explanation of its meaning. In this regard, the reason for its placement should first be understood as follows: Although the Blessed One did not preach this Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta in this specific sequence, it is placed here because it is a counterpart to the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, which was preached by way of appreciation (anumodanā). Alternatively, it should be understood that it is placed here to show the success of those who have performed merit through this Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, after having shown the ruin of those devoid of merit through the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta. This is the reason for its placement here.

## Suttaṭṭhuppatti (The Origin of the Sutta)

The circumstances of its origin (atthuppatti) should be understood as follows: In the city of Sāvatthī, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and great resources. He was faithful and devoted, living the household life with a mind free from the stain of stinginess. One day, he gave an offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. At that time, the King, being in need of wealth, sent a man to him, saying, "Go, fellow, and bring the householder named so-and-so." That royal messenger went and said to the householder, "Householder, the King summons you."

The householder, while serving the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with a mind endowed with qualities such as faith, said, "Go, good man, I will come later; for now, I am occupied with burying a treasure." Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal and having declined further food, spoke these verses beginning with "Nidhiṃ nidheti puriso" for the sake of showing that the perfection of merit is the only treasure in the ultimate sense, and for the sake of gladdening that householder. This is the origin of this Sutta.

Thus:
"Having stated the reason for the placement of the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta here,
And having shown the circumstances of its origin,
I shall provide the explanation of its meaning."

## Paṭhamagāthāvaṇṇanā (Commentary on the First Verse)

In that context, regarding "Nidhiṃ nidheti puriso": it is called a treasure (nidhi) because it is stored away; the meaning is that it is placed, guarded, and secured. That treasure is of four kinds: immovable (thāvara), movable (jaṅgama), limb-like (aṅgasama), and following (anugāmika). Among these four, the immovable treasure refers to silver, gold, fields, property, or any other such thing devoid of posture (inanimate), whether situated in the ground or in the open air...
184: After feeding the Sangha of monks, the householder said, "O man, you go ahead; I am burying a treasure pot and will come after staying a while." At that time, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, spoke the verses beginning with "Nidhiṃ nidheti" to gladden the householder and to show that, in the ultimate sense, the perfection of merit is the true treasure (nidhi) to be stored. This is the origin (atthuppatti) of the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta. Having thus explained the reason for its placement and the origin, I shall now provide the commentary on the meaning. In the phrase "Nidhiṃ nidheti puriso," it is called "nidhi" (treasure) because it is stored, placed, guarded, and secured. There are four types of treasure: stationary treasure (thāvara), movable treasure (jaṅgama), limb-like treasure (aṅgasama), and following treasure (anugāmika). Among these four, stationary treasure (thāvara-nidhi) refers to silver, gold, fields, houses, or any other such thing devoid of posture (stationary) located in the ground or in open space. This is called stationary treasure (thāvara-nidhi). Movable treasure (jaṅgama-nidhi) refers to female slaves, male slaves, elephants, cattle, horses, camels, goats, sheep, poultry, pigs, or any other such thing associated with posture (movable). This is called movable treasure (jaṅgama-nidhi). Limb-like treasure (aṅgasama-nidhi) refers to professional skills, arts, sciences, great learning, or any other such thing acquired through training and connected to one's own being like major and minor limbs. This is called limb-like treasure (aṅgasama-nidhi). Following treasure (anugāmika-nidhi) refers to merit consisting of giving (dāna), observing virtue (sīla), developing meditation (bhāvanā), listening to the Dhamma, and teaching the Dhamma, or any other such merit that follows one through various lives and yields desired results. This is called following treasure (anugāmika-nidhi). In this context, stationary treasure (thāvara-nidhi) is intended. "Nidheti" means placing, storing, or guarding. "Puriso" means a human being. Although men, women, or eunuchs may bury treasure, the teaching is given with "man" as the primary subject; however, in meaning, women and others should also be understood as included here. "Gambhīre odaka-antike": It is "gambhīra" (deep) in the sense that one must go down into it; it is "odaka-antike" because of its proximity to water. There are pits that are deep but not near water (e.g., a pit seven fathoms deep in dry land). There are pits near water but not deep (e.g., a pit one or two spans deep in a low-lying marsh). There are pits that are both deep and near water (e.g., a pit dug in dry land until water is reached). It is with reference to such a pit that is both deep and near water that "Gambhīre odaka-antike" is said. "Atthe kicce samuppanne": It is "attha" because it is not devoid of benefit; it means bringing benefit or welfare. It is "kicca" because it is to be done; it means some duty or task. "Samuppanna" means simply arisen; it means a task that has appeared as something to be performed. (It means) when such a task related to one's benefit has arisen. "Atthāya me bhavissati": This shows the purpose of burying the treasure. That person buries the treasure with the intention: "When some beneficial task arises, it will be for my benefit; it will be for the accomplishment of that task." For when a task arises, its accomplishment is indeed the benefit for that person. ## Commentary on the Second Verse. Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to show the benefit of burying treasure, has shown the desire for attaining benefit. Now, to show the desire for escaping harm, He spoke the verse beginning with "Rājato vā uparuddhassa".
185:
“Whether it be for an accusation by the king, or for being oppressed by thieves, or for release from debt, or in times of famine, or in calamities (it will be of benefit).”

The meaning of this verse should be understood by connecting it, as far as possible, with the words “it will be for my benefit” and “for release from debt,” using the two terms mentioned here: “will be” (bhavissati) and “for release” (pamokkhāya).

In this context, the connection is as follows: A man does not bury a treasure pot solely with the thought, “It will be for my benefit.” Rather, it will be for release from the king when he is falsely accused by enemies in such ways as, “This man is a thief,” or “He is an adulterer,” or “He is a tax evader,” and so on. Or, it will be for release from thieves when he is oppressed by them, either through the stealing of wealth by breaking into a tunnel and so forth, or by being captured alive with the demand, “Give this much gold and silver.” There are creditors of mine; they will demand, “Pay the debt.” When thus demanded, it will be for release from debt. There are times when a famine occurs, when crops fail and alms-food is difficult to obtain; at such a time, it is not easy to survive with little wealth. When such a famine arrives, it will be for my benefit. Whatever calamities arise from fire, water, or unloved heirs—when such calamities arise, it will be for my benefit. Thinking thus, a man buries a treasure pot.

Having thus shown the two kinds of purposes for burying a treasure through these two verses—namely, the intention to acquire benefit and the intention to avoid harm—he now says, wishing to conclude those two kinds of purposes:

“For this purpose, what is called a treasure is buried in the world.”

The meaning of that verse is: For this purpose—for the sake of achieving these benefits shown as “it will be for my benefit” and “when falsely accused by the king,” etc., namely the acquisition of benefit and the avoidance of harm—in this world of space (okāsaloka), what is called a treasure, consisting of various kinds such as gold and silver, is buried, placed, and stored.
186:
## Commentary on the Third Verse
Now, because even a treasure buried in this way brings about the desired goal only for those with merit and not for others, he said this to clarify that point:

"Though that treasure is well buried in a deep place near water, not all of it always serves him."

The meaning of that verse is: That treasure is first "well buried," which means it is placed after being well dug in. How well? It is said to be "well" to the extent that it is considered buried "in a deep place near water." "Not all of it always serves him" means that for the man by whom it was buried, the entire treasure does not serve or succeed for him at all times; it means it is not capable of performing the aforementioned tasks. Rather, only some treasure might serve at some time, or it might not serve at all. In this verse, the word "taṃ" should be understood as a mere particle (nipāta) used to complete the verse, as in "yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino," etc. Alternatively, it is said as "taṃ" instead of "so" by changing the gender (lingabheda). This is because the meaning is easily understood when spoken in this way.

## Commentary on the Fourth and Fifth Verses
Having thus said, "Not all of it always serves him," he now said this to show the reasons why it does not serve:

"The treasure shifts from its place, or his memory becomes confused.
Nāgas move it away, or Yakkhas carry it off.
Unloved heirs dig it up when he is not looking."

The meaning of that verse is: In whatever place the treasure is well stored, that treasure shifts, moves away, or disappears from that place. Even though it is an inanimate object, it moves to another place by the power of the exhaustion of merit (puññakkhaya). Or his memory becomes confused; he no longer knows the place where the treasure was buried. Or Nāgas, prompted by the exhaustion of his merit, move that treasure to another place. Or Yakkhas carry it off to wherever they desire.
187:
They take it away. While he is not looking, unloved heirs also dig up the earth and unearth that treasure. Thus, for these reasons such as shifting from the place, that stored treasure does not benefit him.

Having thus spoken of the worldly recognized reasons for not benefiting, such as shifting from the place, now, in order to show the single reason which is the root of even these reasons, known as the 'exhaustion of merit', he said: "When there is exhaustion of merit, all this wealth perishes."

The meaning of that verse is: At the time when the merit that produces the attainment of wealth is exhausted, and demerit that leads to the ruin of wealth has gained an opportunity and stands firm, then all the collection of wealth such as gold and silver deposited by the one who stores the treasure perishes.

## Commentary on the Sixth Verse

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the worldly recognized treasure which, though stored with various intentions, does not benefit according to those intentions and is subject to destruction in various ways, now, in order to show the attainment of merit as treasure in the ultimate sense, and for the sake of gladdening that householder, began this Nidhikaṇḍa. To show that treasure of merit, he said:

"When a treasure is well-stored by a woman or a man,
Through giving, through virtue,
Through restraint, and through self-control."

In that verse, 'giving' (dāna) should be taken in the same way as mentioned in the verse "Giving and righteous conduct" (dānañca dhammacariyā ca). 'Virtue' (sīla) means non-transgression by body and speech. Alternatively, all virtue such as the five precepts, ten precepts, and the restraint of the Pātimokkha is intended here as 'virtue'. 'Restraint' (saṃyama) means restraining; it means preventing the mind from going to various objects; this is a synonym for concentration (samādhi). One endowed with such restraint is called 'the best among the restrained' in the passage: "Restrained in hand, restrained in foot, restrained in speech, the best among the restrained." Others say: "Restraint is saṃyama; it means closing off; this is a synonym for sense-restraint (indriyasaṃvara)." 'Self-control' (dama) means taming; it means the calming of defilements; this is a synonym for wisdom (paññā). Indeed, wisdom in some places...
188:
...is called 'wisdom' (paññā) itself, as in such passages as "Through listening, one gains wisdom." In some places, it is called 'Dhamma', as in "Truth, Dhamma, courage, and generosity." In some places, it is called 'self-control' (dama), as in "If there is nothing greater than truth, self-control, generosity, and patience."

Having thus understood giving and so forth, now the meaning of this verse should be understood collectively: For whatever woman or man, through these four qualities—giving, virtue, restraint, and self-control—(just as a treasure consisting of wealth such as gold, silver, pearls, or gems is stored by placing those gold and other items in one place), so too a treasure consisting of merit is well-stored by performing those acts of giving and so forth well, either in one's own mental continuum or in an object such as a shrine (cetiya).

## Commentary on the Seventh Verse

Thus the Blessed One, having shown the state of being a treasure in the ultimate sense through the attainment of merit by this verse beginning with "When through giving", now, in order to show the object where that treasure, when stored, becomes well-stored, said:

"In a shrine, or in the Saṅgha,
In an individual, or in guests,
In mother and father,
And also in an elder brother."

In that verse, it is called 'shrine' (cetiya) because it should be honored; it means it is worthy of worship. Or it is called cetiya because merit is accumulated. That shrine is of three kinds: a shrine of use (paribhoga-cetiya), a representative shrine (uddissaka-cetiya), and a relic shrine (dhātuka-cetiya). Among them, the Bodhi tree is a shrine of use. A Buddha image is a representative shrine. Stupas containing relics are relic shrines. 'The Saṅgha' means any one among the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. 'Individual' (puggala) means any one among laypeople or monks. One who has no fixed date or who arrives on any day is a 'guest' (atithi). This is a synonym for a visitor who has arrived at that moment. The rest is just as previously explained.

Having thus understood shrines and so forth, now the meaning of this verse should be understood collectively: That treasure of merit which was said to be 'well-stored' is well-stored in these objects. Why? Because of the ability to provide desired results over a long period of time. For indeed, by giving even a little to a shrine, people become recipients of desired results for a long time. As it is said:
189:
“By offering a single flower, for eighty billion aeons I have not known a miserable state; this is the fruit of offering flowers.” And, “If by renouncing a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure” (Dhammapada 290). In this way, the distribution of the fruits of giving in relation to the Saṅgha and other objects should be understood according to the method taught in the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta, Velāma Sutta, and so forth. Just as the practice and the excellence of the fruits of giving toward shrines (cetiyas) and such are shown, so too, in all instances based on various objects, one should understand the practice and the excellence of the fruits of: virtue (sīla) through the power of performed and avoided conduct (cāritta and vāritta); restraint (saṃyama) through the power of the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati); and self-control (dama) through the power of insight (vipassanā), attention, and reflection based on those objects.

## Commentary on the Eighth Verse
Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the objects such as shrines where the treasure of merit is stored through giving and so forth, now wishing to show the distinction between that treasure well-stored in those objects and a treasure buried deep in the earth near water, said:
“This treasure is well-stored, unconquerable, and follows one along. Among things that must be left behind, one takes this along.”

In that verse, with the first phrase, “This treasure is well-stored,” he points to that treasure well-stored through giving and so forth. “Ajeyyo” means it cannot be conquered and taken by others. There is also a variant reading “acceyyo”; the meaning of that version is that it is something to be accumulated, worthy of honor, and to be collected by one desiring welfare and happiness. In this reading, after connecting it as “this treasure is to be accumulated,” one should then ask “Why?” and connect it with “because it is well-stored and follows one along.” Otherwise, it would imply that what is already well-stored is yet to be accumulated; however, what is well-stored is not currently being accumulated. That treasure follows along only because it has already been accumulated. “Anugāmiko” means it follows; the meaning is that even when going to the next world, it does not abandon one, providing results in various existences.

“Among things that must be left behind, one takes this along” means that when the time of death arrives, among all possessions that must be abandoned and left behind, one takes this treasure and goes to the next world. This is the intended meaning. However, that meaning is not appropriate. Why?
190:
Because wealth cannot follow. Those various possessions are only to be abandoned; they are not things that can be gone with. Rather, it is to those various destinations (gati) that one must go. If this were the meaning, it would be said, “Having abandoned wealth, [it follows] to the destinations where one must go.” Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: in the manner of “the treasure shifts from its place,” etc., when the mortal being goes, abandoning their possessions, they take this treasure of merit and go. Because this treasure follows along, it does not abandon that person.

In that context, if it is said that in the word “gamanīyesu,” the meaning is “in those who go” and not “in the possessions that are gone with,” that meaning should not be taken exclusively. Just as in the passage “The Noble Ones are leading out (niyyānikā)” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.141), the meaning is “those who lead out” and not “those who are to be led out,” so too here, the meaning is “in those [possessions] which are going [away]” and not “in those to be gone to.”

Alternatively, because at the time of death, even if one wishes to give to someone, one cannot even touch or handle one's possessions; therefore, it is said that those possessions must first be abandoned by the body and later passed over by the mind which is devoid of hope. Therefore, the meaning here should be regarded as: “among possessions that are first abandoned by the body and later gone from by the mind.” In the former meaning, the locative case (sattamī vibhatti) is used in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa); it means that among the possessions that are abandoned and gone from, one takes out and carries away only this wealth of the treasure of merit. In the latter meaning, the locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic action (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa). By the fact of the possessions going away, the fact of this treasure being taken along is characterized.

## Commentary on the Ninth Verse

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the distinction of this treasure of merit over a treasure buried deep in the earth near water, again, like a noble merchant who generates enthusiasm in buyers by praising the qualities of his goods, he spoke thus, wishing to generate enthusiasm in devas and humans for that treasure of merit by praising the qualities of the treasure of merit he had taught:

“It is not shared with others, a treasure thieves cannot steal.
As for the treasure that follows one along, let the wise person perform those merits.”
191:
In that verse, 'asādhāraṇamaññesaṃ' means that which is not shared with others (not owned by others). The letter 'ma' is merely a euphonic particle (padasandhi) used for joining words, as in 'adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā' and so forth. 'Acora-āharaṇo' means that which cannot be carried away by thieves; the meaning is that it is not something thieves should or can take. It is called 'nidhi' (treasure-store) because it is something to be stored or buried. Having thus praised the qualities of the treasure of merit with these two terms, [the Buddha] then inspires effort toward that merit, saying: 'A wise person should perform merits, for it is the treasure that follows one.'

The meaning of that verse is: Because merits are a treasure not shared with others and cannot be carried away by thieves. Not only is it a treasure not shared and not taken by thieves, but it is also the 'treasure that follows one' mentioned here in the words: 'This treasure is well-stored, invincible, and follows one.' Since that treasure which follows one is indeed merit, a person endowed with wisdom and endowed with courage should perform merits.

## Commentary on the Tenth Verse

In this way, the Blessed One, having inspired devas and humans toward the treasure of merit by praising its qualities, now speaks to show briefly what fruit that treasure gives to those who strive and fulfill the making of the treasure of merit: 'This treasure gives all that is desired to devas and humans.'

Now, because the quality of giving all that is desired is connected to aspiration, it does not happen without aspiration. As it is said: 'Householders, if a righteous person (dhammacārī), one who lives evenly (samacārī), should aspire: "Oh, may I, after the breaking up of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of wealthy Khattiyas (khattiyamahāsālā)," it is possible that he, after the breaking up of the body, after death, would be reborn in the company of wealthy Khattiyas. Why is that? Because he is a righteous person, one who lives evenly.' (M.i.442).

Similarly: 'May I, by realizing for myself through direct knowledge, enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind (cetovimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) in this very life. Why is that? Because he is a righteous person, one who lives evenly.' (M.i.442).
192:
Furthermore, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, here a monk is endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. It occurs to him: "Oh, may I, after the breaking up of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of wealthy Khattiyas." He exerts that mind, resolves on that mind, and develops that mind. Those formations (saṅkhārā) and abidings (viharā) of his, thus developed and frequently practiced, lead to rebirth there.' (M.iii.161), and so forth.

Therefore, wishing to show that aspiration—accompanied by the exertion, resolution, and development of the mind in various ways according to the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta—is the cause for that treasure's quality of giving all that is desired, he said: 'Whatever they aspire for, all that is obtained by this.'

## Commentary on the Eleventh Verse

Now, wishing to show individually the various things that can be obtained by this treasure of merit, he spoke the verses beginning with 'suvaṇṇatā susaratā'.

In those verses, first, 'suvaṇṇatā' means having a beautiful complexion, a skin like the color of gold. That beauty is also obtainable through this treasure of merit. That it is so obtainable, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, when the Tathāgata in a former birth... (p) ... being a human in the past, was without anger and not full of despair. Though much was said [against him], he did not take offense, did not get angry, was not hostile, did not resent, and did not manifest anger, hate, or discontent. He was a giver of fine, soft rugs and cloaks, of fine linen, cotton... silk... and fine wool. Due to the performance and accumulation of that deed... having come to this state, he obtained this mark of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa): he is golden-colored, with skin like the color of gold.' (D.iii.218).

'Susaratā' means having a voice like that of Brahmā or the Karavīka bird. That sweet voice is also obtainable through this treasure of merit. That it is so obtainable, the Blessed One said: ...
193:
"Monks, in a former birth, the Tathāgata, having abandoned harsh speech, abstained from harsh speech. He spoke only such speech as is blameless, pleasing to the ear, and of such a nature. Because of performing and accumulating that kamma, when he reached this human existence, he obtained these two marks of a Great Man: he has a long tongue and a voice like that of Brahmā, like the song of the Karavīka bird." Thus it was said (in the Pāthika Vagga of the Dīgha Nikāya).

Susaṇṭhāna means having a good physical form. It refers to the excellence of the physical body through the well-proportioned arrangement of the major and minor limbs in places where they should be properly set. This quality is also obtained through this treasure of merit. How did the Buddha teach this?

"Monks, in a former birth, when the Tathāgata was previously a human being, he desired the benefit of many people, he desired their welfare, he desired their comfort, and he desired their security. He thought, 'How may these people of mine increase in faith, and also in virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, wealth and grain, fields and lands, two-footed and four-footed animals, sons and wives, slaves, workers, and servants, relatives, friends, and kin?' Because of that kamma, when he reached this existence, he obtained these three marks of a Great Man: he has the front half of the body like that of a lion, he has the space between the shoulders well-filled, and he has a well-rounded neck," and so forth.

In this manner, other Sutta passages that demonstrate the attainment of other marks through this treasure of merit should be brought from here and there and explained. I have summarized this for fear of it becoming too extensive. Now, I shall provide the commentary for the remaining terms.

In the term surūpatā, the entire body should be understood as 'form' (rūpa), as in the passage, "The space surrounded [by the elements] is known as form." The excellence of that form is called surūpatā. It means being not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too fat, not too dark, and not too fair. Ādhipacca means sovereignty; it has the sense of being a lord or master, such as being a Khattiya Mahāsāla. Parivāra means the wealth of relatives and attendants for householders, and the wealth of a following for those who have gone forth.
194:
The state of sovereignty and having a retinue is called ādhipaccaparivāra. Here, it should be understood that the term suvaṇṇatā and others refer to the perfection of the body, the term ādhipacca refers to the perfection of wealth and possessions, and the term parivāra refers to the perfection of one's own human retinue. Regarding the statement, "Whatever benefit they desire, all that is obtained by this treasure of merit," it is shown that, first of all, all these things mentioned by way of classification, such as suvaṇṇatā, are obtained by this merit.

## Commentary on the Twelfth Verse

Having thus shown the prosperity of devas and humans, which is superior to the royal attainments obtainable through the power of merit by this verse, the Buddha now spoke this verse beginning with "Padesarajjaṃ" to show the royal attainments of both devas and humans.

In that verse, padesarajjaṃ means kingship over a certain portion of the earth without ruling an entire continent. Sovereignty is called issariya; by this term, the kingship of a Cakkavatti ruling one continent is shown. The desirable, lovely, and pleasing happiness of a Cakkavatti is called "cakkavattisukhaṃ piyaṃ"; by this term, the kingship of a Cakkavatti ruling all four continents is shown. Kingship among the devas is called devarajjaṃ; by this term, the divine kingship of humans such as King Mandhātu is also shown. By the term "api dibbesu," the divine kingship of those born in divine bodies, who are called "divine" because of their existence in heaven, is shown. Regarding the statement, "Whatever benefit they desire, all that is obtained by this treasure of merit," it is shown that, secondly, all these things such as regional kingship and so forth are also obtained by this merit.

## Commentary on the Thirteenth Verse

Having thus shown the royal prosperity of devas and humans obtainable through the power of merit by this verse, the Buddha now spoke this verse beginning with "Mānussikā ca sampattī" to show the attainment of Nibbāna, having briefly summarized the prosperity taught in the two previous verses.

The commentary on the terms of that verse is as follows: It is called mānussī because it is the property of humans; mānussī itself is mānussikā. Perfection is called sampatti. The world of devas is devaloka; in that deva world. The term "yā" is intended to include everything without remainder. It is called rati because devas delight in it, whether it arises within themselves or as an external facility. That rati is a name for happiness, and also a name for the basis of happiness.
195:
This word 'rati' is the name for happiness and the object of happiness. The word 'yā' is an indefinite term. The word 'ca' has the meaning of connecting with the previously mentioned attainments. Nibbāna itself is called the attainment of Nibbāna (Nibbāna-sampatti).

This is the explanation of the meaning: There is human wealth mentioned by words such as 'suvaṇṇatā' (fair complexion) and so forth, and there is delight in the celestial realm. All that wealth, and this other attainment of Nibbāna to be reached by way of being a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) and so forth—all this is obtained by this treasure pot of merit. Thus, for the third time, it is said that all this is obtained by this merit.

Alternatively: Although not mentioned in order by words like 'suvaṇṇatā' in the previous verse, there is human wealth consisting of various types such as abundance of wisdom, which is indicated by such methods as 'being heroic, being mindful, living the holy life in this Dispensation'; there is delight in the celestial realm through jhāna and so forth; and there is the attainment of Nibbāna of the aforementioned types. All this is obtained by this merit. Thus, for the third time, it is said that all this is obtained by this merit. In this way, the explanation of the meaning should be understood here.

## Commentary on the Fourteenth Verse

Thus, having shown by this verse the attainment of Nibbāna which is to be obtained through the power of merit and reached by way of being a faith-follower and so forth, he now speaks this verse beginning with 'mittasampadamāgamma' (having come to the attainment of friends), wishing to show that same attainment of Nibbāna which is also to be reached by way of being one with triple-knowledge (tevijja) and one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta), as well as the means for that attainment.

The word-by-word commentary of that verse: One reaches the excellence of qualities through this attainment of good friends, therefore it is called 'sampadā' (attainment). A friend himself is the cause for reaching the beauty of qualities, therefore it is called 'mittasampadā' (attainment of good friends). Possessing such good friends is called 'taṃ mittasampadaṃ'. 'Āgamma' means depending on. 'Yoniso' means by way of means (upāya). 'Payuñjato' means for one who makes constant effort in practice. Because one knows through this wisdom, it is called 'vijjā' (knowledge). Because one is liberated from defilements through this path and fruition knowledge, or because it is liberated by itself, it is called 'vimutti' (liberation). Knowledge and liberation are called 'vijjāvimuttiyo'. The state of being able to master knowledge and liberation is called 'vijjāvimuttivasībhāvo' (mastery over knowledge and liberation).

This is the explanation of the meaning: When a person, based on the attainment of good friends, depends on the Teacher or another fellow monk in a position of respect, receives advice and instruction from them, and makes effort methodically through practice as instructed, there is mastery without delay in the three types of knowledge such as the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa) and so forth, and in liberation consisting of the eight attainments and Nibbāna, as stated: 'What therein is liberation? The mind's release from defilements and Nibbāna are called liberation.' All this is obtained by this treasure pot of merit. Thus, for the fourth time, it is said that all this is obtained by this merit. In this way, by this verse, [the attainment] which was previously mentioned as part of the mastery over knowledge and liberation, to be obtained through the power of merit, and by way of being one with triple-knowledge and one liberated in both ways...
196:
...there is the state of mastery (vasībhāva) by way of not being slow. All this can also be obtained by this fourth instance of the treasure pot of the attainment of merit.

## Commentary on the Fifteenth Verse

Thus, having shown by this verse the attainment of Nibbāna which is to be obtained through the power of merit associated with the mastery over knowledge and liberation previously mentioned, and reached by way of being one with triple-knowledge and one liberated in both ways, he now wishes to show that those with triple-knowledge who have reached mastery over knowledge and liberation, as well as all those liberated in both ways, obtain the excellence of qualities such as the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Through this attainment of merit, and by way of having the proximate cause for the excellence of those qualities, one can obtain the excellence of those qualities in various ways. Therefore, wishing to show that Dhamma, he spoke this verse: 'paṭisambhidā vimokkhā ca' (analytical insights and liberations).

Because of being well-performed, the wisdom that has reached distinction in the Dhamma, meaning (attha), language (nirutti), and eloquence (paṭibhāna) is called 'paṭisambhidā'. There are these eight liberations (vimokkha) by way of the method beginning with 'one possessing form sees forms'. There is the perfection of a disciple (sāvakapāramī) which is to be reached by the disciples of the Blessed One and which accomplishes the attainment of a disciple; there is the knowledge of a silent Buddha (paccekabodhi) which accomplishes the state of being self-enlightened; and there is the stage of a Buddha (buddhabhūmi) which accomplishes the state of being supreme among all beings. It should be understood that all this is obtained by this merit, for the fifth time.

## Commentary on the Sixteenth Verse

In this way, the Blessed One said: 'Whatever they wish for, all that is obtained by this merit.' Having shown that statement section by section with these five verses, he now concludes the teaching with this verse 'evaṃ mahatthikā esā', wishing to praise this entire attainment of merit known as the treasure pot that gives all desires.

The word-by-word commentary of that verse: The word 'evaṃ' is a term indicating the past meaning. One has great benefit; therefore, it is called 'mahatthikā'. It means it leads to great benefit. There is also a reading 'mahiddhikā' (of great power). 'Esā' is a demonstrative term. By that term, he points to the attainment of merit spoken of from the verse 'yassa dānena sīlena' up to 'kayirātha dhီro puṇyāni'. The word 'yadidaṃ' is an indeclinable used in the sense of making something present. By that word, he makes present the thing pointed to by 'esā' as 'yā esā'. The fulfillment of merits is called 'puṇyasampadā'.
197:
The Blessed One, having shown in parts through these five verses the words he spoke: "All desired benefits can be obtained by this merit," now, wishing to praise the fulfillment of all merit, called the "treasure pot" that grants all desires, concluded the teaching with this verse: "Evaṃ mahatthikā esā." The explanation of the words in that verse is as follows: The word "Evaṃ" indicates the preceding meaning. "Mahatthikā" means having great benefit or leading to great benefit. There is also a variant reading "Mahiddhikā." By the demonstrative word "Esā," he points to the fulfillment of merit taught from "Yassa dānena sīlena" up to "Kayirātha dhīro puññāni." The word "Yadidaṃ" is an indeclinable used for emphasis, specifically emphasizing the fulfillment of merit indicated by "Esā."

Fulfillment of merit (puññasampadā). "Tasmā" is a word indicating the cause. "Dhīရာ" refers to the steadfast wise ones. "Pasaṃsanti" means they praise. "Paṇḍitā" means those endowed with wisdom. "Katapuññataṃ" means the state of having performed merit.

This is the commentary on the meaning. Thus, the Blessed One, having praised the benefits obtainable through the power of the fulfillment of merit, ranging from beauty to the attainment of Buddhahood, now, wishing to summarize those benefits and praise the great fruitfulness of the fulfillment of merit of various kinds as previously mentioned because of those benefits, spoke thus: "This fulfillment of merit, taught by me through the method beginning with 'Yassa dānena sīlena,' has great benefit because it brings about such great welfare. Therefore, the steadfast wise ones, who are not weary in teaching the Dhamma to bring welfare and happiness to beings like myself, and who possess true virtues, praise the state of having performed merit in many ways—both by the words spoken in this Sutta such as 'A treasure not shared with others, which thieves cannot steal,' and by words not spoken here such as 'Monks, do not fear merits; monks, this "merit" is a name for happiness'—they praise it not out of partiality or favoritism."

At the conclusion of the teaching, that lay follower, along with many people, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He went to King Pasenadi of Kosala and reported this matter. The King, being greatly pleased, praised him saying, "Excellent, householder, excellent! You, householder, have buried a treasure that even kings like myself cannot take away," and he performed a great offering.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha
## The Explanation of the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta is Finished.
## 9. Explanation of the Metta Sutta
## The Purpose of Placement

Now, the sequence for the explanation of the Metta Sutta, placed immediately after the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, has arrived. Having stated the purpose of its placement here, thereafter:

"By whom, when, where, and for what reason it was spoken;
Having clarified the origin (nidāna) of these, I shall perform the commentary on the meaning."

In this Khuddakapāṭha text, why? Because through the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, the fulfillment of merit such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla) was spoken. That fulfillment of merit, when loving-kindness (mettā) is developed towards beings, has great fruit and is capable of leading even to the stage of Buddhahood. Therefore, to show the supportive nature of that fulfillment of merit, the Metta Sutta was spoken. Alternatively, for those who have entered the Dispensation through the Refuges (saraṇa) and are established in virtue through the training rules (sikkhāpada), the Blessed One showed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) capable of abandoning lust through the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), and the meditation subject capable of abandoning delusion through the Boy's Questions (kumārapañha). Then, through the Maṅgala Sutta, he showed the auspiciousness (maṅgala) and self-protection in one's life. Through the Ratana Sutta, he showed the protection of others suitable for such a person. Through the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, he showed some of the beings (bhūta) mentioned in the Ratana Sutta and the ruin of those who are negligent regarding the aforementioned fulfillment of merit. Through the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, he showed what was spoken in the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta...
198:
In this Khuddakapāṭha text, because through the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, the fulfillment of merit such as giving and virtue was spoken; and that fulfillment of merit, when loving-kindness is developed towards beings, has great fruit, capable of leading even to the stage of Buddhahood. Therefore, to show the supportive nature of that fulfillment of merit, and also because for those who have entered the Dispensation through the Refuges and are established in virtue through the training rules, the meditation subject capable of abandoning lust through the thirty-two parts of the body was shown, and the meditation subject capable of abandoning delusion through the Boy's Questions was shown; and through the Maṅgala Sutta, the auspiciousness and self-protection in one's life was shown; and through the Ratana Sutta, the protection of others suitable for such a person was shown; and through the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, the showing of some of the beings (bhūta) among those mentioned in the Ratana Sutta and the ruin of those who are negligent regarding the aforementioned fulfillment of merit was shown; and through the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, the success which is the opposite of the ruin mentioned in the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta was shown. However, the meditation subject capable of abandoning anger (dosa) had not yet been shown. Therefore, to show that meditation subject capable of abandoning anger, this Metta Sutta was placed here. In this way, the Khuddakapāṭha is well-completed. This is the purpose of its placement here.

## Clarifying the Origin (Nidāna)

Now, the following thematic summary (mātikā) is set forth:
"By whom, when, where, and for what reason it was spoken;
By explaining these points, having clarified the origin of this Sutta, I shall perform the commentary on the meaning."

In that origin, this Metta Sutta was spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by disciples or others. As for when, it was spoken at Sāvatthī for the sake of protection (paritta) and for the sake of a meditation subject for those monks who had come to the Blessed One after being harassed by deities at the foot of the Himalayan mountains. Thus, first, the clarification of the origin by explaining those words in brief should be understood.

In detail, it should be understood thus: At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī when the time for entering the rains retreat (vassūpanāyikā) was near. At that time, many monks from various countries, having taken a meditation subject from the Blessed One, approached the Blessed One wishing to enter the rains retreat here and there. Then, it is said, the Blessed One gave the eleven types of foulness (asubha) meditation subjects, categorized by animate and inanimate, to those of lustful temperament (rāgacarita); the fourfold meditation subjects of loving-kindness (mettā) etc. to those of angry temperament (dosacarita); the meditation on death (maraṇassati) etc. to those of deluded temperament (mohacarita); mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) and the earth kasina (pathavī-kasiṇa) etc. to those of speculative temperament (vitakkacarita); the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) etc. to those of faithful temperament (saddhācarita); and to those of intellectual temperament (buddhicarita)...
199:
In this way, by means of the analysis of the four elements and so forth, He taught meditation subjects suitable for the eighty-four thousand varieties of temperaments.

Then, about five hundred monks, having taken a meditation subject from the Blessed One and seeking suitable lodgings and an alms-resort village, gradually traveled and saw a mountain in the border region connected to the Himālayas. It had a stone surface resembling blue glaze, was adorned with a blue forest grove providing cool, thick shade, had ground covered with sand like pearl nets or silver plates, and was surrounded by reservoirs of pure, sweet, and cool water. Then, those monks stayed there for one night, and when the night had brightened, they performed their bodily duties and entered a certain village not far from that mountain for alms. That village was composed of a thousand households closely situated. The people in that village were faithful and devoted. Because it was rare to see monks in the border region, as soon as they saw the monks, they were filled with joy and delight. After offering food to the monks, they requested, "Venerable sirs, please reside here for the three months of the rains retreat," and they had five hundred meditation huts built. In those huts, they prepared all necessities such as couches, benches, drinking water pots, and utility water pots.

On the second day, the monks entered another village for alms. There too, the people served them in the same way and requested them to observe the rains retreat. The monks accepted, saying, "We shall stay if there are no obstacles," and entered that forest grove. Being energetic in their efforts throughout the day and night, they struck the wooden gong to mark the time, and dwelling with much wise reflection, they approached the roots of trees and sat down.

The tree deities, whose power was diminished by the power of the virtuous monks, descended from their respective mansions and wandered here and there, carrying their young children.

For example, just as when kings or great ministers of the king arrive at a small village and take up space in the houses of the villagers, the householders leave their homes and stay elsewhere, looking from afar and wondering, "When will they go?", even so, the deities abandoned their mansions and wandered here and there, looking from afar and wondering, "When will the venerable ones go?"

Then they collectively thought: "The monks who have entered the first rains retreat will surely stay for three months. We cannot stay away for so long, carrying our young children. Come, let us show the monks a terrifying object." Thinking thus, at night, when it was time for the monks to practice their recluse-dharma, they created terrifying forms of ogres...
200:
(Those tree deities) stood right in front of them and made terrifying sounds. Upon seeing those forms and hearing those sounds, the monks' hearts trembled; they lost their healthy complexion and became very pale. Therefore, those monks were unable to make their minds one-pointed. For those monks whose minds were not one-pointed and who were repeatedly terrified, their mindfulness lapsed. Then, to those monks whose mindfulness had lapsed, the deities applied unpleasant odors. It was as if their brains were being crushed by those foul smells, and intense headaches arose. They did not tell each other about this matter.

Then one day, at the time of performing duties for the Sangha Elder, when all the monks had assembled, the Sangha Elder asked: "Friends, when you entered this forest grove, for two or three days your complexion was very pure and bright, and your faculties were exceptionally clear. But now, why are you thin and pale in this place, with a body as white as a dried leaf? What is unsuitable for you here?" Then one monk said: "Venerable sir, at night I see and hear such terrifying objects, and I smell such odors. Because of that, my mind cannot be well-concentrated." In this manner, all those monks reported the matter. The Sangha Elder said: "Friends, the Blessed One has prescribed two ways of entering the rains retreat. This lodging is unsuitable for us. Come, friends, let us go to the Blessed One and ask for another suitable lodging." Saying, "Very well, venerable sir," those monks followed the Elder's word. All of them packed their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and because they were free from attachment to families, they departed for Sāvatthī without informing anyone. Gradually reaching Sāvatthī, they approached the Blessed One.

When the Blessed One saw those monks, He said: "Monks, although I have prescribed a training rule that one should not wander during the rains retreat, why are you wandering?" Those monks reported everything to the Blessed One. When the Blessed One reflected, He did not see any suitable lodging in the whole of Jambudīpa, even as much as the space for a small four-legged bench. Then He said to those monks: "Monks, there is no other suitable lodging for you. Only by dwelling in that very place will you reach the destruction of the taints. Go, monks, dwell depending on that same lodging. If you desire freedom from fear from the deities, learn this protection. This Metta Sutta will be both a protection and a meditation subject for you." Thus He taught this Sutta.
201:
Other teachers, however, say: "Go, monks, and dwell relying on that same lodging." Having said this, the Blessed One said: "Indeed, a monk living in the forest should know the duties to be performed. Those duties are: by way of performing them in the evening and morning, twice Metta, twice Paritta, twice Asubha, twice Maranassati, and reflection on the eight objects of urgency (saṃvegavatthu)." The eight objects of urgency are birth, aging, sickness, death, and the four sufferings of the lower realms. Alternatively, birth, aging, sickness, and death are four; the suffering of the lower realms is the fifth; suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the past; suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the future; and suffering rooted in the search for food in the present. Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the duties to be performed, taught this Sutta for the sake of these monks' loving-kindness (metta), for the sake of protection (paritta), and for the sake of Jhana as a basis for insight (vipassanā). In this way, the detailed explanation of these terms—"By whom it was said, when, where, and why"—should be understood as the purification of the introduction (nidāna). By this much, the matrix (mātikā) established as "Having purified the introduction by explaining by whom it was said, etc." is fully detailed in every aspect.

## Commentary on the First Verse

Now, as it was promised, "I shall perform the commentary on its meaning," the commentary on the meaning of this Sutta, whose introduction has thus been purified, begins. Therein, in the first verse beginning with "Karaṇīyamatthakusalena," first is the word-by-word commentary: "Karaṇīyaṃ" means what should be done, what is worthy of being done. "Attho" means practice, or whatever is one's own benefit; all that is called "attha" because it is to be approached (araṇīya). "Araṇīya" means it should be approached. "Atthakusalena" means one who is skilled in benefit, expert in benefit. The word "yaṃ" is an indefinite nominative case, and "taṃ" is a definite accusative case; or both are in the nominative case. "Santaṃ padaṃ" is in the accusative case; therein, it is "santa" (peaceful) by its characteristic, and "pada" (state) because it is to be reached; this is a designation for Nibbāna. "Abhisamecca" means having attained or realized. "Sakko" means one who is able, capable, or competent. "Ujū" means one endowed with uprightness; "suhuju" means thoroughly upright. "Suvaco" means one who has pleasant speech, or is easy to admonish. "Assa" means should be. "Mudū" means one endowed with gentleness; "anatimānī" means one who is not excessively proud.

The commentary on the meaning here is: in the phrase "Karaṇīyamatthakusalena, yantaṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca," first, there is what should be done and what should not be done. Between those two...
202:
In brief, the three trainings (sikkhā) should be performed. Failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti), failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), and failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatti), and so forth, are things that should not be done. Likewise, there is one who is skilled in benefit and one who is skilled in what is not beneficial. Between those two, whoever has gone forth in this Dispensation but does not apply himself properly, is one whose virtue is broken, and lives depending on the twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood (anesana). They are: giving bamboo, giving bowls, giving flowers, giving fruits, giving tooth-sticks, giving face-water, giving head-washing water, giving powder, giving clay, flattery, inconsistent speech (muggasūpyatā), acting like a child-nanny, acting like a messenger, medical practice, acting as an envoy, going on errands, giving alms in return for alms, giving gifts in return for gifts, the art of site-divination, the art of astrology, and the art of body-marks. He also frequents the six improper resorts (agocara). They are: the resort of prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, nuns, and taverns. He also dwells in association with kings, great ministers of the king, heretics, and disciples of heretics, through unsuitable association with laypeople; or he frequents, associates with, and attends upon such families who are faithless, without devotion, who are like a well without a landing-place, who are abusive and reviling, who do not desire the benefit, welfare, or comfort of monks... pe... or lay-devotees. Such a person is called one who is skilled in what is not beneficial.

However, whoever has gone forth in this Dispensation and applies himself properly, desiring to stand in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) by abandoning wrong livelihood, fulfills the Pātimokkha restraint with faith as the head, sense restraint with mindfulness as the head, livelihood purification with energy as the head, and the proper use of requisites with wisdom as the head. Such a person is called one who is skilled in benefit.

Or, whoever purifies the Pātimokkha restraint by way of cleansing the seven groups of offenses; sense restraint by way of the non-arising of covetousness and so forth when objects strike the six sense doors; livelihood purification by way of avoiding wrong livelihood and by using requisites praised by the wise, the Buddha, and the Buddha's disciples; the use of requisites by way of reflection as mentioned; and clear comprehension (sampajañña) by way of reflecting on the purposefulness and so forth in the changing of the four postures. Such a person is also called one who is skilled in benefit.

Or, just as one cleanses a soiled cloth depending on alkaline water (soap), or a mirror depending on ash, or gold depending on a furnace; likewise, knowing that virtue is purified depending on wisdom, he cleanses his virtue by washing it with the water of wisdom. And just as a kikī bird protects its egg, or a yak protects its tail, or a mother with an only son...
203:
Just as a mother protects her beloved only son, or as a one-eyed man protects his single eye, even so, one protects one's aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) with extreme diligence. When reflecting in the evening and morning, one sees not even a flaw as small as an atom. Such a person is also called 'atthakusala' (skilled in welfare). Alternatively, a monk who, established in virtue that brings joy (non-remorse), undertakes the practice of suppressing defilements. Having undertaken that practice, he performs the preliminary work for kasina (kasiṇa-parikamma) and produces meditative attainments (samāpatti). This monk is also called 'atthakusala'. Alternatively, a monk who, having emerged from a meditative attainment, contemplates formations (saṅkhāra) and reaches the state of an Arahant; this monk is the supreme among those skilled in welfare. Among these, those described as skilled in welfare—from being established in virtue that brings joy up to undertaking the practice of suppressing defilements—are intended as 'atthakusala' in this context. And those monks were of such a nature.
