Therefore, the Blessed One, referring to those monks, spoke the teaching based on a single individual: 'Karaṇīyamatthakusalena' (What should be done by one skilled in welfare).

Thereafter, to those monks in whom doubt had arisen as to 'What should be done?', He said: 'Yan taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca'. The meaning here is: one who wishes to dwell having understood through penetration the peaceful state of Nibbāna, which is praised by the Buddhas and their disciples, should do what is to be done. In this verse, the word 'yaṃ' follows the word 'karaṇīyaṃ' mentioned at the beginning. Since the passage 'taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca' is an incomplete statement, it should be understood by adding 'one who wishes to dwell'. Alternatively, 'santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca' means knowing the state of Nibbāna as 'peaceful' through worldly wisdom by way of tradition and so forth; one who wishes to reach that Nibbāna should do what is to be done—this is how the meaning should be understood. Also, 'that which is to be done should be performed by the monk skilled in welfare'—thus the meaning should be understood here. Alternatively, when it was said 'What should be done by one skilled in welfare', to those who were wondering 'What?', He said 'Yan taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca'. Its meaning should be understood thus: having understood the peaceful state with worldly wisdom, that which is to be done should be done; it means that very thing is worthy of being done. What is that? What else could it be other than the means to attain that [Nibbāna]? Indeed, this is stated by the opening words which indicate the three trainings (sikkhā) in the sense of being worthy of being done. Therefore, in the explanation of its meaning, it has been said: 'There is that which should be done, and there is that which should not be done.'
204:
In that [Metta Sutta], it means 'In brief, the three trainings (sikkhā) should be practiced.' Because it was taught in an extremely brief manner, some of those monks understood it, while others did not. Therefore, to make it known to the monks who did not understand, and wishing to show in detail the practice that should be specifically performed by a forest-dwelling monk, He first spoke this half-verse: 'He should be capable, upright, thoroughly upright, easy to speak to, gentle, and not arrogant.' (Sakko uzū ca suhuzū ca, suvaco cassa mudu anatimānī).

What is meant is this: A forest-dwelling monk who wishes to dwell having realized the peaceful Nibbāna, or who is practicing to attain that Nibbāna having understood it with worldly wisdom, should be capable (sakko) of practicing to penetrate the Four Noble Truths without regard for his body or life, being endowed with the second and fourth factors of striving (padhāniyaṅga). Furthermore, he should be capable, skillful, diligent, and competent in undertaking the duties of kasina preliminary work and so forth, in repairing his own bowl and robes, and in the various large and small services (veyyāvacca) for his fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī), as well as in other such matters.

Even though he is capable, he should be upright (ujū) by being endowed with the third factor of striving. Even though he is upright, he should be even more thoroughly upright (suhujū) by acting with unflagging effort throughout his life, not being satisfied with being upright only once or only during his youth. Alternatively, he is upright (ujū) through lack of crookedness, and thoroughly upright (suhujū) through lack of deceit. Or, he is upright (ujū) by abandoning physical and vocal crookedness, and thoroughly upright (suhujū) by abandoning mental crookedness. Or, he is upright (ujū) by not making a show of virtues he does not possess, and thoroughly upright (suhujū) by not accepting gains that arise from non-existent virtues. Thus, through the meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna), through the first two trainings and the third training, and through the purity of effort and intention (āsaya), he should be upright and thoroughly upright.

Not only should he be upright and thoroughly upright, but he should also be easy to speak to (suvaco). For if a person, when told 'This should not be done,' says, 'What have you seen? What have you heard? On whose authority do you speak to me? Are you my preceptor (upajjhāya), my teacher (ācariya), or a familiar and trusted friend?', or if he harasses the speaker by remaining silent, or if he accepts the advice but does not act accordingly, he is far from attaining the special distinction (adhigama). However, if a person, when being exhorted, says, 'It is well, Bhante, you have spoken rightly; one's own fault is indeed hard to see. Please speak to me again if you see such a fault, out of compassion. It is after a long time that I have received advice from you,' and practices according to the instruction, he is not far from attaining the special distinction. Therefore, a monk who accepts and follows the words of another in this way is one who is easy to speak to (suvaco).
205:
Just as one should be easy to speak to, so should one be gentle. Being gentle means not being harsh when assigned tasks such as running errands or being sent on missions by laypeople; rather, like well-refined gold, one should be gentle and fit for use in all duties and the entire holy life. Alternatively, being gentle means not frowning, having a cheerful face, being easy to converse with, and being pleasant to approach, like a good landing place. Not only should one be gentle, but also not arrogant. One should not look down on others based on birth, lineage, and so forth. One should dwell with a mind like that of a young outcaste, as did the Elder Sāriputta.

## Explanation of the Second Verse

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of some duties for a monk—especially a forest-dweller—who wishes to dwell having realized the peaceful state of Nibbāna, or who is practicing to attain it, spoke the second verse beginning with "Santuṭṭhako ca" (And contented), wishing to speak further.

In that verse, one is called "Santuṭṭhaka" because one is contented with the twelvefold contentment as described in "Santuṭṭhī ca kataññutā". Alternatively, one is called "Santuṭṭhaka" because of being contented with one's own property, with what is present, and with evenness. Among these, "one's own" refers to the four requisites pointed out during the ordination ceremony, such as "depending on alms-food," and accepted by oneself. Whether those requisites are good or bad, offered respectfully or disrespectfully, if one sustains oneself without showing any change of mind during acceptance and use, it is called "contentment with one's own." "What is present" refers to the property one has actually obtained; being contented with only that, not desiring more, and abandoning greed is called "contentment with what is present." "Evenness" means the abandoning of attraction and aversion towards pleasant and unpleasant objects; being contented with all objects with such an even mind is called "contentment with evenness."

One is called "Subhara" because one is easily supported. This means one is easy to maintain. A monk who, even when people fill his bowl with fine rice and meat, shows a displeased or unhappy face, or who, in front of those donors, disparages the alms-food saying, "What is this you have given?" and gives it away to novices or laypeople—such a monk is "difficult to support" (dubbhara). Seeing such a monk, people avoid him from afar, saying, "This monk is difficult to support; we cannot..."
206:
...support him." But a monk who, having received anything—whether coarse or fine, little or much—is delighted, has a clear face, and sustains himself, is "easy to support" (subhara). Seeing him, people become very trustful and support him, making a promise: "Our venerable one is easy to support; he is contented with even a little; we alone will support him." In this context, such a person is meant by "subhara."

"Appakicco" means having few duties. It refers to one who is not busy with many activities such as delighting in work, delighting in talk, or delighting in company. Alternatively, it means one who is free from duties such as new construction in the entire monastery, Sangha affairs, or instructing novices and monastery attendants; instead, after attending to one's own needs like shaving hair, cutting nails, and caring for the bowl and robes, one is solely dedicated to the duty of a recluse's practice (samaṇadhamma).

"Sallahukavutti" means having a light livelihood. Unlike some monks with many possessions who, when departing for another region, have a large crowd carry many bowls, robes, mats, oil, molasses, and so forth, as head-loads or waist-loads, one should have few requisites. Carrying only the eight requisites of a monk, such as the bowl and robes, one who departs for another region like a bird taking only its wings is meant here by "sallahukavutti." "Santindriyo" means having peaceful faculties. It refers to having faculties that are not flighty through the power of lust and so forth towards pleasant objects and so forth. "Nipaka" means one who is particularly discerning, clear-sighted, and wise. It refers to one endowed with the wisdom of guarding virtue, the wisdom of reflecting on robes and other requisites, and the wisdom of discerning the seven types of suitable things (sappāya) such as lodgings.

"Appagabbho" (na pagabbho) means one who is not impudent. It refers to one who is free from bodily impudence (kāyapāgabbhiya) of eight kinds, verbal impudence (vacīpāgabbhiya) of four kinds, and mental impudence (manopāgabbhiya) of many kinds.

Bodily impudence of eight kinds (kāyapāgabbhiya) refers to unseemly physical behavior in the midst of the Sangha, a group, or individuals, in the dining hall, the fire-room, at the bathing place, on the alms-round path, and when entering a house. For example, in this Dispensation, some sit in the midst of the Sangha with knees clasped or with legs crossed, and so on. Likewise, they sit thus in the midst of a group, in an assembly of the fourfold fold, or before senior persons. In the dining hall, they do not give up seats to senior monks or they prevent junior monks from taking seats. Similarly, in the fire-room, they do not give up seats to seniors, they prevent juniors from taking seats, and they light a fire without asking permission from the seniors. At the bathing place, without considering seniority, they descend and bathe according to the order of arrival. Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One...
207:
(In the refectory), he does not give a seat to the elders, and he prevents the juniors from taking a seat. Likewise, in the fire-room (jantāghara), he lights the fire and so forth without asking the elders. At the bathing place, there is a rule spoken by the Blessed One: "One should bathe according to the order of arrival, without making a distinction between junior and elder"; disregarding that rule, he arrives later, enters the water, and bothers both the elders and the juniors. On the alms-round path, for the sake of getting the best seat, the first water, and the best alms-food, he walks ahead of the elders, brushing arm against arm. When entering the village, he enters before the elders and engages in physical play with the juniors; such are these [physical impudences].

Verbal impudence (vacīpāgabbhiya) with four grounds means the uttering of unsuitable words in the midst of the Sangha, a group, an individual, or in the village. To explain: here, someone speaks the Dhamma in the midst of the Sangha without asking permission; likewise in a group or to an elder as previously mentioned. There, when asked a question by people, he answers without asking the elder. In the village, he speaks in this manner: "What is there for such-and-such a person? Is there gruel, or is there some food to be chewed or consumed? What will you give me? What shall I chew today? What shall I eat? What shall I drink?"

Mental impudence (manopāgabbhiya) with many grounds means improper thinking of various kinds, such as sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), solely with the mind, even without reaching transgression through body or speech in various situations.

"Kulesvananugiddho" means he is not greedy for those families whom he visits, either through craving for requisites or through improper intimacy with laypeople. It means he does not grieve with them, does not rejoice with them, is not happy when they are happy, is not sad when they are sad, and does not personally exert himself in their business that arises.

In this verse, the word "assa" (should be) found in the phrase "suvaco cassa" should be applied to all terms as: "he should be contented (santussako ca assa)" and "he should be easy to support (subharo ca assa)."

## Commentary on the Third Verse

Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the further duties for a forest-dwelling monk who wishes to dwell having realized the peaceful Nibbāna, or who wishes to practice for its attainment, now desires to explain what should not be done, and thus spoke this half-verse: "One should not do even the slightest [wrong] for which other wise men might censure him."
208: The meaning of that verse is: one performing these duties should not practice even the slightest unwholesome action of body, speech, or mind, which is called "minor" or "lowly". It means that one who does not practice should not only avoid gross misconduct but should not practice anything at all; he should not practice even a tiny bit, even an atom's worth of unwholesome action. Then, he shows the visible disadvantage of such conduct with the words: "for which other wise men might censure him." Here, other unwise people are not the standard. For they may treat what is blameless as blameworthy, or what is a minor fault as a major one. Only the wise are the standard. For they, having investigated and scrutinized, speak blame only of those worthy of blame and speak praise only of those worthy of praise. Therefore, it is said, "other wise men". Thus, the Blessed One, having explained through these two and a half verses the preliminary practice of meditation—the distinction between what should and should not be done—for one who wishes to dwell having realized the state of peace or who wishes to practice for its attainment, especially for a forest-dweller, and for all those who wish to dwell having taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) under the heading of a forest-dweller; now, in order to ward off the fear caused by deities for those monks, to provide protection (paritta), and for the sake of the meditation subject through the power of jhāna as a basis for insight (vipassanā), he began to deliver the discourse on loving-kindness (metta-kathā) in the manner beginning with "Sukhino vā khemino hontu". In that verse, "sukhino" means those endowed with happiness. "Khemino" means those who are secure, meaning those who are without fear and without harm. "Sabbe" means without exception. "Sattā" means living beings. "Sukhitattā" means those with happy minds. Here, one should be understood as "sukhino" through physical happiness, "sukhitattā" through mental happiness, and "khemino" through both or through the absence of all fears and harms. Why is it said in this way? It is to show the method of developing loving-kindness. For loving-kindness should be developed thus: "May all beings be happy," or "May they be secure," or "May they be happy-minded." ## Commentary on the Fourth Verse Thus, having shown the development of loving-kindness in brief from access concentration (upacāra) to the peak of absorption (appanā), he now speaks two verses starting with "Ye keci" to show it in detail. Or, because a mind accustomed to various objects does not settle on a single object from the very beginning, but follows and follows the diversity of objects...
209:
The mind tends to become settled gradually; therefore, for the purpose of making the monk's mind settle by repeatedly following the objects categorized into dyads and triads such as tasa and thāvara, He spoke the two verses beginning with "Ye keci". Alternatively, for whichever monk a particular object is clear, his mind dwells happily on that object. Therefore, desiring to settle the minds of those monks on the objects that are clear to them, He spoke these two verses beginning with "Ye keci," which illustrate the various objects of dyads and triads such as tasa and thāvara.

In these verses, He shows four dyads: the tasa-thāvara dyad, the diṭṭha-adiṭṭha (seen and unseen) dyad, the dūra-santika (far and near) dyad, and the bhūta-sambhavesī (those who have come to be and those seeking birth) dyad. By means of the six terms beginning with dīgha, because the meaning can be applied to the three triads of the middle term (majjhima) and the two triads of the small term (aṇuka), He also shows three triads: the dīgha-rassa-majjhima (long, short, medium) triad, the mahanta-aṇuka-majjhima (large, small, medium) triad, and the thūla-aṇuka-majjhima (gross, subtle, medium) triad. In those verses, "Ye keci" is an inclusive term meaning "whatever without exception." Since living beings themselves are called bhūta, they are referred to as "pāṇabhūtā." Alternatively, they are called "pāṇa" because they breathe; by this word pāṇa, He takes the five-constituent (pañcavokāra) beings who are connected with inhalation and exhalation. They are called "bhūta" because they have come to be; by this word bhūta, He takes the one-constituent (ekavokāra) and four-constituent (catuvokāra) beings. "Atthi" means they exist or are clearly present.

Thus, by this phrase "Ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi," He shows all beings who are to be included in the dyads and triads together in one group, and now He shows them by including them in this dyad: "tasā vā thāvarā vā anavasesā."

In that context, they are called "tasa" because they tremble; this is a designation for those with craving and those with fear. They are called "thāvara" because they stand firm; this is a designation for Arahants who have abandoned craving and fear. They are called "anavasesā" because there is no remainder among those beings; it means "all beings." The words spoken at the end of the second verse should be connected with all the dyads and triads: "Whatever beings there are—trembling or firm, without exception—may all these beings be happy-minded. In this manner, up to 'those who have come to be or those seeking birth,' may all these beings be happy-minded."

Now, among the six terms such as "dīghā vā" which illustrate the three triads of dīgha, rassa, and majjhima, "dīghā" refers to beings with long bodies such as Nagas, fish, and monitor lizards. Indeed, in the Great Ocean, the bodies of Nagas are many hundreds of fathoms (byāma) in measure, and the bodies of fish and monitor lizards are many leagues (yojana) in measure. "Mahantā" refers to beings with large bodies, such as fish and turtles in the water, elephants and Nagas on land, and among non-humans...
210:
Long-bodied beings include nāgas, fish, monitor lizards, and so forth. This is true; in the great ocean, the bodies of nāgas have a length of more than a hundred fathoms. The bodies of fish and monitor lizards also have a length of many yojanas. Large beings (mahantā) refer to large-bodied fish and turtles in water, and elephants and nāgas on land. Among non-human beings like yakkhas and devas, beings such as the Dānavas also have large bodies. The Blessed One spoke of the physical form of Rāhu the Asura; to explain in detail, the body of Rāhu the Asura is 4,800 yojanas in height. His arms are 1,200 yojanas, the space between his eyebrows is 50 yojanas, likewise his finger joints are 50 yojanas, and his palms are 200 yojanas each. Medium-sized beings (majjhimā) refer to the bodies of animals such as horses, cattle, buffaloes, and pigs. Short beings (rassakā) are those among various species whose size is less than the long and medium ones. Small beings (aṇukā) are those invisible to the fleshly eye and are only objects of the divine eye. Alternatively, they are subtle-bodied beings born in water and the like, or beings such as lice. Or else, in various births, beings of ordinary size smaller than the large, medium, and stout ones should be known as small beings (aṇukā). Stout beings (thūlā) are those with round bodies, such as oysters and snails.

## Commentary on the Fifth Verse
Having thus shown all beings without exception by way of the three triads, he now shows them by grouping them with the three dyads, starting with "Whether seen or unseen" (diṭṭhā vā ye va adiṭṭhā). In that passage, seen beings (diṭṭhā) are those previously seen by coming into the range of one's own eyes. Unseen beings (adiṭṭhā) are those situated on the other side of the ocean, the other side of a mountain, or the other side of the world-system, and so on. By the dyad "Whether they dwell far or near" (ye vā dūre vasanti avidūre), he shows beings dwelling far from and near to one's own person; these should be understood by way of those without feet, those with two feet, and so forth. Beings dwelling within one's own body are "near," while those dwelling outside the body are "far." Furthermore, beings dwelling within one's vicinity are "near," while those outside the vicinity are "far." Beings dwelling within one's own monastery, village, district, island, or world-system are said to be "near," while those dwelling in another world-system are "far."

Those who have become (bhūtā) are those who have been born or manifested. This refers to those who, having manifested, will not be born again; this is a designation for the Arahants. Those seeking birth (sambhavesī) are those searching for a new existence; because the fetter of existence has not been abandoned, this is a designation for the Sekhas (learners) and worldlings who will seek birth in the future. Alternatively, among the four modes of birth, egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings are called sambhavesī as long as they have not yet broken through the eggshell or the membrane of the womb; once they have broken through and emerged, they are called bhūtā. Moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings are called sambhavesī at the initial moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness; from the second consciousness after rebirth-linking onwards, they are called bhūtā. Alternatively, they are called sambhavesī as long as they exist in a certain posture and have not yet changed to another posture; after that, they are called bhūtā. Thus it ends.

The Blessed One, having shown the development of loving-kindness towards beings in various ways through verses associated with non-anger, such as "May they be happy" (sukhino vā), with the wish for their welfare and happiness, now speaks the words "Let no one deceive another" (na paro paraṃ nikubbetha), wishing to show that same loving-kindness so that there may be no wish to cause harm or suffering (vihiṃsā). This reading is the ancient reading; nowadays, some also recite it as "paraṃ hī," but that method is not elegant. In that text, "paro" means another person; "paraṃ" means another should not be cheated or deceived. "Nātimaññetha" means one should not despise or look down upon. "Katthaci" means in any place, whether in a village, a place of work, or in the midst of relatives.
211:
The definition of 'seeking birth' (sambhavasī) and 'become' (bhūtā) is: moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings are called 'seeking birth' (sambhavasī) at the moment of the arising of the first rebirth-consciousness. From the second consciousness after rebirth onwards, they are called 'become' (bhūtā). Alternatively, they are 'seeking birth' (sambhavasī) while being born in a certain posture, as long as they have not yet reached another posture; after that, they are called 'become' (bhūtā).

## Commentary on the Sixth Verse
Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the development of loving-kindness (mettā) towards beings in various ways through these two and a half verses starting with 'Sukhino vā', by way of wishing for the attainment of welfare and happiness for those monks, now, wishing to show that mettā also by way of the wish for the non-attainment of harm and suffering, spoke the words starting with 'Na paro paraṃ nikubbetha'. This text is the ancient reading. Nowadays, they also recite it as 'Paraṃ hī'; such a recitation is not elegant.

In that text, 'paro' means another (person). 'Paraṃ' means another. 'Na nikubbetha' means one should not deceive or cheat. 'Nātimaññetha' means one should not despise or look down upon. 'Katthaci' means in any place, such as in a village, or in the village's field, or in the midst of relatives, or in the midst of a group, and so on. 'Naṃ' means that person. 'Kañci' means any one person among kings, brahmins, householders, monks, the wealthy, or the poor, and so on. 'Byārosanā paṭighasaññā' means through provocation by way of bodily and vocal distortion, and through the perception of resentment by way of mental distortion. In fact, while it should be said as 'byārosanāya paṭighasaññāya', it is stated as 'byārosanā paṭighasaññā'. For example, just as 'sammad-aññā vimuttā' is said instead of 'sammad-aññāya vimuttā', and 'anupubba-sikkhā anupubba-kiriyā anupubba-paṭipadā' is said instead of 'anupubba-sikkhāya anupubba-kiriyāya anupubba-paṭipadāya'. 'Nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyya' means one should not wish for each other's suffering.

What is meant is this: in developing loving-kindness, one should not develop it only by way of the attention (manasikāra) such as 'May they be happy or secure,' but one should also develop it by attending thus: 'May no other person deceive any other person by means of trickery such as cheating; may one not despise any other person in any place by means of the nine grounds of conceit such as birth; and may they not wish for each other's suffering through provocation or the perception of resentment.'
212:
## Commentary on the Seventh Verse
Having thus shown the meditation on loving-kindness in its meaning through the wish that beings may not encounter harm and suffering, he now speaks the words "Just as a mother [would protect] her own son" (mātā yathā niyaṃ puttaṃ), wishing to show that same meditation by way of a simile. The meaning of that verse is: Just as a mother would protect her own son, born from her own breast, her only son, even with her life—sacrificing her own life to protect that son so that he may not encounter suffering—even so, one should develop this mind called loving-kindness towards all beings; one should generate it and increase it again and again. It should be understood that one should develop that mind of loving-kindness immeasurably, either by way of taking immeasurable beings as the object or by way of pervading even a single being without exception.

## Commentary on the Eighth Verse
Having shown the meditation on loving-kindness in every aspect, he now speaks the words "And loving-kindness towards the whole world" (mettañca sabbalokasmiṃ), wishing to show the expansion of that meditation. In that phrase, one is called a "friend" (mitta) because of the desire for welfare and because of loving, and because of protecting from harm. The state of a friend is "loving-kindness" (mettā). "Towards the whole world" (sabbalokasmiṃ) means occurring in the world of beings without exception. It is called "mental state" (mānasam) because it arises in the mind. This word mānasam is used because it is associated with the mind. "One should develop" (bhāvaye) means one should increase. It is called "immeasurable" (aparimāṇaṃ) because it has no limit; this is said because it takes immeasurable beings as its object. "Above" (uddhaṃ) means the upper direction; by this word, the formless realm (arūpabhava) is taken. "Below" (adho) means the lower direction; by this word, the sense realm (kāmabhava) is taken. "Across" (tiriyaṃ) means the middle direction; by this word, the form realm (rūpabhava) is taken. "Unconfined" (asambādhaṃ) means free from confinement, meaning it breaks down boundaries. "Boundary" (sīmā) refers to an enemy; the meaning is that loving-kindness arises even towards that enemy. "Without enmity" (averaṃ) means free from hatred, being free from the manifestation of the intention to harbor a grudge even at intervals. "Without rivalry" (asapattaṃ) means having no enemies. A person who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to humans and dear to non-humans; such a person has no enemy whatsoever. Therefore, that person's mind is called "without rivalry" (asapattaṃ) because it is free from enemies. "Paccatthika" and "sapatta" are merely synonymous terms. This is the word-by-word commentary in sequence.
213:
'Asambādhaṃ' means free from confinement because it destroys boundaries. 'Sīmā' (boundary) refers to an enemy; it occurs even towards that enemy. 'Averaṃ' means free from enmity, the absence of the manifestation of the intention of ill-will even occasionally. 'Asapattaṃ' means being free from adversaries. A person who dwells in loving-kindness is loved by humans and loved by non-humans; they have no enemies. Therefore, their mind is called 'asapatta' because it is free from adversaries. 'Paccaṭṭhika' and 'sapatta' are synonyms. This is the sequential word-by-word explanation.

The clarification of the intended meaning in this context is: Regarding the statement, "Thus one should develop a boundless mind towards all beings," one should develop and increase this boundless mind of loving-kindness towards the whole world, leading it to growth, flourishing, and abundance. How? Upwards, downwards, and across. Upwards as far as the pinnacle of existence (bhavagga), downwards as far as Avīci, and across to the remaining directions. Or, suffusing without remainder the formless realm above, the sense realm below, and the fine-material realm across. While developing thus, one should develop it by making it free from confinement, enmity, and adversaries, by ensuring the absence of such confinement, the breeding of enmity, and the presence of adversaries. Or, when the perfection of development is reached, it is 'asambādha' (unconfined) in all places by way of the world of space (okāsaloka); it is 'avera' (free from enmity) by removing one's own resentment towards others; and it is 'asapatta' (free from adversaries) by removing the resentment of others towards oneself. One should develop and increase this unconfined, enmity-free, adversary-free, boundless mind of loving-kindness in the whole world in the three-fold divisions of upwards, downwards, and across.

## Explanation of the Ninth Verse

Having thus shown the expansion of the development of loving-kindness, the Buddha now speaks the words "Standing, walking... should resolve" to show the absence of restriction on postures for one who dwells devoted to that development.

The meaning of that verse is: This person developing this mind of loving-kindness does not restrict the posture as in the passages such as "sitting down, having folded the legs crosswise and setting the body erect," but rather, while removing the discomfort of any one of the postures as they please—whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—for as long as they are free from drowsiness, they should resolve upon this mindfulness associated with the mettā-jhāna.

Alternatively, having shown the expansion of the development of loving-kindness, the Buddha now speaks "Standing, walking" etc., to show mastery (vasībhāva). For one who has attained mastery, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, in whatever posture they wish to resolve upon this mindfulness of mettā-jhāna, the standing, etc., do not become obstacles to them. Rather, for as long as they wish to resolve upon this mindfulness of mettā-jhāna, they resolve while being free from drowsiness; there is no sluggishness in them in that regard. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as one is free from drowsiness, one should resolve upon this mindfulness."
214:
The meaning of this is: as stated in the words "One should develop a mind of loving-kindness towards the whole world," one should develop that loving-kindness. Among the postures such as standing and so forth, by whichever posture one wishes to establish this mindfulness of the loving-kindness jhāna, for as long as one desires, one should establish this mindfulness while being free from drowsiness, without paying particular attention to the standing and so forth.

Thus, wishing to show the mastery in the development of loving-kindness, the Buddha encouraged the dwelling in that loving-kindness by saying, "One should establish this mindfulness," and now, wishing to praise such a dwelling, He said, "In this teaching, they call this dwelling a divine dwelling (Brahmavihāra)."

The meaning of that is: it refers to the dwelling in loving-kindness which is praised starting from the words "May all beings be happy and safe" up to "One should establish this mindfulness." This dwelling in loving-kindness is called a divine dwelling (Brahmavihāra) and a supreme dwelling (seṭṭhavihāra) in this Dispensation of the Buddha because, among the four types of dwellings—the celestial dwelling (dibba-vihāra), the divine dwelling (brahma-vihāra), the noble dwelling (ariya-vihāra), and the dwelling in postures (iriyāpatha-vihāra)—it is faultless and brings benefit to both oneself and others. Therefore, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as one is free from drowsiness, one should establish this mindfulness constantly, continuously, and without being interspersed with unwholesome states.

## Commentary on the Tenth Verse

In this way, the Blessed One, having shown the development of loving-kindness to those monks in various ways, now concludes the teaching with this verse beginning with "Not falling into wrong views," wishing to show the attainment of the Noble stage (ariyabhūmi) by making that very loving-kindness jhāna the basis (pādaka), because loving-kindness, having beings as its object, is close to the self-view (attadiṭṭhi), and thus He does so by way of prohibiting the grasp of wrong views.

The meaning of that verse is: having emerged from the dwelling in loving-kindness jhāna which is praised as "They call this dwelling a divine dwelling," one discerns the states such as initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) present in that jhāna, as well as the material states such as the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) of those states. Through such discernment of mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa-pariccheda), realizing "This is a mere heap of formations (saṅkhāra); no being is to be found here," and thus not falling into wrong views, one becomes possessed of virtue through the successive supramundane virtue (lokuttara-sīla). One becomes endowed with the vision (wisdom) called the Right View of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga sammādiṭṭhi) which is associated with that supramundane virtue. Furthermore, whatever greed for the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma) remains as defilement (kilesakāma) that has not yet been abandoned, one should remove that attachment to sensual pleasures by thinning it out and then abandoning it completely through the Paths of Once-returning and Non-returning. Having removed and stilled it, the phrase "Truly, he does not come again to a womb" means that such a person is reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) and, attaining the fruit of Arahantship there, attains Parinibbāna. Thus, the Blessed One, having completed the teaching, addressed those monks, saying, "Monks..."
215:
By abandoning it completely, and having removed and stilled the greed for sensual pleasures, one truly does not come again to a womb, but is reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), and attaining Arahantship there, attains Parinibbāna.

Thus, the Blessed One, having concluded the teaching, said to those monks: "Go, monks, and dwell in that very forest grove. On the eight days of Dhamma-hearing in a month, strike the gong and recite this sutta. Discuss the Dhamma, converse about it, and rejoice in it. Practice, develop, and cultivate this very meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the Metta Sutta. If you do so, those non-human beings will no longer show you fearful objects; on the contrary, they will desire your welfare and benefit." The monks, having accepted the words of the Blessed One saying, "Very well," rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and after circumambulating Him, went to that place and acted as the Buddha had instructed. The deities, thinking, "The noble ones desire our welfare and benefit," became joyful and happy, and they themselves swept the lodgings, prepared hot water, massaged the monks' backs and feet, and provided protection. Those monks, making that very development of loving-kindness their basis and undertaking insight meditation (vipassanā), all attained the highest fruit of Arahantship within that very three-month rainy season and performed the pure Pavāraṇā on the Great Pavāraṇā day.

Thus, having practiced the beneficial practice taught by the Tathāgata, the Master of Dhamma who is skilled in what is beneficial, and experiencing the supreme peace of the heart, the monks of perfected wisdom penetrate the peaceful state of Nibbāna.

Therefore, a wise person who wishes to dwell having penetrated that peaceful state—which is deathless, wonderful, and cherished by the Noble Ones—should constantly practice this beneficial practice consisting of pure virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

## The Commentary on the Metta Sutta
## in the Khuddakapāṭha-Atthakatha named Paramatthajotikā is finished.
216:
## Conclusion

With this sequence of words, there is the statement: "Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, the most supreme among those worthy of homage, I shall perform the explanation of the meaning of some of the Khuddakapāṭha." In this commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, the explanation of the meaning of the Khuddakapāṭha, which consists of nine divisions—namely, the Saraṇagamana, Sikkhāpada, Dvattiṃsākāra, Kumārapañha, Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, and Metta Sutta—has been performed in due order. Because it has been so performed, this is said:

"Whatever merit has been gained by me in performing this explanation of the meaning of the Khuddakapāṭha, desiring the endurance of the True Dhamma, by the power of that merit, may all these beings quickly attain growth, increase, and abundance in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones."

This commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, named Paramatthajotikā, is completed. It was composed by the Elder who is adorned with the qualities of supremely pure faith, wisdom, and energy; who is endowed with a collection of virtues such as moral conduct, uprightness, and gentleness; who is capable of penetrating the thicket of his own and others' doctrines; who possesses expert wisdom; whose light of knowledge is unimpeded in the Tipiṭaka scriptures together with the commentaries and the Teacher’s Dispensation; who is endowed with the beauty of sweet and noble speech arising from the happiness produced by proficiency in the six great grammars; who speaks what is appropriate and supreme; who is a great sage; who is an ornament to the lineage of the Elders residing at the Mahāvihāra, who were lamps of the Theravāda lineage and whose wisdom was well-established in superhuman states adorned with qualities such as the six higher powers and the four analytical insights; who possesses vast and pure wisdom; and who was given the name 'Buddhaghosa' by the venerable teachers.

As long as the name 'Buddha' of the Great Sage—who is pure in heart, who is stable, who is the foremost in the world, and who seeks the qualities such as the aggregate of virtue—remains in the world, may this commentary also remain, showing the method of purity through virtue and so forth to the clansmen who seek an escape from the world.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the explanation of the Khuddakapāṭha is finished.
